speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: She said and I quote, "Our multiracialism is still work in progress.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Each successive generation will bring different life experiences and perspectives.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In each generation, some will want to discuss sensitive issues afresh.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Younger Singaporeans prefer talking about these issues more candidly and openly, which is a positive development.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But the conversation needs to be conducted with restraint and mutual respect, because race, language and religion will always be visceral subjects." Sir, as I embark on my fourth term in this House, I recall my generation's unique experience of multiracialism in Singapore, growing up in the 1960s and 1970s.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It was the era of Mr S Rajaratnam, who's mantra was that we were all Singaporeans, regardless of race, language or religion.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In the 1980s and 1990s, when the self-help groups such as MENDAKI and CDAC were set up along ethnic lines, it was reported that Mr Rajaratnam disagreed as he saw these as running counter to the vision of having a Singaporean identity, where race, religion and language did not matter.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Speaking personally, my own experience is that of a distinct shift between my childhood where talk of race was discouraged, to today's reality of heightened race consciousness.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Equally, it seems to be common ground that Singapore as a society cannot affirmatively say that she has already arrived.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The question, then, is whether it would be prudent for safeguards to be put in place to ensure minority representation in the office, even as Singapore continues on the journey towards that destination.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If this is our desire, it is only logical that we take concrete steps to move in this direction.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We have had painful experiences of raicial stife in the past.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But as the President acknowledges, society's experiences and aspirations are not static and each successive generation may yearn for, and even demand, a different approach.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To that end, I see some encouraging signs from the recent General Election.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Several political parties fielded GRC teams consisting of a majority of non-Chinese candidates and polled well.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I should particularly mention and thank the voters of Aljunied GRC who re-elected the Workers' Party team with three minority candidates out of five.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I believe that Singaporean voters are not fixated with race and there is cause for optimism for the future.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In choosing to speak on this topic, I am acutely aware that there are different perspectives on matters of race, as Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat acknowledged in this House yesterday.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Nevertheless, I believe it is essential for us to move this conversation along so that we inch ever closer towards the ultimate destination of being a race-blind society.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Some may consider that we will never arrive at this destination.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But we must ask ourselves how much closer we can be.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I also acknowledge at the outset that the Government's management of these matters arises from legitimate concerns.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Government is responsible for law and order, and fostering the building of a Singaporean identity in a population that is heterogeneous.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, as society evolves, all of us need to keep an open mind to listen and understand the perspectives of fellow Singaporeans whose aspirations for Singapore may differ from our own.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These are: first, ethnic classifications and data; second, elections along ethnic lines; and third, the HDB Ethnic Integration Policy.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I will call for an open review of these matters to move us along in this journey towards being a race-blind society.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Government has defended the CMIO classification as necessary to ensure that minority rights are safeguarded.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The concept of minority rights itself is problematic as it would be better if we could simply talk about citizenship rights.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Furthermore, with more and more inter-ethnic marriages, where the bride and groom are themselves are of mixed parentage, I wonder how the CMIO classifications can withstand the test of time.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: CMIO also informs the self-help groups such as the CDAC, Sinda, Mendaki and the Eurasian Association.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Over the years, these self-help groups have made significant contributions to uplift the less privileged, especially children.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Notwithstanding the good work they have done, the fact is that they reinforce racial consciousness.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I suspect that the different sizes of the ethnic pools contributing to these organisations would affect the resources available, with CDAC probably having the most resources.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To this end, CDAC has opened up some of its programmes on a race-blind basis.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There is an opportunity here to come together as Singaporeans and contribute to a national pool, helping the less privileged on a race-blind basis.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I am aware of an effort to collaborate in this direction in Yishun called the Self-help Groups Centre and hope we can go much further.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For all the race data the Government collects, it is selective on what it chooses to release.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Though my point today is to move towards being race-blind, it is also true that data is needed to understand issues that may affect particular communities, with a view to narrowing the differences.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As a Member of Parliament (MP), I filed a Parliamentary Question 13 years ago to ascertain the composition of the prison inmate population by ethnic groups.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is information that other governments release as a matter of course.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The answer given to my question was that the Prisons Department was unable to share the statistics.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Why people land in jail is often related to the state of their lives such as whether they have stable income and family relationships.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such serious matters deserve wider study by persons outside the Government such as researchers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There should be public awareness of any challenges faced by particular communities and a whole-of-society approach should be encouraged.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We should strive to foster a national culture where every Singaporean is a stakeholder in the lives of fellow citizens.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As stated by the constitutional commission in 2016, there should ideally be no need for safeguards to ensure that candidates from different ethnic groups are elected into presidential office.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This would be ideal for parliamentary elections as well, when we are so race-blind that candidates of different ethnicities are elected naturally.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These issues have been debated in the past with arguments for and against ethnic requirements.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, that does not mean that these issues should remain as they are over time and forever.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such requirements tend to focus on minority representation which can put an uncomfortable spotlight on minority candidates.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To qualify for parliamentary elections, a minority candidate has to file an application to a committee to determine if the candidate is Malay enough or Indian enough.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Indeed, the committee may come back to ask for evidence to be satisfied that the candidate meets the "kosher" test.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I always wondered how I would fair if one day, I had to pass a test of Chinese-ness.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Being brought up in an English-speaking family and attending a mission school, I find myself constantly feeling inadequate about the state of my Mandarin.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Before I entered politics, my knowledge of Chinese customs and practices was focused on celebrating Chinese New Year.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But being classified as part of the majority Chinese population, I am not required to prove who I am to stand in the GE.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Indeed, there are penal laws against sedition and exciting disaffection between different communities.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Whether having a multiracial Parliament needs to be maintained through the existing laws on minority candidates or whether there are other ways to ensure candidates of diverse backgrounds are fielded can be an area for review.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There is no such requirement for private estate such as landed houses and condominiums.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: After 30 years of EIP, how well is it working?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: From the Parliamentary Questions filed by MPs from both sides of the House, it is clear that the EIP has caused economic hardship over the years.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: When the quotas are reached, residents from minority communities can only buy or sell HDB flats from someone in the same community.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such a price differential could make all the difference to a family in financial need.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Being stuck due to the ethnic quota can leave residents in limbo for months.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I know HDB has allowed appeals on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But the default is that the quotas apply.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As the EIP was introduced only in 1989, it is useful to look at HDB estates where families moved in prior to 1989 when there was no EIP.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, areas like Bedok have clusters where the Malay population exceeded the EIP quotas.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We should note that there did not appear to be extraordinary tensions or disorder there.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It does appear to me that some relaxation of the EIP is possible.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Fourteen years ago when the Workers' Party suggested removing the EIP, it was met with a robust response from the ruling party.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We are also aware that some Singaporeans did not agree with our suggestion.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Today, half a generation later, I hope we can have a more progressive discussion on the issue.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While the Government's position is that the EIP was instituted for a noble purpose, its effect in particular cases has been discriminatory and needs to be addressed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I do not pretend to have the answers that we need.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, what I am convinced of is that our discourse about issues of race has to go forward.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We should include academics with relevant expertise and also ensure there is fair representation of citizens across different age groups.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The scope of the review should involve a wide collective reflection of where society is today on multiracialism, and what steps we can take towards this journey of being race-blind.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I have spoken about Singapore’s continuing journey towards the destination of a race-blind society.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I have also suggested a national exercise to review how this can be taken forward, with specific areas that could be reviewed.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I will like to speak on the issues confronting young Singaporeans and self-employed persons.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They are certain to find jobs difficult to come by in the next 12 to 18 months.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They are uncertain on what their future might hold beyond that.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: With no end in sight to COVID-19, most companies have already put off hiring, if they have not already let go excess manpower.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: First, some younger Singaporeans would take much longer to find a job.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The traineeships have helped but are also highly competitive.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Second, there is a much larger mismatch of skills and jobs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In adapting to the new job market, many young workers had to take on jobs that they were neither trained nor studied for.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Third, their medium term prospects are tenuous because they would also have to compete with later graduating classes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We might possibly have a generation of younger Singaporeans confronted with the most difficult of financial and social circumstances.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Job mobility will require them to deepen or acquire new skills.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Because the COVID-19-induced recession is unprecedented in scale, depth and duration, we might reasonably expect the negative impact to last longer.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We have to invest significantly to safeguard the future of the COVID-19 generation of young Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Many of our younger Singaporeans are understandably anxious.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I hope that the Government can also work with the private education institutions or PEI, and banks to provide similar relief for our PEI students.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Their tuition fees are unsubsidised and the amount owed can be substantial.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We also hope that MOM would allow students to be given a longer moratorium to pay back their parents’ CPF monies used for their education.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We need to help the COVID-19 generation with greater job mobility.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, companies should be encouraged to convert traineeships into permanent positions after the current nine months.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Government can also customise incentives via the Jobs Growth Incentive to employers to hire these trainees on a permanent basis.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: NTUC would extend its assistance to help younger Singaporeans to navigate the tough job environment and provide protection accordingly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: If the economy has yet to turn around after nine months, we can also consider giving the option to extend the scheme.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It would also give our younger Singaporeans more time to pick up and deepen their new skills.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We could then consider providing basic employee benefits such as mandatory annual leave if such arrangements are longer.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For some younger Singaporeans, it might be better to stay in school or go back to school, further their studies or pick up new skills.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For others, a second diploma or degree over the next 12 to 24 months might be needed for greater job mobility.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I suggest that we can help to provide subsidies and loans for their second diplomas or degrees.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This generation will require a career booster more so than other generations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But they would need a helping hand to emerge stronger.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Next, I will like to speak about self-employed workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: COVID-19 has put into sharper focus their lack of protection and income security.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: First, the dependent contractors who depend predominantly on platform companies for their livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They are the workers whose lives are dictated by a couple of apps, whether it is ride-hailing or delivery.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They are affected directly by platform companies’ policies such as incentive schemes or meeting service standards.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They usually have little recourse if they disagree with the policies except to quit and go without their livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They are the coaches and artists, and depend largely on service buyers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: During this crisis, both groups suffered sharp drops in income because mass events and consumption have dropped dramatically.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In fact, many Self-employed Persons or SEPs are grateful to be afforded support previously only available to employees.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Beyond this year’s of support, it is likely that many of them will continue to be in dire financial situation because COVID-19 will continue to shutter events and reduce consumption.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I hope that Government can consider to extend targeted support to them.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: On a longer term, we will need to examine closely and protect their income security.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There are two areas that require closer examination.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: One, because existing laws do not allow them to be collectively represented, their voices might not be heard and interests not advanced.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Thus, the divide in bargaining powers is vast, especially for the dependent contractors.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We need to establish if they are actually contractors or employees.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: And subsequently, the roles and responsibilities of the platform companies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Only when we can strike an equitable balance can these industries or mode of obtaining services continue to thrive.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Second, for the freelancers, it is also critical to establish the responsibilities of the service-buyers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These are naturally difficult and market-altering changes and would take time to study carefully.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, for self-employed persons (SEPs), the lack of work and income security have always been a problem.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The pandemic has aggravated these problems and made us become aware that we must strengthen their protection.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: During the outbreak, the income of SEPs are affected severely.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Government should provide what people need urgently.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I am pleased to see that the Government has recognised the fact that SEPs are not able to receive support from employers, hence the previous Budgets have provided support such as SIRS to this group of people.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This has alleviated their income worries to a certain degree.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Some SEPs' incomes have also been affected but they are not qualified to receive the subsidies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As our economy shrinks, SEPs will face further difficulties in terms of work and income.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Therefore, I sincerely hope that Government can strengthen the support to SEPs as the situation evolves.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Of course, providing support such as subsidies can only solve the immediate problems.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In the long run, we must examine how to better protect SEPs in terms of career and income.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Hence, we must be clear in definitions: are they contractors or employees?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Then we can clearly define the roles and responsibilities of the platform companies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Only by doing this can we ensure that these industries and their operation mode are sustainable.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Second, for SEPs, we must also establish the responsibility of the service buyers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Currently, the way to manage fairness of contract terms is through the Small Claims Tribunal or a civil court.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, notwithstanding these suggestions and comments, I support the Motion.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Does it mean there is discrimination against Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Why are there not enough skilled Singaporeans to take up the good jobs in the new industries as claimed, despite having our "world-ranking" Universities?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Are there no corrective actions taken to increase the number of suitably qualified Singaporeans in areas where we are lacking?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Do we have a net gain in tax revenue after deducting all the infrastructural and social costs incurred in supporting these foreigners?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Unable to get satisfactory answers to the above, many Singaporeans have chosen to believe that the current immigration policy is a bad deal for them and for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I credit the Government for responding promptly to the Singaporeans' message.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Acknowledging the people's wish for this Parliament to work together for better solutions, the Prime Minister has installed my esteemed colleague, Mr Pritam Singh, as the Leader of Opposition.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Over the course of the next few years, we look forward to more information and resources provided to the Opposition for it to function as an effective voice and idea-generator.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Noting the widespread resentment and objections of our countrymen, we recommend immediate actions be taken to restore the balance of interests between the Singaporeans and the foreigners in our country.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We think that our Government might have overlooked the fact that our country is a global city-state and not a global city within a larger state.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: New Yorkers, for example, can choose to sell their properties, pocket the gains and move to another city in the US.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But Singaporeans have nowhere to go without leaving the country.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is disconcerting to have many of our countrymen live outside Singapore in Johor and Batam while we are housing more than two million foreigners on our island at the same time.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Surely, more consideration can be given to Singaporeans who are citizens of our sovereign city-state.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are not being xenophobic or nativist because we have a long tradition of accepting foreigners into our society.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In fact, many of us have fond memories of the old foreign talents who have trained and helped us to "eat other people's lunch" and "not to take away our lunch".

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many of them have contributed significantly to our nation-building.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: From Dr Albert Winsemius, the Dutch economic consultant who worked closely with Dr Goh Keng Swee to develop our economy, to the many unsung heroes like Mr Peter John Bowyer, a British citizen who set up the computer centre at the Singapore Polytechnic, transferred his skills to the locals and then left quietly after the job was done; and Mr John Kovak, my General Paper teacher from New Zealand who planted the idea "the citizen of the world" in my head and coached my school's rugby team.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are very grateful to those foreign talents from the good old days.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government, however, had introduced a different brand of foreign talent to us from the turn of the millennium.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As a high-profile manifestation of that policy, Mr John Olds was appointed the CEO of DBS Bank in August 1998.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At that time, I remembered a senior Japanese banker had called me and commented, "Leong-san, it’s like having a foreigner to run Mitsubishi Bank in Japan.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, I am deeply disappointed now because 22 years later after his appointment, DBS is still without a homegrown CEO.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The current financial industry is very different from the time I started my career at the Government of Singapore Investment Corporation in 1986 when "localisation" was strongly advocated and supported by the Monetary Authority of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: During those times, common conversations among my senior colleagues were "so and so has taken over or is slated to take over the top job at such and such global bank".

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Today, my fellow countrymen are not seeing localisation and have to guard their current positions zealously.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We all agree that to protect jobs is the top priority.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Personally, I regard jobs as the foundation of human dignity.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If a breadwinner is unemployed over a prolonged period of time, a multitude of undesirable social outcomes will follow.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Dr Ang Yong Guan, the former President of the Singapore Psychiatric Association, has said that "economic problems contribute to much of the mental menace we see in our society today".

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So many social problems can be solved by organising ourselves differently in our economic relationships with one another and in relation to foreigners.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As a result, one can expect the group dynamics at the workplace to have changed drastically and we must take the rumblings from the ground about Singaporeans being discriminated against seriously.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This phenomenon is hard to swallow because Singaporeans are being discriminated against in our own country.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Without stricter regulation, this situation is unlikely to improve as foreigners increase further as a share of our total population.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While the 10 million population is not a Government's target, it may still be reached eventually unless immigration is slowed down substantially.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As we are entering unchartered territory, we should give ourselves more time to assess and ascertain the full impact of an outsized foreigner population.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have just been made to pay very dearly by a black swan event – the COVID-19 pandemic – as we try to stop the widespread infection at the dormitories for foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the planning of our country's future, it would be wise not to assume that COVID-19 is the worst possible scenario.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There may be other risks related to immigration that we cannot foresee.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the Government can perform better in its communications.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our foreign talent model is a "free flow of people" model, just like the exporter model, which is based on the "free flow of goods" and the financial centre model, which is based on the "free flow of capital", which we have successfully implemented in the past.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These models can help us attain competitive advantages but there is always a need to balance the conflicts of the foreign and domestic interests in each of them.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The foreign talent model which involves the competition for jobs in our own territory is especially sensitive.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government should provide more timely data to obtain the buy-in for the strategy.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, regular disclosure on PMET statistics broken down into Citizen and Permanent Resident categories and details of the intra-company transfers under the various Free Trade Agreements would be very useful.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Without clearer data, Singaporeans cannot have an informed discussion on whether the existing foreign talent model is benefiting us.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Despite the Government's good efforts, it is difficult to create good jobs in a short period of time and existing jobs are still the best opportunities for employing our people.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Going forward, we need to tweak the foreign talent model to improve prospects for Singaporeans while building Singapore's competitive edge.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They should also satisfy minimum capital and business spending requirements.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We can allow Offshore Companies a freer hand in attracting talents from all over the world provided they uphold the non-discrimination principle towards Singaporeans and follow the minimum salary requirements for Employment and Social Pass Holders.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For all the other companies which we shall categorise as Onshore Companies, we recommend tightening our MOM regulations and procedures to achieve better outcomes for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First and foremost, we stipulate that Singaporeans must be well-represented in the top management and human resource function to ensure that the procedures are followed properly.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This allows us to strengthen the Singaporean Core in our economy and in all the important professions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: An over-presence of foreign PMETs in a particular profession, for example Infotech, may lead to the hollowing out of our locals from that profession in the long run and we will end up lacking crucial skills to run our country and economy in the future.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Further visa extension can only be granted if that manager is due for promotion and his previous position is taken up by a Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Fourth, we should protect entry-level jobs for our new graduates and give them the opportunities to learn and to acquire the necessary skills.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should require foreign PMETs to have longer working experience before they are allowed to join our workforce.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Last but not least, we would like to stress that citizenship is sacrosanct to Singaporeans who are justifiably concerned about the erosion of national identity and the dilution of our citizenship.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Since we are talking about economic relationships, there is no need to put citizenship into the equation.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Citizenships should only be awarded to Permanent Residents who have stayed here for a long time and have passed a stricter set of naturalisation criteria.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We also recommend that a Citizens' Commission be set up to oversee the award of citizenships.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The PSP believes that this Parliament must serve the interests and protect the sovereign rights of our people.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We will stand-by the Government if it decides to take any decisive action needed to achieve that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We assure you that PSP will uphold this Parliament as a Singaporean Parliament and not a partisan Parliament.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We have always depended on foreign migrant labour in sectors like construction, manufacturing and services in jobs that Singaporeans would not want to do, either due to the work conditions, low remunerations or others.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Similarly, in the cleaning and some manufacturing sectors, there are high numbers of foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The pleasant reality is that we have always enjoyed very low unemployment in Singapore and that there are always other better jobs available for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Given the limited size of our local workforce and that we are perpetually in a tight labour market situation, especially in the lower wage sectors, companies in these industries would have to look to foreign labour to meet their workforce needed.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Our manpower policy facilitated that, but with a series of quotas and foreign workers’ levies to keep demand within tolerable levels, both physically and socially.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We have lived with this system for many years and it has helped grow our economy and enabled us to press ahead with the massive infrastructure buildup – the MRT, housing, ports, airports, hospitals, industrial facilities and many others.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: But two major incidents or events have brought into focus our foreign workers policy – how we take care and manage the workers as well as the numbers and our dependence of foreign labour in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The second incident is, of course, the recent major COVID-19 outbreak at the foreign workers’ dormitories.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Many of the workers needed to be decanted from their existing dormitories to provide segregation and to reduce density so as to minimise the risk of further spread.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The entire response has taken a heavy toll on our system and, of course, exerted a high price.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The steep infection rate at the dormitories once again brought to attention the living conditions of the foreign workers and as well calls for Singapore to rethink its reliance and high dependency on migrant manpower.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Following the Little India Riot COI report, there were deliberate efforts to site the purpose-built dormitories away from the residential estates so as to minimise any disamenities to the neighbourhoods.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In the process, it has also reduced the visibility of the foreign workers to the public.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: But the recent COVID-19 outbreak has, once again, brought the issue of migrant workers back into the limelight.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Many Singaporeans were reminded or some were surprised at the sheer numbers of migrant labour in our workforce.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We have, in the past, reviewed our foreign migrant manpower policy on a number of occasions.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The rationale for this approach was that foreign labour should not be too accessible to companies as the companies would have little incentive to invest in productivity improvements.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The outbreak in the dormitories highlighted further unanticipated costs in our reliance of foreign labour.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, the overall real costs of foreign workers may not be as low as we have earlier envisaged, both financial and social.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In addition, the outbreak also reminded us that we need to quickly improve the living condition of the dormitories and, of course, these enhancements will also add further costs to businesses.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, how can we reduce our dependence on foreign labour?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: What is an acceptable number, both physically and socially?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Does the cost-benefit analysis still makes sense to have such large numbers?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I am not about say let us just cut migrant worker numbers to a certain lower level.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It would have far reaching implications and impact on our businesses and industries and also on our efforts to build capabilities and capacities in both the economic and social infrastructures.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: When I spoke to a number of people in the construction industry to seek views on how we can we reduce our reliance, almost everyone was concerned about what I am about to say or ask the Government to do.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: For example, would I be asking for a steep cut in the numbers of migrant workers?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Well, I am fully cognisant of the realities and that there are no quick fixes.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I get it that there is really not much we can do and nothing much can change in the short term.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Our industries, especially the construction sector, would not be able to fulfil their contracts if they are unable to get the sufficient workers they need.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We continue to need high numbers of migrant labour workers for our current and upcoming projects, such as the MRT, the recently announced RTS, HDB housing projects.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Even our climate change mitigation projects will also need workers there to help us build them.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, if we cannot do much in the short term, what can we do in the medium to long term?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: There were a number of attempts in the past to improve productivity.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I read the report on construction productivity by the Singapore Contractors Association done in December 2016 which detailed measures to improve productivity performance.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In the report, it also highlighted the difficulties for firms to invest long term to enhance productivity, given the nature of the businesses where construction companies would tender competitively for contracts, not knowing whether they would win them.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Faced with this unknown of whether they would have work to do ahead of them, contractors would be reluctant to invest in productivity measures in a significant way as they are unsure whether the investment costs can be fully recovered.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Large companies can afford to take a longer term view, but not for smaller companies which are just struggling to make ends meet, given the competitive nature of the business.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The market would not be able to sort out itself to work towards productivity.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, again, the Government has to come in.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: But it has to be well perpetuated and carried out with great insistence to change contractors’ modus operandi.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The other possible radical moves are to identify firms that have invested significantly in productivity improvements and invite them early in the projects to work with planners, architects and engineers on more efficient construction processes that can be less labour intensive.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It will require a mindset shift in the way we look at contract tenders and how we overcome the value-for-money governance.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We can always start something as a pilot, perhaps via a “sandbox” approach and, thereafter, finetune the process for greater implementation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: But we can take this as a price discovery exercise to know how contractors will actually cost a project that involves less migrant labour.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: On the demand side, we can also do more to reduce the overall demand for migrant labour.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We should be more discerning in evaluating if some of our major construction projects should go ahead.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: What comes to mind are the collective sales or en bloc developments that we always hear about.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It is actually wasteful to demolish a building that is still in good working condition, only to build a replacement one that is quite similar.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We should also scrutinise carefully our public projects and plan more judiciously.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: For example, in our neighbourhood, we have a Secondary school that went through a major upgrade, only to announce a few years later that the school would be merged with another one and to be relocated.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: One sector that has been most impacted is aviation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We expect air travel to be much reduced post-COVID-19 and may never recover to its previous levels.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Are our assumptions and parameters still valid in the new permanently changed setting?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Are the risks now too high to go ahead with this massive investment?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Can we work within our existing four terminals, regenerate new value propositions and optimise what we already have with the terminals and the set-up?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We can perhaps still go ahead with the new runway but do we need another terminal building?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I hope the Government will review the decision because such mega projects also consume high numbers of migrant workers and crowd out the more urgent demands by other construction projects.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: One of the key hallmarks of Singapore’s economic success is our human resource and the availability of skilled manpower and talents to our businesses.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Our approach has always been to maximise the potential and opportunities for our local workforce and complement it by allowing some external manpower to strengthen our competitiveness to the extent that it helps create growth and jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Indeed, Singapore is able to seize additional growth opportunities beyond the size potential of our domestic workforce because we are able to leverage on external manpower resource.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This makes good sense, especially when we are in a positive growth cycle where demand for manpower is high and the domestic labour market remains tight.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Notwithstanding these adjustments, we are still one of the most open economies in the world where cross-border manpower flows are concerned.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, I disagree with The Business Time’s headline last Friday that said MOM's latest announcements may put our financial hub aspirations at risk.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: There are not many major financial centres that allow this level of openness.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Global institutions choose to set up presence in Singapore not just because of our foreign manpower policy, but also of our many other very compelling attributes.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Among others, Singapore is the few remaining Triple-A rated jurisdictions in the world.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We are reputed for the excellent global connectivity, the depth and liquidity in our capital markets; sound regulation, integrity and enforceability of our judicial system; and also, importantly political and social stability.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We must therefore be self-assured that from time to time we would necessarily need some re-calibration to our manpower flows in response to the cycles in the labour markets.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: More importantly, we need to focus on the outcomes; and that is – have we been able to develop our local workforce to take on those jobs that are available in these sectors?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: These are the jobs that Singaporeans want to do.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: How can we more effectively minimise the inherent frictions or the biasness working against achieving these outcomes?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We have the data points from our S Passes and EPs – what are the areas of jobs that the companies are asking for EPs and S Passes?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: These can serve as our "skills demand leading indicator”, where we can plan and curate training programmes and traineeships to target at helping Singaporeans compete and take on those jobs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Of course, just tightening EP and S Pass alone would not be enough.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We need other measures such hiring incentives, training allowances, subsidised traineeships to urge companies to hire more locals.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Narrowing the gaps of mismatches and reducing the frictions in job transitions are highly difficult undertakings; we know that.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Left to the markets, it may not resolve into the outcomes that we want.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We therefore need concerted efforts involving a combination of measures and workarounds to achieve this; and importantly, with proactive intervention by the Government.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And this is now the task of the National Jobs Council, led by Senior Minister Tharman.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Let us use the slack in the labour market today as an impetus to help Singaporeans adapt and take on these jobs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Singaporeans, whether they are young graduates or mid-career PMETs, can be up to the task.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We just need to equip them, give them the opportunities and importantly, have faith in them.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We face not just the onslaught of a relentless viral outbreak, but must also deal with the disruptions wrought by COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We will need to respond robustly to this challenge.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Beyond the shock of COVID-19, our living environment is also seeing secular changes.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It has become an increasingly sophisticated world, with a sophisticated population in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As we navigate these changes, I believe that we need to maintain a balanced approach, changing with the times but still holding dear to what we find important as Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: At this point in time, I can think of three key "balances" that we need to strike.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: First, balancing between forging ahead versus bringing everyone along.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The Wright brothers flew their first flight in 1903, but it took 50 years before air travel became commonplace in the 1950s.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Similarly, the steam engine took almost half a century since its invention to disrupt the shipping industry.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Today, a single app, if it is the right one, can change the world within a year or two.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Grab first launched in Singapore in 2015, and they quickly revolutionised the way we book private hire cars.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Grab has also found its way into our daily lexicon, from getting a ride to getting a bite.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Similarly, Douyin was first launched in China in 2016 and its international incarnation, TikTok, started building steam in international markets soon after in 2017.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Clearly, change has been accelerating at breakneck speed.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In the past, breakthroughs in technology would take decades to disrupt economies.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Now, only a matter of two to three years.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Put it differently, our Pioneers might only see one to two major disruptions for the most part of their career, but the young today will see many disruptions in their lifetime.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As a nation that must constantly adapt to survive and thrive, agility in our economic strategies and the way we govern is crucial.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Digital economy, digital Government and a smart nation – these are important and have to pick up speed.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But this imperative also comes at a price.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Countries like the US and China have huge domestic markets; for example, China's hospitality industry is almost fully recovered with some sectors seeing growth – thanks to domestic consumption.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, going digital is an important way of helping our businesses to reach markets in the region, if not the world.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Going digital will also help our people access a wider pool of international job roles even as they focus on their lives here.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Businesses, for instance, may have different reasons for not digitalising fast enough.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Unlike MNCs that have vast amounts of resources at their disposal, SMEs may find themselves lacking the capacity to transform and therefore, risk getting left behind.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Our seniors and the more vulnerable, including workers who had a tough start in life, may find themselves unable to acquire the digital skills fast enough to catch up.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It can be both painful and frustrating for these businesses and individuals, and we risk losing them.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Does this mean that we should leave them behind as we "chiong" ahead, or should we abandon the idea of transformation altogether, or is there a better, more balanced, way to press on while still maintaining a safe space that allow the smaller ones amongst us to grow strong?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It will be a difficult balance to make.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Move too slow, and we risk being overtaken by hungry competitors.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Move too fast, and we risk leaving behind a large segment of our population, who face difficulties in adjusting to our rapidly changing society.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This is a perennial dilemma that we face, almost cliché to mention.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But it will be absolutely critical for us to strike the right balance.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Singapore is in a time of a changing of generations.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: How do we, as the Government, meet the aspirations of the Millennials and the Centennials?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: How do we strike the appropriate balance between the wants of the Baby Boomers and Gen X, while making space for the Millennials and Centennials to shape the world which they want to live in?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: He said that the question we have to ask ourselves is how do we evolve in a way that is self-sustaining.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: How do we do it in a way that protects the liberties that matter most to people?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: How do we effect change, while safeguarding freedom of religion, and the freedom to aspire in life and achieve what you want through hard work?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These, I think, are questions that this Parliament has to ask ourselves.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Millennials and Centennials have an idea of the future we want to live in.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We have a certain view on climate change and protecting the environment.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We have views on social justice and social mobility which cannot be ignored.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We have ideas on work-life balance and social security which, in many regards, may not completely align with the views of the earlier generations.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As we pass laws and policies, there will be trade-offs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The question is, where should the appropriate balance lie?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Conversely, if we choose to spend more on combating climate change and protecting the environment, for example, then something that is important to us today may have to give.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In some instances, it can be a zero-sum game, and there will be trade-offs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This Government has to weigh the different interests, hear the people, and find balanced solutions that care for the older generations, while creating space for the younger generations to shape this nation into one that they can be proud to call home.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Third, balancing openness and fairness, as some put it, between the foreign and local.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Allow me to share that our workforce has also changed.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Singaporeans today enter the corporate world armed with world-class degrees from our tertiary institutions.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: A second time voter told me during my campaign visit that her boss, her boss's boss and her boss’s boss’s boss are foreigners in the MNC that she works in.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: She could not understand why even the middle management positions are held by foreigners.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Another mature resident, who is now in a senior management role in another MNC, told me about how a European candidate with no relevant APAC experience was chosen over him for an APAC role in a previous job application.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Is this because Singapore's education system is inferior and therefore cannot produce capable mangers, CEOs and other senior staff?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, this Government must continuously evolve it to prepare it for the future.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: While paper qualifications and examinations are important, soft skills are invaluable to the working world.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Most businesses place considerable value on the ability to articulate thoughts and ideas clearly, to communicate effectively, and demonstrate willingness to collaborate and work as a team.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Greater emphasis must be placed on such areas.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Perhaps, say, we have two equally qualified employees, but there is only one opening for a promotion to a managerial position.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Like for like, one can imagine that the candidate who is more willing to work with anyone, more apt at building relationships with clients and more enthusiastic about going out of the way to network, will secure the post.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Our education system has to ensure that more often than not, that preferred candidate is a Singaporean candidate.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: At the same time, the Government should formulate a plan to cultivate young adults in our workforce for potential leadership positions.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I firmly believe we have considerable talent in our young adults.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We just need to equip them, guide them and mentor them.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: There are many schemes that focus on building technical knowledge and skills.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These include the likes of SkillsFuture and TeSA.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: There are others that help Singaporeans switch tracks like PCP.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These are wonderful schemes that allow Singaporeans to adapt in a fast changing world.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But, we also need programmes that help push Singaporeans further along their career path – to become leaders.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: There is a need for greater transparency to what firms, especially large firms, are expecting of their corporate leaders.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Having a framework identifying the key criteria, skills, behaviours and attitude, needed at various levels of management would offer Singaporeans clarity on what they have to do to attain a promotion.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The framework could provide a useful roadmap with signposts to better guide younger, high potential Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: On top of that, to create a network for mentorships, whereby prominent, successful and more experienced professionals or business leaders can guide younger Singaporeans in a similar profession or industry.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Some of these mentors could be older Singaporeans who have made it big and now want to give back.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Or they could perhaps be specifically headhunted from overseas by our Government.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These mentors can guide the younger Singaporeans along in their careers, offer invaluable advice based on their wealth of experience and provide insights into how they can be better.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: There is, of course, no guarantee that by going through the above, one will certainly land himself or herself in that coveted top position.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But, it shows our Government and our nation's determination to develop our young and climb the ladder.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: If we can find a way to cultivate a critical mass of Singaporean talents who not only are technically skilled but also with leadership skills and acumen, the eco-system will be so much healthier and competitive.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: (In Mandarin):   State governance is a complex social task involving many aspects including politics, economy, society, culture and law.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The Parliament is a place where laws are made, and an important platform for us to discuss issues affecting Singapore and Singaporeans at present and in the future.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: One can thus imagine how issues debated in Parliament can be equally complicated.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As the world changes and Singapore progresses, Singaporeans' minds have also become more complex.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Similarly, this Parliament has also become more diverse and colourful than before.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, it is now even more important for us to build a model of governance that is more holistic and balanced, one that can overcome divisions in political ideologies.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The new term of Parliament has just begun, and I believe that the Government needs to achieve balance in three areas.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We must maintain the right pace for high speed economic growth, while ensuring that no Singaporeans are left behind, and growth is inclusive.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: While we welcome foreign talents to enhance our competitiveness, we also need to nurture domestic talents, to ensure that Singaporeans are given the fair employment and advancement opportunities that they deserve.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Singapore is now actively implementing the Smart Nation initiative to develop the future economy.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: A digitalised future has become inevitable and our youth can easily adapt to this digitalised environment.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, we need to create an environment where young Singaporeans can maximise their potential.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, there is still a group of Singaporeans amongst us who need help and they include our seniors.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Rapid digitalisation has made life difficult for them.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For example, when the Safe Entry QR code was first made mandatory, they could not cope.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Although they had mobile phones, they did not know how to scan the QR codes, and some of them did not even dare to visit their doctors.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We all know the importance of Safe Entry.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: To the young, it is very simple and straightforward, but to the elderly, it was extremely difficult.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Thankfully, within a few months, everyone has become familiar with how Safe Entry works, and is now more at ease.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Considering this experience, we should constantly remind ourselves to empathize with the elderly and take care of their needs, even as we charge ahead with full speed.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: At the same time, I hope the Government can do more to encourage seniors to learn technology in a stress-free way, so that they can make use of technology to aid their daily lives.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Going back to my main point, it is not an easy task to achieve balance in governance, to take care of the needs of all communities, to ensure that all of us can complement each other and progress together harmoniously.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: (In English): These are questions that we need to answer through community conversations and then translated into legislation in Parliament.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I am constantly reminded that as a Parliament, we bear the responsibility of shaping the future for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We can – and we should – react to the changing tides around us.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, we also need to be deliberate about designing a future that every Singaporean can look forward to and is confident of achieving for himself or herself.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As Mdm President observed in her Opening Address, politics today must be conducted in a manner which cultivates conversations and offers opportunities for individual citizens to be heard.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We need to listen and engage our citizens actively; it is a two-way traffic.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As a developed nation, our children grow up having dreams they want to fulfil and an idea of the future they desire for themselves, families and children.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Many of my residents and volunteers do, and they are willing to put in the effort.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They know there is no free pass in life, there are trade-offs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But sometimes, the trade-offs that need to be made for that desired future are not immediately apparent.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, we need to have frequent and earnest conversations with each other.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We need to discuss and foster an understanding of the trade-offs for each major decision taken.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Better still, forge a consensus on the kind of trade-off we are prepared to make.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So, in determining the kind of Singapore we want, the future we desire and the path and speed to get there, how can we balance the need for agility and the need for meaningful citizen engagement?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But I think being more open to explore difficult issues with Singaporeans is a start.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And of course, we need to make better use of technology so that we can conduct more sessions to reach out to more people.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The Fourteenth Parliament has our work cut out for us.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But we can enlist ideas and advice of Singaporeans from all walks of life, to help us chart a balanced path forward.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Today, as we rise from the shadows of the COVID outbreak, I remain confident that we will overcome this "challenge of a generation" and work together to bring Singapore to the next level.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We can do it, so just do it!

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has brought to the fore the importance of careful planning and being prepared for any future shocks and surprises which may hit us.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Two is better than one, one is better than none.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Diversification is a vital part of resilience planning.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With the SkillsFuture programme, Singaporeans are encouraged to pick up new and different skills.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, what good is a skillset that cannot be put to use?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A worker would be back to starting from square one if he applies for a totally new type of job.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There must be a way for a worker to put learning to use concurrently.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many employers bar their full-time employees from taking on a second job.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The worker could choose to learn and apply new skills to pursue an additional vocation within the same company or in a second job.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Encouraging such a practice would allow the worker to develop a broader set of skills that will allow more flexibility in career switches within a shorter window of time should there be a need to.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Companies also need to identify complementary sectors which are sufficiently differentiated to provide resilience through diversification.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In doing so, the company could allow their workers take up concurrent positions in different business units.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is because people are indeed still eating – at home.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, if a company runs a restaurant and also sells and delivers food ingredients, it will be able to ride out this storm better.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Stock prices go down, gold prices go up.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Brick-and-mortar retail goes down, online retail goes up.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A loss here is a gain somewhere else.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Maybe conglomerates with diversified businesses can try this first – have their employees take on dual roles in their different companies.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While this dual-job thinking may seem out-of-the-box, we should recognise that there are many Singaporeans who possess multiple skillsets and would be able to contribute at a higher level within the same company or seek a second vocation to diversify their income sources.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This approach may not suit certain jobs nor appeal to certain people.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What I am proposing is to encourage companies and workers who are willing to try to be allowed to do so, without compromising their productivity and work-life balance.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Government could incentivise companies and workers to adopt this approach.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The President has reaffirmed the Government's commitment to support our young families to own their homes.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We discussed the topic of housing affordability in March during the debate in the Committee of Supply for MND.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Minister had reiterated that our HDB flats are accessible, as our flat prices are kept at below five times our median household income.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Minister also shared that most applicants could use the Government grants to pay for the down-payment.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They do not need to pay any cash upfront and can pay their monthly mortgages with their CPF savings with 25-year housing loans.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The employment situation today is less favourable to holding long mortgage tenures, compared to the past.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: People of my parents' generation used to hold jobs for life.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For our generation, most of us would have changed jobs a few times.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For the future generations, job cycles will likely get even shorter.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: More and more people are making a living from the gig economy as well.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: All these new factors, together with the higher macro-economic risk backdrop, should be captured in the analysis of the affordability of HDB flats.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Should financial circumstances of the buyer change over time, there is then flexibility to structure lower instalment payments by stretching the loan tenure when needed.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The next point I would like to make is on financial assistance schemes.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: All Singaporeans should be entitled to assistance and benefits regardless of the types of residence they stay in.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: No one should be left behind as all contribute to society.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many of our current assistance schemes are based on housing types, with their annual values determining whether one gets certain assistance or not.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We have to reassess this basis as we can already see convergence in the value of some HDB flats with the level of pricing ascribed only to private housing properties in the past.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There is a group of asset-rich-cash-poor Singaporeans who have problems monetising their assets during this pandemic.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They also need assistance to tide them over this difficult period.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There is also a "sandwiched" group, including low income earners living with family members in private properties which they do not own, resulting in them not qualifying for some types of assistance.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Both groups certainly receive some of the general voucher distributions given to all.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But these may not be enough for those who have sunk into financial potholes for various reasons.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We should not lump them together into one big group.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We could start by tagging everyone to a category, with or without home ownership.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The relevant Committee can also issue cards like it did for CHAS.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Once a person is assigned to a category, he gets benefits in that category for two years.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If there is an immediate change, such as retrenchment or permanent disability, that person can apply for an urgent review.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In this way, those with genuine need for help would be moved to an appropriate category which will receive relevant grants and support.

text: (In English): The important thing is to do our best to ensure that no one gets left behind or left out.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am confident that we have the resources and capability to lift everyone up and together, we will emerge stronger from this crisis.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has caused major disruptions to businesses and impacted workers’ livelihoods in an unprecedented way.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In her Address, President Halimah Yacob called on all of us to build a fair and just society and to look after our low-wage workers, especially during this crisis.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The strong interlinkages of these three components in the “Triple Uplift” formula have increased the overall take-home salaries and retirement savings of our low-wage workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Importantly, this uplifting of wages is significant for our workers, without imposing additional burden on companies, especially during an economic crisis like this.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As a result, the income gap between the low-wage workers and the workers at the 50th percentile has narrowed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
