text: The wages of low-wage workers have also been growing faster than those with higher income, hence income inequality in Singapore is at its narrowest in almost 20 years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: So, the "Triple Uplift" formula has helped significantly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: It is good but it can be better.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Despite all this, I thought this would be an opportunity for me to address areas in which we can improve on this "Triple Uplift" formula.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I will first start with the Progressive Wage Model.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The Progressive Wage Model or PWM, championed by NTUC, was introduced in 2014 and aims to help our low-wage workers to upskill and benefit from higher wages and better work prospects.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This is done through a four-ladder approach – skills upgrading, productivity improvements, wage progression and career advancements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In other words, a "wage ladder" is coupled with a "skills ladder".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Wages go up as skills and productivity improve.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: It looks at raising wages sustainably to match the necessary productivity growth for each different sector, which is beneficial for businesses, workers and the Singapore economy at large in the longer term.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Cleaners saw their real median wages go up by 30%, while the increases were 31% for security sector and 32% for landscape industry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: For example, the starting monthly salary for a cleaner in Town Councils after we introduced PWM is $1,442 a month.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: So, we should do more and expand PWM to more sectors to help more low-wage workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In fact, over the last few years, SkillsFuture Singapore or SSG, has comprehensively mapped out the skills framework for many job roles.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Leveraging on these skills ladders, we should now move towards universal PWM across all the low-paying job roles.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This is in line with our ITM wants to achieve; some of the objectives of which are upskilling, job redesign, productivity growth and wage progression.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The Labour Movement is also now in discussions with our stakeholders to see how we can implement PWM for the waste management sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Understandably, it is not the best time to raise wages during a global health and economic crisis when businesses are facing challenges of cashflow and disruption.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We do not want to put businesses out of action through escalating wage costs in an economic downturn, nor do we want to deter hiring of workers in a distressed job market with rising unemployment rate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As brother Heng Chee How said before in an earlier commentary speech, even as we endeavour to help low-wage workers, we must make sure a balance is struck, so that "low wage" does not become "no wage".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As a doctor, I think it is quite clear that there are no magic bullets and there are actually no magic wonder drug that can heal everything without side effects.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: So, I think in trying to push for intervention, we need to find the right timing but when the timing is right, we must be bold and move quickly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I hope Tripartite Partners can come together even now to conduct an in-depth study on the universal implementation of PWM across more sectors, so that we can move faster in this aspect when the economy recovers post-COVID-19.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: If we truly want to build a more inclusive society and narrow the income gap, the pace of PWM implementation across more sectors must quicken.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: To build a more inclusive society that President Halimah Yacob spoke about, companies must find a way to translate the increased productivity into tangible benefits for our essential service workers, many of them are in the low-wage segment, so that they can see how industry transformation will benefit them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The Government must also be prepared to use more regulatory levers to widely implement PWM.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Clearly, waiting for the market to respond on its own will not produce results we hope to see.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This can be done through leveraging various data sources that we currently have, such as the Occupational Wage Survey data.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: And inn sectors with a more variegated employment landscape such as food services and retail, sectoral wage benchmarks may help catalyse more companies to embark on uplifting the livelihoods of our low-wage workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This of course can eventually evolve into a formal PWM.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Next, let me talk about Workfare Income Supplement enhancements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: To raise the wages of those in the lower paying jobs, society at large must also play a role.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Many low-wage workers are in sectors that provide essential services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: During this circuit breaker period that we have just emerged from, many Singaporeans appreciated the work that essential services workers do, to keep our estates clean, our utilities functioning and our transportation nodes running.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Members would have also read articles and social media commentaries calling for these essential workers to be better paid for the work that they do.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I hope service buyers would price the contracts fairly, so that our workers can be paid fair wages.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The adoption of Outcomes-based Contracting must also be ramped up at a quicker pace.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We need more progressive service buyers to start awarding contracts fairly to companies based on performance and quality, instead of just looking at price alone.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In this way, we can truly recognise the importance and value of the work performed by our essential services workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This means that as consumers we must also be prepared to pay more for essential services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: But in reality, there is a limit to how fast we can raise wages and how much the consumers are prepared to absorb price increases, especially during an economic downturn.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Through this enhancement, our low-wage workers get to experience strong real wage growth.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This in itself is an expression of social solidarity that Mdm President spoke about in her address where the larger pool of taxpayers, through taxpayers’ money, has helped to uplift the wages of those earnings less.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In addition, the Workfare Special Payment of $3,000 announced in the recent Budget was a good measure to tide lower income Singaporeans over this difficult period.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This was much welcomed by many of the low-wage workers I met.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I hope the Government will continue to strengthen this WIS scheme and ensure that the earnings of the low-wage workers keep pace with the rising cost of living.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The third aspect – on the National Wages Council.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The broader articulation of this social solidarity is also embodied in the recommendations by the NWC.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Some of these recommendations include freezing the wages of workers instead of pay cuts when the company is not doing well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Conversely, increasing the wages by up to $50 if the company is looking at increasing wages across the board.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I hope during this review the NWC will continue to protect the wages of our low-wage workers and recognise their contributions in the essential services sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: To benefit more workers and protect workers from stagnating wages, NTUC calls for PWM to be expanded at a quicker pace and be made universal to cover all sectors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Sectoral wage benchmarking could be explored as a first step towards eventual universal PWM to uplift wages for sectors such as food services and retail industry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: WIS should also be strengthened to better provide for low-wage workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Taking care of our low-wage workers and giving them the dignity of earning a fair wage must be an important and tangible manifestation of the social solidarity that President Halimah has called upon all of us to do as one united Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: (In Mandarin):   The COVID-19 pandemic has caused major disruptions to Singapore’s economy and the employment market.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In her address, President Halimah called on us to look after our low-wage workers, especially during this unprecedented crisis, to demonstrate the spirit of Social Solidarity in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The pandemic has made us realize the important contributions made by workers in the essential services sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: And there is now more focus on the many low-wage workers in this sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In Singapore, we uplift low-wage workers' salaries through three complementary measures- Progressive Wage Model (PWM), Workfare Income Supplement (WIS) and National Wages Council (NWC).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: While these three measures have lifted low-wage workers’ salaries significantly, there are still areas that we can improve on.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Hence, I would like to raise these points below to strengthen our support for low-wage workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Led by NTUC, the Tripartite Partners introduced PWM in 2014 to help our low-wage workers in essential services sector upskill and increase productivity, leading to higher wages and better career progression.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We should expand PWM to more sectors to help more low-wage workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: NTUC is also in discussion with stakeholders to implement PWM in the Waste Management sector in the near future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Nonetheless, I hope the Tripartite Partners can quickly conduct an in-depth study on the universal implementation of PWM across all sectors, so that we can move faster in this aspect when the economy recovers post-COVID-19.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: At the same time, we should explore setting a sectoral wage benchmark as a first step towards PWM.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This could help encourage more companies to uplift the wages of our low-wage workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In addition to PWM, the Government has also introduced WIS which contributes to almost one-third of the take-home pay of our low-wage workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This is a demonstration of our Social Solidarity as mentioned by President Halimah.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We do not know how long the pandemic will last.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I hope that the Government can increase the WIS assistance to low-wage workers when necessary.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The NWC has recently made recommendations to further protect the interests of our low-wage workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Amidst economic uncertainties, employers may resort to pay-cuts or retrenchments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: NWC recommends that employers in distress should try to maintain the salaries of low-wage workers, or freeze wages temporarily in order to protect jobs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I hope that when NWC reviews the wage guidelines again in the next few months, it will continue to pay attention to and protect the welfare of low-wage workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In order to benefit more workers, NTUC calls for the Government to expand PWM and for it to be made universal to cover all sectors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I also hope that the Government can strengthen WIS to better support low-wage workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In the face of economic challenges, we can leverage the NWC platform to protect the welfare of our low-wage workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: (In English): With that, Mr Speaker, I support the Motion.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The pandemic has posed a threat to Singaporeans in two key spheres – at home and at work.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Just as these anxieties have, at a global level, caused governments to turn inwards, it is increasingly tempting for us, as a people, to do the same.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This could bring us down the slippery slope of apathy and distrust.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Therefore, at every juncture, we must evaluate the lengths to which we go in the name of self-preservation and what it would cost us as a people.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Though I have not been back there in the past decade since his passing, I have fond memories of the sincerity and kindness the community lived by.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I remember the neighbourhood and the people living in the neighbourhood as if it was yesterday.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Right next to my father's clinic was the neighbourhood hair salon run by aunties.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It was the neighbourhood water-cooler where residents came by, not just for the latest fashion tips, but also to find out how they are neighbours were doing.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Further down the street was a stationery shop run by Uncle Muhammad, an Indian-Muslim from India.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: He would affectionately call me Ling Ling every time I came back, and remembered the comics I like to read.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And I never left his shop without a sweet in hand that he would give me.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: At Tat Lee Bank next door, all their businesses ran on the currency of trust.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our neighbourhood sole proprietors and hawkers knew the names of the bank staff and sometimes, even those of their families, their children, their spouses.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And all the shopkeepers need to do was to place their day's earnings in cash on the counter and could count on receiving a faultless chit the next time they came around.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: My father, the neighbourhood doctor, delighted in the service he provided to the community.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There were many occasions where he did not take money from patients because they could not afford it.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, without fail, we would receive a gift at our doorsteps from them.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If they raise chickens, would get eggs; and if they made sauces, we would a bottle.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The kindness and trust I saw in the community were not naive.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It did not ignore the challenges and struggles that faced the community but stood strong despite these trials.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: When times were tough Uncle Muhammad had to sell his business and started selling magazines under the bridge, but it never did break his spirit.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It never caused us to turn cold towards each other.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The bond that held us together as a community ran deeper and would not tear at the sound of trouble.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This was because of the intimate interest we had in each other's lives.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: My dad knew Uncle Muhammad both as a patient and as his friend.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: My mom knew his wife, Aunty Gowri, and the troubles she had raising three children.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And I knew one of their daughters and chatted with her often when we were growing up.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Within the community, we knew the challenges others faced, and we knew the stories behind these faces and, more importantly, the stories behind the challenges.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the same way, my hope for Singaporeans is that we will continue to be champions for kindness in the community, built on understanding and apathy towards the challenges others in our community might face.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The incessant shouting you might have been hearing at home could actually be a couple in financial distress.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The tired homemaker who has been moving furniture at odd hours could have her hours stretched in the daytime because there has been more people at home.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is on us to open our hearts to the stories that run deep and to extend a helping hand to those in the community who might need it.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Sometimes, I wonder: have we been too quick to judge?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: When I was previously running my company, we had an employee who had been consistently putting in good performance.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, one day, the HR department came to me and raised some serious doubts.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The employee had started to make a habit of sleeping on the job and it caused him to miss many calls.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: That was an issue because he was a call centre operative.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But what we decided to do was to give him the benefit of the doubt and asked him about his recent performance.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: When we are willing to listen, everyone is a winner.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Be it at home or at work, it will go such a long way if we all fostered an interest in each other's lives and uncover the stories that lie beneath.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I believe that Singaporeans will only be able to build a rich national identity when we allow ourselves to deep dive into the richness of the lives around us.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As many of us spend more time at home than ever before and as we are faced with the anxieties of this age, the bonds we have with our community are exposed.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As much as the Government will work hard to build social safety nets and implement policies to ensure Singaporeans emerge from this pandemic stronger, norm is but a distant relative.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: When the rubber hits the road, it is our Singaporean community that must band together.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is these communities that Singaporeans can have to hope to be able to lean back on.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In this House and in the many households across our Singapore, we must heed our President's call to embrace our plurality and diversity, under girding it with a deep appreciation of the lives of those around us.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Then, and only then, can we work out community solutions that will allow us to become greater than the sum of our individual parts.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker Sir, earlier, I shared the challenges faced by our society as a result of COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Is a "job" considered as one only if we work from nine to five?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If an employee needs to take care of his family and wish to break up his work hours, will employers be receptive?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This pandemic has prompted some women to return to the workforce to support their family.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: At the same time, they still have to take care of their family or elderly parents.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They would prefer to work on project or freelance basis, so that they can manage their time more flexibly.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I know a nurse who provides home nursing care.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: She is a kind and capable person who chooses to work night shifts.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: She has almost no rest days and is always toiling over her patients.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I often wondered why she did not choose to work in the hospitals instead.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We found out later that she worked so hard because she has to support her adult son, who has cerebral palsy.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: She looks after him in the day, and works at night to earn a decent livelihood for her family after her son has gone to sleep.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: She is a great mother, taking care of her child in the day, and working hard as a home nurse to support the family at night.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The situation that the nurse is in, is a common one faced by many.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I believe that during this period, more women will become freelancers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Some have chosen to reenter the workforce as freelancers because of the economic hardship brought about by the COVID-19 pandemic, while others have chosen to go off the beaten path to pursue multiple career pathways.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Whatever the reason, everyone hopes to supplement the family income by making use of pockets of their available time.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, I support the Motion.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I am heartened by her encouragement to new politicians, like myself, to continue the good work done by those before us, in shaping an effective and sound Government.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Globally, this year, economies have been paralysed, businesses decimated and livelihoods impacted.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The virus has altered the way we live, work and play.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: But, this pandemic is not going away anytime soon.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The CEO of renowned pharma giant Merck has said that a vaccine is at least a year away.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: So, dealing with this crisis will be like running a marathon – there is a finishing line but the run will be long, exhausting and painful.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Today, I wish to talk about some of the lessons we can draw and how good policies must be complemented with good execution for us to emerge from this pandemic, a stronger Singapore.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Those not included could submit their applications to the NTUC.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: However, there has been a lot of feedback from residents about not being able to access the relief package.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: They are upset and perceive the unfairness of the scheme.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: First, those whose appeals were rejected and do not know why.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Rejected resident applicants received a rejection letter without any reason stated.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Although the NTUC website has been upgraded for answers, it was not clear and specific to their own situation.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Many were disappointed and described NTUC's response as cold and not helpful.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The second group are those who know why their applications were rejected but cannot come to terms with or do not fully comprehend with the basis.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Fellow Members in this House had raised this yesterday and one today, and I share their views.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The principle of having "means-testing" as a basis to identify those needing help is logical and NTUC's website stated that this is "consistent with other Government schemes".

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: But COVID-19 relief is not a normal Government scheme and in implementing this blunt tool, it needs to be recognised that it will exclude residents whom the relief measure was intended to help.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Additional data points could have been used proactively to identify those falling in the "should help" category so that a portion of this relief measure can be considered, given this challenging period.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The last group are those who do not know why they did not qualify for SIRS and do not understand the eligibility criteria.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Some in the category, includes our resident hawkers and freelancers who have not been declaring their net trade income.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Whatever their reasons for not doing so, they are hard hit in this pandemic.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Perhaps, instead of an outright rejection, they could be brought back into the fold and set on the right path, by nudging them to, for example, start tax filings and adopting e-payments – a great initiative by the IMDA – to qualify for some portion of SIRS assistance.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In this way, we can give the needed help and at the same time provide better guidance of their role in the community to file taxes and for the more successful ones in the future, to contribute their share of taxes too.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: SIRS aside, let me provide another example from a different angle that also illustrates how leveraging technology can improve policy implementation as a key imperative.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This relates to the task at hand of guiding the re-start of construction projects that is underway.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: What we need is the ability to do quick tracing, accurately.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: However, new COVID-19 cases detected at cleared dormitories indicates we still have not yet implemented better capabilities.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The TraceTogether app has limitations such as performance consistency across phone brands, inconvenience, and battery usage even after the software fix to slow down battery drain was done.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Perhaps, better wearable technologies or tokens could be prioritised for earlier implementation.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: However, given the rumblings and the noises at the ground, I asked myself why and what is the real gap?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: My view is that at the heart of the issue in these two seemly unrelated examples is about the importance of good execution where we fell a little short on delivery.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Good governance is not just about "Good Policy" but also about "Good Implementation" that goes hand in hand.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: And I want to share that the bank focuses on what we call "The Job to be Done".

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: It is the maniacal focus on customer experiences, the practice of agility, applying data analytics and incorporating feedback quickly and so that the targeted objectives are done and achieved.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This, DBS, took over a decade to try and get it right.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The challenge for Singapore is how do we continue to refine and develop a more citizen-centric governance model, where policies are not sacrosanct but rather a means to an end?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In concluding, I want to say that on any global scale, Singapore executes well.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I can attest to that having lived over a decade overseas and raising my family in the major financial centres in the world.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Our President in her Opening Address assured Singaporeans that the Government will listen to and examine new ideas, and that it will continue to evolve its policies and models to cater to new circumstances.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I am also heartened that Deputy Prime Minister assured the nation that the Government will take a stance and be open to improvise and adapt.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: When we do that, I am optimistic that we can beat the crisis together and emerge even stronger as a nation.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Having world class policies and world-class execution, only then, can we have world-class governance.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, the year 2020 is an extraordinary year for everyone.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Fighting COVID-19 is like running a marathon, we must persevere.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The Government has introduced many good policies to help Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: However, to help more people, there is room for improvement in terms of policy execution.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This has caused concerns among residents who work in the construction industry.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: We all hope that the Government can develop more effective technologies for contact tracing and put in place clear guidelines in terms of division of labour and accountability.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Only by helping the slower runners, can we come together as one united Singapore and cross the finishing line together.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: (In English): With that, Mr Speaker, Sir, I support the Motion.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In our recent memory, the most severe economic downturn in Singapore had been the Global Financial Crisis.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Barely 12 months after the collapse of Lehman Brothers that precipitated the Global Financial Crisis, there was talk about "green shoots".

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In 2009, Singapore’s GDP did not shrink; it actually managed to grow 0.1%.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The following year, our economy powered ahead to double digit growth.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Fast forward to 2020, having battled COVID-19 for about eight months, we see how much more severe the impact is going to be.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Although unemployment has not reached the highs of past recessions, we know this is not a given.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We are still in the middle of a raging storm, and it will be sometime before we see "green shoots".

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Against this backdrop, there is anxiety and a heightened sense of insecurity about jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I appreciate it has not been an easy time for many of them.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For today’s debate, I want to focus on two groups in particular – workers who perform essential services but do not earn much and PMETs in their 40s and 50s.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For over a decade, we have made concerted efforts to raise wages at the lower end.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As part of our social compact, we introduced Workfare in 2007 to mitigate income inequality.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In 2016, the Government launched the Silver Support scheme to provide better retirement support for Singaporeans who did not earn as much throughout their working lives.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Dr Koh Poh Koon has a slightly different take on the Government's holistic support.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Right now, concerns about job and income losses must weigh on us as Parliament debates our next moves in raising wages for workers who earn less.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: What is our preferred approach to moderating income inequality in Singapore?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Specifically, do we continue with the expansion of PWM over time as the NTUC has advocated or do we shift towards a national minimum wage or a living wage, as some parties have called for?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Although in Singapore, we have not legislated a single minimum wage across the board, we have in fact implemented features of a "Minimum Wage" through the PWM in several sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Members of Parliament from the Workers' Party acknowledge this too.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In March 2015, Mr Gerald Giam urged the Government, and I quote him, "to look into introducing sectoral minimum wages under PWM to more domestic-oriented sectors".

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: On 15 July this year, Mr Yee Jenn Jong said and I quote him, "The Government is also not alien to the concept of Minimum Wage, except that they practise it for selected industries only via the PWM."  At the same time, we have complemented the PWM with Workfare and skills training and the results have been good.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Ramli Bin Mohd Hussin, my long-time brother from the Labour Movement, sees first-hand how these schemes have helped workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As senior operations manager of an environmental services company, he supervises about 120 cleaners.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In fact, for many years, Ramli himself worked as a cleaner.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Workfare supplemented his wages, but it was PWM that gave him a chance to move up and build a career.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: At age 47, he has upgraded to a 4-room HDB flat in Yishun.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Of his four children, the eldest was encouraged by him to join the cleaning profession.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Number two has just completed NS after getting his Polytechnic diploma.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Number three started a small business and the youngest is still in school.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Ramli also feels a great sense of accomplishment that an ex-offender whom he had been nurturing was recently promoted to Team Leader.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The result of our approach in Singapore is what two local economists, Kenneth Ler and Ivan Png, described as a unique kind of Minimum Wage policy that succeeded in raising wages without apparently reducing employment.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Outside of sectors with PWM, Workfare and the Special Employment Credit or SEC, have also raised wages without risking unemployment.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Take a 60-year-old worker whose employer had been prepared to pay $1,200 a month.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: When SEC and Workfare are added, the worker actually earns $1,593, 33% more than the employer’s willingness to pay.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Had a national Minimum Wage or living wage been set at, say, $1,600 instead of boosting incomes through SEC and Workfare, would this worker still have a job?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Perhaps, if the labour market is very tight but perhaps not when economic conditions take a dive.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Therefore, to uplift workers who earn less, the Government’s preferred approach that is also supported by the Labour Movement, has four prongs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: First, to regularly adjust Workfare to support employability while ensuring that we continue to mitigate income inequality.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Members like Mr Gan Thiam Poh support this.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Second, to raise wages in PWM sectors at an appropriate pace, taking care of the need to preserve low unemployment among the workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Third, to expand PWM over time to more sectors, taking care to assess the capacity of businesses in those sectors to absorb the change, especially our SME employers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Fourth, to raise standards of living for lower income workers in other meaningful ways, such as acquiring skills to progress, achieving home ownership, providing access to quality healthcare, education for their children and adequate support in their retirement.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is a holistic and sustainable approach to uplift our lower income workers, and is an extension of social mobility beyond the schooling years into working life.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We have been building on this approach, steadily and with focus.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Dr Koh Poh Koon called for the universal implementation of PWM.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The real question for expansion of PWM is one of timing.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In the security sector, 38-year-old Raymond Chin has been similarly able to progress to his current position as Senior Operations Manager.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: However, during a recent conversation, Raymond told me his concerns about security officers earning less this year.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: When calling for new tenders, clients are asking for fewer workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Full-time workers have fewer overtime hours or may lose their seniority when displaced.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Similar trends are observed in the hospitality and F&B sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Businesses are still trying to find a firmer footing.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Therefore, any moves to expand PWM into new sectors immediately, in the midst of great uncertainty in the labour market, carries higher risk.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Given our overriding priority to preserve jobs, we should proceed with care.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: While it may be risky to mandate PWM in more sectors right away, we can still promote its voluntary adoption by progressive employers that are able to do so.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Companies that voluntarily pay progressive wages and provide job progression pathways to their lower income workers will be recognised with this PWM Mark.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Several sectors, including Food Services and Retail Trade, have the potential to come on board.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For the PWM Mark to work, there must, however, be a broader movement involving society at large.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As consumers, we must be prepared to pay slightly more and intentionally support such progressive companies by purchasing their products and services.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This will spur more companies to be progressive and adopt the PWM Mark, which in turn will benefit our lower income workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I hope Members will agree with me that we must have it in our hearts to consider this a small price to pay for better jobs and income security for those among us who need it most.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: At the same time, they, as well as Members like Ms Jessica Tan and Mr Henry Kwek acknowledge that foreigners are still needed to complement the Singaporean workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In fact, we have adjusted work pass policies regularly and slowed down the growth of EP and S Passes considerably.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is less than one third of the average annual growth of 30,400 in the earlier five-year period, and that would be from 2009 to 2014.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In the first five years, 2014 to 2019, the number of EP and S Pass holders has grown on average, less than 9,000 annually.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is less than one third of the average annual growth of 30,400 in the earlier five-year period.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: At the same time, in the last five years, 2014 to 2019, the number of locals in PMET jobs has grown on average, around 35,000 annually.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: So, we have the 9,000 in growth of EP and S Passes, average annual in the last five years and during that same period, what is the growth in locals in PMET jobs?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In other words, for every new EP or S Pass holder added in the last five years, about four more locals took up PMET jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It should also be noted that throughout this period, the population of PRs has remained stable, at about half a million.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It would therefore be wrong to attribute the growth of locals in PMET jobs to an increase in PRs, as some have suggested.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In the 1990s, about three in 10 locals were in PMET jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Leong may not have realised this but it could almost be said at that time to have been the privileged minority.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Fast forward to today, nearly six in 10 locals are in PMET jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In fact, local PMETs outnumber EP holders – 7:1.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For every EP holder that you can find, there are seven locals in PMET jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: With COVID-19, the number of EP and S Pass holders has come down sharply.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: While the numbers are moving in the right direction, PMETs in their 40s and 50s are still concerned.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In this period of great uncertainty, two questions loom large.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: First, when retrenchments become inevitable, will they be targeted by employers because of age and wage-seniority, especially when compared to their younger foreign colleagues?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: When applying for jobs, will they be passed over, especially with employers having continued access to EP and S Pass holders?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: MOM actively monitors retrenchment practices and looks into how retrenchment exercises are conducted.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There are the 10 key questions we ask.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: (a) Did the employer implement any other alternatives, such as cost-saving measures before considering retrenchment?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: (b) Were efforts made to reskill and re-deploy staff, before embarking on a retrenchment exercise?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: (c) Does the business situation warrant a retrenchment?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: (d) Did the employers put in place clear criteria to identify workers to be retrenched?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: (e) Did these criteria discriminate against any employee on the basis of age, gender, ethnicity or family circumstances?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: (f) Did the company provide retrenchment benefits commensurate with its financial position?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: (g) In a unionised company, were the selection criteria and retrenchment benefit discussed and agreed to with the union?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: (h) Did the company put in place measures to support the workers' transition, for example, engaging WSG or e2i for job assistance?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: (i) Did the company communicate its business situation and plans clearly, sensitively and with adequate notice to affected employees?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: (j) Lastly, but certainly not the least of it, was the company's Singaporean Core weakened as a result of the retrenchment exercise?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: And last and not least of it was the company's Singaporean Core weakened as a result of the retrenchment exercise?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Where older Singaporeans have been let go, this has generally been the result of criteria like relevance of skillsets to core functions that the company must retain.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This factor explains why in some retrenchment exercises, seniors comprise a higher share.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: By and large, there has also not been a weakening of the Singaporean Core.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In fact, this is quite an often-seen criterion that companies introduce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Notwithstanding these reassuring observations, we will remain vigilant.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will also work with tripartite partners to advance sound practices, through updating the Tripartite Advisory on Managing Excess Manpower and Responsible Retrenchment, for example, or the Fair Retrenchment Framework proposed by NTUC.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Besides actively monitoring retrenchment practices, we will intensify other efforts to ensure fair treatment of locals applying for jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In substance, this achieves what Ms Foo Mee Har would like to see, a tilt in support of local PMETs that goes beyond fair consideration.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Among other things, an employer's record in how it handles retrenchment exercises will certainly have a bearing.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, is an EP or S Pass applicant a replacement for a local who was only recently retrenched?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: If so, MOM will ask why and turn down the application unless there are very good reasons.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will also place additional emphasis on whether the employer has been responsive to efforts by the Government agencies to help it recruit and train local PMETs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng supported a balanced work pass policy that is neither too restrictive nor facilitative for employers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: He felt that continued access to EP and S Pass holders can help businesses to grow, which in turn expands opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Businesses, however, should not exploit this access but must instead make serious efforts to build local capabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: She calls on employers to look past paper qualifications and consider local job applicants who do not necessarily tick all the boxes, but who can be nurtured with support from Government.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This should, in fact, become pervasive, a regular feature of our employment landscape, the norm and not the exception.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Therefore, in specific areas of skills shortages and where there is strong interest from locals, we will also assess if agencies like WSG, MAS and IMDA have been able to get an employer on board their many programmes to strengthen the development of local PMETs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This will also have a bearing on their EP and S Pass applications.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Conversely, we take into consideration whether an employer has discriminated against qualified local PMETs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Of all possible infringements, this is what offends Singaporeans most, that they have the qualifications but lost out to a foreign candidate who did not appear to be better.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To curb such unacceptable behaviour, MOM has regularly taken employers to task for practices like pre-selecting a foreign candidate and disregarding qualified local candidates.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We agree with Ms Foo that if, in fact, there are equally or better qualified local candidates, it would be only logical that they be given priority consideration.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In one instance of a healthcare multinational, investigators found that 26 local candidates had responded to an advertisement on MyCareersFuture.gov.sg.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Although seven out of these 26 applicants met the job requirements, none were shortlisted or interviewed.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Other candidates were rejected for not meeting requirements that were not stated in the job advertisement in the first place, for example, six-sigma certification.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The company rejected them, saying that they do not have six-sigma.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But when we look back at the job advertisement, it did not say six-sigma certification.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This company was clearly not serious in considering local applicants.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Anyone in business knows that this is serious.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To stay in business, they will have to recruit more locals, something they should have done all along.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We are re-stating them to remind employers of the need to step up their hiring practices and HR management, and also the efforts they must make to help sustain a business-friendly work pass policy.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: At the same time, we will build on the Fair Consideration Framework or FCF to engage more employers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: So, we have the 1,200 in the last five years but we also have this 40,000.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Some Members, including Mr Pritam Singh and Mr Leong Mun Wai, may not have realised this: firms that are scrutinised have not flouted any rules yet, unlike the example I cited above.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Instead, we have identified them through proactive surveillance because of their unusually high reliance on foreigners in their PMET workforce, when compared to industry peers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Until they improve, we will reject or hold back their work pass applications.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: At the same time, TAFEP engages them to understand their problems and help them strengthen their hiring practices.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, we found that one firm dealt, almost exclusively, with high net worth clients from a particular country with language and cultural preferences.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: So, this company need not have been in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They could have served these high net worth clients from somewhere else – Hong Kong, for example.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Nonetheless, through TAFEP’s advice, this company agreed that non-client-facing roles could be filled by locals.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In another instance, the company had been genuinely unfamiliar with local recruitment channels and welcomed WSG’s assistance.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In yet another case, the local office sought special approval from their overseas headquarters to expand recruitment criteria to take into account local conditions.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They were in fact grateful to TAFEP for having helped to bring about this change with their headquarters.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In other words, this targeted approach has helped to keep and expand local PMET employment in these firms.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: If instead we had chosen to vilify them through a name-and-shame approach, we would have frustrated their efforts to expand local hiring.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is ultimately counter-productive, not advantageous to us.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In the case of the company that served high networth clients, it very easily could have gone somewhere else.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: And all of those opportunities would have been lost to us.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Our alternative approach of scrutinising and engaging employers is highly resource-intensive but in fact, a more effective way to get businesses to reshape their HR practices.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is why MOM plans to engage an expanded group of employers to review their hiring practices.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This expanded group will include firms whose Singaporean Core has been weakening; or whose EP and S Pass workforce are overly concentrated from a single foreign nationality source.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Through active intervention, we will help them reshape their workforce profiles.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will do this together with economic agencies like EDB and MAS.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: And as Mr Ang suggested, we will also engage the HR community to do more.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They write to tell me about specific job application attempts where they felt they had been sidelined, or retrenchment exercises where they felt that they had been treated unfairly.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They may also share observations about FCF rules being ignored.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: MOM takes all such feedback seriously, as they complement our own proactive surveillance.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We investigate thoroughly by interviewing the parties concerned and going through relevant records and exchanges – sometimes, mountains of records – to ensure that the retrenchment and hiring decisions have been conducted fairly.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, a whistle blower told us his former employer, an IT consultancy firm, had hired an EP holder through the recommendation of another EP holder who was a friend.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The problem here was that the employer had not considered other possible local candidates as well.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This decision was cleared with the General Manager which made it worse.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I do not think they will forget such an experience.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I hope these examples reassure Members that where there’s evidence of unfairness, we will not hesitate to hold employers to account and lean on them to do better in future.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: However, such actions do not always bring satisfaction to the victims.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Something is inevitably damaged in the process – the sense of fairness and trust in the organisation's value system.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As Members have pointed out, for every errant employer caught, there are other bad hats – at least one other bad hat – who still try to circumvent the rules.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is why MOM calls on employer groups to also step up.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: No amount of rules will be enough if employers do not have the shared sense of commitment to fair hiring and responsible retrenchment.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: No amount of enforcement resources will catch enough employers if they are determined to hide.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: What we lose then is not just a job opportunity for a local, but the trust that the system is fair, that the odds were not stacked against people who are trying.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We need employers to do your part: be fair to locals when you hire or have to retrench.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: At the Work Permit level, we use levies on top of quotas to regulate demand because the numbers are big.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: At the EP level, where the numbers are not as big, our key objective is to regulate quality.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: By raising the salary requirements, over time, this sets a higher bar that EP holders must be able to cross to work in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: You raise the bar, and the hurdle is higher.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: You are going to need more skills, more talent to cross a higher bar.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: That is what the EP salary requirement is – a high hurdle.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The other effect of raising the hurdle is to push EP holders at the lower end, down to the S Pass-level where there are quota controls – something which levies will not do.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: So, you raise the hurdle; those who cannot cross it, what choice do you have?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: And if the company does not have enough quota, well, then, that is it.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In all past adjustments to EP salary requirements, a good number are downgraded to S Passes.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: What about employers who falsely declare salaries to meet the higher bar?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The answer must be to strengthen enforcement which we have been doing, and not to withhold the raising of the bar.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To similarly impose quotas at the higher end of EP holders is not unthinkable, but it is probably unwise.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: When competing for the most cutting-edge investments and sophisticated activities to be moved to Singapore, we need to give agencies like EDB and MAS flexibility.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For this purpose, it is much better to use salary requirements to ensure companies get access to foreign professionals of the right quality and marry them with firm-level commitments to build up local capabilities over time.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Without such flexibility, many of the top-quality investments would have been lost to our competitors and the job opportunities along with them.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As several Members have alluded to, there is no shortage of takers ready to eat our lunch.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, Sir, the usual practice at MOM is to adjust the EP and S Pass salary requirements regularly, based on the situation in our local job market.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There is only one reason behind these adjustments, and that is to safeguard the livelihoods of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Take the EP for example – we adjusted the salary requirements in 2017, and in May this year, there was another round of adjustment.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Some people may be concerned that the raising of salary requirements for foreigners may result in employers who insist on hiring foreign employees simply raising their salaries.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Some Members mentioned this yesterday and suggested that we impose quotas on EP holders to restrict the number of higher-end EP holders working in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To impose quotas on EP holders is not unthinkable, but it is probably unwise.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Most of the foreign workers in Singapore are primarily Work Permit and S Pass holders.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Therefore, MOM uses quotas and levies to regulate the number of such foreign workers that a company can hire.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: What we are more concerned about is the quality of these EP holders.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, they may possess specialised skills that can help businesses venture into cutting-edge fields, and may, in time to come, transfer these skills to Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Therefore, the Government updates the EP salary requirements to ensure that the foreigners that businesses hire are indeed top-tier talent.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: If the expertise and experience of these foreigners are not commensurate with the salary requirements, then they will not be able to obtain an EP to work in Singapore, but will only be able to obtain an S Pass instead.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In past rounds of adjustment to EP salary requirements, a good number of EP applications were not approved as they did not meet the salary requirements.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: And if the company's S Pass quota was already fully utilised, these foreigners would not be able to work here or get their contracts renewed.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In fact, the number of EP and S Pass holders has already come down sharply.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Nevertheless, I would still urge business owners in these extraordinary times that if they must hire foreigners because of business needs, they should continue to give fair consideration to local jobseekers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Businesses have a duty to grow and maintain a Singaporean Core in their workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is especially critical in the current climate.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In these difficult times, we will place additional emphasis on these considerations and pay close attention to the hiring practices of companies.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We want to remind businesses of the importance of nurturing their local workforce, and help Singaporean jobseekers find good jobs and return to the workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: (In English): Sir, I still have a bit to go.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Unless Leader of the House moves a Motion.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Members in the House are agreed that while we keep Singapore open, we need to ensure fair treatment and we must also do everything possible to give our people a leg up.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: How can we enable more of them to take up good jobs created and grow into roles that employers presently hire EP or S Pass holders for?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: First, businesses that retain and hire locals get an extra dose of support from the Government.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is exactly what Ms Mariam Jaafar called for.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Jobs Support Scheme or JSS is one.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Jobs Growth Incentive or JGI is another.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Another way to tilt the balance is to support the cost of skills retraining for employers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Take, for example, our Professional Conversion Programmes or PCPs.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They have helped her bounce back from retrenchment.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Merly was with her previous company for the past 13 years carrying out system support of IT certification systems.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: When searching for a new job, she realised that her IT skills had become obsolete, as she was performing traditional IT tasks all this while.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Hard as it was, she accepted the need to upgrade her skills.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Through the PCP for Salesforce Platform Professionals, she managed to start in a job that she did not have any prior experience for.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Kudos to the employer for taking her on as well.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: A third way to tilt the balance for local PMETs is by plugging hiring gaps with attachments and skills training opportunities for mid-career individuals.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: While recognising the preference for a job, these company-hosted attachments and skills training programmes will nonetheless position jobseekers better with industry-relevant experience.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: When the economy recovers, their CVs will be more polished and they will stand a better chance of bouncing back into jobs they prefer.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Beyond these efforts, agencies like MAS will continue to press on with their bold and significant plans to support and encourage financial institutions to build up Singaporeans for senior roles, like how Ms Tin Pei Ling has advocated.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Minister Ong Ye Kung will speak later today and share some of these plans.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In many ways, these specific programmes and initiatives will be more effective in growing the local talent pipeline for the top jobs, complementing broad-based tools like work pass policies.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We must, therefore, not miss the woods for the trees, by focusing narrowly on keeping foreigners out, and missing the larger picture of growing the pie and giving Singaporeans the chance of the best slice.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We understand the anxieties of PMETs in their 40s and 50s and their concerns about fair treatment and fair opportunities.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We also appreciate the need to keep supporting workers who earn less to grow their incomes over time and address income inequality.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Every single day, workers like Ramli, Raymond and Merly remind the MOM team what our work is about.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We are always here listening to their struggles, thinking deeply about the support that they need, recognising the constraints, adjusting policies in their interests, finding better ways to protect them against unfair practices, ultimately, helping them to get onto the path of growth in their work lives that they so deserve.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To all the other Ramlis, Raymonds and Merlys out there, we know that, in your hearts, you care most about the well-being of your families and loved ones.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: You want to do well not just for yourself, but for them.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Please know that you, too, are always in our hearts.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However long this storm lasts, MOM will walk this journey with you.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However tough it may be, we will help you bounce back.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Our mission is to help each and every one of you emerge stronger by never giving up hope and by working with employers in Singapore to treat you fairly to make your hard work bear fruit.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have taken firm steps forward and we will press on, whatever the challenges, with you, for you, for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I happen to have a number that tells me that the average increase for every year during that period was 50,000.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, I think what Mr Leong is trying to suggest is that all of your gains are meaningless because they are all occupied by PRs and new citizens.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: First, I would like to point out that he is wrong in imagining that all the new citizens and all the new PRs are in the workforce.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: A significant number of them are still children, still in school.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: That is how we top up our population.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: A good number of those new citizens and PRs are married to our citizens.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Is Mr Leong suggesting that these new citizens are any less of a citizen?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Is Mr Leong suggesting, therefore, that we should discount them, not include them?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I would like Mr Leong to share his views with us.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And do we then say that within the Singapore citizen ranks, we start drawing a distinction between a new citizen of two years ago, 20 years ago, or how far back must you be a citizen to be a real citizen?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These are questions that I hope that Mr Leong can help us understand the PSP's thinking.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, the situation is not as rosy as what the Minister has painted.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And we have said right from the beginning that we understand the anxieties of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Having said that, I think it is also important for Mr Leong to recognise what I have just said – which is, if we look at the number of new citizens and we look at the PRs, significant numbers of them are not yet in the workforce; significant numbers of them are also married to citizens.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Are we to say that, therefore, please do not work, please be out of the workforce?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I do not believe Mr Leong is saying that at all.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, this constant obsession – if I may put it that way, with drawing lines – I am not sure it is good for us as a society.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There have been occasions where Singaporeans have stepped up and asked us, "Your policies differentiate between citizens and PRs.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Why can they not get the same level of support from the Government too?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Is their well-being not important to me, the citizen?" What answers do we give to this person?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Do we then say, "If your husband or wife is a new citizen or new PR, okay, even if they are not working, that is fine." I do not think that is what we are heading for.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, I call on Members and ask that you consider this very carefully whenever you raise points of this nature.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is not that the question cannot be asked but I think we have to search our hearts and ask ourselves before asking these questions: what is our thinking?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: What is our attitude and what is the value that we are expressing by even putting these questions forward?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is well and good to say, "This is all about information, transparency" and so on.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
