text: But dig a bit deeper and ask ourselves: what does this question belie?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: What sort of values are we trying to reflect in asking these questions?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Would you like to answer the questions posed to you?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Are you answering the questions or are you posing another clarification?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Are you answering the questions or are you raising another clarification?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I only said that on an annual basis, we have said consistently that in the last couple of years, what the number of new PRs is, what the number of new citizens is.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, I am not sure I understand his question.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: That said, I would like to clarify if Minister Teo believes that simply slowing down the rate of EP and S Pass holders is sufficient to ensure that local PMETs do not get displaced.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I say this in part because this strategy is a very blunt strategy, and for starters, we need to take into account base effects.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even if the rate of issuance has slowed, as Minister Teo has shared, it is misleading to actually compare the two.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For instance, a 20% increase, from 50 people, for example, is 10 people.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But a 10% increase from 200 people is, in fact, an increase of 20 people, which is larger in absolute terms.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Now, I understand that 35,000 people is larger than 9,000 but the point is that the slowdown in the rate of EP and S Pass issuance is less dramatic than Minister Teo claims.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, we should be aware of the effect of diminishing returns by which I mean many PMET positions may already have been secured by foreign talent and so it is no surprise that the number that is now required actually goes down.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I did not say that one contributed to the other.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But I thought that I should perhaps address Assoc Prof Jamus Lim's other question: are we satisfied with slowing down the rate of growth of EP and S Pass holders?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The perspective that I would like to share is this.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Those are the four things that MOM is always looking at.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Then, we ask ourselves what is the best way to achieve these outcomes.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But the important thing really is what does it take to deliver and bring about these good outcomes for Singaporeans?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And then, we ask ourselves: within the options that are available to us as a tiny red dot, how can we mitigate the difficulties, the shortcomings and the worries that people have, legitimate worries that people have, about a very sizeable foreign workforce.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I do not think that the destination that we want to head towards is a different one.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But we have to ask ourselves, looking at the opportunities as well as the constraints we have as a tiny city-state, which Mr Leong Mun Wai reminds us – we are a tiny city-state; we are not a tiny city.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And a tiny city-state has got its opportunities but it also has its constraints.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Within those constraints, what is the best way to help Singaporeans move forward?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: That has to be the answer and not some predetermined ideas about what you bring it down to.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Suppose we can bring it down to a different number and so on, but at the same time, the job opportunities for Singaporeans have shrunk.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Your children, my children one day coming to us and say, "Mom, Dad.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Sorry, cannot find a decent job in Singapore anymore." And they really no longer have that opportunity of the six in 10 PMET jobs that we talked about – which many countries have found themselves in that sort of a situation.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Is that going to be better for us?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Well, we will have to think very hard about whether the answer is yes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Just one point of clarification as regard the treatment of employers found to be engaged in discriminatory practices.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I think in discussing this issue, a number of Government spokespersons have talked about the process of curtailing work pass privileges as a penalty and that is certainly one lever in the Government's toolkit when it comes to employers who discriminate by nationality against Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And where the employer may not necessarily depend on work passes or that is not a very important thing to that employer and therefore, as a lever of control or influence, that may not be so powerful.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I think the Member may have underestimated how serious it is for businesses in Singapore to have their work pass privileges curtailed.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It means that whoever it is that they have in their workforce, they are not going to be able to supplement with a work permit holder or S Pass or EP holder as they had previously.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I should also take this opportunity to address the Member's question about how we secure better employment outcomes for vulnerable groups.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It has been mentioned several times in this House that other countries have anti-discrimination law, but the proof of the pudding is whether as a result of those anti-discrimination laws, they have better employment outcomes than us.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Are we more interested in the form or are we more interested in the substance?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And I think Members of this House have consistently been more interested in the substance.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Actually, we are above quite a few countries in terms of our senior employment rate.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And these countries may well have anti-discrimination law.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, look at the substance of it, I think the results are encouraging.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We are not giving up trying to push the agenda more.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We are concerned about it during this time whether the women, whether the seniors, they will be well taken care of.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But the answer to this cannot be, "let us come to Parliament, let us debate a law, pass another law" and expect that it will be done.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I think that is not a very realistic approach.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: He made the point about EPs and S Passes, and the numbers not tallying.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: If I could ask a clarification, what is his recommendation and what is his proposal in terms of the approach or the numbers that we should take?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: If I may clarify, Mr Speaker, I was not suggesting that the numbers were incorrect.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: What I was suggesting is that, when we think about decreasing the rate of EP and S Pass holders, and we simply think about applying it as a blunt instrument, by saying that just because reducing it is sufficient, that itself is misleading.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I think this was something that Minister Teo clarified – that ultimately we do not want to look for a single number in which we can reduce EP or S Pass holders.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: What we want ultimately is the ability to think more flexibly about how we approach PMET issues and displacement, potential displacement by the foreign workforce.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: I do not think that that was what was being said by many of us in this House.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: In fact, in my speech yesterday, that was precisely the point and together with many of our colleagues, that was precisely the point that we made.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: It is not the only thing that needs to be watched and that it has to be done in a balance.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: In making that statement, I think you were the only one that was making that statement.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: And therefore, that is why I was asking, what is your approach then?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Are you suggesting that we stop the number of EPs or S Passes completely?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: What would the implications of that be and what would that mean for companies?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Not just foreign companies, foreigners coming in, but what would it mean for Singaporean jobs as well?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Because some of these jobs need to be complemented by some foreign workers as well, or foreign talent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But during Minister Teo's speech, she had explicitly said, that at the lower end one instrument that they were using was through the restrictions of quotas, quotas of EPs and S Passes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, I wanted to clarify that, that alone was is a very blunt instrument and is insufficient.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And more importantly, I also wanted to clarify that the numbers themselves are misleading.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Just as Minister Teo said, the numbers were reduced to almost zero this year.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, it is unsurprising, of course, that the number of EP and S Pass holders fell dramatically.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, we should not be looking at pure numbers in order to make our conclusions about whether PMETs are being displaced or not.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The more important question is can we have our tea break?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.55 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.34 pm until 4.55 pm.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So much has changed and the way ahead is full of uincertainties.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The slew of assistance measures by the Government have blunted the full force of this health, economic and social crisis.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, the storm is not over yet but signs of fatigue may be gradually setting in or have already set in.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope that we can all remain vigilant and push back against the weariness and complacency.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: At the same time, let us harness our inner reserves of strength and courage for the transformation we need to survive and thrive in the aftermath.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In addition to those fresh out of school and tertiary institutions, there are many middle aged career jobseekers, who have the dual responsibilities of providing for elderly family members and young children.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Mid-career applicants may have to consider new roles, even in different sectors.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They may have to go for training and learn new skills.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It can be a challenging and intimidating process, especially if the required skill sets are very different.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need more of these certified career coaches to support and journey with them, with more hand-holding if necessary, to encourage them to take the big leap into the unknown.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For Singapore to remain competitive and relevant in the world market, we have to support Singaporeans as they may have to change jobs every decade in the new, fast-evolving economic environment.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our countrymen should never be alone in their search for work and opportunities, regardless of economic cycles.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Government should always have their back, while working in close partnership with employers and investors for a win-win outcome.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For the last few years, as a nation, we have been working to strengthen the Singaporean Core in our workforce, in every sector and at every level.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is not only to protect Singaporean’s labour rights and privileges but also to ensure that our citizens have key competencies and knowledge necessary for national sustainability, independence and security.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As this crisis has highlighted, we should strive to be as self-reliant as possible, even in the face of our limited resources.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For certain jobs and sectors, we have not been able to grow our local core because the jobs and sectors are not attractive to Singaporeans and we have to depend heavily on foreigners.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Jobs that immediately come to mind are construction workers and sanitation workers.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We should intensify our efforts and review how these jobs can be redesigned and done differently, supplemented with technology or incorporate new work processes to make them more attractive.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Second, as a nation, we must be prepared to pay more for services or goods made by fellow citizens, so that they will receive better wages, as the President has pointed out in her Address.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We should escalate the implementation of PWM for more jobs and in addition, raise their wage levels.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We should continue to professionalise the training, upgrading, licensing and organisation of our local workmen and tradesmen.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They are an important part of our local economy and they provide essential services to our population.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We should provide options for them to access certification exams in languages that they are comfortable with, or even allow for verbal rather than written assessments, or even practical tests, given the nature of their work.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The same goes for skills upgrading and training, where we should continue to encourage them to learn new skills and go digital, but in a format that is accessible to them.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If they can offer additional new services or reach new customers through digital platforms, this will ensure their livelihoods and the survival of their trades.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: At the other extreme, there are jobs desired by Singapore Citizens, such as Professional, Managers, Executives and Technicians or PMET positions, but seem to be taken by a significant number of foreigners, giving rise to complaints that our citizens have been discriminated against.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I applaud the efforts to increase the level of government scrutiny to ensure fair hiring practices by both local and foreign firms.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Last month, one of my residents, a PMET, shared with me, in tears, that she was retrenched, a plight which she accepted, in view of the economic crisis.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, she later found out that her job was given to a foreigner, who performed all the same tasks that she used to do in her company.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We must do more to prevent employers from abusing our system.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Just as it is the Government's responsibility to look out for Singaporeans, it is no surprise that companies focus on their own organisations' priorities, such as profitability or their own national interests if they are foreign entities.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is important to nurture Singaporeans by giving them the opportunities, exposure and experience provided by these coveted jobs.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We should also fortify our reporting hotlines to make it easier for employees and whistleblowers to make reports and complaints, and provide more resources to our investigative teams.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While higher qualifying salaries, penalties and levies can be effective, these are blunt tools that may end up driving up costs for companies.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As the global economy is undergoing extensive transformation due to the COVID-19 crisis and the trade tensions, this is also a good opportunity for us to take a deeper look at how our economy and jobs are transforming, and to make the process a beneficial one for employers and Singaporean employees.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Though it is important for us to remain an open society, we should also keep an eye on the statistics to ensure that we are on track to reach our goal of building a strong Singaporean Core within our desired time frame.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I would also like to appeal for more social assistance, including family counselling, for our sandwiched class, many of whom are middle-aged with young children and elderly parents to support.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They are under a lot of stress under these difficult times and may not be aware of our myriad of assistance programmes in place.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For families in crisis, it does not take much to derail them.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need stronger and more holistic social support networks to catch them at the first signs of distress and quickly put a stop to prevent them from sliding further.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We could proactively send materials to employees and families affected or contact them, checking if they need help to tide them over difficult periods.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Knowing that processes are in place to ensure that their children’s and elderly’s basic needs, such as food, housing, healthcare, education and transport, are taken care of will lift a load off their minds, allowing them to focus on the next step – training and trying new jobs.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need more family counsellors during this critical period to share with them how to avail themselves of help and take care of themselves and their families.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):   Finally, I would like to appeal for more social assistance including family counselling for our sandwiched class, many of whom are middle-aged with young children and elderly parents to support.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They are under a lot of stress under these difficult times and may not be aware of our myriad of assistance programmes.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For families in crisis, it does not take much to derail them.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need a stronger and more holistic social support networks to assist them at the first signs of distress and quickly prevent their situation from worsening.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We could proactively send materials to employees and families affected or contact them, checking if they need help to tide them over difficult periods.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Knowing that assistance policies are in place to ensure that their children's and elderly's basic needs, such as food, housing, healthcare, education and transport, are taken care of will lift a load off their minds, allowing them to focus on their next step – training and trying new jobs.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need more family counsellors during this critical period to share with them how to avail themselves of help and take care of themselves and their families.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In English): Sir, in conclusion, we face a daunting task ahead of us but I have faith that we can overcome this crisis.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We are a resilient and determined people who are not afraid to work hard.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Let us put our trust in one another and fight this good fight together.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Together we stand and we shall emerge from this crisis stronger than before.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I conclude with my support for the Motion of Thanks to the President for her Address.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I join Members before me to address the issue on foreign manpower.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As a member of the Board of the Monetary Authority of Singapore or MAS, I will talk about the issue from the perspective of the financial services sector, the people who work in it and the people who want to work in it.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is a key sector of the future economy, a very bright spot in a COVID-19 stricken economy.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Through agility, hard work and good fortune, we have carved out a place in the borderless and fast changing world of global finance.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The fundamental challenge we have is this: how do we defend and grow this position, against very tough global competition, in a way that provides the best opportunities for Singaporeans?

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Let us talk about how we grew into the global financial hub that we are today.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It all started in the late 1960s, when we seized the chance to become an international foreign exchange trading centre.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It was born from a simple but powerful insight.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Due to our time zone, we could seamlessly bridge East and West, to facilitate US dollar transactions after the New York market closed, before London opened.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This became the Asian Dollar Market or ADM, which grew into a vibrant activity in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The earliest banks to obtain licences to operate in the ADM market were foreign banks, the first being the Bank of America.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But over time, these foreign financial institutions trained a whole pipeline of Singaporean talent.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Singapore is now one of the top international wealth management centres today.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: To get to where we are, we had to overcome our initial lack of knowledge, expertise and networks.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, we attracted a critical mass of global players and international talent to get us started.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, it employs close to 3,000 employees across its various business lines.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It has instituted a range of training programmes, including converting our former Command House into the UBS APAC Business University, and one of its objectives is to develop local talent.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Last year, it appointed a Singaporean to oversee the bank’s entire business in the Asia Pacific.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, we have come a long way, from the ADM in late 1960s to a complex eco-system of activities today, from retail and corporate banking to trade finance, investment banking, insurance, wealth management, infrastructure finance, FX and derivatives trading.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In essence, keep bringing in new activities, keep developing new capabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In the build-up phase, inject foreign expertise where necessary – people with track records in the area.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But over time, grow our own timber and when Singaporeans gain the expertise, we take on more roles in multi-national teams, here as well as abroad.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Using the same approach, we are now developing FinTech and Green Finance.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As a result, the sector continues to create jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There are also positive spillovers, contributing to jobs in the legal and accountancy fields, many of which also go to Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is one of our most promising sectors, especially for the young.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We observe this in the way financial institutions and our fresh graduates mutually seek out each other.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For example, every year, up to a third of SMU fresh graduates, and that includes this year’s graduates, are hired by the financial services sector.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Being a former Minister of Education, I observed the same pattern from NUS' Business Administration faculty.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Students from other disciplines such as Accountancy and Engineering also find the financial sector a very attractive destination.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The financial institutions know that our education system prepares our young well for this sector.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And then our students know there are bright careers in the sector too.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, there is no doubt that being a global financial hub has benefited Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I also think that, by and large, Singaporeans are not uncomfortable with this approach.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Why then has foreign manpower raised concerns amongst Singaporeans?

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, let us start by examining some of the data, including the details of manpower in different activities and at different levels that MAS has been painstakingly compiling in recent years, and which it has released recently.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These proportions have remained stable in recent years.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The non-Singaporeans in senior roles have diverse backgrounds.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The largest group comes from Europe, with other significant nationalities across Asia and North America.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The worry is that the large number of foreigners in senior positions may then crowd out Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This concern is understandable, and I will address it.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The reason for a higher share of foreigners in senior roles is mainly due to the large international component of activities here.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Singapore has grown as a global financial centre as more financial institutions set up regional or global functions in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They have made us the hub for expertise, networking and oversight of operations in other markets.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And I think if you ask Singaporeans if this is a good thing for our country, I think most will also say yes.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These functions tap on growth outside of Singapore, support the region’s development and in so doing, they bring opportunities and bring jobs here.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Moreover, for financial institutions to site these operations here is a concrete show of confidence for Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It raises the stakes the world has in Singapore, and makes us safer and more secure.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But the staff profile of regional and global activities, like in any leading financial centre, tends to be more internationally diverse.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As MNCs, financial institutions will fill these ranks with global expertise that they deploy across their offices around the world.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But this does not mean that Singaporeans are getting the short end of the stick, because it is not a zero-sum game.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: First, while the share of Singaporeans in senior roles has remained steady, the absolute number of Singaporeans in these roles has increased.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is because as we grow as a financial centre, the base has expanded significantly.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So same share, but of a growing base.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That is more than a 50% increase in five years, or an additional 900 Singaporeans taking up senior roles, embarking on a new and fulfilling stage in their careers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The second reason, when these functions come here, Singaporeans gain precious global and regional expertise.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This complements overseas assignments and exposure, which are key to preparing Singaporeans to assume senior management roles in global firms.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There are promising signs that more locals are taking up roles with international exposure.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We spoke about the Bank of America being one of our earliest licensees for the ADM earlier.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, the bank’s electronic FX business in Asia Pacific is headed by a Singaporean, who is now based in Hong Kong after having previously worked for them in Singapore and in London.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It currently has 140 Singaporeans working overseas, in key markets like Indonesia, China and the US, and as far afield as Nigeria.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There are many more Singaporeans working overseas in the financial sector.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MAS and EDB are in touch with about 2,000 such overseas Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: About 120 of them are C-suite executives, Singaporeans working overseas; another 750 hold Director/Vice President positions or higher.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Compared to the good old days, the financial services sector has grown to become a global hub.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There is competition but Singaporeans are seizing the opportunities, and taking up these important positions.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Still, there is more that we can do to create opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MAS is working with the industry to groom Singaporeans to be leaders and specialists in financial services.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Another is the International Postings or iPost scheme, which incentivises financial institutions to send Singaporeans for international exposure.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: A further concern that I have heard, is that amongst some firms there may be an unconscious bias amongst business heads towards hiring people from their own nationality and they do not give Singaporeans a fair shot.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We know that it is within the cultural DNA of most international financial institutions to cherish diversity, and this is a value Singapore strongly believes in because of our multi-culturalism and openness.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, let me also be very clear – there is no place for unfair hiring practices for the financial services sector.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MAS holds our financial institutions to high standards and will not condone firms that fall short of fair hiring practices.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We are aware that there are financial institutions that are on MOM’s Fair Consideration Framework Watchlist.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MAS has been engaging these firms actively to understand the reasons for this.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Where their HR practices are found wanting, we will make sure improvements are made.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Another concern is the high concentration of one nationality in the technology departments of financial institutions.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It happened because the adoption of technology is a worldwide phenomenon.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There is an explosion of demand for technology professionals and we are unable to fill all the posts domestically.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We are furiously growing our local talent pipeline in this area, through mid-career skills upgrading and expanding computer science places rapidly in our Universities.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But this is not likely to meet the demand, and foreign manpower is still needed.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, the concern will remain and we will need to address it.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: After all, over-reliance on a single source leaves us more susceptible to unexpected disruptions.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We saw this as borders began to shut amidst the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MAS has been stepping up engagements with the top leadership of key financial institutions on the need to maintain robust HR practices that are merit-based and support workplace diversity.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, foreigner-heavy technology functions may move offshore together with some good quality jobs in Singapore for locals.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have to look at this very carefully and not rush to chop off businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I think the discourse can go either way.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, the world is globalised and digital with its attendant benefits and problems.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The apprehensions are real, but are also shaped by the social media.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, in times of economic difficulties and job insecurity, nativism, and the "us-versus-them" perspective may take hold.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have seen how toxic the discussion can become in other countries and how it can change the course of history.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is not a discourse Singaporeans deserve, nor do I think this is what Singaporeans want.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have forged a very close partnership with our financial institutions over the years.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We could not have come so far without them.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They are here because our location, our rule of law, our stability as a country, our inclusivity, our openness, the ethos and talent of our people, make us a great place for them to put their business here.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: I am honoured to be here today and I am humbled to be allowed to serve my country and my community in these challenging times.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The spread of COVID-19 around the world has affected all of us in one way or another.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The economy has also been affected, and the impact will be a lasting one.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The social value of our essential services workers and being a part of the Labour Movement family in these last few months has opened my eyes further to the plight of our workers, especially those in the essential services.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Many of them have bravely stepped up and continued their work as front-liners during this time of crisis.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This pandemic has made us rethink the social value of many jobs that society has not always viewed as important such as cleaners, security officers, waste management workers and building maintenance personnel.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The services provided by these workers are necessary and without their hard work, Singapore would have come to a complete standstill.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: I am heartened that, as mentioned by Mdm President, this Government will continue to look out for our essential service workers and once this crisis has passed, I hope that we continue to value the work of our essential workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: I urge the tripartite partners to continue to support them and their efforts to continue to upskill and earn a dignified living.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: NTUC stands ready to ramp up discussions with industry players and I look forward to playing a part in realising the vision for these industries and our workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: I am also inspired that these workers' needs have also been considered during this pandemic.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: To complement the PWM, many workers in the essential services have their incomes and retirement funds supplemented by the Workfare Income Supplement Scheme or WIS.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Despite their sacrifices and selflessness, I have met residents who struggle to cope and face financial, physical, mental and emotional stresses.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Their struggle is further impacted by an inability to find gainful employment to support themselves and their loved ones.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Recently, I had visited a resident in her early 30s who is facing the uphill challenge of being the sole care-giver for her father, while surviving on the salary of her elder brother who is working as a security guard.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: One can imagine her stress of not able to earn a living, socialise with peers of her age and more importantly, build a family of her own.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: As a community, we must ask ourselves what more we can do to not only provide her sustainable employment, but also peace of mind when she is at work.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Currently, while there are grants to defray the cost of care-giving, we should also consider households that only consists of a care recipient and the care-giver such as a youth who may be schooling looking after an elder.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Difficult questions such as would additional counselling be conferred to youths who are juggling their academic and care-giving responsibilities, and if there are necessary safeguards put in place to ensure that youth care-givers have adequate access to support networks, need to be asked.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: We must rally ourselves around these care-givers and I encourage businesses to adopt flexible work arrangements and for our Government to strengthen our current policies around care-givers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: As a society, it does us no favours to continue to tiptoe around mental health issues as they may have life-altering consequences.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Instead, we should consider mental health and physical health as equally important and in tandem with one another.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Part of this change must include more frank conversations on mental health issues, especially when concerning our youth.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This statistic is alarming, but we must bear in mind that these numbers represent the portion of our youths and they are empowered and are able to seek help.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Many youths may not be comfortable reaching out for help due to social stigma and the fear of being viewed as weak.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This is further compounded by families who may not be supportive due to reasons ranging from the impact this will have on securing scholarships and jobs, to the social impact a diagnosis may have on the family.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: One way to tackle some of the mental health issues faced by the youth is to equip educators with mental health knowledge so that they can identify warning signs and refer youths-at-risk to counsellors or other resources.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: We should also seek to create safe spaces for youths, parents, teachers and school counsellors to talk about mental health issues in a safe and supportive way.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: I look forward to understanding the concerns and working together with our stakeholders on this issue.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: It is important that we continue to raise awareness and educate ourselves about mental health for people of all walks of life so that we can build a more resilient and caring society.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: (In Malay):   Another area of interest that I would like to focus on is the improvement of our madrasahs.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Much good work has been done by M3@Towns to organise events, conduct house visits and galvanise resources to uplift and aid the community.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This opportunity for them to interact with others, share learning experiences and build friendships, will help integrate them further in the community.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: I hope that more of such initiatives can be adopted.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: While the academic standing of madrasahs has improved over the years, there is a need to find a sustainable model to uplift and support madrasahs and their students so that they further develop as educational institutions.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Part of the role of our madrasahs is to nurture future asatizah, who will guide the community to practise Islam within Singapore's context of social cohesion, peace and economic progress.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Achieving this vision, however, will require effort from many different stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Given the finite community resources, we must explore how else madrasahs can be better supported to ensure that the community's vision of future asatizah is achieved.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: While this is a difficult undertaking, I am looking forward to working with government agencies and stakeholders to continue to provide the madrasahs with better resources and training opportunities so that the students can receive a more enriching learning experience.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: As the Malay proverb goes, if something is worth doing, it is worth doing well.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: As a country, we have just celebrated a very different National Day in a very challenging time.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: But what continues to hold true is our aspiration of a more inclusive, resilient and caring society.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: While some of these are tangible changes like better wages and welfare of our workers and a more sustainable model to uplift our Madrasahs, more importantly we strive to make intangible improvements like a better social safety net and the destigmatising of mental health issues.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: I will strive to work on these issues and more with the support of my colleagues so that together we can emerge from this crisis with a brighter future and a better Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This Parliament and one united people must and will rise to the challenge that will define our generation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We are all of one mind that the crisis should be a pivot towards emerging stronger.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I wonder, Mr Speaker, Sir, the example of the Titanic in 1912 can serve as a useful metaphor here.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The Titanic was the engineering marvel of its time the product of all the best that capitalism and technology had to offer.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It was deemed unsinkable and yet it struck an iceberg and sank, killing over 1,500 people.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The disaster occasioned major reform of international maritime methods.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The link between what went wrong and the lessons that were drawn is interesting.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: If you will, let us use the Titanic as a metaphor in considering Singapore's condition One sobering fact about the Titanic was that it did not carry enough functioning lifeboats for everyone on board, leading to a change in norms after the disaster.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The civil servant who inspected the Titanic and recommended more lifeboats later revealed that he felt his job would be threatened if he did not give the ship the go-ahead to sail.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Insufficient lifeboats will undermine the confidence and peace of mind of Singaporeans, not to mention desirable risk-taking and entrepreneurial behaviour.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Some commentators have asked if now is the right time to introduce such a scheme, but that is precisely the point, should have been done earlier.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And even now when we debate such issues, those debates should be guided by what we should do to meet the next crisis.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Some would say that our system of social safety nets contains some sand in the system.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This is a process that can be excruciatingly embarrassing to the applicant to the point where I know of people who withdrew their applications for that reason.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: These processes also consume the time and resources of social workers and public servants.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Is there a better lens through which to think about such issues?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Can we focus not only on social justice, which is paramount, but also pragmatism, a value much lauded in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But by helping them, society may actually benefit in the longer term.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: If they fail to get that help, they may, for example, not obtain timely medical interventions, which may lead to a worsening medical condition and more state and social cost downstream if they need a more costly medical intervention.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, many such cases may raise MediShield premiums or the fiscal burden of state hospital subsidies, or the applicant may cut expenses for their children for meals and miscellaneous school-related costs, which could hurt their children’s prospects later in life, curtailing the future talent pool and tax base for our economy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: When there are applications for financial aid, could we, for instance, ask applicants to make declarations that they do not receive family support, bearing the risk of penalties for false declarations?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Could we ask applicants to provide permission to the agency to access financial or other records on a need-to-know basis, rather than requiring them to bring physical copies to a physical meeting?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Could we handle more interviews remotely using now ubiquitous videocall technology?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, Sir, I turn to the economy, and in doing so, I declare my interest as the CEO of an international research consultancy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The designers of the Titanic engineered it to be unsinkable, thanks to the latest fail-safes, and yet it failed.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The dominant narrative holds that our economy has also been brilliantly engineered and painstakingly maintained through sound policy, but the post-COVID landscape is changing, with many of the deeper trends having been accelerated, but not fundamentally caused by the COVID crisis.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is a commonplace to say that economic nationalism is on the rise.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: National governments are doing more to root economic activities like manufacturing and food production domestically.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In time, foreign direct investment, or FDI, may be harder to win; but there are also more subtle changes taking place.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Countries and companies are becoming more conscious of food safety, sustainability and unfair labour, trade and tax practices.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The UN’s sustainable development goals, or SDGs, are a widely recognised attempt to address such concerns.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: National governments as well as multinational companies, or MNCs, will come under increasing pressure to address such things.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The COVID crisis has crystallised a few key questions about our economic strategies.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: While unemployment and underemployment affect many Singaporeans, many foreign, special, and employment pass holders continue to hold jobs that many Singaporeans would see as desirable.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: To be sure, Singaporeans as a whole has never rejected a role for foreigners in the workforce throughout our history, and I certainly do not.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Talent from abroad can augment our economic prospects.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Many local SMEs have struggled to weather the storm.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: After years of schemes to support SMEs and start-ups.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Do we have enough regionally and globally competitive companies to anchor this local pillar even as the external pillar becomes more challenging.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There are several industries that are facing structural disruption.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Many jobs in delivery and driving will be replaced by autonomous vehicles and drones in the decades to come.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, the same can be said for jobs that involve pure coordination and narrow clerical functions which may be overtaken by AI-driven bots.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, we could look at programmes like Scale-up Singapore, a programme to scale up promising local start-ups and incentivise them to hire locals specifically from such so-called sunset sectors and give them opportunities in fast-growing companies and industries.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I am sure many of these workers would value the opportunity to prove themselves in such an environment.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: With sufficient time for local firms to adapt and with strong support given to local companies to retool and invest to make that transition.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We owe a huge debt of gratitude to our foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But having such a large population of foreign workers raises questions about longer term sustainability.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Low cost today may not mean low-cost tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: As my colleague, Mr Gerald Giam, and ex-Non-constituency Member of Parliament Mr Yee Jenn Jong, spoke about on the same panel, there is scope to redesign some of these jobs in the construction sector, for example, for locals at higher rates of pay and higher levels of productivity to minimise the impact on costs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Thirdly, there are many foreigners who occupy senior corporate positions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Some employers anecdotally comment that it is not easy to find enough Singaporeans who have the higher-order skills to lead large teams at the local, regional or global levels.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Skills like resilience, strong communication abilities, finding unconventional solutions to novel problems, and so on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There are some employers who engage in discriminatory practises against Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: That is deplorable and needs to be address.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Indeed I and other Workers’ Party Members of Parliament have often spoken about this.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There are many Singaporeans who have been incredibly successful as business leaders in MNCs and local firms.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But can the Government consider engaging with employers to understand this kind of feedback where it exists?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Assess if there is any basis to it and circle back, as it were, to our curriculum development in our school system to understand why locals with these skills are not being produced in sufficient numbers, if this is indeed the case.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Fourthly, Sir, I would suggest that in the uncertain world that faces us, domestic entrepreneurship and innovation are going to be more important in driving growth, vis-à-vis FDI attraction.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Are we doing as well as we could on entrepreneurship?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: How do we fare in global indices of entrepreneurial performance?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Do we have enough entrepreneurs, including, and especially, women entrepreneurs, who can start up and scale up?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This is a subject that warrants serious study.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: If there are impediments to entrepreneurship as regards access to financing, for example, an unlevel playing field due to gaps in competition policy, for example, or any other such issues, these should be identified and addressed.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Many developed country governments and MNCs are facing pressures to ensure traceability in their supply chains in respect of sustainability, fair labour and trade practices, food safety and so on – concerns given expression in the UN's SDGs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Being ahead of the curve of these attributes can be a competitive advantage for Singapore firms.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Our economic agencies should consider deploying relevant tools to incentivise and nudge our local firms to develop tangible programmes that ensure traceability of supply chains and sound practices in these respects.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This will enable them to more competitively export to developed economies in North America, Europe, Japan and elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Over time, this can be expected to become a bigger advantage.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: On the Titanic, the lookouts had no binoculars, and the wireless operator dismissed the key iceberg warning.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: So, we collect unemployment data using the labour force survey every month and publish data every quarter.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Going back to the Titanic metaphor, despite the strict women-and-children-first policy, a greater proportion of men in first-class survived than of children in third-class.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The COVID crisis is testing our fault lines of class.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The gap will widen between those with plenty of future-ready skills, financial and social capital, versus those that have less.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: How do we deal with this as a nation?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: As our social fabric becomes increasingly tested by these powerful forces, we must ensure that our social contract, our political institutions, culture and norms will not crack under the pressure.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: COVID has illustrated how, in this new era, Singapore needs to build an overarching political social and economic eco-system that is not fragile.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The writer, Nassim Taleb, who has studied this issue, writes and I quote, “It is far easier to figure out if something is fragile than to predict the occurrence of an event that may harm it.” And in a separate quote, “The classic example of something antifragile is Hydra, the Greek mythological creature that has numerous heads.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: When one is cut off, two grow back in its place”.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: That means the systems do not over concentrate power, thought leadership, social capital and initiative in one organisation, grouping or class, unless fragile.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And in the new world that is dawn in Black Swan events, may be effectively unpredictable, and antifragility may become more important than efficiency.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Singapore is characterised by a strong and well-resourced state, but a less strong civil society in a political landscape that is less plural than in almost all other developed countries.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There is, Sir, a pragmatic case for pluralism, not only a philosophic one.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Many Singaporeans have asked if the explosion of COVID-19 cases would have happened if we had heeded the warnings of civil society groups about our current system of housing foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Some groups had repeatedly warned of the risk of outbreaks of infectious diseases in these dormitories.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Do we have a sufficiently strong civil society, meaning independent not-for-profit organisations, or NPOs, media academia and so on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In a speech in 1967 on how the intelligence here can make the contribution to society, Dr Goh Keng Swee attacked what he called a curious view that the Singapore Government’s disapproved or dissenting opinions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I quote from an intellectual biography of Dr Goh by Ooi Kee Beng which describes Dr Goh’s speech as saying that the marginality of open debate in Singapore was serious and had to stop.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: What was valuable was open debate unencumbered by timidity and carried out by intellectuals who linked abstract principles with experience of ground reality.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We can do more to nudge and incentivise wealthy Singaporeans to set up philanthropic foundations that not only provide charity but engage in research on policy issues to provide alternative perspectives and ideas.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, I cite the Lien’s Foundation’s paper on pre-school education in 2012, which was impactful, but we need more.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Actions like the Government's removal of a grant from cartoonist Sonny Liew’s award-winning comic book due to its interpretation of Singapore history do not help matters.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We must do more to reboot our notion of meritocracy as the President alluded to in her Address.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: To celebrate unorthodox pathways to success, redefining what success is.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: To be honest, this is not an easy undertaking and requires the whole-of-society effort.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: One suggestion I have would be to identify those who have succeeded in some way, making an impact in life by pursuing unconventional pathways and accord them the status of ambassadors of the unconventional as it were or some such term.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: These individuals could be engaged to speak to students in IHLs, to TACs in the professional groups.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: To promote unorthodox pathways, we also need to uncage unorthodox thinking.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Here again, I would like to return to the education system.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: All of those who are parents are familiar with Primary school examination questions where extra points are awarded for expressing the right answer in the right way, rather than the right answer in an unconventional way.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Habits and mental models ingraining from an early age tend to stick.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: He seems to suggest that it is because we do not have redundancy policies in place and hence our self-employed persons could not be adequately supported during this crisis.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: This suggestion seems to be premised upon that self-employed persons are necessarily self-employed due to redundancy and not by choice.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Does Mr Leon Perera have anything to substantiate or to ascertain that people necessarily become self-employed chiefly due to redundancy and not by choice?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I said in my speech that self-employed persons who are receiving various forms of aid like SIRS have to go through multiple steps and there are different ways of thinking about the process that they have to follow to pursue those steps and to obtain the aid that they need.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I did not say that self-employed people are self-employed because they are made redundant or that self-employed people are somehow not worthy of help.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, I think perhaps also the Member may be alluding to my reference to redundancy insurance.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: My reference to the redundancy Insurance scheme, which we have proposed in the last term of Parliament in this House is not specifically about self-employed persons.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: It is about people who become involuntarily unemployed.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I just hope that that serves as some clarification for the Member.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I would just like to ask Mr Leon Perera, in all humility, whether he is aware of any other country that has introduced a scheme, not like SIRS, but perhaps something else that has delivered as quick support to self-employed persons that we could learn from, that we can do better.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Perhaps he could share with us so that we can learn.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I think she asked about specifically about the SIRS scheme.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I am aware that it has provided help to a large number of people who are in need of help, who are self-employed.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I will say in all candour that I am not aware specifically of any country that has a similar scheme.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: But having said that, I have not specifically researched into that issue.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The point that I made in my speech was really about the process of application for SIRS and in fact, for other forms of aid and how we could improve on that process.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: For example, by applicants being able to make a declaration that they are not receiving family support rather than having members of their family interviewed for the degree to which they support them.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, that was one aspect of the speech that I made.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: But I think the point is well taken that in times like this, in times of crisis, forms of aid had been delivered by the Government to persons in need including those self-employed.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And we have seen forms of aid being delivered by governments in other countries as well.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: There are eight packages that are certain percentage of GDP.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The point that I made in my speech was not to take away or detract from the value of SIRS that has helped a number of applicants but really how that process could be improved.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I should state since the Minister raised this point that perhaps one other area of improvement that I did not allude to, would be when cases are turned down, if there could be more specificity about the reason why they are being turned down, that may actually be helpful to make the appeal process or the follow-up process a little bit more efficient.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: When COVID-19 hit us in the most unexpected ways, we had to think of a way to help self-employed persons.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They are, by their very nature, not captured easily by our systems.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, how to reach them, how to deliver the help to them in a very timely manner, that is not an easy question to answer.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In the end, NTUC put up their hands and said, "Look, this criteria is very useful.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, we believe that there is still another group that will not be captured.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will put ourselves in a position of taking in applications or appeals." I do not know of any other organisation that stepped up to try and do this.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We were just about to enter into the circuit breaker period, it was very difficult to get people to come on board and set up the system, get it properly tested and ensure that it was able to respond to the volume of appeals.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But NTUC, to its credit, accepted that if there were appeals, it must mean that there is a need.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Therefore, they soldiered on and put a lot more manpower, which they did not really have the budget for.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, from MOM's perspective, on behalf of the Government, all I can say to NTUC is a huge "Thank You".

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Had we not had a symbiotic partner like the NTUC that was prepared to stick its neck out, even though it knew that its capabilities in this area had been untested, even though it knew that as a result of that, they could get a lot of flak.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But thinking on behalf of the self-employed persons who might need it, they did it anyway.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I think that has got to be the spirit and I think acknowledging all the areas of improvements, that is well and good.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We would want to do in the next time.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But let us not forget what the NTUC stood up to do.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And I think that the NTUC has certainly processed many cases and attempted to do well in very trying circumstances.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The Minister spoke about how NTUC raised its hand.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I just like to ask for a little bit more clarity on the thinking behind that decision.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have partnered the NTUC for other schemes before.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Before I begin, on behalf of the NTUC, I want to thank Minister Josephine Teo for her acknowledgement of our partnership and of our symbiotic relationship.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We will never shy away from stepping up at a time of need to look after workers, to look after everybody who have to earn a living, to work with the Government, to work with our symbiotic partner, to do the right thing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We believe in action, we believe in learning.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We will do our best and we will do better.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And it is always hard when you are doing things, something that was not pre-existing; and you would learn.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: But we are committed to that and our actions and our results speak for themselves in that they have touched lives.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Singapore depends greatly on trade and global demand for manufacturing, logistics and financial services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: A big chunk of employment is also dependent on tourism and air travel, as these directly and indirectly create jobs for the air hub and related services, tourism services, local transportation, hotels, retail, F&B and so on.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The economic and social disruptions brought about by COVID-19 and by geopolitical and trade tensions have upended lives and livelihoods throughout the world.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The world today continues to be shrouded in COVID-19 infections.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: There is also a rising number of countries facing new resurgence of COVID-19 infection, forcing them to re-tighten on the painful restrictions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: So, when everybody freezes up, that has an impact on a trading nation, on a logistics and air hub.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: It means that our economy will continue to be squeezed which then means that jobs will be lost and the labour market will see jobseekers chase after vacancies, instead of the one that we are a lot more familiar with for years which was jobs chasing after workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: In this scenario, which may persist for quite some time, I want today to speak up for a segment of the workforce who will then face an increased risk of job loss.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: But there are, and one of them is ageing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: It happens – that is, ageing happens – regardless of whether there are geopolitical or trade tensions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The economy was growing and there was a chronic shortage of workers in most sectors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Coupled with low population fertility, both the need and the benefit of enabling older workers to continue contributing is obvious – obvious to the older workers themselves, obvious to their companies and to the country.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Also, with the economy continuing to grow, companies and workers had the time to adjust.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Given this, the most critical outcome for Singaporeans is indeed jobs, jobs, jobs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The question is: whose jobs will go, and who will get the chance to be hired for the new jobs?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Many in this House have spoken already of the need and the means to protect and safeguard the Singapore Core.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Senior Minister Tharman, in an interview dated 17 June this year, said and I quote, "This is, and must be, a national effort.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And it needs new thinking among employers, to give middle-aged and mature Singaporean workers a fair chance to prove themselves." He said, "Employers need to reorient their management philosophies and their human resources and talent management practices." "No Singaporean who is willing to learn should be 'too old' to hire.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And no one who is willing to adapt should be viewed as 'overqualified'", he said.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Therefore, i just want to call attention to this – do not take this lightly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I know the situation is difficult, I know everybody says that they are the most important, "Look after me" but do not take this as the easy way out.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: These two deserve due consideration and serious consideration too.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: On this I want to thank Second Minister for Manpower Tan See Leng yesterday for speaking out also for fairness for older workers and also Minister Josephine Teo earlier.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: If a displaced older worker remains unemployed for a longer period, then that unemployment may turn sticky or become structural.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: There will then be a knock-on effect on retirement adequacy and that will in turn impose a heavier call on community, family and state financial resources, not to imagine what it does to the morale of the people.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I say all these not to pretend that all older workers are somehow better at work than younger ones.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I am saying this in order to help forestall a resort to a quick fix by stereotyping older workers as a category and then making hiring decisions unfairly on that kind of a basis and denying them a fair go.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: That is the one that I am warning against and let us pay attention to it.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The risk of this happening goes up in a recession and we hear on the ground anecdotes of such thinking and such behaviour.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We must therefore warn against and stand up to it.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I propose a five-pronged approach, which I will use the acronym "Heart".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: H-E-A-R-T. "H" is for Holding On to Jobs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Of course, this is the most preferred of options.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The Government on its part has set aside much funding to help improve the cost effectiveness of employing older workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The extension of the Jobs Support Scheme will also help to defray payroll cost of older workers, as it do other workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This is to remind employers of all these special fundings for the hiring of older workers and giving a fair chance to older workers, so that they will not neglect these facts when making decisions concerning their older workers to continue their employment and hiring.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
