text: At the same time, schemes such as e2i’s Lift and Place programme which keeps workers on payroll while they are on temporarily seconded to other jobs in another industry should be tapped wherever possible to minimise and delay retrenchments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: On the part of older workers, I also want to continue to stress the importance of looking after our health the best we can while at the same time demonstrating a positive work attitude and willingness to adapt and be flexible.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This makes it easier for employers to adjust their operations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Such an older worker would also more attractive to an employer compared to another who is not like that.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Despite best efforts by all, some workers will be displaced.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: When this happens, the most important task is to help the person get back into work as quickly as possible.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Prolonged unemployment erodes hiring prospects, especially for older workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: In this context, the work of the National Jobs Council under Senior Minister Tharman and the NTUC’s Jobs Security Council led by NTUC Secretary-General Ng Chee Meng, which leverages the Labour Movement network, and now acts in concert and in support of the National Jobs Council – these are important arrangements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Within the NTUC it is not only the Jobs Security Council but there is also another network which is the Company Training Committees or CTCs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I just wanted to make reference to this because the hon Member Mr Leon Perera talked about the Titanic.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The Titanic once it is made and it sets sail until it comes back into port, that is what you live with.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: He warned against a Singapore economy that it is like that.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: That is why we have from the Government side, indeed, industry and tripartite efforts and we came up with the Industry Transformation Maps or ITMs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I recall Deputy Prime Minister Heng also in his speech talked about 2.0.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: So, in other words, we knew that it is not invent for one time and then just use until it falls apart.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This is not the truth of our economy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Our economy is one that is constantly changing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: In fact, the very name "Industry Transformation Maps" tells all of us that we know we have to transform.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: In fact, it is not fast enough and that is our worry; not that we are so fixated with this sophistication of our model that we say we do not need to change.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We say we need to change, we have to transform, how to transform.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: So, in that sense, we are not the Titanic.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: For the Jobs Security Council, what does it do?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: One of the things that it does is instead of doing job matching, jobseeker by jobseeker, it goes in and works with industry partners, participating companies, by industry, to say, "What are your needs?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Who is having vacancies, even in today's situation?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Let us know and then you say how do you match ahead, retrain and go." So, this is exactly what Mr Leon Perera was talking about just now. "What is sunset?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Find out early, make the arrangements, help the workers go." So, on this we are agreed that it is important and we are doing it.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We will press on to continue to help more.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: One critical success factor in job-matching is indeed the availability of jobs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Aside from public and private sector vacancies in existing and growth areas such as health, long-term care, biomedical and logistical fulfilment for online sales, there are also many other initiatives.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I recall Minister of State Gan Siow Huang elaborating on all the different initiatives under the SGUnited banner.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: In the area related to age, it has actively and steadfastly upheld the principles laid down in relevant tripartite guidelines such as those on fair employment practices, re-employment of older employees and non-discriminatory job advertisements when dealing with complaints.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The NTUC has over the years also pushed for protections for older workers and these have been variously incorporated into laws such as when we amended the Industrial Relations Act and the Retirement and when we created the Retirement and Re-employment Act as well as introduced various tripartite advisories, guidelines and standards.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We will continue to pay attention to this and to do what is right by our older workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We do that in order to reflect the fine balancing of interests between companies and older workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Flexibilities between the parties can be discussed, will have to be discussed because we are in a serious situation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: But whatever we do, the spirit of how we do it and do it together, and hold together not only now but for the long term, that is important.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Those principles are important and we must adhere to that spirit as we discuss.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Where it is really unfair and in egregious cases, then we all know, TAFEP also works with MOM to add bite to its advice and recommendations for improvement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: To have teeth in something like that is key if you are to be taken seriously.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: What I want to say is, in the situation we are facing today, it is of a scale and depth that is quite unlike things that we had done before, that we had faced down before.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We also have to continue to look at this situation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I know Minister Teo had elaborated just now painful curtailing work pass privileges can be, and it is indeed so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And so, we will monitor and we will see what other regulatory teeth might be needed as the situation goes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: But I would much rather that companies treat every worker, including your older workers fairly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Then, we all work this out together and we emerge together.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: For mature workers who are displaced or who face severe wage cuts, the journey ahead will be tough as they seek to provide for themselves and meet family commitments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: As the slowdown wears on, calls by individuals to tap into their CPF savings to tide over this difficult period will grow.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: While I hope that MOM and the CPF Board, when they receive such requests, that they will look at each case sympathetically and be flexibe as much as possible, I am also very mindful that early drawdowns will inevitably translate into weaker eventual retirement adequacy for those workers who have to resort to such early withdrawals, if approved.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I therefore still hope that the CPF savings of our older workers can be safeguarded for as long as possible, as much as possible.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: These are already schemes that are already there to help seniors, the lower wage workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: There is already within the WIS, also a certain extra consideration for older workers and I thank MOM for that.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: But in this situation, can we look at reviewing it to help them in a more timely and effective way, and a more meaningful way, because more would need this, and we do not want the build-up.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Older Singaporeans will also face higher medical expenses compared to younger citizens, on average.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: He said that it was really very, very difficult to do so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: It would be better if they could be allowed to withdraw more, maybe on a temporary basis during this crisis period.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I think we should consider that but in terms of the cash impact, to families who may not have the financial resources.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Beyond the specific help measures, it is the collective will of the people to stand as one, to not let adversity cow us, split us or break us that sets the tone of our society and decide our fate as a nation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: So, let us gather our strengths and our wits, and tough it out to emerge stronger together.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: At the outset, I wish to express my gratitude to the voters of Sengkang for sending our team to this House to represent their voices in what is an immensely challenging time for our country because of prevailing systematic problems, tough economic times and the pandemic we find ourselves in the midst of today.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: But Singaporeans are also tough people whose resilience runs deep.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: When I think about resilience, I think about my Apa, my father, who was an exceptional student but had to drop out of school at 14 after the death of his father.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: He dropped out out of necessity to support his mother and siblings.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: His first job was a labourer at a factory and at night, he would wash the petrol station.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Though this story of his rise to success is inspirational, it does not negate the fact that he suffered immensely for it.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Not only was he subjected to labour-intensive work at such a young age, but he was also unable to continue his education.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: He often speaks about how he could have been a surgeon if not for his family's circumstances.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: He wrote to us and his first line was that he was the sole breadwinner in the house, living with his lovely wife and is a proud father of four daughters.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: We must, as a society, ensure that we have equal opportunities in this country.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: I believe that the meritocracy our past leaders have placed so much importance on, has achieved a great deal for generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: But in the midst of this pursuit, we have inevitably left many behind, short-changed, and sadly, made to believe that they deserve their stations because they were simply not good enough.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: The Primary school student who feels discouraged from even trying to score in exams anymore while watching kids in other classes go for expensive tuition classes outside of school.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: The teenager who stops dreaming of what the future could look like.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: The pre-university student who can sense the condescension from relatives upon telling them he or she will not be going NUS or NTU.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: The eager young graduate from a private university who keeps applying to the Public Service for a job but never gets a call back.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: And even, the NUS graduate who suffers from imposter syndrome because he or she is simply not good enough to apply for jobs their peers seem to have in the bag.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: It is time that we shift our perception of what being a good Singaporean means.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: A good Singaporean to me is someone who is able to define successes in their own way.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: It is often argued that under our meritocractic system, Singaporeans enjoy equal access to opportunities, and that this access drives social mobility.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: From Prof Syed Hussein Alatas in the 1970s to Assoc Prof Teo You Yenn today, academics in Singapore have long painted detailed pictures of inequality on this island within the framing context of local reality.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: There are few questions relevant to our local context.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: We must confront every one to give young Singaporeans a better deal.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: There is a deep sense prevailing in this country that even in 2020, one's socio-economic background is still too tightly linked to the accessibility of opportunities one enjoys.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Reforms have been made and will be made to our education system where grading and testing are concerned.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: We will need to take steps to better support students from young.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: We need to train teachers to be adapt in not just providing academic guidance but also holistic support to students from disadvantaged backgrounds.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: We need to be prepared to have open, honest conversations about whether recent reforms in grading, streaming and testing are working.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: And we need to be prepared to go beyond these reforms.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: And also reforming teaching and learning in a careful but ambitious manner to support learners with different skillsets.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: We need to assess and track the accessibility of opportunities at every phase of education and in the workforce too.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Make jobs in the Public Service and Civil Service more accessible to candidates from a wider academic backgrounds which would help improve the diversity of skills, perspectives and talents our administration can draw from.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Put simply, how can we maximise the opportunities available for young Singaporean students and workers.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: We need a bolder, long-term approach to creating jobs for young Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Let us look for these opportunities everywhere we can.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Let us make a concerted effort to support the creation of green jobs in industries from manufacturing and retail to finance and hospitality, by recognising the reality that economic growth is contingent upon social and environmental needs.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: And let us not forget to educate Singaporean students to re-imagine the possibilities which lay ahead.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Thirdly, Mr Speaker, putting aside the issue of the accessibility of opportunities, we must also ask whether there are Singaporeans for whom that availability of opportunities in the first place is not as real as you may imagine it to be.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Many young Singaporeans of all backgrounds I have spoken to have echoed these views.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: These young people are more than willing to start the conversation and contribute their ideas.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: We see it in young people who organise rallies and beach clean-ups, who want to see Singapore do its part to tackle climate change.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: We see it in young people, who time and time again, have stood up to speak out against sexual harassment.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: We see in young people who have been using Instagram, Twitter and even TikTok to convey, convince and correspond on issues that matter to them.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: And young people whose activism also extend beyond the bounds of social media and in the offline world too.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: I believe that this is what young people envision for a country.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: We envision a country that is able to have open and frank conversations about the direction we would like to see our home move towards.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: We may be young in age and less experienced in life but it does not mean we do not understand the important issues that the country faces.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Young people worry about their future just as much as any of our country's leaders do.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: We worry about our parents' retirement, job opportunities and living a life that is fulfilling.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: We too have anxieties about starting and providing for a family.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: I hope that Parliament will listen closer to the hopes and the worries of young Singaporeans and have them inspired as in making the changes we need for a better future, a better Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Not quite a Perfect Storm, but still a hurricane.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some say it will be as deep as the Great Depression of a hundred years ago, or even worse.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We must be clear-eyed about where policy and implementation can be improved.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: As I said in this House in March 2016 during an Adjournment Motion, it is about "seeing through the eyes of our people".

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This includes looking after our people in sickness and in health.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I will speak on five areas, on health – our elderly; our workers; access to insurance; access to new treatments; and our nurses and our allied health staff.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some in older flats that cannot easily have ramps installed through the EASE programme and these elderly cannot afford to pay for transport assistance to get to the clinic.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In our community outreach, we do our best to help.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But I ask, has MOH systematically studied seniors in such a situation?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Are such seniors less likely to keep up with primary care appointments and necessary follow-ups?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Are they more likely to be admitted to hospital?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And when they are hospitalised, do they stay longer when they are admitted?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I have met elderly seniors who tell me that when they apply for a personal mobility device, they were told part of the process involves a doctor signing off on the paperwork.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But some seniors, Mr Speaker, are confined to the home because they are not mobile, to begin with.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some have a care-giver who also has mobility needs and is home-bound.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some do not have family to bring them to the doctor.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, it becomes a difficult situation – have to go out to see the doctor as part of the process to get the mobility assistance, but they need that assistance to more easily go out.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Again, in the community, many of us in our constituencies are trying our best, but we must continue looking at improving the implementation.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We must make sure that residents do not fall between the cracks of policy implementation and we must continue to try and improve.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I have older residents who have mixed feelings.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Every time there is a new Smart Nation app or digitalisation programme, some are excited, the more techno-savvy uncles and aunties.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: They are excited that Singapore is innovating with new technology, new platforms.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But there are some older seniors who are less IT-literate.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Otherwise, digital progression broadly will have regressive impact on the less well-off, the less IT-savvy, and all those elderly who are less literate.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, again, we must continue pushing, to inculcate IT skills in our elderly, but we must also continue to keep the face-to-face and telephone option open for interacting with Government services.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And the telephone option must be meaningfully available, which means not a half-hour wait on the line before there is a human voice.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It maintains the human touch to have that face-to-face, that human telephone option.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And in an economic downturn, it is an opportunity to hire many more Singaporeans with people skills and life experience to help fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: There are low-wage workers and those without flexible working arrangements, who cannot get time-off for a polyclinic consult during the day.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: If they go to a GP after hours, the cost is higher.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Just because their workplace had healthcare benefits, does not mean the workers were rich to begin with.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Our residents, especially in the COVID-19 crisis, should not face unnecessary challenges to means testing when trying to return to subsidised healthcare.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is also a very visible sign that individual patients and customers do not have bargaining power to stop insurance companies from such practices.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: When an insurance company moves the goal posts for an integrated shield plan, it is not so easy for a patient to switch provider because existing conditions become pre-existing conditions under the new policy.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We must find new ways to ensure affordable access to the newest treatments, not just for today but for tomorrow.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: For new and emerging treatments, such as cell-based therapy, which are capital intensive and where very few firms currently have the capability, we should invest in our own domestic capability, so that we can shape the local and regional market, and not be held ransom by overseas manufacturers who will charge what the market can bear or what the wealthiest segments of the market can bear, as we have seen in some other jurisdictions.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I am sure that MTI and MOH can explore this further.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Many residents in this COVID-19 crisis have shared how COVID-19 has been a reminder of the contributions and good work of our healthcare workers, especially our nurses, our allied health workers, our healthcare frontliners.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In a pandemic, our frontline healthcare workers are part of our national defence.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: If the pandemic frontline cannot hold, Singapore will be overrun.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some residents have asked if we are paying our nurses enough and if we can have more Singaporean nurses and staff in our public hospitals.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I have met older uncles and aunties, pakciks and makciks.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: They say there is something comforting about having a fellow Singaporean looking after them in the hospital wards, even just having someone bringing them between the ward and the clinic an assistant who understands them, with whom they can connect instantly, someone who can connect in our seniors' languages, in their dialect, it is that much closer.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But to survive and surmount these challenges, our domestic policies at home must also be ready for the future – looking after our people, making sure no one is left behind or falls between the cracks.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: When a grandparent falls ill, it affects the grown up children and their own households.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Is Ah Kong, is Ah Mah going to get better?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Would Ah Kong be there when "didi" finishes his PSLE?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: When a breadwinner is struck down, the whole family worries.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: When a child is unwell, the hopes and dreams of an entire family are at stake.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We are facing tough times but it is during times like these that our mettle is tested and we are given an opportunity to shape our norms as a nation.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We decide how we respond and the path we take.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: She needs to adapt and change to adjust to the changing global environment.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: She needs to evolve economically, politically and socially.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: But she can choose to be different from everyone else and do things the Singaporean way.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: For some time now, there has been a call for alternative voices to represent the diverse interests in the community.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I am encouraged to see our electorate maturing and many people from different backgrounds stepping up to contest during the last General Election, offering different perspectives, aspiring for a better Singapore.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: What we have in Singapore is an adversarial process.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This process, when carried out in the best traditions of democracy, brings out the best in all of us as we seek to continually improve.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Healthy competition is good, as we challenge each other to do better and, in the end, the nation benefits.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: However, when people take the adversarial process to its extreme and assert their opinions in a very vicious manner, there is a danger of the society being divided and polarised.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: During the campaign, in the online space, we saw some constructive discourse but also some malicious comments being passed, vitriolic remarks being expressed and personal attacks being made which strayed from the substance of the debate and became an attempt to bring people down instead.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: An election, is an emotive exercise, I appreciate that.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: However, all of us must continue to push for decorum and constructive debates always.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: As we evolve and mature as a nation, we have to find a better way to have discourse and for each of us to express our views and challenge opposing ones.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Society had always rallied against what it deems wrong and groups of people have campaigned against individuals to censure them.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: However, the Internet and social media have amplified and caused an evolution of this phenomenon and its repercussions.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Thirdly, people are quickly pushed to take sides and the very person or groups that need to be edified about the error of their ways, or to be shown different perspectives, are then disengaged.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: A more serious side effect is that those with genuine views become muted as they fear being judged or lynched by the angry mob.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The cancel culture can manifest itself in many different ways.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Several months back, there was an issue that arose within the Malay/Muslim community.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Many women and men, called out the hosts.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Misogyny is unacceptable and has no place in a progressive society.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: However, what was actually an opportunity to address an important issue, turned out to be a highly polarising exercise for the community.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Online, people were pushed to take sides – you are either on the camp asking for the hosts to be de-platformed or are seen as their supporters and, by affiliation, accept misogyny.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Some people I spoke to about the matter felt that there was so much negativity and people missed the point about the need for the community to address misogyny.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We must take a stand against things which are morally unacceptable.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: However, we need to learn to do so constructively so that the community can learn, have discourse and shape new and better norms.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Another trend that we have been seeing is the online movements that have been waged in other countries to change norms and push back against years of repression.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: There is value in rallying people to call out injustice and shift norms to be a more just and fair society.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We should encourage people to be conscious of social issues and do their part to bring about positive developments as a society evolves and matures.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: However, we must be conscious of the impact to the community.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Inevitably, there will be different opinions and we need to ensure the expression of opposing views does not cause polarisation.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The movements in the US have had their fair share of criticisms, even among liberals.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: So, even as we may be inspired by some of these developments abroad, we should not follow them blindly but, instead, find the Singapore way to evolve.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We have much to learn from the experiences of other countries.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: However, as we look to others for lessons to develop norms in our nation, we must pause to appreciate the impact of the same in our context.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We should be cautious not to jump on the bandwagon and copy and paste the playbook in other countries without adjusting the same for our needs.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In particular, we must be keenly aware of our special demographics as a multiracial, multi-religious society.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We must, therefore, ensure that in our debates and discussions, we are mindful of the impact of our comments and the danger of fraying our social fabric if we pit one group against the other.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We must, therefore, take the necessary action to ensure that we shape the norms of discourse in our nation.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We all need to play a part in creating a safe space online that encourages meaningful debates and curbs vitriolic discourse.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I sit on the Management Committee of OnePeople.Sg (OPSG) and have been involved in a few discussions with our youth volunteers and participants of our programmes recently.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We were discussing what were acceptable boundaries when discussing race and religious issues and whether current laws or frameworks need to be adjusted to changing times.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: So, while the Government can do its part by putting in place laws and regulations to set the necessary boundaries that circumscribe our discourse, as individuals, we all have a personal responsibility to behave fairly and call out any action that threatens healthy discussions.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Beyond having safe spaces for discussions online and even offline, to truly shape norms, we need to translate our discussions into real action.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: For this, too, we all must play a part.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We must ensure that we ourselves do not discriminate, especially in our conduct with others who are different from us and that we teach the right values to our children.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: (In Malay):    We are increasingly seeing various views expressed on current issues affecting Singaporeans, especially online.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: What is good is that it shows the maturity of the community in discussing important issues such as Government policies or community norms.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Therefore, it is very important for us to ensure that, in Singapore, we develop our own norms and ways to conduct online discussions, especially when touching on hot and sensitive issues.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Issues related to religion and racism, or discrimination issues, for example, are important issues that we should face in a plural society.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We must be bold enough to speak out and be firm in calling something out if it goes against our societal values.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We should also want to continue contributing suggestions that can improve the lives of our people.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: But we must always rely on facts, and not just accept all the stories that we hear; and when we are faced with different views, we need to discuss with wisdom and have a constructive attitude.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: But in times of difficulty, our character and integrity as a society are tested.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We have the opportunity to shape the norms in our country.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I hope, we can choose our own way, the Singapore way, in debating important issues in our country.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Hopefully, with constructive contributions, Singapore will continue to grow and become an inclusive society, where we all have the opportunity to work, build families and achieve our aspirations.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: (In English): How we treat each other will determine how we evolve as a nation.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Our individual actions accumulate to create the culture of our society.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I hope to do my part to make this world kinder, more compassionate, more accepting of differences.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I hope to make this place a better place for my son, Ayden.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: As a parent, I worry about how he will be treated when he grows up.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I wonder if people will be patient with him, whether they will be kind and whether he will have the support he needs to live well.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The efforts in improving the support and infrastructure has been a work-in-progress.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We have made many big strides and Ms Denise Phua deserves special mention for all the efforts that she has done in this House as well as outside to champion the needs of the special needs community.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We can and should continue to build on these efforts.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I do hope that when we look at reviewing some of the support given, we go beyond lip service and truly work towards changing attitudes and norms.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I hope that we truly learn what empathy is.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We should not tick boxes and be content to just address one feedback at a time.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: When we talk about improving infrastructure, it is not enough to just build ramps and a few inclusive playgrounds.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We must really nudge behaviours to facilitate and make it convenient for those who have disabilities to join in all the activities that others are involved in.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We must encourage understanding and conversations amongst employers and co-workers.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We must learn to see the value and contributions of people who may be differently-abled.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: More importantly, they are differently-abled and should be seen an equally valued member of the community.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: People with special needs are conduits through which we all learn to be kinder and more compassionate.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This I have learnt from you, Mr Speaker.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: A kind and compassionate society is one that can brave through difficult challenges and emerge stronger.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: It is so important that in the midst of all the turbulence, we remain steadfast in preserving and shaping our values as a nation and remain a fair and just society, a society that is truly embracing of diversity.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: It is a great honour and privilege to be able to debate in this august House.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: As I have said in my maiden speech, in this House, we may not always agree with each other, but we debate respectfully.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I believe this decorum can extend beyond this House and I hope, as a nation, we always seek consensus, not conflict.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I hope, as a nation, we embrace our differences and be kind and compassionate always.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Before I begin, I would like to mention that I am not part of the National Trade and Unions Congress (NTUC), but in support of the Labour Movement, I would like to thank our Labour Movement for all the efforts that it has done for the Self-employed Person Income Relief Scheme (SIRS).

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I had the pleasure to work with some of the NTUC staff as they did their outreach, delivering over 30 to 40 Zoom sessions with different groups in different languages, and I saw their dedication in trying to process as many applications as they could, even till the wee hours of the morning, sacrificing their own family time.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The spirit of togetherness that will get us through this difficult time.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This Parliament sits during our worst recession since Independence and in a world that is increasingly divided.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Conditions that made us thrive – globalisation and stable, collaborative international order – has made way to a fragmented world with countries and economies closing, and tension between the major powers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To quote Mdm President, “We must stand united.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must move in one direction.” Mr Speaker, Sir, I would like to thank Mdm President for setting the tone for us to navigate through this unprecedented storm.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Only by staying united and working together can we emerge from this stronger.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Digitalisation, Industry 4.0 and COVID-19 have changed the world we live in.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The way we work, interact and do business is now different and there is no turning back.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Some sectors such as aviation, aerospace, marine and offshore are gravely threatened.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Having worked in these sectors, I am in support of the Ministry of Trade and Industry’s (MTI) efforts to continue to preserve the core capabilities which we have built over these years.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These support measures have cushioned the impact of COVID-19, but some jobs will still be lost, and some roles will cease to exist.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, there will be opportunities for growth in other sectors.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: New areas in digitalisation, Industry 4.0 and new business models will create new jobs and new ways of thinking.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We need to stay positive and see these risks and challenges as opportunities to transform the way we do things.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In addition, Singapore must stand out in a changing world order to survive and thrive.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To quote Mdm President, “We must do things that others cannot do, and do things that others can do, better.” One example is in the aerospace industry.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Singapore has grown to be the Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul (MRO) hub for the aerospace.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, this position of dominance has increasingly been challenged by competitors in neighbouring countries.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For Singapore to stay ahead, we cannot be solely competing for lowest cost as that means we may have suppressed wages too.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Singapore must compete to be of best value.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For example, an MRO facility in Singapore cannot merely be doing repair and maintenance like any other facility in the world.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must embrace industry 4.0 and leverage on digital and data analytics in order to provide better value for our customers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must transform from merely repairing the product, to understanding the product, providing insights that can deliver improvements in performance and move the value upstream.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It will take the effort of everyone working together to emerge from this storm stronger.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Both within an organisation and beyond the organisation, between Government, businesses, individuals, unions, supporting associations and across industries, we must act collaboratively, for the sake of one another.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Equipping the workforce with the right skills and mindset is crucial in driving this transformation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I am in support of the Government’s push for SkillsFuture and increasing internship opportunities.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, I must caution that the success of SkillsFuture should not be measured solely by attendance and course completion.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Instead, success should also be measured by the ability to transform these learnings into actual improvements or output.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As we work together to transform our economy, transformation cannot happen at the expense of others.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must care for one another and not leave anyone behind.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Businesses must do their part to provide fair opportunities for the workforce.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For displaced workers, I support the efforts in upskilling and providing job support through e2i, Workforce Singapore (WSG) and SkillsFuture Singapore (SSG).

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I am also in support of the Ministry of Manpower’s (MOM) incentives to encourage hiring local workforce.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, these efforts to support displaced workers must be matched with employers willing to change their approach and employees willing to try and make changes in a challenging job market.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must also, collectively as a society, work together to ensure that companies abide by fair hiring practices.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We all agree that we want to keep a strong Singaporean Core, provide equal opportunity to mid-career workers and seniors, provide jobs for persons with disabilities and have better work-life balance.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: During this transformation, we must embody and act on these beliefs that we are all in agreement of.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must think hard to redesign jobs and provide fair opportunities to our local workforce while maintaining our competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As our demographics transit to a higher proportion of workforce above the age of 50, we must redesign jobs to best make use of their experience and abilities.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We have all heard the same narratives from our senior residents seeking re-employment.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Government, businesses and citizens must work together and expand opportunities for our senior workforce.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As we eagerly anticipate things returning to normal, let us pause and reflect on what we have achieved in the past five months.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The past five months has been the biggest exercise in redesigning jobs and reassessing the way we do things.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: When many of us were working from home, we took a while but managed to reach the new norm on work-life balance.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Additionally, some were able to provision more time to exercise.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What is also interesting about this new way of working was the fact that it did not matter whether the person working from home was a senior, someone in mid-life or a person with mobility challenges.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Nor did it matter that they came in at 8.00 am and working every single minute, including extended hours.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We found a way to remain equally productive in this new environment and maintain work-life balance.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: He lost his foot to diabetes and hence, he is immobile.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: He goes for dialysis every other evening from 7.00 pm to 11.00 pm.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Working from home, in front of the computer, he can be as productive as anyone of us.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And yet, he still finds it difficult to land a job.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must learn from this recent experience during the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must provide more equal employment opportunities for the seniors and less abled as well as caregivers seeking employment such that people like my resident would benefit from the inclusiveness of employment opportunities.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must not let the sacrifices we made during this crisis go to waste because within this crisis lies opportunities.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I am in support of the schemes from MOM to improve the employment and employability of mid-career professionals, seniors and persons with disability.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Government, businesses and citizens must work together to create equal opportunities for all.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But I would like to say a word of caution to this House.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While the past five months have taught us how to relook at our jobs and work remotely, this also implies that our professionals, managers and executives (PMEs) will become more exposed to global competition as PMEs need not be in Singapore to compete with the jobs required here.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For many of our PMEs, they have not stepped in office for the past five months.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we deal with that then when quotas are no longer relevant to protect our local PMEs in the global market?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Yesterday, Mr Leong Mun Wai and Assoc Prof Jamus Lim questioned numbers and figures of Employment Pass issuance, possibly implying that the control of quotas may protect our PMEs, to which Deputy Speaker Ms Jessica Tan asked, "What is the alternative number?" Coming from the industry and witnessing how the nature of PME jobs is rapidly evolving, I agree with the Deputy Speaker.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I urge this Chamber to consider that this is not an issue of just numbers and quotas, but the right questions this House should be debating for the future of Singapore are: how do we prepare our PMEs to be competitive in a globalised PME local market?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we prepare our PMEs for jobs not only in Singapore but a globalised firm beyond our shores?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we remain relevant to this world?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For we are a small red dot and can easily be forgotten.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This House cannot be distracted and let that happen; for if we do, we have failed the people and we have failed Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Which then brings us back to my first point.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must work effectively together as one Singapore to transform the economy and define our value proposition for Singapore to secure good, irreplaceable jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Faced with such challenges, we must remain positive and see this challenge as an opportunity to change the way we approach jobs and life.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must open our minds and willingly adapt to new norms, whether as individuals or as businesses.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We should use this opportunity to leverage on digitalisation and be open to accept new challenges.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Some examples of this taking place are in the retail industry.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We need to learn from this experience to adapt to new norms and change our expectations and ways of thinking.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Through digital platforms, small businesses can also rethink the way they do business.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: My favourite nasi rawon stall in Bedok now provides food delivery services to the whole of Singapore through third-party food delivery applications.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Last month, my family and I were able to order the nasi rawon from my in-laws' house in Choa Chu Kang.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The stall owner may not have been able to receive and fulfil orders from a location so far from his stall without a digital platform.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, I agree that this is not just the responsibility of workers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While workers retain and upgrade their skills, employers must also play their part.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For our youths, although these are challenging times, they must remain positive and stay focused on building the future, respond to this rapidly changing economic challenge and move forward to contribute to society and the nation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In English): In summary, Mr Speaker, Sir, the Government, businesses and citizens must work effectively together to transform the economy.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And as we sail through these stormy seas, we must not leave anyone behind.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: On that note, Mr Speaker, Sir, I support the Motion.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Last week, I was sworn in as a Member of Parliament at Old Parliament House.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Standing in that Chamber, taking my Oath of Allegiance, a sense of history overwhelmed me.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: I could not help but wonder how our founding leaders – Mr Lee Kuan Yew, Mr S Rajaratnam and Dr Goh Keng Swee – must have felt in the Chamber, the fate of Singapore in their hands, facing a bleak and uncertain future.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: They must have been in their late 30s or 40s, around my generation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: How did they feel inheriting a newly independent country facing a crisis of survival?

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: What went through their minds as they wrestled with the exigencies of their time?

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Defence, the environment, social cohesion, race and religion; where did they start and how did they start?

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: So, we stand here today as one House in this new Chamber, facing the proverbial crisis of our generation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: And we are again faced with the questions that confronted our forefathers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Our founding leaders found opportunities and hope in crisis by finding new ways of doing business, making tough decisions about race and religion and building a clean and green city.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: While this poses many unprecedented challenges, it also provides us with an opportunity to do things differently, to re-imagine and rebuild on the strong foundations of our forefathers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: I will touch on three such opportunities – the opportunity to protect, the opportunity to create and opportunity to include.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: COVID-19 forced the whole world to a pause.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Unintentionally, this pause gives us a chance to take a step back, examine and be deliberate as we move forward.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: One of the first and possibly the only direct positive outcome of COVID-19 is its impact on the environment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: The sound of planes was audibly replaced by the sounds of birds.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Nature was recovering as humanity stayed at home.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: And now, as we slowly try to unpause, we have the opportunity to better balance the sounds we would like to hear, to better protect and steward the environment for our children as we rebuild our economy.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: And now, we have an opportunity to do this, as Eli Sim of Palm View Primary School wrote in a published National Day essay.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Eli wrote that he hopes that Singaporeans will "learn to protect the precious forests, beaches and reservoir parks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: I hope everyone in Singapore will do his or her part to turn Singapore from a little Red Dot into a big Green Dot in future and be a role model for other countries." Indeed, as Eli says, Singapore must be a big Green Dot in a rapidly warming world.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Global warming has led to higher temperatures and rising sea levels.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We have seen the effects of this in the past right in my constituency where our low-lying Pek Kio and Cambridge Road neighbourhood experienced floods.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: An old flood gauge still sits at the corner of Carlisle and Cambridge Road, reminding us of our vulnerabilities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: One of my first priorities as Member of Parliament of Moulmein-Cairnhill was also to do with the environment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: I am sure many in this House also have been dealing with it – dengue.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We have dengue clusters across our country and even in my constituency, and we have set up a Dengue Taskforce to deal with it decisively.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Locally, we have also set up "Our Green Pek Kio", a popular ground-up initiative to drive awareness and action against climate change.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: It is a popular initiative with our residents, very young residents devoting their energy to transform their communities and neighbourhood.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Specific projects include climate change conversations, which speak about the impact of climate change or the relationship between climate change and our fragile environment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We have our "Bring Your Own Container" initiative which helps our residents reduce plastic waste.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: So, these are all ground-up initiatives we should encourage.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: But these are small steps which are slowly, certainly changing attitudes and practices on the ground, and we should do more of these.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: This pandemic has given us the chance to restructure our economy towards sustainable and green solutions, while remaining economically competitive.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: This reflects the Government's commitment to foster a greener economy and we must press on with these efforts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Protecting our environment is not just about protecting our lives but also securing our livelihoods, which brings me to my second opportunity, which is the opportunity to create.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: It has affected how we consume and how and where we work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: At this juncture, there are opportunities that we can create, find and must seize.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We must be nimble and use it to our advantage for our country and our people.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We must continue to strengthen Singapore's position regionally and globally, an oasis in a COVID-19 world – safe, stable, incorruptible and open to the world.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: These are traits that my former colleagues and I in the private sector, even pre-COVID-19, looked for when deciding where to situate billions of dollars of investments.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: When we draw up plans, our strategic investment plans, Singapore is but one of many countries we considered.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: If we and others decided to choose another investment destination, these jobs would have been situated elsewhere.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: And Singaporeans would certainly be poorer for it.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: So, we must continue to enhance this reputation, as investors look for a place they can trust, unleash their ideas, talent and capital.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: The result is innovation, investments and opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Of course, as my colleagues have said, we must ensure that Singaporeans are treated fairly.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Investments and opportunities can choose us or choose others.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: And they will be choosing a steady ship that is sea-worthy in a storm.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: The hon Mr Leon Perera referred to our economy yesterday as a Titanic.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Our economy has been going on for 55 years, not always smooth but always delivering opportunities for Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We have encountered many major problems and crises – the separation, the British withdrawal, the oil crisis, the 1985 recession, the Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS) pandemic, the Asian Financial Crisis and the Global Financial Crisis.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We have never encountered a problem we did not bounce back from stronger.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: This is the mettle of our country and our people.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Because we do not assume that we are invulnerable.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We are always worried, in fact, about our vulnerability, almost to the point of paranoia, planning for contingencies, learning and adapting.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We have been driving transformation and re-engineering our economy as we keep going.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: During calmer waters, there were voices in this Chamber telling us not to worry, that we can risk our stability and our Reserves.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: So, Mr Speaker, I would like to suggest that we are not quite the Titanic.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: As my colleague, Dr Tan See Leng, had mentioned a couple of days ago, we will live long and prosper.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We had a head start in the race and while we were preparing for a marathon, COVID-19 has forced us into a sprint.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Coming from the private sector, I look forward to working closely with our industry partners, as we step up our digitalisation efforts, supporting businesses, including family-run small and medium enterprises (SMEs).

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Three out of these four jobs are also highest in demand for remote employment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: This means that, as Mr Sharael Taha mentioned earlier, they can be performed anywhere in the world, regardless of their employer's location.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: On the one hand, it means anyone living outside of Singapore can get a job based in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: But on the other hand, it also means Singaporeans can apply for a job overseas while living at home right here in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Jobs are now increasingly not confined by geographical borders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We must prepare our people to compete on the global platform and take on these emerging jobs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Advising a mid-career administrator to take on a software engineering role is tough and difficult.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Upskilling through SkillsFuture can help but once you have acquired that skill, how do you then make that shift?

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: This is a question I have heard many times on the ground from jobseekers and I am sure many in this House have also heard from your residents as well.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: When I was at my previous company, my team and I partnered with the Institute of Technical Education (ITE) to help all of our ITE students showcase their skills on their digital resumes so that machine learning algorithms can help notify them of potential job matches in Singapore but also outside of Singapore, opening the market for our students.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: So, I look forward to working with SkillsFuture and MyCareersFuture teams to better prepare but also promote our people, so that they can better compete for jobs in Singapore and beyond.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: I remember taking on an unpaid internship when I was younger, and the experience and networks I gained stood me in good stead for the future jobs I would apply for and take on the future.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: So, we must continue to support Singaporeans young and old, transform themselves out of this crisis.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We either reinvent ourselves to meet the demands of the future or be relegated to the footnotes of the past.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: This brings me to the third opportunity, that is, the opportunity to include and to be more accepting of people with different backgrounds and journeys.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: I will speak on including Singaporeans of different abilities and emphasise two aspects.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: The first is something close to my heart and it is related to the ability to succeed and the stigma of failure.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: I had to repeat a year in junior college and even so, did not do well enough for my "A" level examinations to qualify for any local universities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: I remember feeling dejected, uncertain about my future and dealing with the societal stigma.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Even later on in my career, I faced other rejections, but along my journey, some took a chance on me, not really based on my grades but on my ability, reputation, values, work ethic and even volunteer experiences, and I will always be thankful for these chances.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: But Mr Speaker, we cannot just rely on these second chances.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We need to level the playing field with policies and norms that systematically empower people and give them the chance they need to prove themselves.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
