text: I remembered years ago, applying for a few mid-career jobs in Government and having to input my Primary School Leaving Examination (PSLE), "O" level and "A" level grades and the recruiters not valuing my experience in the Singapore Armed Forces (SAF) or even volunteer work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Conversely, the private sector firms I interviewed with, did not require those grades and they valued my experience even in the SAF and volunteer work among others in their hiring decisions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: It was an easy choice for me to choose which sector to join.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Work or volunteer experience and, most importantly, one's professional reputation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: The needle is indeed beginning to shift, and we are now seeing some exceptions to the old narratives of success.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: In her Address, Mdm President spoke about the work that schools and Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) and the Public Service Commission, employers and even political parties are doing in this regard.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: This is good progress, but we must make these exceptions the norm.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Embracing failure and giving second chances will help strengthen our social mobility and, at the same time, it will encourage people to be bold enough to try new things and potentially fail or innovate.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Most importantly, it will make us an even more inclusive society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Globally, as we all know, COVID-19 has caused untold mental and emotional stress, and revealed underlying biases and stigma to those suffering silently.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Mental ailments affect us regardless of age, background and where we live in the world.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We all know someone who struggles with mental ailments.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: I have friends and, indeed, immediate family members, struggling with the stigma brought about by schizophrenia, depression and other silent mental illness.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: In my constituency, we have had a number of suicides since COVID-19 started and I just visited the family of one of the seniors I knew, who sadly he took his own life.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: When I worked on cyber safety in the tech sector, I also saw first-hand the impact of social media abuse on social, emotional and mental health all over the world.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: I remember dealing with "live" suicide cases around the world and working furiously with my team and our partners to intervene.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: When we fall down, we suffer physical injury.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: If we can accept seeking help for our body, there is no reason why we cannot accept the same for our mind, and this is a point that my colleagues the hon Mr Don Wee and Mr Fahmi Aliman had mentioned in their own speeches.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: I have a friend, her name is Hui Xin, she was born visually impaired but has yet —

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: All we have to decide is what to do with the time that is given us." Mr Speaker, we cannot choose the moments in time —

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Just a second. "...we can choose how we define the moments of our time." Fifty-five years ago, our Pioneers found themselves in the moment of crisis, thrust into an independent nation, which was never expected to survive.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Heroic as they have may have been too, it is okay to be worried.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Years from now, in this very House, our children and future generations will judge us by how we have met this moment.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We hope they will judge us kindly, but that is for the future.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, I wish to thank Bukit Batok Single Member Constituency (SMC) constituents for giving me the privilege of representing them once again as their Member of Parliament (MP).

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I will do my best in this role.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Second, I wish to place on record, my own thanks and best wishes to MPs who have served in the Thirteenth session of Parliament and have stepped down.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I purposely did not use the word "retire" because I believe they will always continue to be involved in public service, in one way or another.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Last, I wish to congratulate the newly elected MPs from both sides of the House, the class of 2020, who just emerged from the political baptism of fire in the form of the General Elections.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I look forward to engaging them on issues that concern Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The winds are no longer in Singapore's favour.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: A small city-state, reliant on global trade and openness, we are now confronted with closed borders, not just due to COVID-19 but to rising nationalism and populism.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These are strong external forces over which we have no control.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In our country, there is a change towards a more contested and less conciliatory form of politics.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As MPs, we must get used to the rough and tumble of politics, become resilient and engage in robust and searing debate.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I, for one, have been drawn to the edge, and spoken out against what is acceptable and what is not.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: All of us in politics must grow the skin of a rhino as well as the heart of a lion.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These forces within Singapore are those we can influence, debate and in the end, decide upon.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: To help us in making this decision – on what kind of politics we want in Singapore – I thank the President for describing who we could be if we were to realise the best of ourselves.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: She calls us to find "common purpose" and to find strength in our diversity.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He said, "Our constitution does not copy the laws of neighbouring states; we are a pattern to others rather than imitators ourselves.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: A community of people who follow not only a written law, but a social and moral code, which, although unwritten, yet cannot be broken without acknowledged disgrace." How profound and relevant these words are to our circumstances, even after all these years!

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Knowing these two truths, the large changes in the world and in Singapore, and an aspiration of what we could be, the question remains.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Katherine Graham, the former publisher of The Washington Post, said, "News is what someone wants suppressed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Everything else is advertising." Agreement, collegiality and friendliness, all these make poor headlines.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The truth is most of the time, all MPs in this House agree.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Most times, the Workers' Party (WP) agree with the Bills introduced.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Such agreement is boring and almost never makes the news.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Even on the relatively controversial issue of Ministerial pay, the WP agreed with the outcome although the process in arriving at the decisions – "top down" compared to "bottom up" – were different.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Consensus is as boring as contestation is exciting.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But I see consensus as being perhaps the most important outcome of our work here.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, I do not think we should be perturbed if anyone were to say that Singapore’s parliamentary proceedings are boring.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Consensus and the negotiation of shared interests are key aspirations of our democracy.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But consensus is not a matter of sweeping hard truths under the carpet but a process of contestation, persuasion and resolution.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The outcome of this process – decisions and agreements – are sticky and legitimate.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This would require MPs to have a deeper understanding of the policy considerations behind the Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This has already been done by the New Zealand Parliament and has much to commend for itself.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In this way, MPs will be better prepared to debate the Bill during the Second Reading which happens on a separate occasion.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Today, the Second Reading of the Bill comprises largely Members of Parliament reading out their speeches when their turn comes.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They have little time to react to what has been said by their fellow Parliamentarians.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This also puts them up to public scrutiny while, at the same time, creating a more efficient process.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Having done this, time in this House should be spent on genuine debate and points of clarification or disagreement.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We will be able to avoid repetition of points that waste valuable time.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Minister should feel free to berate Members who try to debate without having read his speech.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Through this process, it would then be easier to assess the full diversity of views expressed by all Members, ascertain, as a matter of record, where the consensus lies and the points of disagreement, if any.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This information is already public and can be obtained today, but not without some effort, including manual counting.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I urge such records to be made available more easily with an online search platform.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There should also be a Parliamentary record of the outcome of Members’ proposals which the Minister has agreed to study.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Hansard is replete with examples of frontbenchers providing holding replies without the ability to check whether there have been any updates.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Members of the public reading the Hansard will not be able to tell whether the loop has been closed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We should also entrench a practice of expressly acknowledging MPs should their proposals be accepted by the Government.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This, too, should be accessible by members of the public.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Of course, it could take years for results to be seen.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But I am sure I speak for many others when I say it is far better late than never!

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I do not think this is a laborious task as there exists technology that can be harnessed to generate such reports.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: One may ask what has this got to do with Parliament?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They are also discerning, attentive, rational and fair.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They hold all of us up to high standards and see beyond political colours to the real impact we make on their lives.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Not only that, the proposals that I have suggested will ensure that our constituents have access to such information to make informed political choices and decisions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Pericles highlighted the importance of an informed citizenry in the same speech I quoted from.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He said: “Here, each individual is interested not only in his own affairs but in the affairs of the state as well.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Even those who are mostly occupied with their own business are extremely well-informed on general politics… We do not say that a man who takes no interest in politics is a man who minds his own business; we say he has no business here at all”.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: That was 2,500 years ago and this passage has not lost its relevance.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: How do we know if we have succeeded as a people?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The key test is this: are we proud of ourselves as a people, or do we hold what we have in contempt?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Do we want to build upon what we have done, or do we want to tear down our structures and start from scratch?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They are hard questions which we need to ask ourselves because they will define us, not just for this political term, but for the rest of our lifetime.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If we succeed, we would have built a democracy strong and imperturbable.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Our politics may not be full of sound and fury.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Chairs and fists may not fly in this Parliament – at least, I hope so – but our steady, even-keeled politics will ensure that we, as a nation, will be able to withstand fierce winds and firestorms and so secure our future.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For example, we value multiculturalism but the process of achieving it must no longer be a matter of quiet tolerance but of open debate.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There are many among us still not used to debate, let alone robust contest.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There are many in the silent majority who have views not expressed on social media, but held no less strongly for that.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There are those who prefer not to have to fight for our views but to hope that these views are self-evident.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But I wonder whether this hope is in vain.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Often, we take to “the streets” online, by setting up petitions on causes and let brute numbers speak in place of reason with no chance of reaching consensus or – using the words of the hon Leader of the Opposition – engaging in "reasoned conversation".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I think it is time that we – just like during Pericles' time – as a nation, set a social and moral code under which we should not flinch from actively defending our views and values and also understand an opposing point of view, and debate and discuss these views.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We should do so respectfully with an open mind, always with the hope that the other side has something to teach us.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In the end, whether we succeed in persuading one another to a common view or not, we would have built a stronger shared understanding and promoted mutual respect.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In the end, if we agree to something, it is an active, not a presumed, consent.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is a process that grants legitimacy to our actions and makes our decisions binding.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The rest of the book, we must write together, all of us in this House, and everyone outside.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Like all Singaporeans, our team has been adjusting to the "new normal" in the age of COVID-19, while getting to know our residents and communities in Sengkang and Buangkok.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Once again, we are touched that voters have taken a leap of faith in the Workers’ Party (WP) and are grateful for the opportunity to work together with everyone to make our home a better one for all.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In between setting up Sengkang Town Council and conducting our groundwork, we have also been privileged to receive warm welcomes from residents into their homes, into their preschools, Senior Activity Centres (SACs) and other parts of their community, and also from the various agencies and teams who work tirelessly to serve the residents of Sengkang.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Our friendships and partnerships have only just begun.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Today, I would like to talk about the Singapore that we hope to build together.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In the last two months, set against the difficult backdrop of the COVID-19 pandemic, I have seen much evidence of an "Engaged Singaporean", contrasting against the "Ugly Singaporean" label that we unfortunately sometimes hear being applied.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We have been struck, time and again, by the experience of seeing residents from all ages and all walks of life banding together, looking out for one another and coming together to look after the more vulnerable in our communities, so that no one is left behind.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Being engaged in our community is now a value that Singaporeans hold dear and they expect the Government to support this too.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We are also seeing the Engaged Singapore in the emergence of a more discerning electorate.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I often find myself being asked challenging questions about the WP team, about our work and our policy proposals.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Deeper, more thought-provoking questions are also being asked of us, of society and of the Government’s policies.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These two trends, taken together, mean that we must step up our own engagement with all levels of our community and keep discussing with and involving everyone in deciding Singapore’s future.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We must recognise that everyone has something to add to the conversation and there is no one way to do it.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Instead of relying solely on highly structured Singapore Conversations and Emerging Stronger Conversations, and Government-mandated or approved schemes, we should also look to more informal forums, such as coffeeshop walks, which the WP team has been doing.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We have found that the informal nature of these has a frankness, directness and immediacy which has been invaluable in shaping our understanding of the issues.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Our ground-up movements can also begin with a small spark and do not have to be only possible under the People’s Association (PA) and other "designated enablers".

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Instead, we have already seen some of these initiatives on the ground, with residents chipping in to start community gardens and small projects to look out for their neighbours.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We hope to add to this by organising our own hackathons and town halls within Buangkok and Sengkang and working in close partnership with various organisations and bodies on the ground to ensure that residents feel a greater sense of community and ownership.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The Government, too, must play its part in fostering an environment which enables a more Engaged Singapore – from our youth, workers and enterprises.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Instead of solely thinking about competition between groups, we must learn how to come together to find shared interests and resources while, also at the same time, learning to disagree respectfully when differences arise.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In this way, we can foster a stronger sense of solidarity, be it intergenerational, inter-societal or even inter-regional.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is not just about creating new schemes or another task force.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This will ensure that we do not have to expend too many resources on just keeping a proper track of them all.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It would also make for a much better user-centric experience.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The streamlining would also aid in tracking how effective and productive the schemes are.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: With this, I am glad that we all agree on the "Singapore for all" and that the Government has committed to strengthening social mobility and a society of opportunities for all.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This has been made worse by the ongoing pandemic which has exposed our weak points and hit vulnerable members of our society harder.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The number of residents who are struggling and require assistance appears to be increasing and we believe that this will worsen.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The expansion of programmes such as KidSTART and the increase in the Ministry of Education (MOE) Kindergartens is a good first step.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: How ever many programmes and task forces that we have, I believe that the real danger facing us now is the perception of the lack of social mobility and the presence of elitism.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: When I worked with my university's access schemes to encourage students from disadvantaged backgrounds to apply to top universities, we found that it was often a lack of belief and confidence that held many of these students back.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Often, they showed great potential but it would never cross their minds to even put in an application as they felt they stood no chance.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Even for those who do apply and succeed, this perception can also persist.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I remember once speaking to a volunteer who came from an under-privileged background after obtaining a polytechnic diploma.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: He was successful in gaining admission, a place to read law at one of our local universities and was about to start a training contract with a prestigious firm.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This reluctance to lean in is based on a certain perception of meritocracy, society's ossification, and something that we have to urgently address.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: One way is to encourage more existing university students and members of professions to take a more active role in speaking to and mentoring the next generation of applicants from disadvantaged backgrounds early on.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: They would be available to encourage them, to discuss their concerns and to guide these students through the recruitment or application process, and thus demystify some of the pre-existing notions that these students may have.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Other ways of doing so include smaller class sizes that the WP has been calling for and deeper engagement between schools beyond the bonding activities that are currently planned.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And we must remember that engagement is always two-way and there are always many things that we can learn from segments of society that are different from us.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Next, I would like to touch on sustainability.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is good that we now have a Ministry for Sustainability and the Environment (MSE).

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Climate change and environmental issues are important, but sustainability goes beyond this.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We must also ensure that Singapore is a socially, economically and demographically sustainable.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is a key factor in ensuring the sustainability of a harmonious society.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Instead of berating Singaporeans for being xenophobic, we should instead really listen to their concerns and try to understand why they feel this way.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We should also continue to involve more segments for our society, engage with them and empower them to take the lead in building our Singapore identity and future while, at the same time, involve more in integrating and welcoming newcomers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Economically, the COVID-19 pandemic has focused the world's attention on global supply chains and their vulnerability.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is good that the Government now plans to strengthen our food and essential supply chain security to ensure that we are not so much at the mercy of global forces that are mainly beyond our control.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But the shock to supply chains goes beyond just food and consumption and has severe repercussions for the structure of our economy.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is a commonly held view now that the recovery from the pandemic, together with increasingly complex geopolitical tensions, will further accentuate shifts from truly global supply chains to concentrate manufacturing and production being moved to the continents or regions of end consumers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Trade patterns will correspondingly be affected, and Singapore needs to be ready.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Environmental sustainability does not just have to mean costs and compliance.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Like my colleagues who spoke before me, I instead see many opportunities for Singapore here.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Some potential growth areas can include our move towards Industry and Supply Chain 4.0, by harnessing new technologies such as blockchain and Internet of Things, not only to develop expertise and helping companies and industries digitalise, but to use these new technologies to commit to a completely sustainable supply chain from source to final product.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Such expertise can be developed by our enterprises and be exported to other economies in the region, as we set the gold standard for what true sustainability means.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Similarly, I am pleased to hear of a stronger commitment to green financing and green tech which would also definitely benefit the environment.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This too can be a growth area for our economy going forward.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: There, older students become green ambassadors and are responsible for guiding their younger schoolmates towards green and sustainable practices.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is this type of youth- and community-led projects that we hope to be able to implement in Sengkang.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Our changing social fabric and demographics have accentuated the challenges facing our care infrastructure.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Having to adapt and thrive in a post-pandemic world has made it all the more important that we cohesively tackle this head-on.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Failure to do so would lead to widening health inequalities and increasing burdens on households already struggling to get by.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We must ensure that our care systems keep pace with evolving demands and that carers, especially those who undertake unpaid care and domestic work, are more visible and supported.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This will enable more seamless support for growing elderly population and people with long-term conditions who require care and support.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This means joining up hospital and community-based services for physical, mental and social care needs.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We would see greater efficiencies by breaking down barriers between services and focusing on growing our ability to provide care in our homes and communities.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As care needs are complex, a fully integrated system would also result in less confusion and stress among family members struggling to cobble together – a care plan for loved ones.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: There should also be room for more innovative care solutions and infrastructure, such as situating elder and childcare centres within the same facilities, which has the added benefit of facilitating intergenerational exchanges and solidarity while also tackling the pandemic of loneliness.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We must also consider our informal carers and integrate them into our care delivery system.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These are unpaid workers are unsung heroes, like my mother, who have devoted their entire lives to providing care for those who need it, be it their elderly parents, children, grandchildren or family and friends who have special needs.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Their contributions to our society are equal to any other wage-earning job, but unequally measured by traditional indicators of growth or value.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet, informal and unpaid carers often end up being vulnerable themselves, as their care responsibilities often have a detrimental impact on their own physical, mental and economic well-being.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We know that Singapore is not unique, and that unpaid work falls disproportionately on women.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In addition, in the most vulnerable segments of our society, children may also be called upon to undertake domestic labour by being solely responsible for the care of younger siblings and doing housework, often at the expense of their own education and childhood.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Such an approach immediately recognises this work as being of tremendous value to our society and will be a first step in changing how we think about such work and in understanding the profile of these workers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Having better visibility and measures of unpaid work also mean that it is easier for our policies to pay more attention to inequality.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The US does an American Time Use Survey every year since 2003.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Regular measurements immediately recognise the work as being of value to our society and also give us an idea of how our policies have implicit effects on such unpaid workers and how effective other policies are in addressing the problems that they face.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, countries such as Finland and New Zealand have made concerted efforts in measuring the scale of unpaid work which has resulted in policies that address the gender differential, for example, by providing adequate paternity leave.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Progress Singapore Party (PSP) believes that progress should always be accompanied by compassion and social safety nets play a big role in that.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: During difficult times, they are of even greater importance.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government has introduced temporary relief measures to help Singaporeans and businesses cope with COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While Government support is essential, we should continue to exercise financial prudence in the utilisation of our Reserves.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A significant portion of our relief packages goes towards the Job Support Scheme (JSS), which gives companies wage subsidies in an effort to keep jobs.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is a blanket measure that also pays companies that do not require any wage subsidy.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Most companies in certain industries, for example, the technology and financial sectors, continue to do well.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is too late to do anything about the JSS payments that have already been made, but we can impose conditions for the additional JSS recently announced.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: JSS for Singapore citizens and Permanent Residents (PRs) should also be differentiated to underline the difference in the Government’s duty and obligations to these two groups.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The first duty of any government is always to its own citizens.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Under such circumstances, most will take longer than three months to find new employment.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: An OCBC survey this year found that 70% of the respondents did not have enough savings to last more than six months.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In comparison, Government Reserves, though never revealed, is widely believed to be sufficient for at least eight to 10 years of Government expenditure.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If my figures are wrong, I would be happy to be corrected.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Otherwise, there will be much anxiety and pain in many families, which will in turn slow down our recovery.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Another way we can help families cope with the financial stress caused by COVID-19 is to allow CPF members who have lost their jobs to borrow from their own CPF accounts.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These loans can be repaid after finding new employment.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The CPF system works well for many Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, for those who are experiencing financial difficulties, it can be very frustrating to see their own savings trapped in an account they are unable to touch to help them ease their current situation.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The fact that these savings are being withheld for their future needs is scant comfort in the face of immediate distress.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Coupled with the later withdrawal age and steadily increasing minimum sum, it is fuelling dissatisfaction or even mistrust in our CPF system.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we can allow ways for CPF members to rely on these savings in times of need, for their CPF savings to be a source of financial security at all times and not just in the distant future, it will help build trust in the system and provide a peace of mind.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would also like to suggest that the Government explore the option of indexing CPF LIFE payments to inflation, with the inflation adjustments paid by Government.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To illustrate, if the monthly CPF LIFE payment is $1,000, and inflation is 2%, then the Government can top up the CPF LIFE payment by $20, which is 2% of $1,000.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Based on current retirement age and life expectancy, there are approximately 20 years of retirement life that we need to plan for.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our CPF system is designed for individuals to be responsible for their own retirement needs.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, certain things are beyond our control, despite our best efforts.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the economy and wages grow rapidly over the years, then the wages earned in the early years would be too low to cope with the cost levels in later years.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If inflation is rampant, then retirement funds saved up in the early years would be inadequate.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Twenty years after retirement is a long time, and retirees are at the mercy of economic forces over which they have no control.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, while we do not want to purely rely on our younger generations to support the older generations, to expect every individual to fully fund their own retirement may not be a feasible nor realistic proposition for many.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even in our earlier asset enhancement approach – the idea of owning an appreciating asset that we can then sell to fund our retirement – that involved a transfer of wealth from the younger generation to the older.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would therefore like to suggest that the Government explore a hybrid system, where individuals build up their own retirement sums as much as they can, and Government steps in after their retirement to help them cope with the effects of inflation.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But echo chambers exist everywhere, not just online.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I remember when I first entered politics and joined an alternative political party, I immediately experienced a marked change in my environment.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many with anti-establishment views sought me out to share their perspectives.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: People whom I already know previously became more forthcoming in criticising Government policies.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My environment became decidedly more critical of Government all of a sudden.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It took great effort to maintain my perspective, to remember that the world has not really changed all that much all of a sudden, but simply that people are telling me what they think I am interested in hearing.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If I experienced such being just an opposition candidate, how much more must it have been for someone who wields power?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And the only way we can mitigate this myopia is to acknowledge that these filters exist.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Like any investments, past performance is not a promise of future returns.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singaporeans are intelligent, believe in the core principles of justice, equality and the concept of sacrifice for the common good.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These are pillars of the Singapore identity that we should continue to uphold.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am confident that we can all find the courage to step out of our echo chambers, listen to all sides without prejudice, and act without pre-set agenda, so we can collectively build the next chapter of The Singapore Story.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: One that departs from our daily routine, one which calls for constant adaptation and one where we have no reference except to figure our own way to overcome the challenges brought about by COVID-19.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: When that time comes, we will ask ourselves what we have learnt, what can we improve structurally to prevent fallouts that we see today and what we can do better than before.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: All these are valid questions, and we should seek to find the answers together as a country.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: In Mdm President’s Address, she highlighted the challenges we faced from COVID-19 to global instability that resulted in the issues ahead of us as a nation and how we can evolve as a greater diversity of views emerge and aspirations of each generation change.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Some issues that now surfaced probably existed even before COVID-19, but quickly came under the spotlight when the natural order of things was disrupted, and everyone had to adjust to the new interim rules.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: For me, there are three areas which stood out, which I believe we firmly should have bolder change and further building of trust.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: First, the need to foster an open and collaborative spirit between the people, Government and the authorities.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: During COVID-19, we recognise the heavy dependence we had on essential workers who manage many aspects of our lives and keep our country going.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: During the circuit breaker, when landscaping works were unable to go ahead, the fields of grass and trees in the neighbourhood flourished abundantly.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: To some extent, some of my residents felt it is unkempt and must be immediately tidied once allowed to.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: If we take a look at the work nature of grass cutting and gardeners tending to designated plots of gardens, there is subtle differences and they probably hold the same level of injury if they were conducted in an unsafe manner.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Looking at the larger scheme of things, such community effort is in fact commendable.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: It is not only a good sign of heightened social responsibility.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: It also opens an opportunity for the SG Together movement and for people to feel the sense of belonging and that they are valued individuals in the community.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Another example is how projects involving collaboration can be lost in effectiveness when there is a lack of leadership and accountability.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Citing a case in my constituency when a neighbourhood school turned into single session, it further heightened the traffic congestions in the area during peak morning hours.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: In my view, we need to break some imaginary boundaries and enable more effective cross-collaboration between the agencies and the public to achieve an outcome with speed, simplicity and accountability.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Without which, any strategy will only remain a paper strategy when it cannot be executed with tangible ground impact.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Through this approach, we will develop the attitude of experimentation, learn and form new rules and build trust with each other at different stages.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: In time to come, we will better appreciate and value the fact that we do not simply ask for change but understand why the need for change and how exactly to change.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The idea is not new, and I understand that NTUC, too, has explored this as far back as the early 2000s.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: But in good times when employment rates are low, it is understandably hard for people to be willing to pay the premiums for such an insurance.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Of course, in a more volatile future, this idea should be revisited.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: But first, we need to understand what we seek to address with such an insurance.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: For example, unemployment that is arising from structural skills mismatches may not be easily insurable.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: So, what are the costs that are involved, whom to pay, the willingness of the parties to pay them and the trade-offs that are tied to the proposal, all these have to be studied carefully.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: We need to be honest and upfront to see if the insurance can be effective and to understand if the math really works.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: For a crisis like COVID-19, the negative impact on the economy and jobs are wide and deep.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: No one will quite have the answer now.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Will an insurance alone sufficiently cover the needs?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: It is even more relevant post-COVID-19 as the nature of jobs change, the movement patterns of people and businesses globally will deviate from the past and the geopolitical tensions will result in different business decisions.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: So, I suggest we look at solutions more holistically, on whether the proposed solutions aim to resolve the structural of fundamentals if they exist or whether they serve to complement and fill the gaps.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: At the end of the day, it is the people who need the help the most that we do not want to disadvantage.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: COVID-19 had brought out the best, the good and the ugly of individuals and society.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Social media had enabled actually many thoughtful	ground-up initiatives that strengthened the cohesion in our country during this crisis.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: But what truly made the difference are the people who stepped forward.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Those who had the heart and those who cared enough to make us realise there is always someone or some other families who need the help more than ourselves.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: These kind-hearted souls put their skills to good use for good causes and rallied their family, friends and also strangers to join them.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I am sure all of you felt the same as me – our hearts and spirits were uplifted each time we hear of all these heartwarming stories amid the daily numbers of infected COVID-19 patients being reported and announced.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The fallouts and negative situations that COVID-19 brought about had actually set us thinking about the larger meaning of life, family, aspirations and social needs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: For many of us, we have experienced so many firsts in 2020 that yet another first will not really surprise us.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Despite the rumblings, I think we pulled through it, with the hope that COVID-19 will soon pass.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: But if we look deeper in our society, there equally exists many individuals who can barely survive this episode or are further disadvantaged against their own situation pre-COVID-19.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Vulnerable seniors, families with little financial and support, individuals with special needs and people who are mentally challenged and stressed, these groups are particularly displaced in coping with the pressure and stress that is brought about by the external environment.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Any impact to their livelihood, their living conditions and financial status will almost leave them hanging by the thread.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: While state resources had always largely been channelled to assist the vulnerable and the low-income groups, have we considered what other safety nets they require or what may make them feel more comforted in knowing that they are not left behind as Singapore progresses?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I think Singaporeans are broadly shy to show open empathy and acts of goodness towards others.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: However, I am not surprised that many would have thought of helping someone else and doing something to ease their pain and burden if they are aware that someone is suffering or needs help.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Why do we not begin to allow these, what I call "silent voices" and acts of kindness to surface naturally and be cheered?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I say schools should acknowledge and reward children who look after other classmates, or co-help one another in areas to excel, depending on their own capabilities and taking care of others who are living in the community.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Such self-initiated actions from the students are far more valuable than Values-in-Action programmes that is initiated or school-organised.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: We need to inspire, not calculate or rank, the spirit of volunteerism and acts of kindness.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: A points system to measure the efforts of one's contributions is counter-intuitive and is fair.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: If a student in school constantly helps another child who has learning needs and make him or her feel less isolated or different from others, I would say this child has learnt beyond the books and school and is a person that we should celebrate and be exceptionally proud of.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: It is not the scores or ranks that he or she has achieved, but the values and ability to pay it forward that we should celebrate.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Over time, we will hear fewer conversations that children from disadvantaged families are unable to cope to have the same opportunities that they can afford tuition or extra classes.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: These children will have new starting lines and the ability to break the cycle of poverty as it begun on the day that their own classmates and those with more resources are already partnering them and helping them to get ahead in school or the community.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Our society will have a chance to become kinder and cherish every individual for who they are, the values they stand for and recognise that everyone's abilities are essential in this country.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I believe, by then, the stress that many face today will correspondingly reduce as our definition of success has more dimensions.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: It is multifaceted, it becomes less superficial and the fanatic race to a top single prize is no longer relevant as more people are champions of their own rights and causes.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: And lastly, Sir, how can we be more constructive moving forward?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Often, we hear feedback that we need to strengthen our Singapore identity as we evolve and even more so now getting through a crisis.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This begins from conversations between the Government and the citizens, which have been taking place over the years.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: While conversations and exchange of thoughts and ideas are a great starting point, I feel we need to deepen the understanding of perspectives that are raised and effectively listen without biasness from all parties.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The assumptions used and basis in which policies are being crafted can be more actively shared during public consultations.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: And whether feedback have been considered, the reasons for implementation or not and new circumstances that may arise from the point of feedback and implementation, we require more flexibility to adapt as we implement.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: If the flexibility required does not exist today due to a need for compliance, how then should we change?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The authorities to take the lead or the community and citizens to share the ownership of ideas and implementation?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: It is time we relook at our fundamentals and not take all feedback and requests as radical changes or criticisms.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Processes do exist but constantly require fine-tuning or removal if it is no longer relevant for the times.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: But what we should not forego is the need to widely consult and gather diverse views from groups, big or small, and robustly review all options available at each point of time.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, COVID-19 has brought the world into a critical time.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: People need to adapt and change in this uncertain environment.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Only by doing this can we survive the adversities.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: To learn and grow from these difficult times is critical for future crisis management and system reforms.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: In her Address, the President emphasised that the Government cannot overlook the diverse views and aspirations of each generation.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Only when the development is balanced and holistic can the country grow in a healthy manner.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I suggest that we make bolder reforms in the following areas.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: We need to break some old mindsets and boundaries, create more collaboration opportunities between the people and Government and enable more effective cross-collaboration and platforms, so that we can achieve an outcome with speed, simplicity and accountability.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Through this approach, we will develop the attitude of learning, form new rules, build trust with one another at each stage and create a Singapore in a new era.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Although the Government has always believed that we should provide more resources to the vulnerable and the low-income groups, have we thought about whether our existing safety nets are strong and suitable enough or have we considered the feelings of the recipients?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: After COVID-19, people will need not only financial but also emotional support.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Conversations and exchanges of thoughts and ideas between the Government and citizens over the years are a great starting point.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I think we need to deepen the understanding of perspectives raised and effectively listen from all sides.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: During public consultations, the assumptions used and the basis in which policies are being crafted can be more actively shared.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: We can then communicate with the people again after feedback has been considered and tell people the reasons for implementation and new circumstances that may arise.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: (In English): And in conclusion, Sir, this is an inevitable journey we must trod with determination and be inspired to share.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Regardless of circumstances, the leaders of the time have to demonstrate leadership in order to gain the trust and respect of fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: To build a more just, a more fair and a more equal society that is not just idealistic, but one where every Singaporean feels they are a valued member and a country that we can all proudly call our home.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Depending on context, it can be a tango, waltz, hip hop or line dance, but this coordination and partnership is exactly what we need to keep the society and country going.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I emphasised that we needed to become a more caring and compassionate society, that the heartware of this nation is just as important as the hardware and software.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My focus on a caring and compassionate society will continue in my second term as an MP.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I will speak up for a more equal and just society where discrimination becomes a thing of the past.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I will push hard for an inclusive society without labels.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Today, I will speak about how we can make our workplaces, schools and community more inclusive and how we need to remove the labels.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The first label we need to remove is that of being a mother so that we can have more inclusive workplaces. "I cannot find a job"; many Members would have heard this over and over again from our residents.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In this economy, we need to do our best to help Singaporeans find new jobs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But some will find it harder than others.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Last month, a female resident shared worrying concerns with me during my market walkabout.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She said, "I have just been to an interview.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The human resources (HR) personnel called me a 'mother' before they even called me by my name.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am in the line of recruitment and such stories are a dime a dozen.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My take is that the focus should be on whether we are up for the job.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It should not be on whether we are a mother and then assumed that we are not able to do the role." Was this a one-off incident or a more widespread problem?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I took to social media to do a public consultation and the results were alarming.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many more people shared about the bias they faced.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One lady said, "I have faced bias because my daughter was under the age of one when I was applying for a job with a large corporation and they said that while I was extremely qualified for the role, they needed someone who could travel at short notice and was therefore unencumbered.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Nobody asked me if I was willing to travel even with a young child.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They just assumed. 'Unencumbered' also gave the impression that my child is a burden." Another shared, "I have been asked in an interview before if I am planning to have a fourth kid in future.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The hiring manager said he is not a sexist but if he had to choose between me and a male candidate, he would choose a male candidate over me as I have three children." Even worse, another lady shared, "At a final interview with a local bank (with HR sitting in as well), they blatantly told me that I should not get pregnant if I were to take on the role." There are many more stories, and the numbers paint the same picture.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The unfortunate reality is that study after study show that at job interviews and at work, many women are second-guessed for no other reason than being a woman and a mother.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: MOM's figures also show that there is a problem.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our female labour force participation rate has stagnated for the past five years.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I know MOM is working hard to address this problem.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But Sir, one of the main causes of this problem is the assumption that women are supposed to take care of the children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I saw this problem first-hand when we built the Oasis Water Park in Nee Soon East, which opened just last year.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I made sure that the water park is family friendly.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We have a nursing room, a nappy-changing room, hot-water dispenser, child-friendly toilets, the whole deal.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But what I forgot was this gender stereotype.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The builders installed the nappy-changing room inside the women's toilet.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: When I asked them why, they said women are the ones who change nappies.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We managed to resolve this by installing a second nappy-changing station in the disabled toilet so men can help change nappies as well.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But these builders are not alone in thinking that only women take care of babies.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Such an attitude makes it harder for women everywhere.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: First, we need to legislate to make it illegal for employers to ask interviewees and employees about their marital status and whether they have or plan to have children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our Tripartite Alliance for Fair and Progressive Employment Practices (TAFEP) guidelines are clear and state that questions related to marital status and family responsibilities should not be asked during an interview.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But these guidelines are clearly not being followed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We really need to go beyond guidelines and follow the US, the UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Israel, China and Hong Kong to legislate and make it illegal for employers to ask about marital status and child-bearing plans when hiring.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, we need to legislate to give employees the right to access flexible work arrangements, which employers can turn down only for valid business-related reasons.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This pandemic has given fathers more opportunities to be involved with childcare at home.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It has enabled both men and women to feel they can contribute at work and home equally, and this change is good.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should legislate this flexibility to work from home, so that we can facilitate this change and help break the gender stereotype.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She was judged on her ability and competence, and I am privileged to have her in my team and for her to lead the passionate staff and volunteers in Nee Soon East.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our workplaces can be more inclusive, and our schools should as well.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point today is about more inclusive schools and the label of being a child with special needs or, a more progressive term which I will use, a differently abled child.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need to make sure that every school is also a good school for differently abled children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am glad we are abolishing streaming, which will encourage more social mixing across socioeconomic statuses in our schools.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need to work towards more social mixing with differently abled children, starting with our preschools.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I met a group of parents with differently abled children last month.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Their children were only five to six years old.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They shared their worries about what would happen to their children when they pass on.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will they be left alone and be abandoned by society?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They have to think so far ahead, and I can see how worried they are.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They are fighting hard for their children who have mild to moderate developmental delays, to enter a mainstream preschool because this helps their children integrate into society.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Ultimately, they hope that when daddy and mummy pass on, they would pass on knowing that their child would be respected and valued members of our society.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But the reality is they are finding it difficult to find preschools that accept their children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They face constant rejection, which does not help in the already difficult journey they are in.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Early Childhood Development Agency (ECDA) has worked hard to make our preschools more inclusive, and Mayor Denise Phua has spoken passionately about this.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Such specialists provide in-class support to the mainstream teachers to integrate the differently abled children in various group settings.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: By supporting the integration of differently abled children, I hope we can make schools more inclusive.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third and final point is about an inclusive community.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They put themselves at risk during this pandemic to keep us safe.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They are labelled as cleaners, and worse and ironically, the people who give us a clean environment to live, work and play in are sometimes labelled as "dirty".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Most of these cleaners are our migrant workers who do the work that many Singaporeans do not want to do.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As Senior Minister Shanmugaratnam said, "It is because of foreign workers that 57% of Singaporeans have been able to become PMETs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They clean Singapore, they build our Housing and Development Board (HDB) flats, they handle our waste management, they form the base of our economy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And therefore, they are helping us build our prosperity."  Sir, last year, I joined our Nee Soon Town Council cleaner, Hanif, on his trip back to Bangladesh to welcome his first child into the world.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our plans failed slightly as his wife delivered early and he missed the chance to be there when his son was born.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He was already absent for the whole pregnancy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In Bangladesh, I saw first-hand how difficult it is for our cleaners to be so far away from home and so far from their loved ones.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It was both a heartwarming and heartbreaking experience.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In Bangladesh, I saw how much his family loved him and missed him.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Hanif's wife, Tania, said, "Sometimes, I think, if he can come back to Bangladesh, how amazing that would be.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I feel sad and I miss his presence.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, reality is very tough, so he has to work hard abroad for us.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Obviously, I feel sad for my son, that he will be deprived of his dad's love and affection." When asked how he felt knowing that his son may not see him for a long time, Hanif replied, "We are poor people and to survive we have to make these kinds of sacrifices."  During that trip, I also invited all our Nee Soon East cleaners' families to lunch in Dhaka.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We arranged for them to do a video call with their loved ones in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It was heartbreaking to see them cry as they spoke to their husbands, fathers, brothers and sons.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I met our cleaner's, Mazibur, daughter who was seven years old and he has never met her.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I met Newton's daughter who was about a year old, and she too has never met her father, and it will be years before she meets him.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To be honest, I felt bad that their daughters had met me before meeting their fathers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As a father, I cannot imagine not being able to meet my daughters for so many years.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should show a lot more appreciation to our cleaners for the work they do for us.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I learnt this from Mr Speaker, when I was serving with him in Kembangan-Chai Chee.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We bring them to explore Singapore to see a different side of our beautiful country that they seldom get to see.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I see how much they value these outings.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many do video calls during the outing to share the experience with their families back in Bangladesh.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In Nee Soon East, we have placed posters at every block to share who the cleaner for that block is and also their personal stories.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope that residents will see them not just as a cleaner but as a person.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In Nee Soon East, we had a beautiful barbecue party hosted by Hanif.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Together with our cleaners and residents, we celebrated the birth of his son.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These labels should not define who we are or our place in society.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For the past three years in this House, I shared the story of a Singaporean sex worker.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Her story was in my speeches on the Women's Charter (Amendment) Bill and the Massage Establishments Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I shared that, "She was only 19 years old when she became a sex worker and did this for four years.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Her parents divorced when she was five years old and both parents did not want her.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She was left with her grandmother who raised her.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For her entire childhood, she was constantly reminded that she had no parents.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I cannot imagine the impact that had on a young child.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She did not do well in her studies and could not get into a polytechnic.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She tried to enroll in a private polytechnic but did not have enough money to pay the tuition fees.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She tried to get a bank loan but failed, as she could not find a guarantor.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Not knowing where else to go for help, she ultimately entered the sex trade to fund her education."  Many have discriminated against her as she was labelled a sex worker.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If we remove the label and give her a chance, help her like any other person rather than discriminate against her, then like any person, she can succeed as well.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I was invited to use a giraffe sculpture as a canvas to "share about any cause you would like to champion for or any related thoughts or ideas".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Sometimes, we need to view the world through the eyes of our children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: So, instead of me painting the giraffe, my daughter painted it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Here is the description of the giraffe she painted that was published: "My five-year-old daughter Ella painted this.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She views the world as a rainbow with colours mixing.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There is beauty in looking at the world through the eyes of our children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They view the world without labels we adults created.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Ella has been with me to help refugees, cleaners and many others.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To her, they are not refugees or cleaners but simply, her friends.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Children remind us that there is no us or them, only us, one human family connected in ways we sometimes forget."  Sir, I am often asked which animal I resemble the most and I have always replied "a housefly", mostly because a housefly is very persistent and never gives up.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Or, as my sister would say, I am as irritating as a housefly.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Some people now say I look like a housefly, so I am glad and very humbled that Mayor Denise Phua has named me a "Giraffe Hero" for sticking my neck out for the common good.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A giraffe is much cuter than a housefly and so I am very glad to reply to people now that I resemble a giraffe.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I will continue to fight for a more caring, compassionate and inclusive society, and one with a strong heart-ware.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We are still in the midst of a pandemic, and it is our hardware and software that will save lives and livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But it is about being inclusive and our heartware that will determine whether we will get through this pandemic as One People, One Nation and One Singapore.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I rise in support of the Motion to thank the President for her Address.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: There are three key questions I would like to raise for this House to consider, as well as for our citizens to reflect on and contribute their views to, to help shape our policies.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: My first question: how do we maintain the fighting spirit of our people, maintain our unity, even as the loss of jobs puts increased pressures on families and make people feel like they have to compete for resources?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I think the best way to do this is to change the way we think about welfare and social assistance.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We will need to provide strong social support to those hit hard.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: This will require our social policies to be more generous.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: It also gives us an opportunity to evolve the existing narrative and notion of welfare recipients beyond having to be deserving and needy.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: COVID-19 has shown us that anyone can fall onto hard times.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: With global trade and economy being so volatile, we can now clearly see that the willingness to work is not the main factor that makes someone seek help.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
