text: More often than not, people seek welfare because of many forces outside of their control.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   The Government's schemes are meant to help the people but, for some, the application process can be very frustrating.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Many low-income earners cannot qualify just because they have Medisave account arrears.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Is it because the schemes are not designed thoroughly or because public officers lack empathy?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I do not think the problem lies with the frontline officers because their job is to do what is instructed to do.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: The Government should study where the problem lies and avoid unnecessary conflicts.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: What is meant to be “sending coals amid snow” should not end up becoming “adding frost to snow” and damaging the morale of public officers at the same time.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: (In English): While we support those who have lost their jobs with the usual practicalities of upskilling and employment matching, it is imperative that we uphold their dignity.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We must maintain their self-esteem and we must upkeep their morale.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Heng affirmed this in his speech on Monday.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Hence, let us remove the shame of people feeling that if they resort to welfare, that it is because they did not try hard enough.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: If COVID-19 cannot convince us to be more compassionate and less judgmental in the way we help and support our people, what else can?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We can make more of such improvements to help reduce the anxiety, stress and erosion of self-esteem that affects many recipients of support.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: As my colleague, Mr Seah Kian Peng, also advocated, let us err on the side of being kind.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I am certain our social assistance policies were designed to get people out of poverty and not keep them poor.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: But did we unintentionally create a perverse situation for people to stay poor because the system forces them to show us how needy they are before we can help them?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: The human spirit is intangible, and it is so important to preserve, especially in such difficult times.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: The cost to rebuild it is far too high.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: My charity, Daughters Of Tomorrow, was set up to help low-income women from challenged families rebuild their confidence in order to step back into the workforce.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We intervene at the right time with the right measures without judging them.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: All these help us rebuild the spirits and revive the potential of hundreds of women.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: It might sound like semantics, but the choice of words can remove unhelpful labels and refocus our social assistance approach towards removing the barriers faced by these families who struggled.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I also urge the relevant Ministries to create funding for individuals and social service agencies to reward effort and progress.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We should reward individuals and families for making progress.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We should also reward social service workers and officers for successfully enabling these families.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I believe we can change the vicious cycle to a virtuous cycle.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: With compassion, empathy and the correct key performance indicators, we can lift the plight and spirits of our people, one person, one family at a time.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: My second question: how do we rebuild our economy to ensure equity while balancing fiscal sustainability?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I believe the best solution lies in better harnessing the potential of women and allowing their talents and wisdom to shine, and to contribute better by reducing work-care conflict.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: During the General Election, I made a promise to my constituents that I would look after the sandwich generation of families and ease their stresses and burdens.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I, myself, am a self-confessed millennial woman guilty of not choosing marriage and childbirth, not because I do not wish to, but because I am hesitant to.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I grew up watching my mother be a tireless and self-sacrificing full-time homemaker.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: This gave me the unchangeable impression that a mother is someone who willingly takes on all chores in the household related to cooking, cleaning and taking care of the health and happiness of everyone in the family.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: As a 38-year-old woman with a career I find immense fulfilment in, there is no way I could see myself being a mother the same way mine was while continuing to advance in my personal and professional aspirations.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Despite more and more women graduating from university with a degree, we still face the pressures and penalties that come with being a wife and a mother.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: All over the world, once a woman bears children and stays home to rear them for a few years, there is little chance, if ever, that her income can catch up again with the level she otherwise could have gotten.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: When her parents get old, again, she may have to give up her job to look after them, especially if they are in ill health.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: This then means she ends up poor in her old age, because she has not made enough income during her productive years to ensure that she can retire well.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: As we already know, the low fertility rate in Singapore has serious implications for our society.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: The lack of caregiving support, opportunity costs in career for women, as well as the increased stress in their lives are all barriers to women having more babies.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: As my colleague, Mr Louis Ng, spoke passionately about, if we do not remove these barriers, we have little hope of reversing the trend of low birth rate.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I look forward to discussing and debating these strategies in future Sittings.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We need MOM, MSF, the Ministry of Health (MOH) and the Ministry of Finance (MOF), as well as domain experts from civil society working in gender as well as the care sectors to come together.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We need to ensure that the complex interconnections among employment, caregiving, domestic labour, healthcare and retirement adequacy are considered holistically from a woman’s life journey approach.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I believe if the Government also works with social innovators and entrepreneurs and focus on enabling women, we could see the rise of a Care Economy that creates economic activity and new jobs for our citizens, both men and women, while serving the care needs of our ageing population.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: The third and final question that Singapore needs to address is this: how do we cater for the aspirations of the younger generation while meeting the desires of our older generation for social cohesion, peace and stability?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: To do this, we first need to step out beyond ideologies, theories and frameworks, away from emails and keyboards, and into people’s lives, to truly understand how they feel and why they feel the way they do.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: My colleague, Ms Yeo Wan Ling, spoke about knowing people for the stories behind the faces and the stories behind their challenges.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Related to gender and poverty is a larger conversation about discrimination in our society.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: For those of us who are privileged, whether by race, class, gender or education, we may not always notice that it exists.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: However, for those without such privileges, I have come to understand that it is ever present, seeping into their daily lives.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Discrimination is real to minority communities, not just in daily life and social interactions, but also from people in positions of power over their lives.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Minority communities have spoken up again, with some in the majority listening with an understanding ear, but some not.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: As I, myself, am learning right now, sometimes I say and do things that come across as unwittingly hurtful to our minority communities.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: In the past, I know that I have held and maybe even perpetuated some of these biases without knowing better, but I am trying to learn from my mistakes and be better.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I invite all of us to reflect on what are the biases that we have inherited from the society around us and how do such biases affect the way we speak to and treat our friends and fellow countrymen and women who are in the minority.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Did we behave in ways that have been insensitive and unmindful that we should remedy?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Outside of these, I would also like to extend a challenge to those who are passionate about working on these issues.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Can we make our activism and advocacy more accessible?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Can we explain concepts like microaggressions and intersectionality to our elders?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Can we include our parents and grandparents in these discussions about equality and justice?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I encourage our youths and others who are passionate to step up on these issues, not just on social media, but also in real life.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Real life is where we build strong relationships.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: And we need strong relationships in order to have these difficult conversations.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: There are those who may not have the finesse to talk about such topics with the level of sensitivity that would be ideal.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: There are those who are well-informed and well-researched but may sometimes be hindered by passion and inexperience.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I see and I empathise that our leaders bear the weight of Singapore on their shoulders.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: They bear the burden of protecting us, protecting our security, and protecting our stability.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: They have dedicated much of their lives and uncountable sleepless nights for the good of our country.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: It is a heavy cross to bear, but there is no need to bear it alone.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: The youths of today are passionate because they care so much for Singapore.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Many have good ideas, and many are capable.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: It is now our cross to bear too.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I have confidence that if we balance circumspection from the youths, with guidance and mentorship from the elders, we will find a sweet spot.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: A sweet spot of unity, cohesion and shared purpose together, across generations.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I look forward to an awakening and participation of our people that stems from compassion and empathy and future discourse that roots itself in mutual respect.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 3.30 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 3.14 pm until 3.30 pm.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This year, we opened Parliament sooner than we usually do after a General Election, because we have urgent business dealing with COVID-19 and the economy.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: COVID-19 has caused a massive upheaval in our lives.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: After eight gruelling months, we have stabilised our situation.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But it has taken a tremendous effort to get here.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: From the very beginning when COVID-19 hit us, our overriding consideration was to protect the lives of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Many countries talked about flattening the curve, the infection curve, of letting the disease burn through the population until herd immunity developed.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But that would have meant many Singaporeans getting ill and perhaps thousands dying, especially the old and vulnerable.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We were determined, right from the very beginning, not to go down that route.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We did our utmost to contain the outbreak and keep Singaporeans safe.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We built up contact tracing and testing capabilities so that once we detected a new case or cluster, we could immediately isolate them and their close contacts, before they could infect others.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We set up temporary community care and isolation facilities at the Singapore Expo, Changi Exhibition Centre, PSA Tanjong Pagar Terminal, old schools and SAF camps, where we could accommodate and treat patients with mild symptoms.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Implementing the circuit breaker in April was a very big move.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We knew that it would cause extensive social and economic disruption, and demand major sacrifices from Singaporeans.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But we decided, Cabinet decided, we had to go ahead, to slow down the infection rate and get things firmly under control and buy us time.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Fortunately, we timed the circuit breaker right and luckily, it worked.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Each of these operations was huge, and all of them had to be done in parallel.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Thanks to the heroic efforts of many unsung heroes, working quietly behind the scenes, we have got here today.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Judging by the health outcomes, we have done well, so far.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: New infections in our community are down to just a handful a day.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This has given us the confidence to re-open our economy and society – gradually and carefully.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Of course, our COVID-19 response was not without shortcomings.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: COVID-19 has severely tested every government in the world.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: No country has been perfect in its pandemic response.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Some have done better than the rest, like South Korea and New Zealand.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But even for them, the fight continues, with new cases surfacing as they open up again.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: With hindsight, we would certainly have done some things differently.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: For example, I wish we had known earlier that people with COVID-19 were infectious even when they were asymptomatic, did not show any symptoms.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Then, when we brought Singaporeans back home from all over the world in March, we would have quarantined all of them earlier, instead of only those returning from certain countries, so that the virus did not spread to their family members, or their colleagues and friends.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And we would have tested all of them before releasing them from quarantine, whether or not they showed any symptoms, instead of assuming that no symptoms meant no infection.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We would also have recommended that everyone to wear face masks sooner than we did.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But at the time, we took the best available scientific advice.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Once the World Health Organization (WHO) recognised that asymptomatic transmission was a major problem, we changed our policy and distributed face masks to everyone.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We would also have acted more aggressively and sooner on the migrant worker dormitories.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We knew that communal living in the dorms posed an infection risk.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Communal living in any form poses risks – onboard ships, in army camps, in student hostels and nursing homes.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But then, bigger clusters broke out in the dorms, which threatened to overwhelm us.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We must learn from these errors and do better the next time.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But in the fog of war, it is not possible always to make the perfect decisions.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The key is to watch things closely, learn from experience and adapt our responses promptly as new information emerges and as the situation changes.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Because of the scale and complexity of our operations, there have inevitably been some rough edges.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: For example, now that we have cleared the dorms, we are helping the migrant workers resume work, especially in the construction industry.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But this has to be done safely because the risk of cases re-emerging is still there.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I know we have made things more difficult and burdensome for employers, especially the contractors and sub-contractors.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They have found it frustrating to deal with all the new rules, approvals and inspections, even as they try to get their businesses up and running again.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But I hope they understand that we are doing our best to smooth things out for them and doing all this in order to keep our people safe.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is better that we make these measures work and get businesses to operate safely, than to suffer a new outbreak and have to shut down again.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Overall, we have been able to deal with COVID-19 only because the Public Service, the political leadership, our businesses and the Singapore public have worked closely together, each doing their part and more.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In the Public Service, the officials, Ministries and agencies have worked tirelessly, building new capabilities on the fly and stepping up to do things way beyond their normal scale or scope.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Without a high quality, dedicated and adaptable Public Service, we could not have carried out all these major operations.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The political leadership has also played a role to define the priorities, to make the major decisions, to direct the civil servants implementing the decisions, win public support for these measures and take responsibility for them, for example, whether to impose a circuit breaker, what activities to restrict, which businesses to keep open, whether to close schools or reopen them.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We explained these decisions to the public at frequent press conferences, video addresses and in Parliament, so that Singaporeans understood what we were trying to do and what each of us individually had to do.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: These are the responsibilities of the Ministers and ultimately of the Prime Minister and the Cabinet.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Without political leadership, the Public Service alone could not have done their job.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Businesses came forward, also, to do sterling National Service.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They put their people to work furiously on solutions, often going well beyond their business mission.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They set up mask production lines, constructed Community Care Facilities, built up testing capacity, scoured the world for test equipment, test kits and reagents, and designed booths to swab patients safely and much more.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Their contributions were a vital complement to what the Government agencies were doing.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Our COVID-19 response also depended critically on Singaporeans working together and giving the Government their trust and support.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They understood the need for tough and painful measures and complied with them.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Many Singaporeans' lives have been severely affected, but they have borne the difficulties calmly and stoically.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They had confidence that the Government would see them through the crisis and beyond.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Many volunteered to take part in the COVID-19 operations, sometimes on the frontline, and also in the community efforts to help others through these tough times.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I am very grateful for their cooperation and support.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Their support will remain crucial as we continue the fight to keep Singaporeans safe.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The situation is currently stable, but we must not let our guard down.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I recently received an email from a university student.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He complained that our reaction to COVID-19 was “one of the greatest overreactions to a public health issue”.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: As proof, he pointed out that our hospital systems were far from overwhelmed.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He said that, instead, we should let young Singaporeans “do us the service of achieving herd immunity”.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: You only have to look at the situation in other cities that have let this happen to imagine how this could have turned out for us.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: What has changed is that we have taken measures and we have built up our capabilities to contain it.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Just look at Europe and many other places in the world.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: COVID-19 will not be our last public health crisis.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: After SARS, we knew that, sooner or later, another novel pathogen would appear and pose a threat to humanity.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We had H1N1, which was highly infectious but, fortunately, it turned out to be relatively mild.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Then there has been Ebola, but we escaped it because it was confined mainly in some African countries.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Next, there was the Middle East Respiratory Syndrome (MERS) but, fortunately, that is not so transmissible and we have been lucky not to have had any cases here, although the Koreans had.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They had an outbreak, they learned painful lessons from it and the lessons served them well when COVID-19 came.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Scientists talk about Disease X being overdue – a new disease, unknown, that is highly infectious, deadly and mutates easily.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, when COVID-19 appeared, people asked whether this was Disease X.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: COVID-19 has been a disaster for the world, but it is not Disease X.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, we had better learn from COVID-19 on how to deal with a pandemic and be as ready as we can when a worse one befalls us.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We should build up our resilience, instincts and preparations, so that when Disease X comes one day, we will be prepared.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Even as we manage the immediate situation, we must look forward and prepare for life after COVID-19.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: As the President said in her speech, we are headed into a very different world.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: What must we rethink and reinvent, so that Singapore can continue to be successful in this brave new world?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Members have touched on several topics already in this debate, including social safety nets and foreign worker policies.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In times of economic uncertainty, it is natural for people to be anxious about these two issues.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, let me give Members my perspective and explain to Singaporeans what we intend to do in these areas.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Then, I will talk about the future of politics in Singapore, which underpins how we will manage and respond to all these different issues.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Social safety nets are there to protect the vulnerable in our society and ensure that everyone has full access to opportunities to improve our lives.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They also give people the confidence and assurance that if some bad luck trips them up in life, society will be there to break their fall and help them pick themselves up again.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In our early decades of nationhood, we did not need extensive social safety nets.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The economy was buoyant and unemployment after the first few years was very low.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If you lost your job, a new one was just around the corner.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In fact, sometimes, people were happy to be retrenched because you collected your retrenchment benefits and then you went into a new job straightaway; get paid twice.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, we invested heavily in our social infrastructure – universal education, basic healthcare and public housing.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This improved everyone’s standard of living and allowed all to benefit from the country’s progress.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: More importantly, it levelled everyone up, giving them the means to improve their lives through their own efforts.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Now, we have moved into a different phase of development.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Our economy is maturing and incomes are growing less rapidly.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: There is a higher premium on specialised skills and education.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: As a result, when someone loses his job, especially as a mature worker, it is harder for them to move to another job, especially across different sectors.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: These schemes, and many others, are targeted at the lower-income and those who have fallen on hard times.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They supplement their wages and CPF contributions, so that the recipients gain both current income and also retirement security.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: As we expanded our social programmes, we have also extended the coverage of other schemes and subsidies beyond the lower income, to include middle-income households, too, for example, with preschool subsidies, and bursaries for universities and other post-secondary institutions, which almost all our students now attend.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We also gave special support to our Pioneer and Merdeka Generations to help them see through their retirement years.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: These are emergency measures; they are crucial for now.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We have to start thinking about what comes after them and about the level of social support we will return to after COVID-19 is over.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In the "new normal", we fully expect more economic uncertainty and turbulence.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And the longer-term trends of an ageing population and rising healthcare costs remain unchanged.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, we will certainly need to strengthen social support for our people, during and after their working lives.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Several ideas have been raised, including in this House, on this debate.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The Government is not ideologically opposed to any proposed solution.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Our approach has always been pragmatic and empirical; make the best use of our resources to meet the needs of different groups in our society, in a targeted manner.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Because if we help everyone equally, then we are not giving more help to those who need it most.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Having been in the workforce for longer, they tend to draw higher salaries than younger workers, but their skills may be less current.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If they lose their jobs, they find it harder to find another similar job, particularly at the same pay, so they are at greater risk of long-term unemployment.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Solutions, like unemployment insurance, can offer older workers transient relief, at best.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But retraining and upskilling older workers will enable employers to continue finding value in them and to be less likely to make them redundant.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And if the older worker does get retrenched, with these skills, he or she can find a new job more readily.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This is a structural solution that helps older workers get their careers back on track and feel that he is making a worthwhile contribution.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They are the most vulnerable ones in our workforce.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They worry about the day-to-day and how to make ends meet.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They often feel stuck in their jobs while others around them seem to be doing better.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We need to support them to improve their lives, so that they can catch up and narrow the gap with the rest of society.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The Workfare Income Supplement has made a material difference to them, and we have been enhancing the Workfare scheme every now and again.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In this downturn, we made a special payment under the Workfare scheme because we want to help those who are most in need and we do not want to put the burden on employers.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The Progressive Wage Model has also helped them and we will extend the Progressive Wage Model, as you have heard from Minister Josephine Teo yesterday, to more sectors over time.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The Government’s efforts, supported by unions and employers, have worked.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We need to do more, and we are ready to do more.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The question is: what more will we need to do and what is the best way to do it?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We should take some time to assess the landscape after COVID-19 to see how things unfold and what specific problems develop.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We must keep an open mind as we build and improve on the systems we have and consider solutions that can work in our context.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is not just floating ideas like minimum wage or unemployment insurance, but assessing their impact carefully.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Who wins and who loses within the workforce?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: How will our SMEs or the public be affected?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We must identify pragmatic solutions which will make a real and sustainable difference and give people justified assurance that, when they need help, they will get the help that is relevant to them.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And it must not create new problems in the process, for example, by eroding our spirit of self-reliance.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: One permanent imperative as we think about new schemes is to keep our programmes fiscally sustainable.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: When our founding generation were building up our Reserves, they never asked themselves whether they had too much savings.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We were in our early days of nationhood.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Things were so uncertain, and no one knew what the next day would bring.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But it was never a question of how much Reserves would be enough.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The question was whether we could steadily squirrel away a bit more in our Reserves, year after year, decade after decade, as protection for a rainy day.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: After several generations of frugal prudence, we have built up significant Reserves.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And because we have taken such an approach consistently, decade after decade, in this enormous monster storm, we have been able to draw on past Reserves and fund our essential Budget packages and help people on a very big scale.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The opposition says, "Show me how much we have in the reserves before I decide whether I support your Budget and tax plans.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Let us have a look at the money".

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Basically, they are asking, "I have something in the bank already.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: How much of that can I touch?" This was not the attitude of our forefathers, the founders who were building for the future, but the attitude of inheritors who think they have come into a fortune and want to consume the fruits of their predecessors' labours.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: How much Reserves are enough or too much?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: There can be no good answer to this question.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We have no way to tell what may hit us from out of the blue.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In January, before COVID-19, MOF was preparing Budget 2020, and we were quite confident.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We have had to draw heavily on past Reserves to fund four, five Budget packages and explain to the President why this has been necessary.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Therefore, we should not think of ourselves as inheritors spending what we have been lucky enough to be endowed with.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Rather, we should take the attitude of founders, even though we may be the third, fourth or fifth generation in reality, but we should think of ourselves as founders for the future generations.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In Chinese, it sounds better because it is a coffin fund.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Every year, we live within our means and whenever we are able to, we add a bit more to the rainy-day fund, to make ourselves a bit more secure for when it really pours.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And that is the way to build Singapore for the long term and secure the future for our children and grandchildren.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: A second area that we will review is our foreign worker and work pass policies.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Minister Josephine Teo spoke about these yesterday, but I want to give my take on this too.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But in an economic downturn, this issue becomes sharper.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is the case not just in Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: All around the world, anti-foreigner sentiment is on the rise because people are feeling worried and insecure about their futures.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Many Singaporeans are feeling anxious and pressured about their jobs.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Their sense that foreigners are competing with them for jobs is palpable.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Some feel unfairly treated when they see foreigners replacing them or taking up good jobs ahead of them.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: To grow our economy, we have no choice but to top up with foreign workers and work pass holders.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And yet, we cannot throw open our doors, just throw open our doors, nor have we done so.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We only have three and a half million Singaporean Citizens and half a million Permanent Residents.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In Southeast Asia, there are 650 million people.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In Asia, China and India alone add up to nearly three thousand million people.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: All can potentially come in, many would love to come.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And that is why we have our foreign worker policies.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They help us control the inflow and ultimately, ensure that the foreign workers who do come in add to the workforce in Singapore, rather than substitute for them and benefit Singaporeans rather than hurting them.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: How we control the flow depends on the type of foreign worker.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: At the lower levels, we have got work permits and we use a mix of levies and quotas – we call them dependency ratios – to directly control their price and quantity.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is a rough and ready approach, but it helps us deal with the large numbers and limit them effectively.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In the middle levels, we have the S Pass.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is not just a matter of numbers, but we also want to look at the quality because the S Pass are competing with people who are graduating from our polytechnics, diploma holders and slightly above that, and we want to make sure that there is a balance.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, the S Pass still has levies and quotas, but we also impose other requirements on minimum salary and qualifications.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Then for the upper levels, the professionals, managers, executives and technicians (PMETs), we have the Employment Pass (EP).

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Here, the key issue is about controlling the quality and making sure the people we bring in are those who are able to contribute to Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, we have been using salary benchmarks as a proxy, along with other qualifying criteria.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: While the perception of foreign competition is sharper during this downturn, actually, both the EP and S Pass holders have been coming down since COVID-19 this year.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But we still have to make adjustments to our work pass schemes because there is now more slack in the job market but also because, over time, the education levels, capabilities and incomes of our local workforce have gone up.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: More Singaporeans are now ready and available to take up PMET jobs.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And the purpose of the EP scheme is to top up at the higher end of these PMET jobs.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Therefore, we need to tighten the EP qualifying criteria.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And that is why, at the lower levels of the EP holders, the proportion of Singaporeans is higher and at the higher levels, the proportion of Singaporeans is slightly lower because we are deliberately bringing in EP holders who are at the higher level and can contribute to us.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We have to pay attention to market conditions and adjust at the right pace, but this is the correct long-term direction.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But I know Singaporeans are not just concerned with the macro overall numbers but also, at the micro individual level, they are also concerned about fair treatment, that Singaporeans are being considered fairly for jobs, promotions or when it comes time for retrenchments.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: There is no comfort in knowing that the total numbers are not too many, if personally, we feel that we have been discriminated against at the workplace, or that the EP holder working beside us somehow has an inside track because of old school ties or some other personal connections.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And that is why we have the Tripartite Alliance for Fair and Progressive Employment Practices (TAFEP) where Singaporeans who feel unfairly treated can seek redress.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We also have the Fair Consideration Framework, which we are tightening further as you have heard.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And we are working with unions to make sure any retrenchments are done fairly, and no company is retrenching a Singaporean only to fill the same post with a foreigner, without very good justification.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The Government takes this issue of fairness very seriously.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In evaluating EP and S Pass applications, we take into account whether the employer has kept up support of local PMETs in their employment and has been responsive to Government efforts to help them recruit and train more Singaporean PMETs or conversely, whether the employer has discriminated against qualified Singaporeans.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This has always been the Government policy, but we particularly want to emphasise these considerations now, in these uncertain times, to remind all employers to play their part in building up their Singaporean workforce – the Singaporean Core.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This concentration, if it is unchecked, can cause social resentment and workplace problems.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It makes it harder for the company to blend into and be accepted by our multiracial society.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They stick out; it is a lump unable to be digested or integrated.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It suggests that the company has not really taken root in Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It can cause problems within the company too, because employees of other nationalities – Singaporeans or others – may find it harder to fit in, take pride in their work, and see a future for themselves in the firm.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Therefore, when that happens, we ask the firm to please relook at their hiring practices.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Most companies are responsive, and work with us in good faith.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In fact, many global companies understand that a diverse workforce is to their advantage and have explicit HR policies for this.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The issue of concentration can be easily played up and we know that there are some people who are stirring this up.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: For example, a Facebook page posted a wefie of DBS CEO Piyush Gupta with a room full of Indian employees last September.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It was captioned "Eyesight test: Find a Singaporean or Chinese in this DBS photo".

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The picture resurfaced recently and went viral, which just shows that during tough times, this subject is more neuralgic.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The person who put up the post surely knew this, yet he irresponsibly misused the wefie to insinuate that DBS in Singapore was not being fair to Singaporeans.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The Government will always be on the side of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: What is the point of creating jobs for foreigners if it does not benefit Singaporeans?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Ultimately, our aim is to grow the economy, create good jobs for Singaporeans and raise our standards of living.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Foreign workers and work pass holders help us to achieve this.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: By being open to talent from all over the world, we create more opportunities for ourselves.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Singapore has succeeded by being an international hub, tapping talents worldwide and serving a global market.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, even as we adjust our work pass policies, we must be careful not to give the wrong impression that we are now closing up and no longer welcoming foreigners.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Such a reputation would do us great harm and we have to watch this because we are being watched.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The Financial Times had an article just a couple of days ago to say Singapore, the mood is changing, we are turning inwards.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: There had been articles in the South China Morning Post a few months.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The grapevine buzzes and we have to do the right thing for ourselves, but we must also avoid sending the wrong signals to others.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It may surprise you, but even in this depressed economic climate, where some companies are consolidating and laying off workers, many investment projects want to come to Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: All over Asia and in the world, societies are under stress and politics is in flux.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In places where investors already have regional headquarters and projects, they are rethinking the merits of their locations and looking for alternatives.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It does not look the same as before.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: You will start thinking, "Where can I go?" Investors starting new projects are also anxiously scanning the globe, searching for the right place where they can safely make a commitment now.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Companies are seeking a safe harbour, where the politics is stable, there is rule of law, the people are hardworking and united, and where the country will come through the pandemic safely and have a bright future.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We take no joy in the troubles in the world, but it is a fact that in a troubled world, Singapore is one of the few trusted countries that stands out.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Indeed, EDB and the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) tell me that many companies have expressed interest in coming to Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But there are others yet that have not been announced or are still under wraps, are being discussed and are hopefully on the way.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I cannot tell you these confidential discussions, but I can give you a small peek.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Another company specialising in pandemic risk insurance wants to set up shop here.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: These are opportunities which are directly coming out of the crisis.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We want vaccine plants here so that we can get access to vaccines when they are available.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We want to build up our financial sector and pandemic risk insurance is now something on peoples' minds, and they are looking for a safe place where they can put their insurance company.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: There are other companies which are coming to Singapore or looking seriously at coming to Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Major financial institutions want to grow their operations in Singapore too, and these include IT and operations; backroom operations.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And we look at them, they are good projects.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We are conscious that IT is one of the areas where we worry about an over-concentration of foreign work pass holders.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But when you get a good project like this, an IT centre for a major foreign bank, a major global bank wanting to come to Singapore, and therefore going to recruit a proportion of Singaporean IT professionals and other management staff, should we say no?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They see us as a stable base to work from.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We want to talk to them to see how they can fit in here in Singapore to create good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But for them to come here, they must feel welcomed and be allowed to bring in the talent that they need.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Because we do not have the full complement of specialist engineers and other expertise for all these types of work yet.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And also, regional and global headquarters, by design, need to draw talent from around the world and to be run by international teams.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: That is the nature of a regional and global headquarters.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The companies which have headquarters run by all one nationality – the Japanese used to be like that – they did not thrive.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The American companies which had headquarters with people from all continents, they did well and they could adapt.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This is how we have always done it.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: For example, pharmaceutical companies began to invest in Singapore 20 to 30 years ago.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Later on, as these facilities grew, some of the pharma companies set up regional headquarters and research labs, like GlaxoSmithKline (GSK).

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: GSK's site director is Lim Hock Heng, a Singaporean.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He joined GSK in 1992, nearly 30 years ago, as a production engineer, picked up skills and knowledge from his foreign colleagues and rose up the ranks.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Today, Hock Heng runs most of the Singapore sites, which manufacture key GSK products for the whole world.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In other words, it is a drug which belongs to GSK and Singapore is the one place in the world they are making it and exporting it around the globe.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In the late-1980s, Singapore was recovering from a major recession and trying hard to grow our financial centre.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Several global banks came to Singapore, including Citibank.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They had no shortage of staff to choose from, with tens of thousands of employees globally.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But they hired Singaporeans, including Susan Kwek, who had a polytechnic diploma in Computer Science.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They saw her potential, groomed her, rotated her through several operations and technology roles, here and in the region.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And, today, Susan oversees operations and technology for Citibank in Hong Kong.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: There are many more Singaporeans in senior positions in semi-conductors, oil and gas, and IT.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If we had not welcomed these companies in the past and encouraged them to bring in global talent, Hock Heng, Susan and others would have been deprived of these opportunities.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But it is not just global companies that need foreign manpower.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Local companies also need global talent to grow and develop.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Our SMEs need skills, knowledge and expertise that they may not have in Singapore, for example, to develop an external wing and to move up the value chain.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But there is a more fundamental question which we have to ask ourselves, and that is, what sort of society, what sort of people do we want to be?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We have always been a people open to the world, welcoming others who can add value to our society and bringing the best out of us.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This is our history and our ethos, from our beginnings as an open port and an immigrant nation.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The Bicentennial last year reminded us of that.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This generosity of spirit gives our society and economy, vitality and resilience.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It has made Singapore the exceptional, cosmopolitan city that we are today, plugged into the global economy and making a living by making ourselves valuable to the world.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Social safety nets and foreign worker policies are just two of the many difficult issues that we will have to deal with, as our society matures.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We will study them carefully and, of course, debate them thoroughly, including here in Parliament.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The Government will lead this conversation with Singaporeans, build a political consensus around the right solutions and move us forward.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Whether we succeed depends on how well our politics work.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Singapore has achieved a high degree of political consensus on many of our social, political and economic issues.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This is one major reason for our rapid progress and one major benefit of the People’s Action Party's (PAP) dominant position.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Each new generation of Singaporeans is more educated, more connected to the world and surer of themselves.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They desire more diversity, alternative voices and checks and balances.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The desire has always been there, but it is growing.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In the last General Election, many people voted for the Opposition, while fully expecting that the PAP would remain in power as the Government.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In fact, the Workers' Party (WP) campaigned on this platform, if I am not mistaken, seeking to form a strong Opposition, but explicitly not seeking to form the next government.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Senior Minister Teo Chee Hean told me that on the second last day of the General Election campaign, a middle-aged lady came up to him, a little agitated.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: She asked him, "Mr Teo, is it true?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: My friends tell me it is okay to vote for the Opposition.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Because the Government will still be in charge.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: All the programmes the Government has promised, they will deliver – MRT, upgrading, new facilities, polyclinic.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, do not worry – all the things will still get done and that PAP will work even harder for you.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: You get everything they promised, and two persons working for you instead of one." She was very perturbed and asked him, "Mr Teo, is that true?" Her question really was, "How can this be true?" It troubled her profoundly that she did not know how to rebut the argument, yet, in her heart of hearts, she knew instinctively that something was very wrong.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The PAP will respond to these social and political trends, as we have always done.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We have not stayed on top all these years by being static, but by adapting to our evolving society and changing needs.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We have been assiduous in our leadership renewal.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Each new generation of PAP leaders has developed their own leadership styles and their own policy priorities.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They have created their own bonds with their generation of Singaporeans, to be in sync with their mood, to win their trust and support, and develop new ideas that resonate with them.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Mr Lee Kuan Yew and his founding generation of leaders governed Singapore in a direct, no-nonsense way.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It was necessary and appropriate at that time, and Singaporeans then strongly supported Mr Lee, although today's Singaporeans would probably consider the style hard and uncompromising.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: You read the old speeches, the directness and the force of the language, it makes you sit back and say, "Could we say that today in a different way?" The truths are the same.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The presentation has to change with the zeitgeist.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Mr Goh Chok Tong and his team had a different touch.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: His approach was about bringing people together and building a societal consensus on the next lap of Singapore's growth.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It was a contrast to Mr Lee's approach, but it was appropriate for his generation of Singaporeans and Mr Goh made it work.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: My team and I are not like Mr Lee, neither are we like Emeritus Senior Minister Goh’s teams.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We found our own ways to engage with this generation of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We have gone through many ups and downs together over these last 16 years and adapted and changed policies to meet the new needs of the population.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And, by now, I think Singaporeans all know what I am like and how I work.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They have always given me strong support and together, we have taken Singapore another step forward.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: My successors will have to do things in their own different ways too, establish their own standing and build their own bonds with the next generation.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The 4G leaders have been doing this for some time.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They are conducting the SG Together conversations now.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They want to accommodate this growing desire of Singaporeans not only to be heard but to be involved.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: For our part, the Government will take an open and constructive approach.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And let me explain what I mean by this bland term "open and constructive approach".

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: On the specific details of policies, we can be quite relaxed about it.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We will be open-minded, and we will listen to the different voices.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We will take in all constructive views and perspectives.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We will still have a full discussion, in fact, probably an even fuller discussion.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But at the end of the discussion, if there are still different views, the Government will have to make the decision it judges best and take responsibility for it.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is the Government’s duty to make such decisions and to be accountable to the people for them.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, discussion is fine, but discussion must lead to action and, finally, if it is an important issue and we are not yet entirely at one, the Government has to decide, we shall go.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And in the end, we put it to the voters.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The voters have to decide; do they support this, or do they want something different?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But politics is not only about issues but also about power.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And if the issue is not policies and priorities but a challenge to the Government’s fitness to govern, then the Government will have to stand up and defend itself vigorously.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It must put down the challenge and prove that it deserves to be the Government.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Because, otherwise, it must step aside and let another team take over.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This is how the political system is supposed to work.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We have a Westminster style of democracy, modelled on the British and adapted as we have gone along with it.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In Parliament, the Leader of the Opposition sits on the opposite front bench, directly opposite the Prime Minister.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: That is why Mr Pritam Singh is there, sitting opposite me.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He is not there as a supportive cheerleader, helping the Government to perform better.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He is there to challenge the incumbent Prime Minister and the Government, to point out their faults, to highlight where the Government has fallen short and to keep chipping away at the Government’s and the Prime Minister’s credibility.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And so, at the next General Election, or sooner if the opportunity arises, the Opposition can knock the Government out of power and take its place.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I am saying this not as a criticism of any political party in Singapore or anybody in Singapore, but I am saying this as how the system is designed to work.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In the British House of Commons, you have seen Jeremy Corbyn as the Leader of the Opposition taking on David Cameron and later, Theresa May, during Prime Minister’s Question Time.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He was not very successful at this, which is why he is no longer there.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Now, the new Labour Party leader, Sir Keir Starmer, is doing his best to show up Boris Johnson and to make his own name in the process.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In the Australian Parliament, Question Time for Prime Minister Scott Morrison and his predecessors happens every day when Parliament is sitting and often lasts for more than one hour.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Lots of drama and theatre and prepared soundbites.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The British or Australian Prime Minister has to stand his ground, defend his government’s policies and maintain psychological dominance to show that he deserves to be the Prime Minister.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If not, members of parliament on both sides will sense it and so will the public, and this will influence election outcomes as well as leadership contests in their parties.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In today’s Singapore, the tone of our Parliamentary debate is less combative than in Westminster or Canberra or, indeed, than how the Singapore Legislative Assembly was in the early 1960s, when the Barisan Sosialis was a formidable presence on the Opposition benches.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Our political traditions have developed differently since then.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Speeches in the Chamber are more substantive, with less verbal fireworks.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The Opposition is generally more restrained in its style of questioning.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Sometimes, their questions sound like questions which could have been asked by PAP backbenchers.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And, no doubt, it helps that they know if they take a more strident tone, Ministers are on top of their briefs and will be more than capable of taking them on.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But that does not stop them from trying their hand and their luck from time to time, and Mr Low Thia Khiang was particularly skilled at this.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I listened carefully to Mr Pritam Singh on Monday, describing how he intends to perform the role of Leader of the Opposition.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The Government benches will do our part to work with him to keep Parliament a constructive forum for debate.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I believe that it is good to have an adequate number of Opposition MPs in Parliament.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But that does not mean that the more Opposition MPs and the more fiery the debate in Parliament is, the better.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Or that the tone of our political debate cannot change for the worse.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The adversarial dynamic that is inherent in the Parliamentary system can go wrong.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We all hope that diversity will make a hundred flowers bloom.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But how do we prevent diversity from producing polarisation?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: How do we make sure disagreement does not result in paralysis?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It has happened in so many other countries.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Even public health issues, whether to wear a mask or not, becomes a partisan issue.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If you wear a mask, you are a Democrat; if you do not wear a mask, you are a Republican.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This is my side and that is yours.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: There is no middle ground, only sides to take.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: There are no truths or facts, only different versions of reality — facts and equal standing, alternative facts!

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The country is divided and goes into a downward spiral.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If this happens to Singapore, we will not just cease being an exceptional nation.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: MPs must speak up for what they sincerely believe in.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: You are elected not just to repeat what you have heard others say, but to think on behalf of others and to make arguments which make sense, which will benefit the interest of the people you are representing and of the voters who elected you.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If we do that, then there is a basis for us to manage the inherent tensions in our system and for politics to work out productively.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Ultimately, what sort of politics Singapore has depends on Singaporeans themselves.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The standards they demand of political leaders, PAP and Opposition, will influence the quality of the political leadership and the level of discussion and debate in Parliament.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They will determine whether our politics enable us to thrive and prosper, or divide and destroy us.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is a responsibility that the PAP carries, but no other political party in Singapore shares, to make our system work.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The PAP is inextricably linked with Singapore’s founding, its history and development.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It was Mr Lee Kuan Yew and the PAP who pledged that Singapore shall forever be a multiracial nation on Separation Day itself and made good on that pledge.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It was Dr Goh Keng Swee and the PAP who decided on National Service and built up the SAF into the respected force that it is today.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It was Mr S Rajaratnam and the PAP who penned the National Pledge and strived to live by it every day for the last 55 years, and counting.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: These are among the reasons why the PAP has won every election since Independence.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Singaporeans have trusted us, and we have never let them down.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Last week, Ms Sylvia Lim posted a beautiful picture on her Instagram of herself with Mr Low Thia Khiang, Mr Png Eng Huat and a few others.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They were dining al fresco after the Opening of Parliament at what looked like a rooftop bar near City Hall.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Behind them, you could see the National Gallery, Raffles Place and part of the new downtown in Marina South, brightly lit and spectacular.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In the caption, Ms Lim wrote: “What a skyline”.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I thought to myself, "She has paid an enormous tribute to the PAP Government and to the people of Singapore"; my predecessors as well as my colleagues in the current Government and generations of Singaporeans who worked with the PAP Government to make this happen.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I do not think she intended it and, therefore, I appreciated it all the more.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: How politics and Government work in Singapore is quite unique.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We have put enormous emphasis on the quality of government – the public service as well as the political leadership.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We have gone to great lengths to recruit the best people we can find to enter politics, join the Government and serve Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This quality of government, coupled with the trust and support of Singaporeans, enables us to deal with problems rationally, comprehensively and effectively.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Sometimes, we have paid the price in the vote, but overall, we have continued to win elections.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And therefore, the Government has been able to think long term, well beyond the next General Election.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: As a result, the country progresses, Singapore benefits, and the PAP continues to win elections, so far.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Once broken, it will be very difficult to put back together again.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Several years ago, I made a trip to a former Communist country in Europe, quite a big one.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: A distinguished business group hosted me to dinner, serious-minded people interested in Singapore and some of them knowledgeable about Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They asked me how the Singapore Government operates, and how we have made Singapore succeed.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I gave them my usual answers – our strong anti-corruption stance, our long-term planning and our unremitting efforts to promote social inclusion.
