speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: My hosts looked at each other in amazement.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They were familiar with how the politics in their own country worked.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: To them, what I described was completely unimaginable.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Surely, it cannot happen in this real world!

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But it happens here in Singapore, and every one of us thinks that it is just normal.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But even in Singapore, it is not normal at all.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is the result of sound politics, hard work and the will to put together, pull together and make Singapore a success.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We have come this way; we have kept it like this.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is like being in the Garden of Eden – things are going right, they stay right; you leave the Garden of Eden, you cannot go back.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: With more diversity and contestation, can we keep our focus on the long term and plan and build ahead for Singapore?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Can we continue to get good people into politics to maintain the quality of our Ministers and MPs, and make things happen for Singapore, if more and more citizens prefer the PAP to form the Government and yet vote for another party’s candidates to be their MPs for diversity, for checks and balance?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Is it really true that one day if there is a change of government, a new party can run Singapore equally well because we have such a good Public Service, as Mr Pritam Singh suggested on Monday?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is just like saying, if you have a New York Philharmonic orchestra, anybody can be the conductor.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In the nature of politics and of human societies, things can and do go wrong.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Each successive generation of Singaporeans has to keep on doing its best to keep the system working right.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Of course, there is no guarantee that even under a PAP Government, Singapore will forever be successful.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The world is not quite the same as it used to be.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: She said she felt sad when she came through Changi Airport.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It used to be bustling, crowded and full of life.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: When Changi Airport first opened in 1981, it was a coming-out party for Singaporeans of that generation.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: When someone was flying out, the whole extended family would come to Changi Airport to see him or her off and, at the same time, take pictures with the trishaw display and the water features.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I remember it fondly; I suppose it dates me.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Over the years, we expanded Terminal 1, and built Terminal 2 and Terminal 3, and now Terminal 4.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We built Changi up into the best airport and home to the best airline in the world.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: When Jewel opened, Singaporeans took immense pride in it.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I showed it off in my National Day Rally last year to demonstrate what we are capable of and explain why Singaporeans can look forward to limitless possibilities for our nation.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But Jewel too went dark during the circuit breaker.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We did not know whether we could survive after the Separation and the British withdrew East of Suez.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We rode through major economic storms like the Asian Financial Crisis and the Global Financial Crisis, not knowing if we would sink or swim.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But each time, we did survive and actually came back stronger.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Each time, the dire circumstances became the occasion and the platform for ambition and daring.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And each time, we transcended ourselves and built again.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We should fight COVID-19 with hope in our hearts because there is a silver lining.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This searing experience will help a whole new generation of Singaporeans appreciate and treasure what we have and what makes us an exceptional nation.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We are here by dint of will and imagination.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In defiance of all the odds and of all those who said we would not make it, we did.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Singapore Airlines will be a great way to fly once more.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Our children and our grandchildren will continue marching forward to build a fairer, ever more just and equal society.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I have a few clarifications and I will start with the first one – the framing of suggestions that the Opposition puts forward about the use of the Reserves.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And there is nothing unusual about this because the PAP does it too.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Does that not reduce the growth of the Reserves?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, the argument cannot be that when the Opposition tries to put that proposal forward, somehow, we are engaging in some sort of chicanery to steal what previous generations have toiled and perspired over to bring us here.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: When we look at alternatives, what are we looking at?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For the same Singaporeans who worked hard, toiled hard, and are now in their retirement years who have some difficulties, questions of intergenerational equity come up.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And that is the context through which some of these proposals are put forward.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I believe in the last term, Deputy Prime Minister Heng said no, this is a secret weapon; you do not reveal these numbers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But this House, this platform, provides us the opportunity to do so, if not in session, in Committee.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And yes, there is Parliamentary privilege, but I am prepared to give up my Parliamentary privilege if I divulge those numbers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Then, I will have to be taken to task under the Official Secrets Act.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We are doing it precisely because we are looking for alternatives to better consider the welfare of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Prime Minister spoke about the social media post of Piyush Gupta and, obviously, it was posted with completely mala fide intentions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But similarly, when an issue is not framed accurately and the Opposition is made to look like charlatans, surely, we have to stand up and say, no, that is not the agenda.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, I hope that clarification is helpful when we talk about Reserves and why those numbers matter to us.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The second clarification deals with the anecdote the Prime Minister shared about a lady who spoke to Senior Minister Teo and that choice, that difficult choice, she had to make about, "There will enough people voting for the PAP, they will be the Government.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But there are also people who are saying two-for-one".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It has come up before in previous elections.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And there is another side of the coin – that is one perspective.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There are conversations that Opposition MPs hear: "Mr Singh, why is it that when new citizens go to the Community Clubs, the elected MP is not there?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Is the elected MP, who is an Opposition candidate, not part of this larger political firmament?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Is that not unfair?" And there are other questions too and these have come up as well.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: More recently, I put up a post about restarting the Meet-the-People sessions and a pro-establishment Facebook page goes on and says, "Hey, look at them, trying to engender sympathy from the public by doing MPS at the void deck".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And, of course, people come up to me when I go on the ground and walk the markets.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Actually, the Government says you can build your own offices." I said, "That is true".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Because the argument was there was a competing need for void deck space.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Even though in the later Parliamentary sessions, that number is only 1%, I understand, that was dedicated for that purpose.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And so we have to deal with some of this reality as well.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Poor understanding, call it what you want of the situation; people feeling that there is something inherently unfair and so, when they say, "I want the PAP in the Government, but I also want an Opposition," they are giving voice to the situation many Singaporeans actually feel, which is, "We want that an Opposition in this House!

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There must be an Opposition in this House!" So, my duty and the duty of my colleagues is to be responsible about our role.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We come under pressure to from our own supporters too.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But as the Prime Minister rightly said, I think we owe our loyalty to something larger.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And we will do our best by Singaporeans, and if we are not good enough, we deserve to be voted out.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And that is how the system should work.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Prime Minister referred to a point I made about the political system and whether it would still run and so forth.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I refer the Prime Minister to the unofficial biography of the PAP which was published by The Straits Times Press, if I remember correctly.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In it, Mr Lee Kuan Yew, our first Prime Minister himself, says this and I quote, "At the end of the day, if you are running the system properly, you must have a distinction between what is the party, what is the Government, so, if you are voted out of office, the machinery is there for the next party to take over.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, although we do not have much of an Opposition, we keep the system going, so that at any time the party is out, the Government, the Parliament, the Civil Service will be there.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is not going to happen with people just hoping someone else does it.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Somebody has to plant his flag in the sand and say, "I am going to do it".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And then, it is the duty of myself and my party colleagues, to make sure that the people who are onboard do their very best.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is my commitment to Singaporeans, and this is my commitment to the Prime Minister as well.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: On Reserves, I am not arguing on the technicalities of percentages, drawdowns, NIRC and so on.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: That our mindset should be: what is a rainy-day fund, what is my daily expenses, and I meet my needs.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: We do draw from the rainy day fund a certain stream of income to spend.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Mr Singh says we are not talking about bringing the Reserves down.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But, as you know in financial investments, there is no certainty about Reserves going up.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: It can come down because the markets can come down and bring the value of our investments down, despite our best management of GIC or Temasek, as it has happened from time to time.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And there is a balance of risks, which we have to accept.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: What are you depending on for the future?

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And I suggest that our mindset should be that what I have planned for the future, I think of as only touching them in extremist.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: On Monday, when Mr Singh spoke about trade-offs and difficulties, he said, yes, he knows that there is more spending which is necessary, there are old folks, there will be trade-offs and we can raise income taxes.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But he is prepared to raise income taxes.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Well, these are political judgements which you have to make.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But finally, you have to be able to spend what you are able to earn.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I suggest that our fundamental mindset should be that we pay our way forward.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And we do not depend on another little bit from the Reserves, another little bit from the Reserves, another little bit from the Reserves; each time, I am not really compromising a principle.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I am just getting a little bit more pregnant.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I suggest that is not the way we should think as a generation.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: We should be thinking for the future for the next generation, and I am, as their founder, I want to help to provide for them.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: That is a mindset which has brought us here and that is a mindset which will serve our children and grandchildren well.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: On Senior Minister Teo's anecdote and Mr Pritam Singh's arguments, his arguments do not respond to the anecdote.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Because the basic point is this: whatever happens, there will be Opposition MPs elected to this House.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: It has worked out and the Opposition has been making use of this system.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: The WP in the last election had NCMPs, the PSP in this term has NCMPs.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But, if you say, "Vote against the Government because somebody else will look after getting the PAP Government", you just become a free rider.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: If you vote Opposition, "No harm, the PAP will still be there", then I think the system must fail.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: If they vote tactically, the consequence must be, one day, they will get the result which they mark the "X" for but which they did not intend.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I think that is a wrong thing to teach people to do.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: You go to the elections, you vote for the person whom you have trusted in, who will run your system and who will run your government.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Our system is designed so that if you do that, it will be stable.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: If you do not do that, I think you are courting trouble.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I can understand why Mr Singh, as Leader of the Opposition and not in a position yet to challenge the Government, would like to make this argument; that the PAP Government will be there, do not worry, you can safely vote for me, I am not going to be the next Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But I put it to you that that is not the right thing to do morally, and it is not the right thing to do for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Thirdly, on the system still running, he quoted Mr Lee Kuan Yew and, indeed, we have designed it to the best of our ability so that if the PAP is out of government, it shall not collapse straightaway.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But let me just ask you whether you really believe, that if this team, that the PAP, one day, hands over to a new Opposition party, the system can work the way it has been working?

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: There is an autopilot, you can fly straight and level for some time.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: There are countries where the political system continually produces revolving-door Cabinets.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Japan, for a time, was like that, before Mr Abe became Prime Minister a second time.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Every six months, they have a new Prime Minister, a new Minister for Trade and Industry and so forth.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: When Mr Abe came in, and I think this time he was eight to nine years in government, eight years; and got the team together and set directions, the country moved.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: So, to say that the system is such that with civil servants, the SAF and so on, therefore, it does not matter who is the government, I think that is not being honest.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: In that case, we can dismiss all the Ministers, they can go on leave, you do not need Ministers, and anybody can be a Minister.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But you need to run a system which is finely tuned and capable and you need a very capable hand at the top.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: They are expected to know all about the Ministries, every in and out of the policy.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: When he comes here to answer in the Committee of Supply or in case there are Parliamentary Questions, he does not refer to his Administrative Vice Minister, which is what the Japanese have or, in our equivalent, would be the Permanent Secretaries.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Civil servants and the elected can make this happen, can carry this.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I think that is not in this world.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I do not think the residents in Aljunied, Hougang for 30 years now and even Sengkang, as a result of the results of the last election, would appreciate being called free riders.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The residents of Aljunied, I can speak more authoritatively for Aljunied residents because I am a sitting Member there, we are not just doing nothing, having been voted in.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: We are not just letting the other guy, the government of the day do something.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: We have got to do what we have to do.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: We have got to run the Town Council, which is why Mr Lee Kuan Yew conceived of the Town Councils in the first place.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Because if you want to move forward in the system as an Opposition MPs, you have got to prove your worth in the Town Council.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But if we were bungling things up, I would not be here today.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: We have tried our best in the circumstances that we are in.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The Sengkang team is not going to have an easy time.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: For the first term, it is always going to be tough.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But the voters of these constituencies put their faith in us because they know an opposition in Parliament is ultimately good for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And it is not just – and if I can suggest this – it is not just the NCMP version of the opposition, with full respect to everyone who was an NCMP in this Parliament and those who came before, but it is when you have elected Opposition MPs, the Government listens harder.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I am sure the PAP may have a different on it, but that is my perspective.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And that is why it is important for there to be elected Opposition MPs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The Prime Minister alluded to a dishonest sort of packaging of what I am suggesting.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The bigger moral imperative that I have, and it is a huge burden, and I felt this burden before the last elections, was whether the people who are standing as WP candidates could follow through.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And if you choose someone who is not committed, not vested, that is the biggest pain for me as the leader of one party that aspires to represent Singaporeans in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, I will have to do what is good and what is right by Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Do I want to contest all the seats, more seats, slowly grow?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: A lot of it depends on the quality of people that come and are attracted by the WP and our platform.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: If Singaporeans are attracted to it, then sure, there is a prospect of growth.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But it is not growth for growth's sake.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I am not desperate for power, Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But we have got to get good people if we want to bring this country forward.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The PAP has been doing that as the Prime Minister has alluded to.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: At this point in our growth, we have to grow our roots as a loyal Opposition.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: After more than 50 years of Independence, this is the first time the Government has recognised the Office of the Leader of the Opposition.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: We have many, many more miles to go.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I am in no way undervaluing his motivations, his passion and his desire to do right by Singapore, his wish to have a high-quality Opposition built up in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I think it is good for Singapore that you have honest people in the Opposition, people who believe in what they are trying to do and people who will stand up and fight for their ideals.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And from time to time, agree very strongly with the Government.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I think it is also good that you have Opposition who take their Town Council responsibilities seriously, who look after their constituencies assiduously and conscientiously and do their best for their voters and give the voters a reason to vote for them.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Because the argument which he makes is that he is very careful, he only chooses candidates he can trust to be WP candidates.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: It is the right and responsible attitude to take.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But I think other opposition parties may say they have been trying to get good candidates too.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And they could make the same argument as you have, that it is good to have an Opposition in Singapore, "Vote for us.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Somebody else will look after the government of Singapore".

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: So, supposing that the PSP had been as persuasive as Mr Pritam Singh, and the Singapore Democratic Party had been as persuasive as Mr Pritam Singh, and more voters had taken such an attitude, where would Singapore be?

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: So, therefore, something is wrong when you say I really want one government, but I will vote for another one.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And the system will go wrong when you do that.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I think it is necessary that people understand this and understand what is at stake when you elect a government of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: They are also about electing the government for the country and that is necessary for people to bear firmly in mind.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am mindful that this is the first time I am attending Parliament and also just an NCMP, thank you for the opportunity to ask the Prime Minister a few clarifications.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I do not know what privileges I have in terms of how I am going to speak but it may be a bit of my own opinions plus a bit of clarification and questions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, it will be a mixture of that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First of all, I think the Prime Minister had given a very touching presentation on the situation in Singapore today.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But what we want to say is that, on the point of the free rider, I am not sure whether that concept is being used in line with what economists have in mind.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But nevertheless, we do not go into that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, as a result, there is a very comfortable margin.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Let us try." And I can tell you, Mr Prime Minister, I am a very new politician.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But in the process of the last one year, when I interacted with voters on the ground, I felt that the Singaporean voters are really, really, very smart.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, what they are thinking now is, "There is a buffer, so I leave it.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And I will wait until that buffer shrinks and I am not going to vote everybody, anybody in.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even if PSP is not good enough this round.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I want to get the best people to go in.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And as the buffer shrinks, I will make my decision again." So, whether it is the Opposition or the electorate, from the position of the electorate, there is no question that, at the moment, everybody wants the present Government to continue.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But that does not mean if, going forward, the performance of the Government does not improve, the electorate is going to sit by.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But that is going to be very, very long down the road.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, I wish to ask Mr Prime Minister to clarify whether what I said is something that is useable in the current political climate we have.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is no long-term plan that they can be comfortable about.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We want to maintain our current foreign talent model as well.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But, at the same time, when we were to create jobs and have a new economy, we need to have new capabilities, we need to have Singaporeans who can think independently and with the leeway to think.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, these are the two questions I want to pose to the Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: On his first point, we have addressed the questions extensively.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: He does not add anything new to it.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: As for the other issues of rebalancing and not a revolution, I think these are matters which can eminently be discussed and are suitable for debate in this House.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But it is not the focus of my speech today.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I am talking here about which way Singapore politics is going, what their risks are in going in this direction, what we must do in order to make it turn out right and how it has worked out well for us in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And how we must try to continue to let this work for as long as we can, to serve Singaporeans, a new generation, new desires, but the same high quality of service of Government of commitment in order that there can continue to be more Reserves to argue about in the next Parliament.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister, Minister for Finance and Coordinating Minister for Economic Policies (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I want to reiterate the point which the Prime Minister has just made about the difference between a founder's mindset and an inheritor's mindset, and address Mr Singh's suggestion about the use of the Reserves, as somebody who has been directly involved in using the reserves twice.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister, Minister for Finance and Coordinating Minister for Economic Policies (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It was a very difficult decision because we never wanted to do it, until all the neighbouring countries have created bank deposit guarantees to guarantee all the deposits in the banks.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister, Minister for Finance and Coordinating Minister for Economic Policies (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And if we had a bank run, the consequences on Singapore would have been far worse.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister, Minister for Finance and Coordinating Minister for Economic Policies (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: At that time, Mr Goh Chok Tong was my Chairman.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister, Minister for Finance and Coordinating Minister for Economic Policies (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: After long discussions with him and Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam, who was in MAS at that time, we decided to discuss with the Prime Minister, and we went to see the President.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister, Minister for Finance and Coordinating Minister for Economic Policies (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: If you ask me today: could I have predicted it when I first went to MAS?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister, Minister for Finance and Coordinating Minister for Economic Policies (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Could the world have predicted there was going to be a global financial crisis?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister, Minister for Finance and Coordinating Minister for Economic Policies (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Did we know that there would be governments around the world creating bank guarantees of that form?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister, Minister for Finance and Coordinating Minister for Economic Policies (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, I think the Reserves, as a contingency fund to meet unexpected events for a small country with zero natural resource of any kind, is something which we must never forget.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister, Minister for Finance and Coordinating Minister for Economic Policies (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The second aspect is, this year, as the Prime Minister said earlier, we were projecting a fairly rosy picture before the financial year.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister, Minister for Finance and Coordinating Minister for Economic Policies (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Therefore, the Budget was made on the basis of even the amount that we will return and keep in past Reserves.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister, Minister for Finance and Coordinating Minister for Economic Policies (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But within 100 days, I did four Budgets and also, very recently, a Supplementary Statement.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister, Minister for Finance and Coordinating Minister for Economic Policies (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In those five Budgets and Statement altogether, I saw the President and the Council of Presidential Advisers five times and, each time, I can tell you, they asked very tough questions about all our assumptions and what we were looking at, what was the contingency and what could get worse.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister, Minister for Finance and Coordinating Minister for Economic Policies (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Mr Pritam Singh also spoke about intergenerational equity.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister, Minister for Finance and Coordinating Minister for Economic Policies (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I have been looking at how other countries have funded all these programmes.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister, Minister for Finance and Coordinating Minister for Economic Policies (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: A lot of them have funded them through borrowings.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister, Minister for Finance and Coordinating Minister for Economic Policies (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As the Minister for Finance, I can tell Members that I felt so grateful to our founders for that founders' mindset in leaving us with these Reserves that my team and I were able to focus fully on what would best serve the interests of Singaporeans, how would we best help our businesses and how would we best provide resources for the frontline agencies, especially MOH, to tackle this major crisis.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister, Minister for Finance and Coordinating Minister for Economic Policies (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I did not have to worry about what terms I would have to negotiate with lenders and how we were going to pay for it.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister, Minister for Finance and Coordinating Minister for Economic Policies (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Again, let me emphasise that, for a country with no natural resource of any kind who really live by our wits, having those Reserves gives us strength and allows us to keep jobs for our people, to restructure, to reform and that, even in the Budget, even in this crisis, we are talking about how we can emerge stronger, we have proposals on looking beyond COVID-19 and how we will re-establish relationships and even seek to emerge stronger.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister, Minister for Finance and Coordinating Minister for Economic Policies (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I think there is a certain mindset that we owe something not just to ourselves but to our future generations.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister, Minister for Finance and Coordinating Minister for Economic Policies (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Therefore, I hope that Mr Pritam Singh will bear that in mind when looking at this.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister, Minister for Finance and Coordinating Minister for Economic Policies (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: On the contingency question, one could ask what contingencies there could be in the future for which the Reserves may have to be used and whether the Reserves are enough.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister, Minister for Finance and Coordinating Minister for Economic Policies (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Today, on the front page of The New York Times, they spoke about the situation in Spain and the worries in Europe about how things could get worse, whether a vaccine would be found soon enough and, even then, how would that work because now people are talking about the risk of re-infection.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister, Minister for Finance and Coordinating Minister for Economic Policies (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, we have to have a mindset that we have to prepare for contingencies and not think about, "Well, if I know how much it is, I can tell you how much to spend." Because the one big unknown is what are the contingencies that you have to prepare for.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister, Minister for Finance and Coordinating Minister for Economic Policies (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And I do not want to elaborate on the range of other contingencies that we have to prepare for.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister, Minister for Finance and Coordinating Minister for Economic Policies (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But a pandemic is certainly one very big area.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister, Minister for Finance and Coordinating Minister for Economic Policies (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The global economy does not go on a straight line all the time.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister, Minister for Finance and Coordinating Minister for Economic Policies (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And we, being so open, will be exposed far more than many other economies.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister, Minister for Finance and Coordinating Minister for Economic Policies (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, I hope that Mr Pritam Singh will think about these carefully before thinking about "I must know how much before we know how much to spend".

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister, Minister for Finance and Coordinating Minister for Economic Policies (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The principles on why we do it are quite clear.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The exchange of views has certainly added to the robustness of the debate in this House.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic is disrupting every aspect of our society.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: There is no road map for a solution and no one knows exactly what to do.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We must finish this race that is full of twists and turns.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: What good will come from COVID-19 is dependent on how Singapore runs as a team in this marathon.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: To run this race, we must be able to respond to the challenges and be able to adapt and transform.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We must nurture strong and new runners and let them start racing when they are still really young.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Our youths must have a strong mindset and must always stay hungry in order to compete globally.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We must invest resources in them to accelerate the building of new capabilities for our future economy.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The youths need to feel a strong sense of ownership and feel that they have a role in shaping the future of our country.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: So, how do we prepare and motivate our youths?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Digital transformation has accelerated the change necessary for productivity.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The changes to the workforce we put in place now will greatly impact the future of our young Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Our millennials ought to play a bigger role in articulating their vision of Singapore in a post-COVID-19 world and the roles they want to undertake in shaping our collective future.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Our youths must have more opportunities and responsibilities to lead the change and shape the future society they want to live in.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: To prepare them to be able to compete globally, we need to invest and build deep capabilities, not just in growth sectors, but also to solve our nation’s fundamental problems like the shortage of manpower.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Our youths must find a way to customise solutions with the use of more industry 4.0 technologies to seek ways to reduce the reliance on foreign workers in sectors like construction, hospitality and nursing.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Our youths should also focus on how the rising sea level is a slow boiling frog problem but with real existential threats to our nation’s survival.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We also need to create conducive environments to spawn creativity and innovation.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Better solutions often come out of intersections of different disciplines.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I hope our education institutions will provide more opportunities for cross-disciplinary training for the students.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: This will broaden their knowledge and skillsets instead of being part of the current unemployed pool.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: As marathoners, we must trim fats, stay lean and stay light.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We can take supplements, but avoid quick fixes like steroids.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Steroids may boost our performance very quickly but, in the long run, they do more harm to our health.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: As an open economy and an international brand, Singapore will certainly need the help of international talents.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Having said that, they should not cripple our organic capabilities.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We need to spread foreign talents across various industries so that there is more even growth and to create more opportunities for Singaporeans to excel in every sector.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In a 45- to 50-year career lifespan, we should then take time to build a strong foundation to be good in developing a craft or a career, grow and develop our practical skillsets and experience, before moving into managerial or management roles.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: This will help our workforce not to be too top-heavy, resulting in us becoming expensive and uncompetitive.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: At this point, I would like to take the opportunity to talk about our women marathoners.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Women provide diversity and a different style of leadership at all levels and across diverse fields.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: While men work hard and tend to be strong and aggressive sometimes, women are naturally nurturing and resilient.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: These are qualities that are crucial when surviving a crisis or rebuilding the economy and society.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Many talented and capable Singaporean women have traded-off careers for their young families and children.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: These women do have the requisite skillsets, experience and maturity to contribute and lead in the workplace.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: They just need to be given that opportunity to rejoin the workforce.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We should increase accessibility for these women to return to the workplace, especially after their children have grown up.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: To attract and retain women in the workplace, the work environment must also transform.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Ironically, COVID-19 has made flexible work arrangements workable and acceptable.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Echoing Mr Louis Ng's suggestions, I would like to suggest that we consider the possibilities of ensuring that all companies be more gender neutral.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The vision of Singapore in a post-COVID-19 world will be completely different from how we thought it would be a year ago.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We must now undertake the responsibility to reshape our future creatively.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We must be different to succeed, to seek autonomous solutions to build new areas of growth and to embrace deep capabilities to improve on our competence.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We must be conscious of environment conservation solutions to live better.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In our resource-scarce nation, everyone must work together to succeed in this post-COVID-19 world.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: There is a Zambian proverb that says, “When you run alone, you run fast.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Around this time last year, 200 Singaporeans came together to run "Relay Majulah", to celebrate Singapore’s Bicentennial and to raise funds for President’s Challenge.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: It was a race that showed us that so long as we stayed determined to help one another, we can achieve our goal no matter how difficult it may seem.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: As a nation, we must keep running this uphill marathon together, no matter what extremely harsh weather condition we may all need to go through.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I am confident that we will eventually finish this race together, stronger and trimmer than when we started off.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Deputy Speaker, let me conclude my speech in Chinese.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The fight against COVID-19 and economic recovery is like a marathon, and the key lies in perseverance.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Every member of the team must do his or her best and overcome the difficulties without fear.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The youths must be brave to innovate and be entrepreneurial and use advanced technologies to solve the most challenging issues that the country is facing.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: They should also take on the responsibility to shape our future.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Women are known to be soft and resilient.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Hence, we should encourage them to participate more in the decision-making process at the senior level to work out a more holistic solution.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: However, as long as we persevere and help each other with a strong belief in mind and a united team spirit, we can complete the run and reach our destination.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Team Singapore is a group of unremitting marathon runners who are determined to win!

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, I support the Motion.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It will not be easy for us or the world to emerge from COVID-19 and its economic fall-out to recover fully any time soon.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But I have confidence that we can grow and emerge from this difficult time.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What we can and must count on and empower is our people, Singaporeans, young and old.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have been reflecting on the last few words of our pledge: happiness, prosperity and progress for our nation.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What truly does happiness to a nation mean?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To me, "happiness" is about ensuring and engendering the social and collective well-being of our society as a whole.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Economic growth is crucial, yes, and is the lifeblood of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But addressing the softer human needs and the collective well-being of our people can be a counter-balancing force when our economic growth may no longer be as fast as in the past decade.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A balance in the pursuit of what is most important to benefit the wider population, especially the at-risk groups, will become increasingly important.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As such, my speech will focus on building our people, not just on the "bread and butter" issues affecting livelihoods and jobs, but also social and mental health of our people, and social cohesion.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First, I would like to talk about one group of at-risk people particularly impacted by this crisis, and many in this House have also spoken up about them: the older workers and how we can assist them.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is important that we recognise and appreciate the wealth of experience and skills of our older workers, who will make up an increasing share of our workforce.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I commend Moovaz, a Singapore-based startup specialising in international moving services.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In a The Straits Times article reported on 24 August 2020, they employed Mdm Becky Chang, 60 years old, after she was let go from her company in the shipping industry.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Moovaz valued her four decades of experience in the shipping industry and, importantly, her willingness to learn.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As Members of this House have quoted, and I would like to reinforce, as Senior Minister Tharman Shanmugaratnam has aptly said, and I quote, "no Singaporean who is willing to learn should be 'too old' to hire.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And no one who is willing to adapt should be viewed as 'overqualified'."  As a society, we must make every effort to continually support a more mature workforce in meaningful and dignifying work.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What is even more important is for us to respect the emotional journey they are going through as they cope with the rapidly changing job market.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have met older adult residents who have lost or are at the risk of losing their jobs and they shared with me their anxiety in finding new jobs.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Not for the lack of will to learn, but for the steep learning curve of acquiring new skills in growth areas and the learning pace they need.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My constituency volunteers and I keep them supported by encouraging them not to give up.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Government has started many good schemes to provide assistance to this group.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These are all commendable schemes, but we need to also systematically redesign jobs, shift workplace culture and HR policies to institutionalise new possibilities for our maturing workforce.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We need to help them overcome the workplace barriers which may stand in the way of maximising their potential.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In my view, social service experts are adept in designing systemic environment and practices, designing new job roles, breaking down tasks and coaching them in partnership with employers, doing these in a way that build psycho-social wellness of people, bringing in elements of respect, dignity and empowerment.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We saw that in the hard-forged efforts in the movement for employment of persons with special needs, which organisations like the National Council of Social Service (NCSS), SG Enable alongside community-minded corporates like Pan Pacific Hotel Group, as well as Social Service Agencies like Autism Resource Centre led by our capable Mayor Denise Phua have made impactful progress in.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We need a similar movement for our older workers.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am glad to share that there is much keenness to support this segment of our workers.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that more public, private and people sector organisations will collaborate and join in such efforts.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Change in workplace culture, mindsets, HR policies and practices that will ensure non-discriminatory hiring and retention of older workers will require relentless and collective efforts.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Because of the important element of self-worth and self-empowerment that work brings, we must continually improve status quo to give assurance to our older workers and help them increase job security.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This brings me to the next part of my speech – the impact of the current crisis and uncertainties on social and mental health of our people.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Centre for Research on Successful Ageing, a research centre based in the Singapore Management University (SMU), undertook a study recently to understand the possible impacts on elderly Singaporeans during the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In my opinion, this has potential impact on our people’s mental health.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These two reports show that the impact of the current crisis on mental health is a complex one that affects different groups of Singaporeans in different ways, both young and old.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My hope is that our younger people today, who are more likely to talk about mental health more openly and honestly, can increasingly exercise "self-care" and be part of their normal vocabulary to be able to find support and care that they need.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am heartened that compared to five years ago, the awareness when talking about the stigmatisation of mental health among youths and young adults has vastly improved.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But we must keep on this journey of bringing down the stigma for youths that need the help to find help.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some of the older adults may find it difficult to talk openly about mental health.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They may not dare to tell people that they are not doing well.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Perhaps they feel that their dignity may be impacted, or they do not want to be a burden.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Social cohesion amongst all generations for a collective destiny is increasingly important.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In dealing with the issues I have mentioned so far, we can see that we are facing more complex challenges among our people, both young and old.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, I remain hopeful that if we pull our strengths together, not seeing the emerging issues like what I have mentioned as solely the problems of one specific group or another but affecting our common destiny ahead, we can find new solutions together.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: After all, all our futures are closely intertwined with each other and how Singapore will continue to thrive ahead.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We can build intergenerational "Communities of Support" at work, in the neighbourhood and at home out of the Singapore Together conversations.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such communities can act as platforms that promote intergenerational bonding through embarking on shared projects with common interest that value each other's strengths and provide support that is enriching in a meaningful way intergenerationally Mr Deputy Speaker, I would like to end my speech on a note of hope.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hope for all Singaporeans, young and old, during this period of uncertainty.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hope for a better nation as a whole.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: No matter how diverse our views are and no matter how complex the challenges we are facing, we can all prevail in a common destiny ahead if we know how to harness each other's strengths and will.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Beyond the current fight with COVID-19, the real battle we have ahead of us is a virus of disillusionment in the longer-term future of Singapore.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: I am a recent father to a baby boy, all of 77 days young.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: On occasion, where I have the luxury to lull him to sleep, questions inevitably flood my mind.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: When he completes National Service some 20 years later, what will Singapore be like?

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Can Singapore still work for him, as it did for me and my cohort?

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Indeed, in the past couple of months, I have narrated my life story several times, since being introduced as a candidate.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Juxtaposed against the life stories of many of my fellow first-term Parliamentarians, my story does seem a little "familiar", and some might even say, "cookie cutter".

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: And may I also suggest that these stories could not have been possible if our system had been running on the fuel of tokenism.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: These stories are not only emblematic of our generation of Singaporeans, but to impose broad and inaccurate characterisations on these life stories make a mockery of what the Singapore system stands for.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Being both blue-collared workers, my parents worked very hard.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: At their urging, I too studied hard and was often reminded that getting good results was my ticket to a good life.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Two years ago, CNA ran a documentary titled "Regardless of Class." In that programme, six youngsters from the Integrated Programme (IP) and Normal streams were brought together and had a visibly uncomfortable time together, as they shared about their ideals in life.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: That social experiment generated a fair amount of heated discussions around class divides in Singapore.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: And that reminded me that I, too, had my fair share of awkward brushes on the topic as I grew up.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: There was once in primary school when we had to write a composition about our fathers.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: As a few of us strayed into casual chatter in that class, questions that are usually taboo in conversations between adults innocuously sprung up, "How much does your father earn monthly?" I remember wondering in amazement when a classmate of mine shared that her dad was a manager and that he earned a handsome monthly salary of $5,000.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: That was several times my household income at the time and was, to me then, an astronomical sum.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: When I became older, another episode left a deep impression.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: I remember I was getting to know a group of new teenage friends when the conversation veered into where each of us lived.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Amongst this group was a friend who had known me for some time and was quick to answer, on my behalf, albeit a little insensitively, "Oh, Eric lives in Ang Mo Kio, the slums near the Town Centre!" I remember feeling uneasy momentarily while another friend with a better emotional quotient, I think, quickly steered the conversation away to lighter topics.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: To be sure, socioeconomic differences are present in every society.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: But what powers people forward and what keeps successive generations striving is the hope of a better future.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: The idea that if one works hard, he or she can potentially earn a train ticket for a better cabin class on our collective trip into the future.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: For families not far behind, this statistic serves as an aspirational target.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Being born to a family of a lower socioeconomic status should not be a handicap.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Who you are at birth should not determine who you will end up being in life.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Conversely, problems occur when one gets entrenched in their situation at birth, essentially, being stuck with the hand you are dealt, with little to no means of getting a better deck of cards.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: The bad news is entrenchment is the natural order of things.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Most, if not all parents, regardless of their ability, will naturally want to provide their children with the best they can afford.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: In fact, no social order in the world organically ensures parity of opportunity.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: So, if left unchecked, our train of hope will eventually run out of fuel and tank.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: But instead of simplistically alleging the failure of our meritocratic system, I suggest we need to take intervening steps to keep our systems going.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: The tried and tested path of studying hard for a degree and landing a comfortable white-collar job remains the mainstay for most.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: But this remains only one out of the kaleidoscope of possible ways that one can succeed in life!

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: After all, each of us are unique individuals, and I am not making a feel-good Disney statement here.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: It is high time we celebrate the diversity of our talents and just think about how much we can achieve if each of us pursue life to the fullest by mining our individual reservoirs of unique talents, instead of trying to fit square pegs into round holes.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: It takes a paradigm shift in our mindsets that beyond the typical, white-collared roles, there can be many other viable routes to success in life.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Along with this attitudinal shift, we need to take concrete steps not just to signal, but to tangibly show that there can truly be multiple pathways to different pinnacles of success.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Apprenticeships offer individuals the chance to grow both in the classroom and at the workplace.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: It is a good way of enhancing the development of one's skillsets and preparing the individual for his or her career all at once.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: And it is not uncommon to hear of individuals working up the ranks to senior appointments, often without even a basic degree.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: To be sure, designing and provisioning for apprenticeship programmes is an arduous process involving many stakeholders poring over details such as remuneration, time allotted for classroom instruction vis-à-vis productive work.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: But the key obstacles we face today are the tinted lenses through which we view apprenticeships.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: We need to ask themselves the right questions when a young family member considers taking up an apprenticeship.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: It is not about whether the family can afford full-time classroom learning.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: It is much more about whether an apprenticeship provides the best pathway for the child to develop his or her full potential.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: At the same time, employers also need to see apprenticeships as a pipeline for talent development, not merely a manpower supply line.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: I know our education institutions have been exploring work-study progression pathways for our children in recent years.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: They face an uphill task of changing deep-seated beliefs that we have held for a very long time.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: But if we are determined for our future generations not to trip over ourselves by sticking to narrow definitions of success, we have every collective interest to make sure apprenticeships flourish in our system.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Beyond pathways, we need to do more to help Singaporeans in non-white-collared roles as well.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: We can do so by helping our local industries, some of which are Uniquely Singapore, flourish.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Today, few would actually raise an eyebrow when they find food selections that made it to the Michelin Bib Gourmand list in our hawker centres.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: That alone is testimony of the quality of our hawkers' products.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: We can help our hawkers innovate their business models, scale up operations and even help them go regional!

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: For other industry segments that are fledgling or non-existent locally, we can connect Singaporeans with aptitude to overseas centres of excellence.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: It is after all my belief that Singaporeans of all stripes, not just those with degrees, can make waves the world over.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: It is most certainly not about having our own master watchmakers, or expert sommeliers simply for the vanity of it.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: At the heart of it all, we need tangible change to help Singaporeans reimagine and re-visualise a multi-dimensional definition of success.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: And replying to the same question, respondents from the upper class cited; (a) knowing the right people, (b) ability, and (c) hard work, as their answers.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Indeed, one's networks has an impact on how well one does in life.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: As a general rule, it is not inconceivable that a family that is better off will be able to leverage a larger network to their children's advantage.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: And this speaks to our earlier point on entrenchment as the natural human order.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: But this is where we need to take intervening steps to level the playing field.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: I have been mentoring ITE students since 2014.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Many mentees do well and go on to complete diploma courses in the polytechnics.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: One of them has even gone on to sign on with the Republic of Singapore Air Force and is now a pilot trainee.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Another one, recently left Singapore, to pursue a hospitality apprenticeship in Switzerland.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: I do not lay claim to any of my mentees' successes, but simply being able to journey with them for part of their formative years has made me a better person.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: So, to unlock the full potential of every Singaporean, we need to avail mentoring for our youths at skill and tap on the many who are willing to step out as mentors.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: I am sure many among the 14% who got uplifted in a single generation need no nudging.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Many will want to make a difference by mentoring a younger person.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: We can tap on our collective energy and create conditions where people can step up to pave forward and for successive generations of young Singaporeans to do likewise.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, I venture an assumption that whether society views its future with optimism or otherwise can have a unifying or divisive effect on its constituents.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: According to the Pew Research Centre, when asked to gaze at the crystal ball into 2050, many Americans are pessimistic about many aspects of life in the US, including a perceptible decline in living standards.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: (In Malay):   Sir, President Halimah Yacob's speech at the opening session of the Fourteenth Parliament of Singapore, touched on the importance and need for Singapore's political and community leaders from all walks of life to unite, despite having their own different principles and philosophy, working together and contributing towards a happy, prosperous and developed Singapore.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In my speech, I would like to share my thoughts on strengthening unity in diversity.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It is natural that humans are created differently or in a state of diversity.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This is normal and we must agree with and accept this natural state.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Whether this diversity results in something good or not, the outcome depends on the way we accept and how we go through it.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: My life experiences, especially as a counsellor, make me view diversity positively and accept it as a blessing and wisdom.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This is because diversity offers choices, and it can also help and facilitate efforts to complement each other on any matter.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: However, we must acknowledge that some differences that may arise from diversity are sometimes awkward and can pose challenges.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In addressing such differences, we must be open, tolerant, have mutual respect and practise the principle of agreeing to disagree.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It is natural for us to practise the values of diversity in life.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: People who live in a community cannot live alone without engaging in the existing ecosystem, as the English saying goes “No man is an island”.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: A combination of ideas and efforts is necessary in going through all aspects of life, especially within the challenging global situation today and in the future.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
