text: In short, we need each other to complement each other.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The “ownself check ownself” political approach is unhealthy.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: As human beings, we are exposed to the phenomenon of “blind spot” and “group thinking”.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: But we must also accept the fact that diversity can also cause anxiety and the possibility of fault lines.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This is something that may not be avoided but can still be addressed or mitigated.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Diversity should not have a negative impact such as being divisive and discriminatory.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: There should not be any feelings or opinions by any party that their ideology or philosophy is more “superior” than the others.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: As I said earlier, this diversity is meant to complement each other and, if differences cannot be resolved, we should be prepared to agree to disagree.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Efforts to assimilate and practise unity in diversity in our society should start from the country's political leadership.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The actions of political leaders will serve as examples and role models for the public.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The ways leaders deal with and discuss sensitive and hot issues, whether inside or outside the House, to some extent, will shape and influence the tone of debate and discussion that will take place among the public.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In short, whether there is a live telecast or not, it is not the reason for a Member not to showcase their acting, because they know their acting can still be watched through recording clips over social media channels.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Members of this House should realise that whatever qualities they display, whether through verbal or verbal conduct, will have an impact on the public.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This House is meant to discuss matters that can have a positive impact on the well-being of the community and the country.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It is not an arena to launch personal attacks against anyone.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Debates that incorporate personal attacks are unsuitable for this House as it will tarnish the integrity and status of this House as a legislature.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The portrayal of a leader who makes personal attacks against another leader shows an unhealthy example to the followers.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: However, a robust discussion should be based on good order so as not to erode the value of unity.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: As elected leaders, it is best for us to be more vigilant in the way we debate because it will become a model and example to the public, because negative examples can create unease and anxiety, and thus will likely lead to polarisation and disunity among the community.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Justice is central in achieving unity especially in a multiracial, multi-religious and multicultural society.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The desire for justice is part of human nature and when there is an injustice, there will be uneasiness.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Their question is, why are MPs elected from non-ruling parties not given the post as was done to the ruling party MPs?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It has been said in this House repeatedly that the PA is a statutory body and is not political in nature, it is neutral and is not inclined towards any political party.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Several reasons have also been shared on why an opposition MP is not appointed as the PA's grassroots adviser.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The experience of serving in ministries and statutory bodies is valuable and most appropriate for such individuals to hold this post.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I believe such appointments will eliminate the issue of injustice, that is, the PA's tendency towards partisan politics.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Once again, I ask that my proposal be given serious consideration if the Government is sincere and honest in further strengthening the principle of unity in diversity.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I would now like to touch on the issue of religion and race, which is considered taboo and sensitive to be discussed openly.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: According to some leaders, such matters should only be discussed behind the scenes.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I think it is time for this matter to be given due attention.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Minister Shanmugam, as reported by the media, said that Singapore should find suitable ways that can be accepted by different generations to discuss issues of religion and race.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: More recently, Minister Edwin Tong also stated, “less confrontation, more mediation, when talking about sensitive issues”.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Such discriminatory incidents are deplorable and should not happen, given that efforts have been made over 55 years to develop a multiracial and multi-religious society.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: These two recent incidents indicate that there should be more open and dynamic approaches to further strengthen understanding, acceptance and tolerance among Singaporeans so that the discriminatory attributes, whether consciously or indirectly, can be better curbed.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: And such efforts should start at a leadership level.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Leaders should be open and not narrow-minded whenever an endeavour or discussion on issues related to religious practices are put forward.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Avoid the use of words or phrases that can cause unease in society, words like “divisive” and “problematic”, when discussing religious issues.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Speeches containing such words and phrases are not helpful to anyone and, in fact, it will give rise to anxiety that can lead to cracks to social cohesion.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: These qualities will enable discussions to be conducted rationally and constructively so that, in the end, they can result in consensus and good solutions for the community.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: If no solution can be agreed upon, at least the discussion can end in a “agree to disagree” situation and mutual respect.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This is what is best in order to maintain unity in diversity.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Humility, openness and tolerance will strengthen unity while negative qualities will create fault lines instead.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This is because leaders are role models to people who follow them.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: While our seniors strive to stay healthy for as long as possible, it is quite inevitable that at some point in time, disease sets in or an injury occurs.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, today, I would like to speak on how we, as a society, can also care well for our seniors and their dignity, in sickness and in infirmity, when they are at their most vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Our seniors may have multiple siblings, but few children.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Their siblings may offer some degree of support to each other, but all are ageing at the same time.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Their children, on the other hand, have to balance the demands of supporting parents while building their own homes, raising kids and fulfilling career aspirations.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In my house visits, I have met many seniors.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: They would tell me about their family portraits, their children and grandchildren.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So often, their children would have moved out and built their own families.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Against this backdrop, we have to recognise the practical limits of the family unit in caring for our seniors if and when their healthcare needs become the highest.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Any intervention would have fiscal or social implications or both.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, as a society, we would need frank and thorough discourse and seek to refresh our compact on personal and shared responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Allow me to touch on some specific areas that we need to look it collectively.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The Government has steadily grown nursing home capacity and continues to do so.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: While we must avoid the moral hazard of institutionalising care as a society, we must also recognise that more families would require the support of long-term full-time institutional care for our seniors.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In the last decade, the sector has improved its quality of care significantly, but I believe it is time to go beyond basic care to dignified care.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: We can do more, in terms of integration with the community, rehabilitation and thoughtful design to improve residents' quality of life.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: For instance, could residents continue to enjoy their favourite hawker food in a nursing home?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Could residents mix with children regularly and bond?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Could our nursing homes be more home than nursing?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: To achieve even better standards, cost of care in the sector would have to go up.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Ultimately, we must keep long-term care dignified and affordable for those who need it the most.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And yet, we must guard against runaway healthcare costs in general.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Indeed, in the COVID-19 "new normal", we face serious fiscal challenges.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I believe we need to start with our hospitals, our tertiary care setting.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: At this point, I would like to declare my interest as an employee in a public healthcare institution.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In our hospitals and tertiary care setting, we must continue to make difficult decisions on standard treatments and therapies.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Even as the range of treatments and therapies available to patients continue to grow, our society would need to constantly review and refresh our consensus on this.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: As importantly, we must continue guarding against fragmentation in tertiary care.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: An encik once told me, "Jantung (heart) got problem, better see jantung doctor lah".

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: That is very understandable, but I wondered, "Hati (liver) also got problem, how?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Paru-paru (lungs), tulang (bone) also got problem, how?" The point is more seniors will be affected by multiple conditions.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And while we would expect to see a specialist for each organ, it may neither be sustainable nor lead to the best overall outcomes.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, increasingly, we should move towards having a single doctor to coordinate care around a patient's whole range of conditions.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: For our healthcare system, this reduces duplication of resources and reduces costs.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But, as importantly, for the patient, it means less visits and more convenience.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Indeed, when illness is stressful and becomes more complex, care should become simpler – one patient, one principal doctor.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This would require patients to shift their expectations about care fundamentally.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And this would require our healthcare professionals to also refresh both mindsets and skillsets, starting with a training framework that must emphasise broad skills on top of deep skills.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But ultimately, no bed matters quite as much to our seniors as the bed at home.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I have attended a number of wakes in my constituency and almost all of these residents who passed on have either passed on at home or wanted to do so.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: We should strive to provide what has traditionally been hospital-level care outside the hospital and in the home.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Providers around the world are exploring this in earnest and we will need to evolve our own way.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This may be a moonshot for our healthcare system, but one that I believe is worthy for us to apply our minds and energies to.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: There had been several debates on this topic in this House, around qualifications, culture and language.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Allow me to share my views with a simple story.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: On 16 March, it was announced that the flow of people across the Causeway would all but cease within two days.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Yet so many of our non-Singaporean nurses decided to stay with us in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Some rushed home to pack before crossing the Causeway just in time, even on foot.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: These nurses have not seen their families for months.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Some have postponed weddings or missed funerals of loved ones.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, if there is anything that COVID-19 has taught the healthcare sector, it is that everyone, Singaporean or Work Pass holder, has made sacrifices and everyone has worked as one team to care for Singaporeans and keep Singaporeans in the community safe.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: COVID-19 has taught us that we need resilience.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: We need a buffer in our system to anticipate disruptions.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And so, I hope Singaporeans can recognise that going forward, we need more locals and more foreign nurses to continue working together as one team to ensure the best care possible for our seniors.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: At the same time, we have to care better for our caregivers.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: We need to define full-time caregiving carefully and guard against abuse in implementation.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But fundamentally, we must recognise that full-time caregivers have sacrificed much in terms of career and income.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Both childcare and parent care are key burdens for Singaporeans in the “sandwich generation”.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, our policy principles for childcare and parent care should be consistent.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Introducing parent-care leave entitlements send an important signal to workers, employers and the whole of society on our collective compact to care for seniors.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: At the same time, we have to recognise the impact on businesses.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Therefore, flexible work arrangements must remain as our most sustainable strategy.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: COVID-19 has changed the way we think about workplace and collaboration, and we must use this opportunity to further cement flexibility of work as part of our new normal.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Thirdly, we should work with caregivers to raise the uptake of Lasting Power of Attorney and Advance Care Planning among seniors.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: These may be difficult conversations, but necessary ones as they significantly reduce caregiver stress down the road.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: We should support our caregivers to plan ahead and plan well with our seniors.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: (In Mandarin):   We all know that Singapore is ageing rapidly.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: When I make house visits, I have met many senior residents.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The good thing is that many of our Pioneer Generation seniors were mistaken by me as the Merdeka Generation and many of those who are from the Merdeka Generation were mistaken by me as being middle-aged.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In other words, our seniors look young and live a good life in their old age.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: As the sandwich class, the children not only have to take care of their parents, but also their own children.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Work and life have brought double amount of stress on them.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Under these circumstances, the society and Government must better support Singaporeans and families, and ensure that seniors are properly taken care of, both physically and mentally, when they get old or fall sick.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Of course, as Deputy Prime Minister has pointed out, our national pocket is not bottomless.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: As a society, how we help to share the burden will be a core issue in our future social compact.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Let us face it squarely, make decisions based on care, protect the dignity of our seniors, and uphold the core value of respecting the elderly.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Keeping our seniors healthy will always be key.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: At the same time, becoming sick and losing functionality is part of being mortal, but it does not have to be morbid.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: We, as a society, must resolve that it will not be morbid for our seniors and the caregivers in our midst.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Families, community and Government must work together to provide dignified care for our seniors and preserve their quality of life as much as possible.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This means even better standards in our nursing homes and allowing as much optionality as possible for care within the home, where our seniors truly want to be.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: He said that both complaints related to his posters being below the 2.2 m minimum height requirement which is meant to prevent posters from obstructing the line of sight for motorists.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Mr Dennis Tan further said that and I quote, "One resident told me that she had witnessed the PAP team pulling down our posters from the original height.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: She showed me where they allegedly took place and I have no reason to doubt what she said." Mr Speaker, Sir, this is a serious allegation.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In its Press Statement on 31 August 2020, ELD invited him to file a report so that it can investigate the matter.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: ELD also explained its enforcement approach when it receives such complaints, which is to ask the Election Agent to rectify the posters in breach of the rules within three hours.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: And in the spirit of constructive politics that we discussed in recent days in this House, it cannot be that a Member stands up to raise doubts and does not follow through to substantiate his allegations.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This is to be fair to all parties involved, protect the integrity of the election processes and continue to uphold trust in our elections.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Would any of Mr Dennis Tan's colleagues like to respond?

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In my walks around Punggol, I meet many young families.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: A young mother shared with me that both she and her husband are essential services workers and as such, she needed a childcare near her home so that she can pick up her young child easily.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: A stay-home mum spoke for an hour with me, worried that her daughter would not qualify via Direct School Admission or DSA to her preferred school as she did not have a certificate to prove her daughter’s talent.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: A young father whose Primary 1 son was diagnosed with mild intellectual disability told me his son is not slow, just relatively slower than his classmates and just needs more time to catch up.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: These stories are diverse and varied, but they all carry a common thread of hope, struggles and dreams that all of us as parents have for our children.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: As parents, we want our children to have the best shot in life, to grow up happy, to have the confidence to chase their dreams and to be successful in life and their profession, whatever that may be.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: As a people, we aspire towards a fair, just and inclusive society where everyone has equal opportunities to develop to their fullest potential, regardless their backgrounds.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Many advanced economies have found that social mobility gets harder to sustain as society progresses and as more well-off parents pass down their resources to their children.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: At the same time, technological displacement to jobs and increasing competition from other markets are demanding a new set of traits for individuals to succeed in life.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Amidst this shifting landscape, what might we expect of our education system?

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I ask this as a mother, and now as an office holder in MOE.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: My hope is that our education system will always remain a social enabler so that everyone, especially those who may have started with less, has the hope and confidence that in Singapore they have equal access to opportunities to do well, achieve their aspirations and find happiness.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I believe that our social conscience tells us that we do not want to create a self-fulfilling class system in Singapore that is entrenched and segregates individuals, limiting them in their endeavours, and stifling hopes and dreams.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I also hope that our education system provides the space for our children to discover their passion and allows them to grow, confidently, in their own time.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Different children flourish at different stages, in different environments and in different realms.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I hope that there are multiple pathways available to them, that schools and parents recognise their diverse strengths and interests and that there is porosity between the pathways to support our children’s varied endeavours.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: And lastly, I hope that our education system serves a wider social purpose of building a sense of solidarity among Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Where our children from diverse backgrounds can learn from one another, interact with each other comfortably and respectfully and through these interactions, find a shared destiny which they continue to believe in even after they grow up.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Globally, research has shown that what happens in the early years is critical in determining how children turn out and how they subsequently fare in life.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The MOE and MSF are therefore intervening earlier, from the pre-schooling years, so that our children regardless their backgrounds, have a good start from which to find fulfilment and joy in life.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Government is also investing significantly in the software aspects of teacher recruitment, progression and professional development.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Taken together, this sends a strong signal that the Government prioritises the early learning years and wants to give every child a good starting point from which they can chart their future paths.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: While the vast majority of each cohort has attended pre-school prior to Primary 1, there is nonetheless a group of children whose attendance is irregular in pre-school and a few who are not even enrolled in pre-school.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We should examine how we can further enable pre-school participation, as the formative years play a critical role in a child’s development.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: With Growing Together with KidSTART, I also hope that more community partners can come forward to partner lower income families in their parenting journey.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: My second point is about expanding educational pathways.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Different children bloom at different stages, in different environments and in different ways.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: To give our children a fair chance to develop and shine, there must be varied educational pathways to better recognise a fuller range of talents and strengths, beyond academic achievements.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: DSA is one way of expanding pathways by providing students an opportunity to progress to their next stage of education through recognition of their diverse talents – in sports, performing arts and so forth.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Our children come from a diverse range of backgrounds and bring with them different experiences, different opportunities that they have had and different personal traits.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We are therefore encouraging schools to dig deeper for potential.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We recognise that the process in trying to identify students’ potential in a particular DSA area is inevitably less straightforward than simply checking if they have demonstrated achievements in the past.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: But if we truly believe in expanding opportunities for all, then we have to try.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Our children can also bring character and personal qualities to a sport or performing art.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Qualities such as resilience, compassion and leadership which help reflect the spirit of the DSA area.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We should also look hard for students that come from a wider range of schools, keep a lookout for them and for talent amongst them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This will truly expand opportunities for more children and offer them more pathways to succeed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I also mentioned earlier that the changing global operating context is demanding a new set of traits for our children to thrive.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We want our children to develop into global citizens, to be able to seize opportunities in the global marketplace, and have the disposition and ability to work with people from different cultures.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We are therefore refreshing our humanities curriculum to deepen our students’ understanding of the histories, cultures and economies of our regional neighbours, and our connections to them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: When the situation allows, we will also expose our students to more global opportunities, through more overseas student exchanges and internships, to strengthen our cross-cultural skills and develop the global perspective to seize opportunities both at home and abroad.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Speaker, Sir, I will like to make a final point about children with special educational needs or SEN in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I visited Grace Orchard School about a month back.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: It is a Special Education or SPED school catering to students with mild intellectual disability and those with mild Autism Spectrum Disorder.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: At the school, students were learning daily living skills, such as personal health and grooming, and picking up work-ready skills such as horticulture.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: But what left an indelible impression on me was how the students interacted with their teachers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: As I walked through the corridors and in the canteen, I heard students spontaneously greeting their teachers with exuberance.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Individual voices rang out, one shouting, "Hello, Mrs Goh"; another one, "Good morning, Ms Low".

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: These were not greetings in unison, they were random, all over the place but full of joy.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The positive energy and love the students have for their teachers was palpable.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We will also actively look for ways to foster purposeful interaction between students with and without SEN to create a truly inclusive environment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Some examples include satellite partnerships between the mainstream and SPED schools, combined teams at the National School Games and joint OBS camps.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: But over and above all that, our children at Grace Orchard School taught me something and reminded me of what education really is about.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Education is not preparation for life; education is life itself, where our children grow up feeling loved, treasured and supported; where they grow up confident and passionate about learning and life; where they are seen for who they are and not what they can or cannot do.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We ourselves hold the keys to building a fair, just and inclusive society – through our efforts in our children’s education.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: (In Mandarin):   I have just shared with you how MOE will work to ensure that our children have opportunities to develop their potential and succeed in many ways, and how we will work to create a more equal and inclusive education environment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: However, for children, family support may be more important for their physical and mental development.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The family is not only a haven for children, but also a basic unit of society, and a cornerstone of national stability.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: However, COVID-19 has resulted in significant pressures to families.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: These are not limited to economic and employment pressures, but also psychological and emotional pressures, which may lead to family conflicts and even family violence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Some couples are worried about financial difficulties, while others are parents working from home but still need to manage their children’s home-based learning, resulting in strained relationship with their children.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: At the same time, we note that COVID-19 has also impacted the formation of new families.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This will have a negative impact on the number of newborns in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: MSF is aware of the challenges faced by families and has taken various measures to help affected Singaporeans and families.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: At the same time, MSF is reviewing other grants and assistance for families, to extend our social safety net.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Besides the Government's efforts, we need more people to look out for those who need help and those who face difficulties but do not know who to turn to for help.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: It is heartening to see the strength of the community and volunteers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I am part of the Youth Mental Well-being Network, which is a collaborative effort with community partners and concerned individuals, involving more than 1,000 volunteers and experts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Through the Singapore Together Action Network, they are working together on issues concerning youth mental well-being.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Inter-Agency Task Force on Family Violence, which I co-chair with Minister of State Faishal, is also pleased to see the participation of many social service agencies, providing their views and helping families in need.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In the area of family formation, we will continue to render assistance to minimise delays caused by COVID-19, so that the newlyweds can collect the keys to their new homes as soon as possible.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: For those whose new flats have been delayed, we will assist them with interim rental housing.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: To mitigate the impact of COVID-19 measures on marriages, MSF has introduced solemnisations via video-link in May and has recently relaxed the guidelines to allow up to 50 persons to attend in-person solemnisations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We will also continue to monitor the situation and explore ways for couples to have memorable weddings despite the pandemic.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We do not wish to see people’s lives come to a standstill because of COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I know that young couples when considering whether to start a family can be concerned about the costs of raising a child.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We will review our policies to see how we can lower the costs for young families in times of crisis.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Looking at the history of mankind, some countries have seen a decline in the wake of a crisis, while others have shown greater social cohesion and vitality.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In the 55 years since Singapore’s independence, we have gone through several crises, such as the social turmoil in the 1960s, the Asian financial crisis in 1997, SARS in 2003, and the global financial crisis in 2008.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: But we become more united after each crisis and emerge stronger after going through a rough patch.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I believe that the resilience of Singaporeans will enable us to ride out the current economic crisis.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Singaporeans' compassion will also enable us to stay together and watch out for one another.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Everyone will face challenges and there will be clear skies for those who ride through the storms.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We will do our best to protect it.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I believe that with the strong corporate and community ties that Singapore has built over the years, and the efforts of our government, community volunteers, community organisations and volunteers, we will take good care of our families, overcome the pandemic and give all Singaporeans and our children a healthy, prosperous and bright future.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Before I begin, I would like to declare that I am a practising lawyer and a member of the board of an Institute of Public Character providing crisis shelter for domestic violence survivors.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: President Halimah Yacob highlighted that we will have to strengthen our safety nets and support every Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Like many other Singaporean parents, I dream of building a stronger and more cohesive society for our children.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: My speech is inspired by my six-year old son and his love for Lego blocks.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But, if you do not connect them properly, then the entire structure may be unstable.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To me, each Singaporean family represents that building block of our society.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These blocks may come in different shapes or colours but when connected together they are stronger and more beautiful.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In order for us to build a more cohesive society, I submit that we will have to continue doing three things.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Supporting families is crucial given the financial and emotional stresses that they now face.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The economic crisis of today may give rise to the social crisis of tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I propose two specific areas of support in healthcare and housing.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For many families I have met in Keat Hong, their common fear is to lose a job or worse, suffer a major illness.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: One of my residents, Mr Tan, suffers from kidney failure and now, a drop in income.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: He is concerned that if the costs of dialysis treatment keep on going up, he would have to dip further into his life savings.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For families like Mr Tan's, we must continue to review how our healthcare safety nets work.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But we must do this in a fiscally responsible manner.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How do we review and increase the limits from MediSave and MediShield Life to help the financial burden now; perhaps we can increase the limit on an interim basis at least during this pandemic period.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Senior Minister of State Heng Chee How has also mentioned such review in his speech.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I have filed a Parliamentary Question related to this.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This will be consistent with the intent behind MAS' relief package initiative which allows residential owners to defer repayment of commercial bank loans up to 31 December 2020.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Besides financial help, we need to explore other ways and frameworks to ease the mental and emotional strains on families to make it easier for family members to share the load and ensure the family stays strong through this crisis.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Especially for those who may need more help.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, the family or the building block is very different now than what it was 30 years ago.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Blended families, unwed mothers, single working adults, taking care of their elderly parents, all make up our building blocks of society.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We must not leave anyone behind especially the vulnerable or what Ms Carrie Tan referenced in her speech yesterday as the "challenged families".

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A chain is no stronger than its weakest link.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We need an ecosystem of stronger connections within our community.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In this respect, I submit that we have to do two things.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: First, we have to work together and then we have to stay together.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To illustrate this, I will refer to the work in ending domestic violence and working with families.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Since the circuit breaker, there is a concern in the rise of domestic violence cases.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, I would caution that these are only the reported cases.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: According to an Ipsos study in 2019, a third of Singaporeans said that they or someone close to them had experienced domestic violence.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Another survey by the International Violence against Women in Singapore found that less than a quarter of victims actually report domestic violence cases to the police.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am using the term "domestic violence" because it encompasses more than just violence between family members.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Under the current legislation, only family violence is specifically defined.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Perhaps it is time to broaden the definition beyond family to domestic violence or revisit the approach in the Family Violence Bill previously proposed in 1995.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Having said that, I am also heartened that the Inter-Agency Task Force on Domestic Violence has been formed, headed by Minister of State Sun Xueling and Minister of State Faishal Ibrahim.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It has connected Government agencies, the judiciary and strategic community partners to address domestic violence issue.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope the Task Force can look at how we can make it easier for the discrete reporting of domestic violence in the case of elderly abuse and immigrant wives.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In Australia, the Department of Home Affairs provide information to immigrant wives on domestic abuse and how to get help upon their entry into the country.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Perhaps we can adopt a similar approach for immigrant wives, so that they too, can understand their rights and protection afforded to them under our laws.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Even after working closely together, we need to ensure that we stay together as one.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: One of my residents in Keat Hong, has been running a foster home in her jumbo flat for the past 15 years.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: People like her create a more stable and supportive environment for these children.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How do we attract and retain more such partners?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We need to find ways to not only incentivise but to also take care of our community partners and volunteers, so that more will be encouraged to step forward.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The broader point I am making is this – we need to see beyond the lens of the beneficiary or recipient.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We need to look at it from the perspective of the provider also.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is in line with the spirit of togetherness that Mr Yip Hon Weng stated in his speech yesterday as well.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With all of these ingredients, we can make it work.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As Henry Ford said, "Coming together is the beginning, staying together is progress and working together is success".

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: At this inflection point for our country, we must embark on our journey together – one of reflection and rebuilding.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Malay):   The process of self-reflection and co-creating solutions is nothing new to the Malay/Muslim community.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I think we should be bold enough to evaluate what is available, revamp what is obvious to us and proceed to build it.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: At the same time, this can help build expertise in the Syariah Court and sensitive issues related to wakaf can be looked into from the lens of the community.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With the existence of the Committee on Future Asatizah (COFA) and the Singapore Community Wakaf initiative, we can build a legal framework that can develop the expertise of religious teachers and meet the needs of the community in the future.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: My hope is that we can make this a success together.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The oft-mentioned spirit of mutual cooperation can change a person's life and unite the community.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Our Malay/Muslim community's sacrifices during the past Ramadan amidst the COVID-19 pandemic gives me hope that we can weather this economic crisis and address the problems faced by our community.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Issues such as drug abuse, divorce and domestic violence are affecting all levels of society and do not differentiate between race or religion.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Therefore, our approach to these issues has changed and should continue to change.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: M3 strategies and approaches should be looked into, not only for our Malay/Muslim community, but also because it can potentially be harnessed by all the communities in our country.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We now face an unparalleled economic crisis and face a single enemy in dealing with COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As we embrace the diversity of recommendations and opinions, we must uphold the core values that were championed by our nation’s pioneers, that is, to place importance on unity in society and diversity.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: When the storm hits the wharf, The anchor is dropped by the seasoned captain, When a crisis hits our shores, Prioritise unity in our nation.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, none of us knows for sure how Singapore will look like after this crisis right now.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But storms draw something out of us that calm seas do not.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If we take care of the building blocks of our society, strengthen the connections and co-create and build together, I believe we can ride through this storm not just surviving but thriving.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What makes Singapore special is that we embrace and celebrate diversity, including the political diversity that makes up this current Parliament.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Political diversity is not the monopoly of any party.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We have seen from the speeches made this week of the diverse views held among all of us.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Yet, we still respect and must hold on to our common values that make us uniquely Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I reflected upon what Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong said in his speech yesterday, about our future and our political discourse.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In Parliament, every word we say here is recorded forever.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I urge and have full confidence that Members of this House will prioritise people over polarising politics.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It must be for the cause, not the applause; the intention and not attention.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We have to set the tone in this House for the discourse of our politics.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It will ring loud here and outside, in our constituencies, in our communities, in our homes.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We have to set the example, history will judge us, our children and their children will judge us as well.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They will either look up to us or look away.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The crisis we face will not define us.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is our responses as a people that would shape our collective future.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Let us continue to play our part to rebuild a more resilient, more inclusive, more vibrant society and economy than ever before.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Together we are greater than the sum of our parts.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But if one part is not connected, then everything else may fall apart.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singapore’s journey in the last 60 years has been remarkable.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: At the time of our Independence, we were very much a developing country.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If we look at the numbers, it is a remarkable growth.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, of course, the growth that that generation experienced would have been remarkable.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This, again, by any standard, is a big number.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But in proportion, it is three times the growth.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This clearly put us very much amongst the First World nations.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singapore has been criticised for focusing too much on GDP.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But I think this is a luxury we have after we have achieved that growth, a luxury that has given us many opportunities.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For comparison, if we compare these figures to, say, the UK – which was also not a very successful country and was our former colonial masters – we actually see how remarkable this achievement is.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In 1960, the UK’s GDP per capita was about US$1,398, about three times ours.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In 1990, the same second timeframe, it was US$19,095, still more than 60% higher than ours – no longer triple but still significantly more.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In 2006, its GDP was about US$44,600, again, higher than ours, but only about 25% higher.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As of last year, the UK’s GDP per capita was $42,300, according to the World Bank figures, and this is actually slightly lower than it was in 2006, and, now, 30% below ours.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is not meant to be a criticism of the UK but just to show how difficult it is to achieve growth once you have become a developed nation and the UK has been maintaining its GDP for the last 14 years but it has been difficult to achieve growth.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, if you compare that as the benchmark, I think the current term of government has done incredibly well.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It has grown GDP from a high benchmark to an even higher benchmark.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is why, in many ways, we are in no-man's land.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There is an old saying in Tamil which goes: “இக்கரைக்கு அக்கரை பச்சை”.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In English, you will be familiar with this.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It means, “The grass is greener on the other side”.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, for many of us, we may look at other developed countries and think we are inferior and then say, "Look, we have to replicate them".

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But I think this sometimes understates how good things are over here.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is not to say we are perfect and this is not to say we cannot learn.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We have to always learn, we always have to look outwards.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But at the same time, we also cannot let go of things that have worked for us and which we have been doing right.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In this speech, I want to touch on three themes that I think are important for this.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The first is openness; the second, equality; and the third is fairness.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The first topic I am touching on is openness.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Openness has been one of the most important themes for Singapore's economy since its founding.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: When the British set up Singapore and planted their flag in Singapore about 200 years ago, the population was less than 1,000.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But at that time, Raffles saw Singapore as a place where the region and perhaps even larger parts of the world could come to trade.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As Singapore grew as a trading port, as part of a bigger global empire, more and more people moved here, including from the Malay peninsular, China and India, where many of our ancestors are from.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, it was, in fact, Singapore's openness from inception that brought many of us here.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: At the time of Independence, Singapore had a choice.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Many countries that won independence from colonial masters sometimes cut roots altogether.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: They said "We want nothing more to do with the rest of the world.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We did not burn bridges with our colonial masters.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The British continued to provide for our defence for some years after our Independence.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We played a part in the Commonwealth, we joined international organisations.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We brought new industries and new businesses here and this is what actually helped Singapore grow during the early years.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In the earlier speeches, Minister Ong Ye Kung talked about the financial sector – one area where many Singaporeans are feeling angst about foreigners taking their jobs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Our senior management, I think, could do better but the numbers still stand at 44% Singaporean and these are jobs that would not have been here if we were not open.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Yesterday, in his speech, Prime Minister Lee talked about many sectors, including oil and gas and pharmaceuticals.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Other sectors not mentioned include areas like manufacturing.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But many of these areas grew on the back of our being open and allowing people to come in and build a base here.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I am also heartened that, during this difficult time, Singapore remains open.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think the Prime Minister mentioned in his speech yesterday that EDB has a longer pipeline of projects this year than last year, including companies looking to develop treatments for COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is good news for Singaporeans and jobs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But in order to benefit from this, we have to remain open.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Equality is something that I think every society strives for.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: During the Cold War, there were two very different conceptions of equality.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: On the one hand, you can say the US perhaps epitomises it.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It talked very heavily about equality of opportunity – whoever you are, wherever you are, you must have a chance to succeed.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But equality of opportunity almost always creates inequality of outcomes.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If everyone is given the same chance, some people will do better than others; the outcomes will be different.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It can be hard work, it can be luck.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Or it can also be privilege – you had a better starting position.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But if you focus on giving everyone equal opportunities, your outcomes will not be equal.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The second side, you might say, is the ideal of communism – equality of outcome.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, the ideal world, in that conception, was that whatever you do, it did not matter.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As long as you did your best, everyone will get the same outcome.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But no society has been able to achieve that.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Even in the more strongly socialist countries, outcomes were still different.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is just that those differences were less.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But one big problem with that conception of equality was that the human desire to do your best to achieve was significantly dampened.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And George Orwell and many other commentators observed that the only way you could have complete equality of outcome is in a totalitarian state and that was undesirable because, ultimately, the state has to take control of everything, tell people what to do and everyone one outcome.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, where we are after the Cold War is that everyone more or less said, okay, equality of opportunity is the way to go.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But, of course, 20 years down, we realised that equality of opportunity also has problems.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One of the biggest problems is the entrenchment of privilege.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is why I think governments still have a role to play to ensure that the playing field remains fair and that everyone will still have a chance to do well, even if we focus on equality of opportunity.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This actually brings me to my point on fairness, which is the third pillar in what I think is important.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Fairness is something which Singapore has worked very hard to achieve.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is something that we enshrine in our Constitution and with express policies to promote.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This was about six or seven years ago at a time when ISIS was brewing as a problem for the world.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: At that time, Singapore was also concerned about this.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But my European counterpart was asking me, "How do you deal with this issue of returning fighters?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: You have a Muslim population that is about the same size as ours but you do not seem to have many people going to the Middle East to fight, whereas we have..." at that time, he said, "...more than a hundred people who were going and there is not much we could do about them because people are free to travel".

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: At that time, he was actually asking us about our Internal Security Act and he thought that that was the main reason we did not have so many people going there to fight.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We had a very interesting conversation because I asked him a little bit more about the Middle East.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: He said that the Muslim community was about the same size in our two countries.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, I asked him, "You said many of them were going to fight.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But how well integrated is your Muslim community with the rest?" He said, "They are not discriminated.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But they all like to live together." Then I also asked after that, "Do you have any of them in parliament?" and he mentioned "No, they are not in parliament.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But, yes, they do not run, so they are not in parliament." So, they have a very laissez faire approach to it.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But the outcome of that laissez faire approach was that it looked like you had a community that was not well integrated, not well represented and, therefore, felt like an outsider, whereas one of the things about our community is that all the different communities are very well integrated.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And, certainly, when it comes to radicalism and so on, usually, most of our leads come from the community itself, the rehabilitation takes place through the community and everyone sees themselves as part of the same project.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, this is a very important part of equality and fairness.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This requires at least gentle legislation to put people together and then people can form bonds.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, yes, we can explore this, but it is something that we should be slow to let go.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But there are three things that I do think we can change and these are suggestions along the way.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, when I talk about fairness, what fairness really means is that wherever you are, you should have a fair shot.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: John Rawls, in his Theory of Justice, said that for any society, the ideal benchmark of fairness is you decide and structure the society without knowing where you will be, so that, wherever you are, you will feel this is a fair society.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think, in Singapore, it should be wherever you are, rich, poor, minority, of whatever ethnic group, you should feel you have a fair shot at life.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There are three areas we could look at to improve.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I had mentioned very early on, even before I became a father, that I actually thought it was important to socialise pre-school course as well.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Everyone had to go in for Primary school.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: At that time, in Primary school, that was where you learn to read and write.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But now, what has happened is that more and more people are starting out at pre-school.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It has been made significantly more affordable but it is still more expensive than Primary school.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And those who can afford it or are deemed to be able to afford it, will have to pay.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Standards are variable and parents sometimes have a perception that some pre-schools are significantly better than others and, therefore, there are different starting points.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I acknowledge that the socialising of pre-school to try and make it equally accessible, free and, potentially, even compulsory, will be significantly more than Primary school.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, this is a big prize to get the item and this is something that we should focus on if the Budget allows it.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These are things we can do, now that we are a richer country.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But, again, it has to be balanced against other priorities.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, this is the pre-school level, the very early starting point.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The second area where we could put a bit more focus on is, once you move to the Secondary level, people diverge between vocational paths and more academic paths.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Germany is a country in Europe which has the fewest number of graduates per capita but it also has one of the highest GDP per capita.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: That is because vocational jobs in Germany pay very well.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, I think it is important for us to look into why there is discrepancy between vocational pay as compared to the pay of graduates.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If a skilled vocational person is able to add value, they should be able to command a higher salary than graduates.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In most developed countries, vocational pay is higher.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The implication for this, of course, is that when you pay for service, you have to pay more as well.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But I think if you are talking about progressing fairly, this will be one area that probably requires more careful study.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The third area is what I would call, a workplace discrimination.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And here we have had very longstanding debates taking place about whether or not Singaporeans are being discriminated in their workplace.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And I think MOM has a very clever lever at the moment.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This, of course, is perfectly logical; it is a very effective tool.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But the group of people who are left dissatisfied with this process are the people who feel they are victims of the discrimination, because they themselves have no recourse.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I would also add that workplace discrimination legislation has had a mixed history in different countries.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In some places because of anti-discrimination legislation, people actually get more afraid to hire from that discriminated community.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Any anti-discrimination legislation has to be careful, but I think if the focus of discrimination is on Singaporeans and foreigners, I think it will be a line that we will be able to maintain.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: What this basically means is that, on the one hand, MOM as the regulator will manage the access to work passes, rights to employ more foreigners and so on, if they are deemed not to be fair to Singaporeans; but at the same time, if legislation is there to give the individual aggrieved recourse, I think that would also make Singaporeans feel they have had a fairer hearing.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: They will know that my specific case was considered, my grievance was considered, and yes, there was an outcome.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think this is an important process that will add to the feeling of fairness.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I have laid out three suggestions that I think would help in the fairness aspect which is ultimately important for us to get support for the Government.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: At the base of this triangle are physiological needs.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The need for safety is at the next level.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Together, these two lowest levels make up what we call basic needs.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The next level is relationship and intimacy needs which we derive a lot from interaction with friends and family.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This is then followed by esteem needs which we derive often from our work and education.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: At the apex of this triangle, is our self-actualisation need – that feeling of achieving our potential through accomplishing something creative or extraordinary.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Maslow's hierarchy of needs is not really just a tool to explain our needs, but really to explain what motivates us.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I think many of us have also realised that our relationships with family and friends are very precious during these last few months, especially during the circuit breaker period.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Indeed, many of us are more attuned to our basic and psychological needs than ever before and realise that in the hustle and bustle of the pre-COVID world, we may have taken them somewhat for granted.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But I would like to say that even when the future looks bleak and the world looks more dangerous than ever, we should not neglect higher needs for self-actualisation and esteem.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Jobs do not just put food on the table, jobs also give us esteem and a chance to self-actualise.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But, Sir, beyond jobs and the economy, which are of paramount importance now, there are also other areas that deserve our attention and resources.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It is part of our nation-building process that goes on every day, with or without COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I had watched this movie made by local director Ms Eva Tang when it was first screened more than five years ago in our cinemas and I watched it again when it was made available on Netflix.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It chronicles the birth and development of a Singapore genre of Mandarin music called Xinyao that began in the late 1970s and flourished in the 1980s.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It was written and performed by Chinese educated students of a transitional generation that faced many difficult challenges.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I belong to that generation, although I am not Chinese-educated and I cannot write music or sing.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I went to Hwa Chong Junior College between 1980 and 1981 when the Xinyao movement was just starting and gushing with creative energy.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In 1981, when Liang Wern Fook, the now famous singer-songwriter and also Xinyao pioneer, was elected President of the Students' Council in Hwa Chong, Xinyao gained even greater prominence.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Subjects such as math, physics and geography, which they had learnt in Chinese previously, had to be relearnt in English.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
