text: On top of that, news of the merger of University of Singapore and Nanyang University to form National University of Singapore in 1980 was already circulating strongly in the Junior College community then.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: To these Chinese-educated schoolmates in our midst, it was a further blow to some of them as it meant there was effectively no more place for them to pursue their dreams of a Chinese-stream university education.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It was also widely reported in the mass media that good job opportunities were far and few between for Chinese-educated students.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It was truly a sink or swim, do or die for them in the English-stream Junior Colleges.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Many of them did not despair, but some did.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I could see it in their eyes then.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Many of them were active in Chinese literary clubs and Xinyao groups that blossomed in many Junior Colleges, even as they struggled on a daily basis in a titanic struggle to master English and wondered what an English-based economy had in store for them.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: They seemed to feel like strangers in their own land, somewhat marginalised and dislocated even.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: As these youths took refuge in their music and writings, many good things happened.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The energy, optimism and purity of spirit of the Xinyao movement and its student performers is exactly what we need now.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This is derived from cultural activities such as music and literature.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The Xinyao music gave these young people strength to face another day and helped them to forget, for a while, the harsh realities that buffeted them daily.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The relationships and camaraderie that were forged during those times by not just the performers but by all who listened to Xinyao in the early 1980s, also undoubtedly helped many Chinese-educated persons to weather the existential questions that they came face to face with.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: There is more to sports than just getting fit and deriving the physical health benefits from sports.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The South Africa rugby team helped Nelson Mandela to unite South Africa during the 1995 Rugby World Cup.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: South Africa was a country that was just emerging from apartheid then.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This story was made into the movie "Invictus" in 2009.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: More than ever now, we need to believe in ourselves.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: To paraphrase the last two lines of the poem, "Invictus" – "We are the masters of our fate, We are the captains of our soul." Mr Speaker, I will end by saying that it is very tempting to relegate culture and sports to insignificance in times of a public health and economic crisis.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Through my admittedly brief time interacting with Sengkang residents, an underlying theme that unites them is the aspirations they have for Singapore in the 21st Century.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Therefore, I wish to speak today about compassionate policy-making.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The word "compassion" refers to a sympathetic concern for others by linking compassion to policy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I am suggesting that the design of our national policies need to be more cognisant of how these policies play out – not just on the aggregate but also how they impact different groups, especially those at the margins of society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Students of policy learn very early on that the policy-making process comprises two key pillars.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The first – efficiency – describes how well policy deploys the resources available at our disposal.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The second – equity – speaks to the sense of fairness inherent in resulting policy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Ultimately, policy entails a trade-off between the two.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Traditionally, our policy-makers have prided themselves on being stewards of rational, efficient policy-making.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Accordingly, Singaporeans have been called to acquiesce to policies of tough love, sacrificing individual justice on the altar of national progress.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be clear, this has worked well for us over three generations and has brought us from Third World to First.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And so, we as a nation have shied away from the sort of policies that will lend support to certain segments of society if it also meant that we had to compromise our deeply rooted sense of personal responsibility for the economic and social circumstances that we happen to find ourselves in.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This, indeed, has been the cornerstone of our national belief in meritocracy and self-sufficiency.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But the truth is, reality is often far more complex than we are willing to allow or admit.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Workers do not simply collapse into a state of dependency when offered supportive handouts by Government because most people find a sense of purpose and meaning in work, even when they draw humble salaries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Children born into poor, broken families leave school early, not merely because they are lazy or lack talent but because when they fall behind, they lack resources to help them catch up and some may be discouraged and question their own abilities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: People fall into debt, not just because they have irredeemable penchant to gamble their lives away but because those little bets they place offer them the best hope for escaping what they perceive to be dreary, hopeless situations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I am not suggesting that we stop rewarding hard work or success or that we squander the fruits of past generations by irresponsible expenditures to prop up undeserving individuals and families in the name of progressive policy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What I am suggesting, Mr Speaker, is that the sort of decisions we make as a society and as a country should no longer privilege efficiency at the sheer expense of equity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Because we are no longer a Third World nation, we cannot continue to operate as if we are blind to the consequences that tough nose policies carry for our people.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is especially so at the time when we need to help everyone pull in the same direction for our collective future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In her speech Mdm President spoke about the importance of building a fair and just society, about sharing the benefits of progress with all citizens.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The hard truth is though, in as much as we have, indeed, progressed over the past few decades, the gains from this progress have not been equally shared across society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is, therefore, undeniable that our existing approach to policy-making can benefit from a greater injection of compassion and thoughtfulness.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet the fear that many policy-makers often hold when they talk about policy reform is that we must not break the system that has worked so well for us.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Sure, we recognise a need for change, but let us do it slowly in careful steps.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, the policies we pursue turn out to be tentative, incremental, "kiasu".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The problem with this approach, Mr Speaker, is that such marginal changes do little to right the boat.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As a nation, we have, fortunately, yet to experience the sort of populist pressures for change that have plagued so many other developed nations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I speak with residents, many who are modest and unassuming who, nevertheless, feel crushed by the dual weight of high costs and low wages, with seemingly little compassion for their plight.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is wonderful if your view of human nature is that people would otherwise while away their time but unconscionable when it requires our elderly to continue working into their sunset years, or if we wish to provide genuine support for single working mothers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We talk about the importance of improving the quality of life after retirement, yet we remain overwhelmingly rigid and insist on ensuring the future adequacy of their CPF savings, even when they face extenuating financial circumstances that are causing severe distress today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We excessively constrain the usage of MediSave, leaving seniors with chronic conditions, the tab of paying for their expenses that exceed the annual withdrawal caps.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We remain stubbornly afraid of policies that involve redistribution even when our workers secure some of the lowest share of income in the developed world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We often default to the mindset that equates redistribution with sloth while glossing over the enormous challenge of making a living while being pinched from below by low-cost foreign workers and out-competed from above by high skilled foreign talent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This leaves are blue-collar workers feeling left behind and our PMETs increasingly insecure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: These policies, and others like these, demonstrate that we are in fact capable of injecting compassion into our policy choices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My contention then is that we are certainly able to do more, much more.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: When we pursue policy-making under the umbrella of compassion, we seek to relieve the suffering of others, which is the key component of the definition of compassion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: When we prioritise compasssion, we become more willing to err on the side of equity, perhaps at some expense to efficiency.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This means a willingness to accept the it may be better to allow for a policy where one or two out of every hundred individuals may end up exploiting or abusing the policy, but at the same time that others clearly benefit from being supported by the expanded social safety net.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But compassionate policy can also be robust policy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Engineers keenly understand that when design becomes too complicated, too involved, too tailored to extract every last ounce of efficiency, it can also be fragile, embedding multiple points of failure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Robust policy is better suited to deal with the sort of high uncertainty post pandemic environment that we find ourselves in.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, when policy is gamed into no longer yielding first-best outcomes, the second best policy is often drastically different in form from the original.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Some may argue that as we face down the worst crisis of our generation, the time is not right for us to pursue such "soft" policies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What we need is a tough nosed policies that require all of us to make sacrifices for the greater good.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: When we call on Singaporeans to make such sacrifices – and I believe we are more than willing to come together to do so – we also need to reassure Singaporeans that the fruits of such sacrifice will not only accrue to certain winners after the storm has passed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Not only that, I also believe that improving the social protections we offer to people can be an important path to blunting the sorts of populist, nationalist pressure that has reared its head in so many countries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I do not believe that Singaporeans are inherently anti-foreigner.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, we are a nation of immigrants and we have been an open trading society for centuries of our history.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But what has inspired recent resistance to foreigners is concern about unmitigated population expansion, a sense that they are not getting a fair shake, of feeling discriminated in their own country.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is a sense that the Government does not appear to have their backs and that their foothold on prosperity is so precarious that once they fall, there is no way back.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Of course, the best time for enacting policies that imply some degree of redistribution and introduction of frictions to unfettered market forces is not when we are in the throes of an unprecedented crisis.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But I also believe we should be able to walk and chew gum at the same time – although the latter is admittedly difficult in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: When the crisis has blown over, we will be prepared to implement the policies we commit to today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Besides, policies that emphasise compassion also matter in the immediate term even as we confront the worst economic crisis of our generation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: When we do so, we are exercising the sort of compassionate policy-making that is necessary to help tide us over this crisis and to emerge stronger.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is understanding that when we fail to adequately allocate schooling spots to nearby schools, we compel hard-working parents to endure additional costs to raising the family – like the Goh family who shared with me about how all their lives, they have always coloured within the lines, live their lives as good citizens and never asked for what they feel is beyond reasonable expectations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet they have been informed that their elder daughter is unable to enrol in any Primary school in their neighbourhood and they are now forced to add additional travel to their already taxing daily schedules.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is understanding that when we insist on the fulfilment of standard feasibility studies before deciding on improvement projects, we impose additional burdens on our elderly – like the case of Mr Tan who has asked for years to no avail that the overhead bridge beside his block install an elevator.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet, the overwhelmingly young demographic of his neighbourhood means that the two senior blocks have effectively been neglected, resulting in their continued difficulties whenever these elderly residents wish to take a bus.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is understanding that when we asked students to study hard and do well, we have also led them to expect that there are opportunities available for them after they have fulfilled their end of the bargain.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, when we have graduates like Danny or JK, who are unable to secure a decent job after graduation because they feel that they are being displaced by globalisation or foreign talent, we should not be surprised when they become disillusioned and angry.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: When their educational training has repeatedly assessed them on what to think instead of teaching them how to think.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We should be unsurprised, when they feel betrayed by the system that they feel has not adequately prepared them for the jobs of the 21st century.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is understanding that when foreign workers under our charge gets sick, we owe a moral responsibility to take care of them and nurse them back to health as we have correctly chosen to do.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And there are many more and we hope to raise these in this House in the months ahead.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Almost eight centuries ago the Sufi poet and scholar, Jalal ad-Din Rumi, wrote of such empathy in his poem "A Great Wagon".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Rumi implored for us to go out beyond ideas of wrong-doing and right-doing: where there is a field, I will meet you there.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is inherent on us in this House to find a better balance to the policies we pursue for the future of Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We can do so by embracing more compassion in our policy-making.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And with that, I support the Motion of Thanks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I have a question for Assoc Prof Jamus Lim.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I agree that we must exercise and demonstrate compassion in policy-making.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: And in fact, I think that is what the Government has been trying to do in many of the policies, and as a result, sometimes our policies become very complicated because we understand that there is no one-size-fits-all policy that treats all problems.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I have a specific question and it is about Minimum Wage.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I am not sure if I heard correctly.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim seemed to have suggested that Minimum Wage can be implemented with minimal impact on unemployment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: There are unintended consequences of some policies with good intent, but I think we must understand the context and the circumstances that we are in, so that we do not unintentionally cause more distress to our lower wage workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: It actually warms my heart that in this very House, others in the PAP ranks have in fact echoed a lot of these sentiments: Patrick Tay and Henry Kwek spoke more about balance in foreign PMET hiring; Mariam Jafaar about discounting paper qualifications; and Louis Ng, in fact, about compassion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, in fact, you could even say that they have become PAP-lite.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So that when we set these plans in place after the storm has passed, we can easily bring them to pass.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: I have a clarification to Member Jamus Lim's point about Minimum Wage.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: There is a fundamental difference between what the Government has said so far about the Progressive Wage Model or PWM versus the Minimum Wage.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: This is not a new concept which was thought of just after the General Election.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: If you were to talk members of the NTUC, for example, they have talked about the PWM since 2012, and there is in fact a key difference between PWM and Minimum Wage, in that it is differentiated across sectors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: These are pains in which the union, the Government and the employers come to a position on, in what is bearable for every sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: And the fact that there is a ladder also tells us that there is recognition that we want to bring workers to different productive levels too, to make sure that workers continue to upgrade and get paid better.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We have seen the impact of the PWM.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Minister Josephine Teo mentioned that in her speech.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: The expansion of PWM is not something new that we just talked about.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: The reason why we have taken a bit of time – and you have seen how PWM has been implemented over the past few years, including the most recent round announced for the lift and escalator sector – is that we have to come to positions that are bearable; that it is not just a blunt tool, a straight line across all sectors, to the point that you will find employment being difficult for some.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Some stalls are family-owned; so some assistants are members of the family helping each other and so, the family businesses are what you have to think about.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: So, there are different considerations and things that we have to work out across sectors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: It is something that we have been working on since 2012 till now.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: In fact, even before that, the unions have really raised this.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: It is just that we have implemented them in stages.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: It is something that we have already announced that we will expand, once times are better.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: The second point that the Member raised is that we have to talk about compassion.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: I think it is easy to talk about compassion when it is just mere talk.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: If you have got to put money on the table, you have also to consider, as a Government, where that money comes from; and how you manage the Budget, whether you have to raise GST.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: I think where the PAP Government has made a difference is that we put the money where our mouth is.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: I think many Singaporeans have also felt the impact of the Care and Support Package.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: The Job Support Scheme, I think, is one of the best forms of unemployment insurance to some extent, where you can see many jobs being saved during this period.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: So, to some extent there is a lot of compassion.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: But I think you have to realise that this is also a whole system put in place.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: The last part where the Member talked about 25% of our population are in the low wage group.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Can the Member let us know what is his benchmark or basis for saying so?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: What is the definition of living wage or Minimum Wage that Workers’ Party subscribes to?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: This translates into up to 30% of extra income for them, so that we – the society – bear the burden, transferring back taxes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: You do not push this onto the consumers so that you also manage the level of inflation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Over time, you have seen wages go up through PWM.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We hope as we expand it, we will get more workers on board.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: What is also important is that you do not just work on the minimum.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: As you can see for the different sectors, the security sector earns more than the cleaning.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: So, why work on one level when we can work at different levels, making it relevant to the productivity and the levels of wages that each sector can afford.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: And last but not least, if you look at the proof of the pudding.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: The transfers that the Government gives go beyond just wages, but they encompass the whole system where I think a large part of our low-wage workers are given that shelter, that stability for their children to be able to grow up in stable homes, given the opportunities to rise.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: And many of us came from those kinds of families too.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: To be able to give good shelter, good education systems.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: All these come to play in how this Government has been compassionate in its policies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: And I hope that with our further debates in this House, there is more that can be done.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: One, he talked about how there is a fundamental difference between the PWM and Minimum Wage, in that it is differentiated across sectors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: That is, in part, why I anticipated that point in my speech and mentioned that when you start to over-engineer a system, you run the risk that it can get gamed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I do not want to get too technical, but there is a theorem in public policy-making that when you are unable to hit your first best policy, it is very likely that your second best policy is going to be extremely different from the original.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, you want to be careful when you try to over-engineer and try to squeeze out every bit of efficiency when you are working with imperfect knowledge about conditions on the ground.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The other issue with the Minimum Wage is that as long as you have the possibility that another sector has a Minimum Wage that is different from the first, you run the risk that there is going to be substitution between one sector versus another.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: You want to shut out this possibility of substituting between workers in one sector and another such that employers end up gaming the system in that fashion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, I am giving you a bigger slice of this pie, but it is still a much, much, smaller slice of the pie than the kind of pie that other workers in other high-income countries are able to enjoy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, I would be willing to trust their numbers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: He also talked about how with the PWM and making it universal, it is a step that has come closer to us.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I am much more of an ideas person.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, rather than looking at the city-scape, I tend to look at the policy landscape.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: When I see that the incumbent's position is now closer to us, I say to myself – what a skyline – and I thank the voters for helping us to get a little closer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: A final point – where does the money come from?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Well, it is important to know and this speaks a little bit to the debate yesterday in this House as well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: We should not think about government budgets in the same fashion that we think about household budgets.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: People can bequest things onto the next generation but by and large, households eventually perish.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Because of that, we can think in a much more longer term.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: There is the possibility that the Government can over-save and in a time where interest rates are at record lows.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Ask yourself, is it time for you, even as an individual, to perhaps re-mortgage your home?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: If you think that re-mortgaging with low interest rates is a good idea, that is about expanding leverage, that is about borrowing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, if I may argue that what we want is to make the best use of financial resources and not cling to some rigid ideology that we should never touch.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The way we should think about expenses such as our reserves, is not that we are people who will spend the reserves.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: We are stewards and as stewards, we are responsible not just for ensuring that the pot will grow over time, but as stewards, we are also responsible for taking the right financial decisions which in certain times may involve spending for higher investment things.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: What are some of these higher investment things?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: These are higher return things from which we can extract higher returns, so that in the future, we will be able to get higher tax revenue that will more than pay for the expenses that we incur today.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Second, is the Member aware of any countries with a Minimum Wage that has a lower unemployment rate than Singapore?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Because I think that would be a case study for us.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I do not know and that is exactly why what we need is a national commission to understand this and to study this.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: That would be what I would argue that we should have, if I were to ask for a practical policy proposal.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: It should be staffed by university professors as well as representatives from both the unions and firms.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: It should be filled with these people to better understand what is a good level and to adjust.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: We are a pragmatic country, a pragmatic policy-making nation, and so we can adjust accordingly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, I should be clear that when I talk about the absence of an unemployment effect, I am not using theory to make this argument.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: It is based on empirical evidence which has been backed by studies from countries all over the world, not just in high-income countries.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: First of all, it is more to clarify my understanding.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: By that, how might it be more efficient?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The third question is that I understand based on the hon Member's response to hon Member Mr Vikram, is that there is no specific number that he has in mind in terms of Minimum Wage.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Perhaps to give us a better idea is, for your Town Council, what is the Minimum Wage given to your cleaners?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I think that would give us some form of reference.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The last question is I can feel his passion about youths and Singaporeans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The first is whether I agree with Member Gan that rolling out Minimum Wage would have adverse consequences.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: It was a necessary but not sufficient condition.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I did say that this is not an ideal time but I do not know if we were to roll out the Minimum Wage, whether this would result in actual adverse consequences.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, it is a necessary but not sufficient condition.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Personally, I do not necessarily think that rolling out the Minimum Wage is a good time, but I would not go the second step of saying that it would imply adverse consequences.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The second point is whether we want to roll in and out of the Minimum Wage.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: In fact, I would argue the complete opposite.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The whole point of something like a Minimum Wage is to provide the kind of social safety net.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: If you were to roll out of the Minimum Wage at a time when you are in a crisis, that would pull the rug out from under those workers who rely on the Minimum Wage in a time of crisis.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, that is an absolutely wrong-headed way to go about implementing this policy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But let me take the more general spirit of the question.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Can we just roll out a Minimum Wage in a given Town Council?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And again, this comes from the fact that you have general equilibrium effects.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: If we were to roll out the minimum wage in only one sector of the country, what would happen is substitution and what would happen is you will have the low-wage jobs migrate out of a given country.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: What you want is an across-the-board, universal Minimum Wage to apply to the entire country and that is precisely why I think that is the way forward.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And at least in so far as the PWM is concerned, I would agree with the notion of universality.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This is tricky in part because youth unemployment tends to be very cyclical.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, when you have unemployment especially by the youth in a crisis period, what happens is that that is often a reflection of a decision to delay entry into the labour force and to end up taking more education.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, you would see an increase in unemployment in a time such as this, when we are in crisis, but it is actually not a bad thing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: You want these people to actually go in and build up their human capital —

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: While I appreciate his erudition in economics – and I am learning quite a lot from him – he has not answered Ms Tin's question.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: If I may clarify, which question did I not answer?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Ms Tin asked if you had a proposal for youth employment, not the principles under which youth employment change or does not change.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Yes, but why that context is important is because we do not want to roll out specific proposals to address youth unemployment in a time when we are in a recession because we are not sure if the unemployment is justified or not.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, that is the reason for me stating that context.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, I do not have a specific policy in mind because I have not thought about it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This is a very slow 8086 processor, that kind of dates me —

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: As an accountant, I am rather perturbed by something Assoc Prof Jamus Lim said just now.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: If I heard you correctly, you said that given low interest rate, it is now time to re-mortgage your properties.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: As an accountant with over three decades of experience, I can tell you that is how people start getting into trouble.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Having a balance sheet is good, having savings is not a sin, having savings like the way we have it, is very good.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: So, may you clarify on what you have just said?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: No, in fact, you did not hear me wrongly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: That is exactly why I mentioned the distinction between a government budget identity and that of a regular household.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Governments have an infinite horizon and so it is entirely possible for governments to over-save.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I used the mortgage situation just to illustrate the point that there are instances where if you borrow against low interest rates and you invest in something that would give you higher returns, that is not just financially prudent, it is in fact going to be better for your balance sheet in the long run.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: You are always assuming that tomorrow will be better than today.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: I do not want to go into an argument about economics here.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: You said because of the low interest rate, I mortgage and then I reinvest to get a better return.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: You are assuming there is a better return which may never come.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: No, I am not assuming a better return.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I am saying if there are projects that give you better returns today, you should engage in those.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Substitute out from the lower returns that are already locked in by your ability to borrow at low interest rates.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, it is not assuming a future euphoria.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: It is recognising that there are higher return projects today, unless you are saying that the youth of today in Singapore are not worth investing in.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I do not think that was the point that was made.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: So, I will start with Minister of State Zaqy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It could be a bit more, it could be a bit less, but that is my inference from answers to Parliamentary Questions that we got earlier.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Let us assume that it is 100,000 earning less than $1,300 per month.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Of course, there could be dual-income, triple-income households.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But for those earning $1,300 per month, I assume that not everyone will be covered by the Progressive Wage Model.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I think that is a reasonable and fair assumption.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Does the Minister of State believe that there is no room for policy improvement for this group?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Should this group wait until the Progressive Wage Model comes to them?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Is there no room for improvement and what would the Minister of State say to those individuals?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: My second point of clarification is to Minister of State Gan.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There is actually quite considerable academic evidence for this proposition.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And I would like to ask the Minister of State Gan would she consider that actually the danger to jobs is not setting a Minimum Wage, but setting a Minimum Wage too high, which is definitely not what we are advocating.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: My third clarification is to Mr Vikram Nair who asked whether there is another country that has a Minimum Wage and has a lower unemployment than we have in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister, Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister-in-charge of The Monetary Authority of Singapore (Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam)
text: I was not intending to speak and I just thought I would make a very brief intervention.

speaker: The Senior Minister, Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister-in-charge of The Monetary Authority of Singapore (Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam)
text: I would not – and I say this to everyone from all sides – I would not exaggerate the differences between the PWM and the Minimum Wage Model.

speaker: The Senior Minister, Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister-in-charge of The Monetary Authority of Singapore (Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam)
text: The sectoral approach actually has a lot to commend it because it allows you to set the minimum rung at a level that is not so low and not so high.

speaker: The Senior Minister, Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister-in-charge of The Monetary Authority of Singapore (Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam)
text: Because if you have a single level, you will have to decide where to pitch it.

speaker: The Senior Minister, Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister-in-charge of The Monetary Authority of Singapore (Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam)
text: How to do it without having gaming is an issue that policy-makers grapple with.

speaker: The Senior Minister, Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister-in-charge of The Monetary Authority of Singapore (Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam)
text: Not such a complicated issue in practice, to be frank.

speaker: The Senior Minister, Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister-in-charge of The Monetary Authority of Singapore (Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam)
text: And you have to watch what happens at the edges, but it is a very sensible approach.

speaker: The Senior Minister, Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister-in-charge of The Monetary Authority of Singapore (Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam)
text: And I say this not to discredit anyone.

speaker: The Senior Minister, Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister-in-charge of The Monetary Authority of Singapore (Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam)
text: In particular, I really respect where Member Jamus Lim is coming from – intellectually, emotionally and so on.

speaker: The Senior Minister, Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister-in-charge of The Monetary Authority of Singapore (Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam)
text: But no one should assume that you have a monopoly over compassion.

speaker: The Senior Minister, Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister-in-charge of The Monetary Authority of Singapore (Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam)
text: I have listened to speeches over the last few days amongst everyone.

speaker: The Senior Minister, Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister-in-charge of The Monetary Authority of Singapore (Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam)
text: I must say some of my PAP colleagues really made an impression on me, not just for the very forceful proposals they were making – often going beyond what the Government is doing – but the force of their convictions and the emotional force of their convictions.

speaker: The Senior Minister, Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister-in-charge of The Monetary Authority of Singapore (Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam)
text: So, please do not assume, none of us should assume – I am not directing this at anyone in particular – none of us should assume that we have a monopoly over compassion.

speaker: The Senior Minister, Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister-in-charge of The Monetary Authority of Singapore (Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam)
text: Also, and here is a bit of advice: try to avoid strawman arguments.

speaker: The Senior Minister, Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister-in-charge of The Monetary Authority of Singapore (Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam)
text: Like saying that the Government is only interested in efficiency and not equity.

speaker: The Senior Minister, Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister-in-charge of The Monetary Authority of Singapore (Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam)
text: By the way, I say "strawman" – should I say "strawperson"?

speaker: The Senior Minister, Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister-in-charge of The Monetary Authority of Singapore (Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam)
text: But women are not made of straw, I think, so let us stick to "strawman".

speaker: The Senior Minister, Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister-in-charge of The Monetary Authority of Singapore (Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam)
text: But try to avoid that manner of argument, or painting everything in binary terms.

speaker: The Senior Minister, Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister-in-charge of The Monetary Authority of Singapore (Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam)
text: It is usually not necessary to reply but I say this as a piece of general advice.

speaker: The Senior Minister, Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister-in-charge of The Monetary Authority of Singapore (Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam)
text: Raising the standard of living of the poor is a complicated matter.

speaker: The Senior Minister, Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister-in-charge of The Monetary Authority of Singapore (Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam)
text: And I say this, by the way, as an economist, as someone who studies overseas experience very carefully, and who together with my colleagues, is a practitioner.

speaker: The Senior Minister, Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister-in-charge of The Monetary Authority of Singapore (Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam)
text: And it is not a job that is done for good; we have to do more – many of the speeches that we have heard in the last few days about how we can do more in a way that really helps those we are trying to help.

speaker: The Senior Minister, Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister-in-charge of The Monetary Authority of Singapore (Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam)
text: But we are frankly not very far away from each other in that objective.

speaker: The Senior Minister, Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister-in-charge of The Monetary Authority of Singapore (Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam)
text: In fact, we seem to be quite convinced, there is a consensus, let me put it that way, that that should be our objective.

speaker: The Senior Minister, Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister-in-charge of The Monetary Authority of Singapore (Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam)
text: But just try to avoid strawman arguments and pretending that you have a monopoly on compassion.

speaker: The Senior Minister, Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister-in-charge of The Monetary Authority of Singapore (Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam)
text: By the way, it is a very small point – I have never heard economists cite a university as a source of research, be it a well-regarded or not very well-regarded university.

speaker: The Senior Minister, Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister-in-charge of The Monetary Authority of Singapore (Mr Tharman Shanmugaratnam)
text: Individuals do research and it may be very credible research.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I regret if it came across that I was suggesting that only I or the party or any individual has a monopoly over compassion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: In fact, that was explicitly why I did cite cases where I felt that existing policy demonstrated oodles of compassion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I even cited other Members not from our party that have also talked about compassion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, I actually believe, like Minister Tharman does, that there is in fact quite a bit of daylight, there is not as much of a gap between the thinking of the two.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: That said, I do not think that I was setting out a strawman argument in talking about an efficiency/equity trade-off, and the reason for this is because this is precisely a continuum.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, I am not suggesting that every policy that is currently in place is only geared toward efficiency.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Likewise, I am not suggesting that every policy that I have laid out in my speech and elsewhere, is only geared toward equity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And I am arguing that we can move more in the direction of favouring equity over efficiency.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And that was the entire point of the argument, not to create an artificial strawman.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Many Members in this House have spoken about the importance of seizing opportunities in the digital age and the tremendous positive benefits that it brings.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Even as we ride the wave of digital revolution, we need to bear in mind that technology is a double-edged sword.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: I will speak today on how we can minimise the downside while we seek and strive to maximise the upside – how we can safely navigate cyberspace when there is danger lurking at every corner; how we can come together to build a safer, kinder, more caring online community for all.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Names have been changed to protect their identity.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Fifteen-year old Joyce had what she thought was an innocent online friendship with a supposedly 18-year-old boy.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: This turned into one of manipulation, where he threatened to harm himself unless Joyce fulfilled his requests – even for nude photos.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Though the relationship has since ended, the episode left her struggling to trust the people around her.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Mr Ong, another East Coast resident, shared with me a harrowing experience.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Inappropriate photos of his daughter were downloaded from her phone without her consent and circulated online.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Though police reports were made, the social media platform was slow to respond, and the photos stayed online.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: His daughter was traumatised and even contemplated suicide.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: The family felt extremely helpless, not knowing what to do and who to turn to.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Seniors are vulnerable, with those aged 55 and above, making up of almost half of all victims of inheritance scams and tech support scams in this same period.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Countries around the world are also grappling with these challenges.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: New Zealand criminalised serious instances of online bullying, and harassment and appointed an organisation "NetSafe" to act as the first port of call to investigate and resolve complaints on online harm.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: For example, NetSafe liaises with website hosts and Internet service providers to take down harmful content through persuasion and mediation.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Australia set up an Office of the eSafety Commissioner, a dedicated agency that was empowered to investigate and take action against perpetrators, by issuing warnings, requesting websites to remove harmful material, or seeking a civil penalty order in Court.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: In South Korea, the government itself operates a "Digital Sexual Crime Victim Support Centre".

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: This one-stop centre provides counselling services, liaises with websites to delete harmful content and refers victims to pro-bono legal services.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Importantly, victims and their loved ones know they are not alone in their darkest hour of need.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Each society has an obligation to protect its citizens.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We too have a duty to keep Singaporeans safe from online harm.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Singaporeans are proud that we have one of the safest streets in the world.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We let our children and loved ones walk freely around the neighbourhood and we trust they have pleasant interactions.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Likewise, we must also strive to build a safe and kind online space – one marked with care and respect, where everyone including our children and our seniors can interact freely without constantly looking over their shoulders, looking for perpetrators and predators.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: A few days ago in this House, Mdm Rahayu spoke passionately about building a kind and compassionate society, both offline and online.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We must act now and decisively, and not wait till it is too late.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Our content classification regime protects our young from harmful or unsuitable materials, while ensuring the rest of us access the whole wide range of content.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: The recently formed Inter-Ministry Committee on Scams coordinates efforts across the Government to tackle scams.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: The Protection from Harassment Act or POHA was enhanced in 2019 to allow authorities to better respond to emerging online trends, such as by criminalising the act of doxxing.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: MOE’s Cyber Wellness education teaches students to recognise risks in the digital space, identify negative influences and navigate online spaces safely.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: The National Crime Prevention Council raises awareness on online scams through a WhatsApp broadcast channel and they run an anti-scam helpline.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Yet despite these efforts, we are often only playing catch up.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: A few days ago, Ms Tin Pei Ling spoke about the immense popularity of the TikTok video sharing platform.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Each emergent platform – be it Instagram or TikTok – brings with it new challenges.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: This requires us to be nimble and adaptable.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Legislation and Government efforts by themselves are insufficient.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Multiple stakeholders need to be involved and each given a stake in this effort.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: The Government can set out the broad approach to regulations, code of practices and norms, but we need ground-up initiatives to experiment with various approaches to meet the needs of our citizens.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: If they are successful, we can scale up these initiatives.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: With these considerations in mind, let me propose three steps how we can achieve this – how we can Step Forward, Step Up and Step In.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: The Government plays a critical role in this multi-stakeholder approach.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: It sets the tone and brings the right parties together.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Consequently, we do not fully understand the shape of the elephant, much less tame the beast.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: This agency should work with a panel of experts so that we can think about this matter holistically, ensure that we keep abreast of global developments, and stay on top of this issue.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Mental health professionals and academics can help us make sense of the social and psychological dynamics of the online space.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Community partners can help us understand the impact on vulnerable groups, and the support they need.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Educators and pedagogy experts can study and share best practices on	how	schools	can	facilitate	learning	on	these	topics.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Industry representatives can advocate for the role of the private sector in working with us to build a safer and kinder online space.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: This panel can be empowered to make recommendations on how to prevent these harms and provide timely help to the victims.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: This could include proposals to strengthen current legislative and enforcement levers, or even establish new ones.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: But the Government’s role is only one part of the solution, which brings me to my next point.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We need every stakeholder group to step up and take action.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: To the private sector, my appeal to you is “Starting safe is half the battle won”.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: It is in your firm's interest to do so – a safe customer is a loyal customer and I will touch on two aspects of how corporates can contribute.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Today, cars and consumer appliances need to meet safety standards before they are allowed into the market.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Similarly, we should consider ways on how we can give users a sense of assurance in the online space.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: There are some early efforts and areas we can further explore in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: For example, banks exploring monitoring elderly customers’ accounts to spot irregular transactions so that they can be alerted in time.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Seniors may be also given the option to disallow cross-border remittances made through their e-banking service.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Caller ID can be a first line of defence for many seniors to spot scam calls.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: For instance, the plus sign is now prefixed to all incoming international calls, to combat spoof calls from overseas.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: This is a good step and more can be done.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Perhaps telcos can consider maintaining a common database of blacklisted numbers and block incoming calls from these numbers, and also consider making many of these functions easily accessible for all seniors.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: In fact just this morning, there was a Forum Letter on this very issue in The Straits Times.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: E-commerce platforms can also better safeguard its customers by implementing measures such as an escrow account to reduce e-commerce scams.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Keeping customers safe online should not be an afterthought or treated as the customer help desk’s problem.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Management needs to take ownership and I commend many responsible companies that are adopting such a mindset.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: I encourage many more to do so too.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: It is the right thing to do and it makes business sense.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Second, social media platforms can step up to detect and resolve online harm issues early, as well as raise awareness on these issues.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Nip the issue early in the bud, before irreparable harm is done.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Platforms such as Instagram and Twitter have existing functions for reporting content, comments, or accounts.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: They can work with the appointed Government agency on how we can better use these tools to combat cyber bullying and cyber grooming.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Facebook has also piloted programmes with TOUCH Cyber Wellness in schools, to equip seniors to use technology safely, or conduct workshops with school counsellors on how to talk about cyber bullying in the classroom.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Singapore has a stellar reputation for trust globally.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: It is a win-win outcome for us and the social media platforms if they can do more in Singapore and set the benchmark for the rest of the world.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: To parents, my appeal to all of us – since I was recently promoted to that stature – would be, “Staying safe online starts at home.” This was the advice that a group of Secondary school girls that initiated "Project Bluetic"’ shared with me.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: The team started off with a simple objective to raise awareness amongst their peers and encourage them to "bluetick" uncomfortable online messages – "bluetick", which is to read the message, get the "bluetick", ignore these messages and report the user.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: However, they soon realised that the key group that needed education were the parents.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: One parent signed up for the cyber grooming workshop, thinking it was online courses on how to improve the kid's appearance!

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: The girls shared with me how important it was for parents to provide a safe space at home, where children can seek advice or help without fear of being judged.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: So, to all parents, I humbly call upon all of us to step up to better understand the dangers of online harm and to create such an environment where we and our children can speak freely, heart-to-heart.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: I spoke about how the Government can step forward and how key stakeholder groups can step up.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We must foster a culture of inclusiveness where we make technology accessible.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We must foster a culture of kindness where we respect each other like we do in real life and a culture of safety so that our seniors and children can learn and enjoy the Internet without fear.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: The Singapore Kindness Movement started in 1997, building on the National Courtesy Campaign.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Many of us, even young kids I spoke to, fondly recall the iconic "Singa the Lion", the face of this campaign since 1982.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: A new movement to rally passionate individuals and groups, and channel their energy and enthusiasm into taking action that would make a difference for society.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: The campaign encourages youths to flag out uncomfortable or predatory online conversations and to have candid conversations on such experiences with their loved ones.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: They ran a powerful, immersive exhibition at the National Library called “45 minutes in the PreyGround”, P-R-E-Y, PreyGound, where visitors were led to step into the shoes of victims to understand their experiences of being preyed upon online.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Because of COVID, they have focused their advocacy effort on Instagram, sharing stories of victims and bite-sized infographics and videos.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: They even came up with a card game to encourage conversations amongst friends!

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Another insight the NTU team shared with me was the importance of peer support, friends looking out for one another.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Each of us can step in and be part of this movement.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We can spread awareness, offer a listening ear to our friends or direct those in need to avenues for help and support.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We can also learn how to speak about such issues in a supportive way – to push back against stigmatising such issues and provide a safe space for victims to come forward.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Ultimately, kindness starts with each one of us.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Put ourselves in someone else’s shoes, think before we click.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: (In Mandarin):   Technologies have brought a lot of convenience to the lives of Singaporeans, but we must also be wary of the dangers that comes with technologies.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Cyber bullying, cyber grooming and online fraud can cause long-term damage to the physical, mental and financial health of the victims and their families.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We must take immediate actions to create a safe and kind cyber space for all, especially the young and the elderly.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Second, we need the full support of different stakeholders groups in society.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: For example, tech companies and social media companies can study how to provide safer online services and products, and work with the government to promote cyber security awareness.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Parents, on the other hand, can pick up relevant knowledge and provide a safe space at home, so that children can seek advice and help when they need it.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We can each do our part too, for example, helping to promote cyber security awareness, lending a listening ear to friends when they are troubled, providing them with guidance, or encouraging them to turn to existing channels for help.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We cannot shy away from the internet just because there are risks.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Instead, we should learn how to make good and full use of it while protecting ourselves.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Everyone needs to take responsibility to protect ourselves in cybersecurity.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, Mdm President spoke about the need to build a fair and just society.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: As our world becomes increasingly digitalised, we must also pay special attention to how the most vulnerable amongst us not just access, but also navigate the digital space.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: My wife and I just had our baby.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Isaac will be turning a month old this weekend.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: He and other children of his generation will grow up in a very different world from all of us, where they will spend a large part of their lives in cyberspace.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: It is the duty of our generation to do all that we can to make sure that our children and seniors can grow up and grow old in a safe and caring online community, where there is no digital divide, where our people have the confidence and skills to ride the digital wave; where just as they are at ease moving around in the physical neighbourhood, they can have the same peace of mind navigating the digital space.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We need to act boldly and decisively now before it is too late.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office and for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: So, let us all step forward, step up and step in to be part of this national movement.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The President mentioned in her speech that we are starting a new term of Government under the shadow of COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, COVID-19 has created unprecedented challenges to the lives and livelihoods of the people around the world and Singapore is, unfortunately, not spared from this global crisis.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Yet, despite the devastating headline economic statistics, I have no doubt in my mind that Singapore will weather the COVID-19 crisis and our economy will continue to grow again.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But the bigger question to me is: what does it mean for us to emerge stronger as a nation and how do we define our success?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It is unfortunate that it takes a crisis, such as COVID-19, to expose some of the weakness of our economic structures and our lack of social protection for the vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
