text: To the lucky few amongst us, COVID-19 is just a passing storm or the proverbial rainy day where we can rely on our past savings to tide us through.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But to the less privileged Singaporeans who are struggling to make ends meet on a daily basis, COVID-19 is a tsunami which threatens not just their livelihoods, but possibly even their lives.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Today, Singapore is already one of the wealthiest countries in the world as measured by GDP per capita.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Yet, we are also often perceived to be an unequal society where the benefits of growth may perhaps not be evenly distributed and with inequality threatening to weaken our social fabric.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To this end, I note that New Zealand embarked on its first well-being budget in 2019, recognising that economic growth, while important, does not guarantee improvements in living standards.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Bhutan, too, has a Gross National Happiness Index which captures multiple indicators across nine domains.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While these may not be directly replicable in the context of Singapore, it is imperative for us to start assessing how each and every Singaporean is doing, and how best to address the unmet needs of our people in a sustainable and equitable manner.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: On that note, I would like to highlight four areas for reform to build a stronger and more resilient Singapore society, post the current pandemic in this crisis.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The first area of reform is in relation to workers' protection.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: COVID-19 has, undoubtedly, been an unprecedented healthcare crisis, leading to a simultaneous demand and supply economic destruction.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Yet, with the shortening of business cycles and hastening of technological disruption, the threat of widespread job losses and rapid job irrelevance is only going to rise in future.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Direct assistance to companies, such as the Jobs Support Scheme, could arguably provide indirect support to employment.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But as we have seen in the second quarter employment change numbers, subsidies to companies and moral suasion cannot prevent job losses.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Many more workers will be without a job despite their best intentions to be employed.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Rather than providing blanket wage subsidies across companies, it is perhaps the workers themselves that are most in need of direct support and financial buffers in the event of unemployment.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Singapore Government has taken pride in creating a pro-business environment through its economic and manpower policies.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It is now time, in my view, however, to strengthen our employment laws to better support and protect workers and raise the standard of work for all.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Global Financial Crisis in 2008/2009 saw the introduction of Kurzarbeit in Germany, a short time work programme that has been a key feature of the German safety net since, which was a useful template for many countries to model on.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Building a more resilient workforce in society starts with strengthening our social safety nets for workers, and we now have an opportunity to do just that without necessarily impairing the incentive to work hard.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The second area of reform is in relation to housing.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This has serious implications for the retirement adequacy of Singaporeans, as much of Singaporeans' assets are being tied to their primary residence, which is their HDB flat.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Government has said earlier in 2019 that it will consider all alternative suggestions and ways to manage the expiring leases of HDB flats and we cannot continue to ignore the elephant in the room.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And this is an issue which I believe should rank high on our national agenda.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: With many Singaporeans entering their golden years, the knowledge of their HDB flats steadily losing value as they approach the tail-end of their leases can become a significant source of mental stress and insecurity.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The third area of reform is in relation to support for families.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Our houses may be built from bricks and mortar, but the family is the basic building block of society.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I believe that sustainable growth is not only defined by fiscal sustainability, but by the future sustainability of our people, our human resource.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We need to recognise that family-friendly policies boost rather than reduce productivity and reject the notion that dedicating time for our care-giving responsibilities hurts the employment prospects of workers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The silver lining to the circuit breaker period was that it institutionalised flexible working arrangements and showed us that economic competitiveness need not come at the expense of our families.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: On a personal level, I started working from home even before Phase 1 of the circuit breaker measures and, as a father to a newborn baby, I am thankful to have witnessed his various development milestones over the past year and to partake in the joys of parenthood while continuing to stay productive at work.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I recognise that MOM will support employers to offer flexible work arrangements and work-life harmony initiatives.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We need the Government to lead by example and demonstrate to companies what progressive HR policies look like.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: More importantly, we need to devote greater resources to families to support their parenthood aspirations.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We need to take bold and decisive steps and provide greater financial and non-financial support to Singaporean families, recognising that the stresses on families and our low fertility rate, if not urgently addressed today, would have significant long-term socio-economic cost to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The last area of reform is on the use of reserves.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I agree with the Government's fiscal prudence and policy that our expenditures cannot and should not be more than our revenues for long-term sustainability.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, national policy proposals that tap on the reserves must be seen in the context of Singaporeans' growing needs across healthcare, ageing and retirement adequacy.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As such, there needs to be thorough evaluation of alternative sources of revenue that remain untapped.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Currently, some Government revenues, including land sales, are excluded from the official Budget.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, capital receipts, such as land sales, represent strong recurring cash revenues that are actually received by the Government, particularly with land being sold on a leasehold basis.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While we would need to safeguard our reserves for potential contingencies, let us also acknowledge that increasing the percentage of returns generated will only vary the pace of reserve growth, but will not cause the reserves to fall.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Arguably, deploying our reserves into more productive uses by investing them into our people, our human capital, could generate far superior returns in the long run and boost the future sustainability of our nation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: (In Mandarin):   Singapore is an affluent country, ranked at number eight in the world in terms of per capita GDP.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, we are often described as an unequal society with a widening income gap, weakening social cohesion slowly.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Perhaps it is time for us to rethink what we should value as a society, and whether we have overlooked certain groups in the society while chasing economic growth.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I urge the Government not to continue to measure the success of governance solely based on economic data, but to adopt a more holistic approach and measure the progress of the country in various ways.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Policies should not be formulated purely on the economic level, but to give priority to the welfare of all Singaporeans and pay attention to the disadvantaged groups in society.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Today, I would like to raise four areas for improvement so that we can build a stronger and more resilient society after the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Global demand is softening, many companies have no choice but to retrench staff, and many Singaporeans have to face unemployment.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For businesses, the Jobs Support Scheme, which has been extended repeatedly, may help them survive, and companies do not need to apply.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But even if the unemployed can apply for other one-off assistance schemes, some will still be rejected after going through cumbersome application processes.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Instead of continuing to subsidise companies, what local workers need more is direct subsidies and assistance to help them mitigate the impact of unemployment and economic recession.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Many older Singaporeans, no matter how hard they work, do not have enough protection if they fall ill or are retrenched.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Direct subsidies and assistance are the most needed help for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The second area that needs to be reformed is our housing policy.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Minister for National Development has mentioned the need to take care of the housing needs of Singaporeans, such as ensuring affordability of HDB flats, allowing young families to own homes earlier, and strengthening schemes to help the elderly use the value of HDB flats to supplement their retirement needs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, the problem lies in the value of our HDB flats.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The third area is support for the family.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The family is the bedrock of our society.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We must realise that pro-family policies will not reduce productivity but raise it instead.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It is also incorrect to think that employees spending time and taking care of their children and elderly at home will affect their career prospects.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We need to take bold and decisive measures to provide more financial and non-monetary assistance to Singaporean families, because if we don’t address early the daily pressure faced by families and the issue of low birth rate, they could have a long-term socio-economic impact on Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I agree that it is important for the Government to manage its finances prudently, to balance revenue and expenditure to achieve long-term sustainability.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, considering that rising healthcare and cost of living have led to inadequate retirement funds, should we not assess our untapped sources of income in a more holistic manner?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: What we are doing is not to cut this tree of reserves, but to allow Singaporeans to take shelter from the forest as represented by the reserves as they are under the scorching sun.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, to conclude, COVID-19 will not be the only challenge for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: There will be many more foreseeable white swan events and unpredictable black swan events which we may not be fully prepared for.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To build a more resilient society, we need to foster a culture of open-mindedness where dissenting views are not only accepted but actually encouraged and where bold, innovative ideas are championed instead of being squashed.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I believe that change has to come from the top and it starts from the context of the Parliament and the Government of the day.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To this end, I am comforted by the President's assurance that the Government will be open to constructive criticism and rational debate, and to new ways of doing things.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As a first-time Member of Parliament, I am honoured and privileged to be a Member of this House, and I believe voters have put their faith in us because of their greater desire for diversity in Parliament, more robust Parliamentary debates and a bigger say in Government decision-making so as to achieve the best outcomes for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We must continue to be the voice for our constituents.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But beyond mere words and statements of intent, it is our actions that define us.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I sincerely hope that the Government will have the courage and political will to translate the breadth and depth of ideas that Members bring to this House into concrete policies to take Singapore forward.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: A united Singapore Together is not one that speaks with one voice.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: A united Singapore is one with a diversity of voices sharing our common belief for a better future and working together as one.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In her address, Mdm President highlighted that we are facing a sea of change in an uncertain and complex world.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Globally, fault lines are growing more pronounced across class, political, racial and inter-generational divides.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We are seeing new waves of protectionism taking root in a world more connected than ever before.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It starts within us and the biases in our mind, whether we admit them or not, and grows in the unwillingness to have conversations to understand the perspectives of people we are unfamiliar with or with whom we may disagree.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This requires us to lean into conversations on issues that may be uncomfortable.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But I submit that if we do not lead the way in navigating these conversations, we leave the space wide open for others to fill in ways that may be incendiary or out of context for our Singapore.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While hope for a better future is a shared aspiration across generations, the common lived experience of a Singaporean life has changed dramatically over the years.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: During my house visits in Cheng San-Seletar, some senior residents shared their fond memories of rubber plantations and farms in Ang Mo Kio.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The world we live in today is one where these residents and people like my grandmother hardly recognise.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My grandmother was given away as a child and tried to find her way back home after the war.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It was a time when girls did not go to school and sometimes were considered less worthy.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Her experiences shaped her own perceptions, beliefs and hopes for her children.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The stark differences in lived experiences have not spared the baby boomers, Generations X, Y, Z and Alpha from inevitable clashes.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is natural for members of each generation to feel that their experience holds the most weight, to reject opinions that do not gel with their worldviews.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And it is convenient to turn to labels, which make it easier to dismiss perspectives.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While these inclinations are understandable, they are unacceptable in a society which appreciates the wisdom and guidance of its elders but also trusts its youth to lead it forward into the future. "OK Boomer" and "strawberry generation" narratives are examples of reductionist caricatures.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Generation Z comes in as interns, millennials move up in their careers to take on supervisory roles, Generation X become top executives and seniors retire later.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We may even feel this in our own homes as grandparents and grandchildren disagree on political and cultural norms.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If we truly want to harness the potential of our youth and tap on the experiences of our seniors, then we must not be dismissive of their thoughts, dreams and fears.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While social media has amplified the space for individuals to have a voice, ironically, it can also make people more afraid to speak up for fear of being judged or flamed.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In a world where tweets and memes dominate, we must also take the time to really listen and consider the details.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The space that our middle ground occupies, carefully built up over the years, should be enlarged, not shrunken.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Social media also accentuates the polarisation of perspectives on a global level, which very quickly trickles down to the local.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We are not only exposed to shifts in global economic headwinds, now we are also exposed to shifts in social and cultural headwinds, which we must learn to navigate with equal competence.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As much as we are pragmatic, we are a nation built on the backs of dreamers with the gumption to tackle the challenges of their time.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have seen this through the efforts of the Merdeka and Pioneer Generations.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Driven by the promise of a stake in Singapore's progress, they pursued the betterment of our society relentlessly.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Fifty-five years later, we are in a different time faced with different challenges in a world battled by COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While there are immediate challenges to tackle, it is also important to keep an eye on the longer term.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: After the dust settles, what does that citizen's stake in Singapore's progress look like for future generations?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What will be the engine of social mobility for our sandwiched class?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In times of hardship such as this, we need to sow seeds of hope for when the rain passes and a strong vision for the future.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the region and globally, we see socio-economic shifts gassed by systemic inequality.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Here in Singapore, we would be in a much worse position if the Government had not invested heavily in trying to protect Singaporeans by motivating companies through stimulus levers to raise wages progressively, upscale workers and keep the Singaporean core employed.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One group that has been deeply impacted are mid-career professionals.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These are individuals with several years of working experience and are on track to becoming specialists in their domains.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They are often at the age where they have children to raise and parents to look after.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many of my residents fall within this category.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While training allowances are much appreciated, the reality is that these individuals and their families will feel the drop in income.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A number of mid-career professionals already find themselves part of the sandwiched class squeeze and at times, the opportunity cost of upgrading their skills in pursuit of a potential future feels far too great.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our workers will need to adopt a longer term earning outlook but this does means that perhaps on the social side, we may need to relook what assistance schemes look like, who qualifies for them, and if there can be interim targeted support so that families can thrive and not just survive.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In her address, Mdm President also spoke about the need to evolve our model of meritocracy.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There are many schemes to support students and families from disadvantaged backgrounds.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the same time, work on the ground reveals that there are people who fall through the cracks and we must deal with these gaps with empathy.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Where individuals miss the qualifying criteria by a whisker, where circumstances require our youth to take on part-time paid jobs instead of a coveted, unpaid internship, or where women drop drop out of the workforce to fulfill care-giving roles at home as hired help is beyond their means.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While it may not be possible to completely eradicate inequality in the world, it is entirely within our responsibility to ensure that Singaporeans from all walks of life are not priced out of opportunities and are able to seize them in a timely way.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At 20, she did not fall automatically within the age criteria to receive certain transfers or benefit from schemes that residents 21 and above qualified for.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Her parents were divorced, did not have regular employment and could not support her.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: She met a young man of the same age, had a baby, got married and got pregnant the second time.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Despite moving in with his family in their rental flat, the youth and her baby effectively lived as a separate family unit while the husband served National Service.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: She shared with me her hopes of finding a job but worried there would be no care-giver for her children as her husband's vocation did not allow him to return home in the evenings and that the flat's monthly rental fees would be adjusted upwards when she became a new income earner in the house.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In my time on the panel of advisers to the Youth Courts, I have also encountered youth who reside in homes under the Children and Young Persons Act.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While family is a building block of society, as spoken about by my colleague Mr Zhulkarnain earlier and the hon Member Louis Chua, sadly, there are some youth who, upon reaching the age of 19, are no longer able to stay in these homes but also do not have families to reintegrate with.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The sudden shift to independent living without a routine while having to find work to pay for accommodation can be overwhelming and these youth, sometimes, are not able to reach their to reach their full potential.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Having served in the youth space for many years, I have seen the shifts and in fact compassion, exercised by policy-makers.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There is no doubt in my mind that our youth are deserving and that the Government recognises this and has heavily invested in building up our youth.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that we continue to do so and reach even more youth segments.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Malay):   I am concerned about the COVID-19 crisis occupying the minds of our community.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am however confident that this crisis is only temporary and we can overcome it.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is because, in these trying times, the Malay community has shown solidarity to help one another in order to move forward together: I have seen the spirit of mutual cooperation and collaboration between M3 and Malay/ Muslim organizations under the SG Teguh Bersatu initiative.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am also touched to see many seniors such as retired teachers as well as qualified business leaders coming forward to help the community.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am also glad to see youths taking the time to embark on initiatives and serve the community.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When I look at our community, I am filled with admiration because our Malay community is a resilient one.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We appreciate the guidance from the older generation and have faith in our youths to progress towards a brighter future.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am also aware that the government has drawn up various programmes to help needy families.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): In closing, we must build bridges of understanding to deal with the shifts in the global World Order and the needs of different generations.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am confident in who we are as a people and our Singaporean values that put us in good stead during these unprecedented times.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat said in the earlier part of the debate: adapt to change but stay true to our values.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The world will change with or without us, and our Little Red Dot’s best shot at driving is to change as we stay united together.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We are a young country and I believe our best days are ahead of us.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Much has been said about how the COVID-19 pandemic has severely disrupted our lives and forced massive changes to the way we work, live and play.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: It is no exaggeration to say that this is indeed a crisis to test our generation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: But it is also not without some silver linings.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: First, people are looking out for one another.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We can take pride and draw strength from this.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Many Singaporeans have gone out of their way to help others – giving out free masks to strangers, delivering groceries to those in quarantine, hawkers cooking for the hungry, customers rallying support for hawkers on social media.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: These are just a few examples of the great many heart-warming acts we see all around us.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Second, our businesses and workforce are seizing opportunities and trying new things in response to the crisis.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Traditional businesses have innovated and accelerated their adoption of tech solutions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Our wet market stallholders are hawking their fresh produce over livestream on Facebook.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Many Members may also recognise getai veteran, Wang Lei, who has sold seafood, durians and even cars online.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In his words, he turned the crisis into a business opportunity, or in Chinese, 把危机转成商机.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Third, the enforced time-out has allowed nature and the environment to recover.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The air is cleaner and humanity’s carbon footprint has shrunk with the reduction of transportation and industrial activities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: It was my nine-year-old daughter who has noticed there are more butterflies and wildflowers in our estate during our evening walks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: These silver linings give us confidence that we shall prevail.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: And we will continue to grow stronger as a nation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This is indeed the time to chart the future we want for Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: And our youth will be key in shaping our collective future, for they are the leaders not only of tomorrow, but also of today.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Our youths, with their ideals and ideas, can play a critical role in building the kind of society we would like to have and to see in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: First, I would like to see a society of opportunities for all.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Second, I would like us to build a liveable and sustainable environment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: And third, I hope Singapore will be a society built on trust.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The economic impact of COVID-19 has not been borne evenly.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: But what weighs most heavily on them is their worry about the future of their four children who are all in school.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: There are families out there who need help.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: And I am most concerned about young children and the opportunities they may lose, if nothing is done.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: While there are various Government schemes to support individuals and families along their life journeys, there is an important role for the community and individuals to reach out to fellow Singaporeans, like what we have done during this pandemic.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Two years ago, I worked with some colleagues in the public service to initiate a social programme where volunteers befriend children from the rental blocks at Casa Clementi and give tuition to them after school.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Twenty-four-year-old grassroots leader, Hameed, played an active role in setting up and sustaining the centre, together with youth volunteers from NUS and ACS Independent, and even MINDEF and SAF regulars.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Besides tutoring, Hameed and his team organised activities and holiday programmes for them, such as coding classes, football sessions, and trips to the Zoo and the Wild Wild Wet.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: During the circuit breaker, they delivered special care packs to each of the children’s homes on top of the regular Zoom sessions, just to remind them that they were not alone.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: It was heartening to see the students improve in their learning attitudes and in their results.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I asked Hameed recently what kept him going.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: His answer was simple – seeing the excitement in the children when they turn up, watching them develop and grow, and simply wanting to make a difference in the community he lives in.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I am sure we have many Hameeds in every community to bring all Singaporeans on board the moving escalator, to give each generation a better future.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I urge Members of this House, many of whom have spoken passionately about this topic, to rally our community to step up and do something for our children who may not have a good start, to ensure they receive a good education.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Together, let us ensure that there will always be social mobility in our society and that this remains deeply anchored in our value system.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Second, I hope that we can build and nurture a liveable and sustainable environment for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Sustainability is about meeting the needs of the current generation, without compromising that of the future generations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This has become more pressing than ever with the gathering pace of climate change and its impacts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: So, it augurs well for the future of our common home that sustainability is a high priority for many of our youth, as studies commissioned by the National Youth Council have shown.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Many of them are also stepping forward to make their voices and their actions count, and some are working together to make a bigger impact with their efforts on sustainability.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In Pasir Ris, we have residents who are keen to turn seaweed and mussels into bioplastics and then into alternative fuel.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We have youth who want to champion rooftop farming, clean up beaches and estates, promote car-lite by improving cycling path networks and so on.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We will create new jobs in the green sector and develop a pipeline of talent to support sustainability in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Besides working with businesses and other partners, we must actively engage and create opportunities for youth to play a bigger role in co-creating and co-delivering solutions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We must take our youth’s efforts seriously because they are not an interest group – they are taking ownership to lead in fighting climate change, to make Singapore a more liveable and sustainable city.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I will certainly do my best to support their efforts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This is more relevant and important now than ever.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: How does a society built on trust look like?

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I believe that such a society is characterised by a sense of togetherness where individuals and groups are willing to sacrifice their own interests for the larger good of the society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: A good example in our history is our Land Acquisition Act of 1967.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: As a young growing nation, our kampungs and squatter huts had to make way for high-rise HDB buildings and industrial development.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Our Pioneer and Merdeka Generations understood that, and they reluctantly moved from places they were familiar with to the HDB flats.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: There was trust that this was indeed necessary for the greater good of our nation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Today, our world class housing bears great testament to what we can achieve when there is trust between the Government and the people.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: As our founding Prime Minister Mr Lee Kuan Yew once said, “Our greatest asset was the trust and confidence of the people.” COVID-19 has shown this trust still exists today.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We saw this when workers accepted wage cuts so that more of their co-workers could remain employed, and when we all responded and stayed home to break the infection cycle and preserve our healthcare system for those who needed them most.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I hope that we can continue to build and nurture this trust.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The question remains: how do we build this trust between the Government and people, and amongst people?

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We often hear the phrase that trust has to be earned.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Over my career in the Army and public service, I found that this adage, while may be true, may be counter-productive sometimes because until someone earns it, we hold back trust to protect ourselves, build policies on the premise that a small minority may abuse the trust, and sometimes we micro-manage down to the dot.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Instead, I believe when we are in a position of leadership, trust has to be given.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: When my firstborn was in Primary school, I was called up by the school for an incident that he was involved in.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Without even verifying with him, I chided him in the car on the way home for getting himself into trouble.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: He remained quiet for some time and then turned to me and asked, "Dad, why don’t you trust me when I said I didn’t do it?" Like all fathers, I wanted to earn his trust.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: That day, I learned that I have to give him my trust first.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I hope we can build a culture of openness and trust and continue one in which the Government listens, consults and engages regularly with citizens.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This may mean being more transparent about our considerations and trade-offs when developing policies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: For instance, since the start of COVID-19, our Prime Minister and the Ministers have been sharing very openly and regularly with Singaporeans about the pandemic, trusting us to rally together to do the right thing.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Beyond sharing information, our policies also need to reflect trust in our people in their delivery.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In some areas, the Government can trust citizen groups to lead and execute policies and projects.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: On the other hand, an engaged citizenry must be prepared to listen and understand the various perspectives, considerations and trade-offs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We must create a discourse that is based on data, science and facts, not one based on rhetoric and ideology.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I hope to be part of this constructive engagement process.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: It is only when we give trust, that we gain trust and achieve great things together.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I urge all of us Singaporeans to come together to build a society with opportunities for all, that is liveable and sustainable, and founded on mutual trust.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Together, let us build on the solid foundation that the Pioneer and Merdeka Generations developed for us, and create a society that we will be proud to pass on to the generations to come.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: With all Singaporeans on board, we will surely get there and grow stronger in the process.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, I would like to share the lyrics of a xinyao song; the title is "Singapore Pie".

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Do not worry, I am not going to sing it, I am just going to read out the lyrics: "Dad said I was born in the 60s.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I was only one-year-old when Singapore was born.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Back then, nobody believed in the Singapore brand and there were people migrating overseas.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Gradually, we went into the 70s, the chimneys in Jurong were rather grand-looking.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Friends said that the more I live, the more I was as real as Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In a blink of an eye, we are in the 90s and now it is people from other places migrating here.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Who do not love the Singapore brand?" Due to the time constraint, I shall not recite the whole song.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: If interested, you can go online and listen to it.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The reason why I mention this song today is because it tells the Singapore success story.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In the early days of nation-building, nobody believed that Singapore would succeed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Those who have migrated also started to return.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The last two lines of the lyrics are: "We will write our own stories.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Do we want a Singapore that people blame each other or help each other to find solutions?

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs and Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Do we want a Singapore where people keep asking "what can I get" or "what can I do"?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Across the world, there is economic chaos, business foreclosures, job instability – perhaps more painful and poisonous than just economic disruption – and a healthcare crisis, its divisions, strife and an "Us versus Them" dialogue.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In Singapore, we have been lucky so far.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We have our reserves, we have strong Government, we have a united people, and we have avoided most of the communal upheavals that others have experienced so far.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Yet, we cannot and must not assume that the worst is over.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The cases of COVID-19 infections may be coming down, may be stabilising, but the economic storm is still yet to hit us fully.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And with that, our societal fabric will be strained, perhaps fray, and may well start to tear as well.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: That we have come through a General Election where passions have been aroused is perhaps a symptom of the times.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Today, more than ever, we need to re-emphasise the importance of coming together, a message that perhaps is both important and well encapsulated in Total Defence.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Even if the enemy that we are facing today is unseen, even perhaps unknown, we can see clearly where our military and civil defence have been important.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: At this point, it is perhaps apt to recognise the work of our SAF, the SCDF, our healthcare workers and many frontliners, who have been serving with great passion, dedication and also compassion during these difficult times.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But just as the Prime Minister said in February 2020, the real test of this pandemic is our social cohesion and psychological resilience.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They have staved off the enemies of joblessness and economic stagnation.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But we, the people of Singapore, must also do our level best.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: COVID-19 has accelerated many trends in our economy – driving automation, reconstruction of value chains, e-commerce, logistics, all sectors that are now growing because they are new norms in our COVID-19 world.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is perhaps the best impetus for us to change.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And as a people, we must not fear adaptation to explore new areas of growth, to re-skill and upskill.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For us, for our families, for our nation, we must remain fearless, relevant, not only to ourselves but also to the world.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is not the time to hide away, or to say that if only we could just turn back the clock, because we cannot.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But there are bright moments and there is a lot of motivation as well.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Just recently, the five CDCs held our SkillsFuture Festival, the first fully online festival, and we had very encouraging participation.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And many, in their feedback, have said that they have learnt something new and they have enjoyed that process.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some have also shared that they had fears initially, but have found that once they take the plunge, it became so much easier.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But, at the same time, we cannot ignore the fact that change will bring with it some discomfort.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Our social defence is, therefore, also at stake.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: COVID-19, as we have seen in the rest of the world, has exacerbated inequalities, built up tensions in communities.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We see this in various forms, for example, as we work from home and also in home-based learning during our circuit breaker.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is not unapparent that most of us who can work from home, perhaps, can claim to be better off.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is those who cannot, who are on the ground, who have to be physically present, that are feeling the true brunt of this crisis.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Home-based learning also shows up the differences in access to technology.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Different family situations give rise to starkly different learning outcomes during the circuit breaker.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In as much as we try to provide more equal access, yet, different circumstances still lead to different learning outcomes.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: All this comes back perhaps to a word that we use very often in our discourse – meritocracy.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Meritocracy underpins so much of our social structures in Singapore and we can justifiably be proud of how we provide equal opportunities for everyone in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is also about ensuring that we have equitable outcomes, not equal outcomes, not as what Dodo in Alice in Wonderland says at the end of the caucus race, "Everyone wins and therefore everybody deserves a prize".

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We must have equitable outcomes because, if we do not, then it is even worse than not having meritocracy.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For this, we must engender change in our attitudes across Singapore in all sectors – at home, at work, in our economy.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We need to rethink our values, redefine success, refocus our beliefs, interests, causes, passions.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is the only way we can stop perpetuating the sense of inferiority or feeling of being unrewarded despite trying our best, amongst different groups in our society.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We should, therefore, revalue vocational and technical skills as much as academic dexterity, shift out perception of value based on work or academic performance alone.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In many other societies, being a plumber, being an electrician, is a valued skill set.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: That way, we can ensure that our social fabric is strengthened, not because we are one giant piece of cloth but like a warm comforting blanket comprised of different multiple equally important layers, so that we can all play our role equally in society.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The Members before me have spoken very passionately also about the digital sphere.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Digital defence is important to us as well.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We see this impact of negative communication overseas.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: All this depends also on the most fundamental pillar of Total Defence and that is our psychological defence.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Our psychological resilience and our sense of security is important.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Again, it is now more than ever that we are in this together.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But we see various examples, many of us in our constituency, we hear more and more comments like these, "My neighbour, formally Malaysian" or "you know, that chap who came from India".

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As disputes arise, we must strengthen our identity of Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Again, regardless of how long you have been here, you must be proud, to belong to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: All of us here are proud to be Singaporeans, but some of us were not born in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Yet, we serve fellow Singaporeans in this House.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many out there in society are doing the same thing as well.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And they too, are valuable Singaporeans, they too, are our brothers and sisters.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A group of pigeons, led by their mother, was searching for food.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Driven by hunger, they came across a pile of rice.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As they started eating, a little sparrow came by.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The sparrow asked one of the brothers, "Could I share in your meal?" The brother said, "No, we found it first." Yet, the mother pigeon said, "There is more than enough, let us share." And so, she welcomed the little sparrow.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As they ate and were filled, they were preparing to fly away when suddenly a huge net came across them.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The pigeons panicked, they flew off in different directions But, as they struggled in different directions the more tangled they got.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In a distance, they saw the farmer coming at them with a club.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It was the little sparrow who suddenly said, "Stay calm.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Let all of us take one part of this net and fly in unison.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As they did so, they managed to lift the net and the farmer could only look on as the net flew higher and higher way.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But, they were still trapped in that net.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And so the little sparrow also said, "I know of a friend, he is a little mouse who lives across the hill.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I brought him food once during the winter.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, they flew across the hill and met the little mouse.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The little mouse said, "I can get you out of this quandry," as he bit through the net and freed them one by one.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And where we have more of, we can share.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But, we should also not belittle those that are smaller than us, or less skilled than us, or appear to be weaker than us.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Because they too, have a role to play in our society and in our country.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Perhaps it is them who have the street-smart, who can tell us when we are in trouble, how to get out of there mine.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I think, in the course of these few months, we have shown the capacity to be proud of who we are, Singaporeans and to be proud of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 5.00 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.37 pm until 5.00 pm.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I will refer to these handouts briefly in the course of my speech.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These four strands hold and bind Singaporeans and Singapore society together, for the long term.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And I would say – they are no less important than the foundations of our country’s economic and security framework.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Like Mr Sitoh earlier, I believe these four strands coming together synergistically is critical not only to providing an outlet to rebound from the current pandemic, but also to our long-term goals in nation-building.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They foster a national identity and consensus in a way that no other facet of society can.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I am honoured and very humbled to be given this opportunity as Minister to lead in this endeavor, to build on the solid foundations established by my predecessors.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In this speech, I will focus on youth, and on the kind of society that we want to foster.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Our young people are a crucial segment of our society.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The youths of today are the leaders of tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They are the people who must have a say in the kind of society they want to be in, and play a part in shaping the kind of future for Singapore that they want to leave behind.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Government is here to help them reach their personal and collective potential, but the future is in their own hands.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is usually used to describe a young person who is capable and outstanding.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Unfortunately, there is no equivalent of this for older people.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: While this saying usually describes young people, it also describes a very positive and hopeful state of affairs with being young and associated with being young – the young are full of potential, promise and eventual accomplishment.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For the young, with the luxury of having time on their side and the endowment of energy and imagination, the sky is the limit.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: However, amid the backdrop of COVID-19, there is a perceptible sense that the positivity in our youths might be somewhat diminished and I understand their concerns, as I am sure many of my colleagues in this House do, about the impact of the pandemic on bread and butter issues.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is only to be expected in the current climate, but we must ensure that while we are realistic and we remain aware of the situation, that our youths do not become discouraged, do not become defeatist or disenchanted.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The pandemic will pass, but our aspirations and dreams must remain. 年轻有为 still applies.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And perhaps even more so in today's context.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In the last few weeks, I have spoke with a number of youths, across a broad range of backgrounds.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I asked them about their concerns and their aspirations, and what they felt we should address in this new term of Government.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I promised them that we would bring these up in Parliament and let me just share a few of their thoughts with you.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Understandably, many of the concerns revolve around the current economic climate: will I be able to find a good job when I graduate?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Will my skills still be relevant in a post-COVID-19 world, where there have been disruption upon disruption?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Will I be able to stay competitive, especially in this climate when foreigners can compete for the job and perhaps even do it remotely from another country?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Will I be able to afford the things that matter to me most at this point in my life: getting married, buying a home, looking after my parents, whilst trying to start my own family?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: At the same time, they are also thinking deeply about the way we live, as a people, dealing with broader societal issues, and the values and ideals that they wish to see in society.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: At the top of their minds are questions such as: how do we care better for one another?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Can we better support vulnerable communities and how do we ensure that we leave no one is left behind?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And can we move from just tolerating, to truly embracing our diversity?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Youths also asked hard questions about the fairness and the tone of political campaigns at the recent General Elections.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They asked to see more diverse views in Parliament, more checks and balances and more open debates on constructive policy alternatives.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These concerns and questions are entirely valid and reflect the rapid changes in our economic, political and social environment, amplified, catalysed by the effects of the current COVID-19 situation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: A participant, one of them from my youth engagements, summed it up as follows, and I quote, “Youths seem to be dealing a lot with uncertainties – clashing ideologies, existential threat of climate disruptions, fundamental economic shifts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It’s scary having to navigate a future that feels so hostile and full of unknowns.” I think all of us would have a lot of empathy for this sentiment – the future is uncertain.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But I would also say to this group and to those out there – that we are at the cusp of a very different future that is promising in so many ways.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Various student groups have helped to share messages of encouragement and also translate content for migrant workers staying in the Changi Exhibition Centre Integrated Community Care and Recovery Facility.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Others have contributed through SGUnited, a movement and one-stop digital portal for Singaporeans to contribute toward the national response for the COVID-19 outbreak, and they do so through donations, through volunteering and, of course, also in taking part with others in community-led efforts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: What is striking about all these initiatives is that they were initiated by volunteers, who stepped up, even as they themselves were, at the same time, worried about their own lives and livelihood.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is very heartening and we need to encourage more of these efforts, work together with them and build on them.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In the best of times, the Government does not have all the answers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Today, in an uncertain environment with complex challenges ahead of us, all the more we must chart a path together.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As a Government, we need to partner with the community including our young people, to leverage on our shared values and forge a way forward.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Today, I hope to address some of these concerns raised – not just through our policies and our programmes – but also in our broader efforts to partner and work with young people to catalyse the solutions and tackle these issues together.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I will be addressing two broad questions that our youths have raised.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First, how can I secure a good future and achieve my aspirations in these turbulent times?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This question deals not only with bread and butter issues in these uncertain times, but also how we can collectively address longer term challenges, like climate change, sustainability and the environment.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, how can I help realise the vision of Singapore as a more caring and inclusive society?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: How do we become the kind of society we want to live in, and would be happy to leave behind, for our children?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This second question is both philosophical and also practical – how do	we weave the Tapestry of Singapore’s society to accommodate a diversity of threads seamlessly, so that the Tapestry is at once both beautiful to behold and also comforting to touch.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Sometimes, the Tapestry can be more beautiful to behold from afar than to touch and feel textually.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Keeping it together, keeping it nice, beautiful, soft to the touch is a constant work in progress.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The threads are woven together, sometimes by suasion, sometimes by policy, and the feel can be kind of uneven and rough on occasion.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Sometimes a thread or two might come loose and we have to put it back with some effort.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But we have to, because each thread that comes loose from this fabric is Tapestry, it threatens the integrity of the thread next to it, and if left unchecked, eventually could unravel the entire fabric.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is an important aspect of the work in my Ministry and I will come back to this point.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The youths of today face intense competition once they start formal schooling.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Globalisation presents new opportunities of exchange, but also opens up academic competition beyond national boundaries.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And it is exacerbated by the current COVID-19 pandemic when global economies are in recession and opportunities are fewer to come by.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: My colleagues have outlined the steps to protect Singaporeans better, but the hard truth is that competition is a fact of life and we cannot influence the trajectory of other countries.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Yet despite this, I want to encourage our youths to realise that competition drives us to excel, competition pushes us out of our comfort zone to be more than what we thought we could be and realise a better version of ourselves.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will support you in this journey as best as we can.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Whether it is in getting work experience, facilitating job and training opportunities or skills development.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Internships and work experience in these times could otherwise be more difficult to come by.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have also set up a portal called gradgowhere.sg that contains resources for youths looking for jobs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These programmes to equip youths with skills and provide more employment opportunities and will help address their immediate concerns about day-to-day living.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For more details on these programmes, I would like to ask Members to look at the handouts that I have just given out.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: At the same time, while youths are concerned about the immediate bread and butter issues, they also reflected to me that they are equally concerned about the broader, longer term questions, such as looking after our mental well-being and how do we better entrench our environmental sustainability efforts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These are important issues, and I know that many young people angst over them.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Our youths are very much at the front and centre of these efforts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They have called for action to reduce the stigma associated with mental health issues, and greater awareness and openness in seeking help.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Young people in Singapore, like their peers around the world, are the vanguard for an environmentally sustainable future, advocating not only new ways of living, but also new ways of making a living.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In this way, they are really our active agents of change and we need to tap on this dynamic resource.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The hon Ms Raeesah Khan said, I think two days ago, that youths need to have a seat at the table to look at such issues, and we agree.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The above are just some examples of how we want to engage our youths to participate and contribute actively to their own future, having a say, being an architect in their own future and also on matters of national importance.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will continue to create more opportunities and avenues for youths to partner the Government and society on issues that matter to them, and we will do so on a regular and sustained basis.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: When we engaged youths under the SG Youth Action Plan last year, they outlined their vision for a better society not just for themselves, but for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And inherent in this push for a more caring and inclusive Singapore are key considerations of (a) reducing social inequality; (b) building a more tightly knit society; and (c) improving civic discourse and participation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Which in turn brings up even more fundamental questions of what kind of social compact and politics we desire for our country, both now and in the long term.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: An important consideration for me is how we can harness youthful energy to bring about positive change, to allow our young to blossom, instead of allowing uncertainty and discontent to fester amongst our young and resulting in negative confrontation?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First, we need to allow the young to give voice to their dreams and aspirations.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We need to give them the space and the avenues to engage with the rest of society, and have conversations with older generations to implement change, whilst at the same time understanding the constraints and trade-offs that age and experience sometimes can give a better insight to.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The older generation in turn needs to be a little more patient, accepting and appreciative of generationally different views.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These shared ideas have indeed help take us forward.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have been working with Singaporeans across the age spectrum, across the generations to reflect on our shared identity, and to think deeply about the values and legacy that we want to leave behind.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We are a society comprising both the young and the old and neither can exist alone, and we must learn to recognise that all of us have a part to play in moulding our future.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, societies need to give the young hope – hope of a brighter future, including good jobs and good lives.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Many of the young in developed countries see the dreams of their parents slipping beyond their grasp and are reacting against a system which they might feel is no longer capable of giving them hope.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We cannot let this happen to us here in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Our society needs to remain meritocratic, but not ossified.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We need to make sure that our society remains fair, transparent, has equality of opportunities and that the fires of the Singaporean dream keep burning.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The story of today's Singapore youth, like the youth before them, must therefore be woven from the fabric of hope.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, I return to the Singapore Tapestry metaphor I mentioned earlier.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That Tapestry is really the heart of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Singapore Tapestry will always have yarns of different colour, sizes and even nature.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Some are old threads, some are young threads.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But whatever the case, there are certain enduring truths about the Tapestry.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Each of us, each thread and each fibre, is part of a larger whole.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: All of us have a role to play in keeping the Singapore Tapestry from fraying or worse, from being stretched and ripped apart.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Yet, even as there is only one single Tapestry, we remain individuals, with our own identities, our own dreams and our own aspirations.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In fact, it is this very diversity of yarns that make Singapore exciting and more beautiful.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In contrast to a Tapestry which had it been spun out of a single spool of fibre, single colour, one type, one nature that would have yielded a uniformly plain and monochromatic Singapore Cloth.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Our differences, our diverse ethnicities, our cultures, different backgrounds and heritage and beliefs, they make for a collective which is far richer, and for a whole which is far greater than the sum of its parts – and that is the Singapore Tapestry.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
