text: There is a lot of progress that has been done in the way we educate our children, because we know these are very important skillsets and values that are required for children in the future.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: Much has been talked about in terms of changes that we have put in place in the education system.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: I invite Mr Leong to look up some of this information.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: If he needs further information at another platform, I invite him to file questions or raise some of these issues.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: I just find that this may not be the right forum because I think there could be many other speakers.

speaker: Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman
text: I also invite Mr Leong to look at my speech again and see how I have elaborated on the various changes we have put in place in our education system.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: I wanted to ask a clarification of Ms Sylvia Lim.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The reason I rise is because I was the first CEO of SINDA.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: At the time that I was CEO of SINDA, we worked collaboratively with MENDAKI which was helmed by Mr Zainal Abidin Rasheed.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We worked with the CDAC which was led by Mr Chan Soo Sen, and also with the Eurasian Association, which was, at that time, led by the Chairman, the father of our Deputy Speaker, Mr Timothy de Souza.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: I understand where she is coming from about the questions that have been raised.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: When I was asked to be the CEO, I had the same questions.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: But I think after involvement and seeing the evolution and not just in individual silos, but I think in the collaborative way in which our self-help groups have operated – be it in the context of educational support, be it in the sharing of expertise, be it in the area of working with the Government on various policy initiatives, I think it is fair to say that our self-help groups have not been ossified.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: There has been a response to not just the feedback from population, but also from the evolving needs of the different communities and how we can work together.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: I think the Member is also fully aware of the range of programmes that are now being mounted individually and collectively by these self-help groups, and the number of people that are being helped.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: With that understanding, with that appreciation of the evolution, the question I have for her is: does she feel that we would be better off without the self-help groups?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: His question is whether I am positing that society be better off be better off without the self-help groups.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: This is something I am calling for an open conversation about.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I am not trying to be prescriptive to say that the answer is to amalgamate.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: But it was put forward as a suggestion from me as something that could be discussed in the national exercise and that was the spirit of my speech.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, I take it that the Member's position is not that she is advocating — because an amalgation is an effective dissolution of the existing entities.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, assuming she is not recommending that, her proposition is that we should have an on-going dialogue in terms of how we can work closer together.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And that in fact is what has been working all along.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That is why the self-help groups have evolved the way they have.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I am not quite clear what the Member's proposition is, or is there a specific proposal that the Member has.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Even if they collaborate, the question is whether it would be something that society wants to move on about, to have these, all the work done under a national body, in that sense.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I can share with the House as well.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I think the Minister is a bit older than me, but it does not matter.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The fact is that there are many people in my generation, as I had mentioned in my speech, who grew up during Mr Rajaratnam's time.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Our distinct memory was quite different from the reality that I sensed today.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: In fact, many of my contemporaries wrote to me thereafter to say that they are very uncomfortable with the self-help groups as they are.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, I respect that there may be different views on this, as I have said.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: But I think it is important for us to have a conversation, and as the President said, in a spirit mutual respect and being open to the possibility that things may not be static.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But there are so many things wrong with that.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: More specifically, calling for an open dialogue, I think is very welcome.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But when you start the dialogue, what is your starting position?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I did not say that this is the answer, but this is something which I think should be in the discussion.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: And at the end of whole national exercise, the consensus is, "No, we should not do it", I will respect that but I think we need to have a starting point for discussion.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: I would just like to reframe the matter.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Perhaps Ms Sylvia Lim is coming to this a little bit late.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Indeed, we have been engaging in such conversations with a wide variety of people.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: And Singaporeans can volunteer for more than one body, more than one organisation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Singaporeans can contribute funding to more than one body, and often do.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: There is plenty room in Singapore for us to work through a variety of means to achieve this common aim.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: I just wanted to put that on the table.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: It has been posited before and there are people who have actually made this happen.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: And if people would like to come and find out a bit more about what these bodies are doing, I would be very happy to provide them some instructions.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In her words: “In all that we do, the interests of Singaporeans are always paramount.” Strengthening the Singaporean Core is an important tenet in nation-building.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It is important during good times when our economy is growing rapidly and doubly important during bad times such as during this recession where we see numerous layoffs and where many Singaporeans, especially Professionals, Managers and Executives (PMEs), are impacted.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Over the past few decades, our economy has grown from third world to first world.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Accordingly, the expansion of business needs has generated demand for workers with specialised skills such as in cybersecurity and artificial intelligence.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As Singaporeans may require time to be trained with the relevant skills, we should not close our doors, but instead, complement our local workforce with specific-skilled foreign PMEs to maintain Singapore’s economic competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In fact, the COVID-19 crisis has shed light on certain critical sectors, which could be the forerunners in calibrating our nation’s reliance on foreign PMEs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: For example, the development of rapid virus test-kits is testament to the complementarity between local and foreign expertise in the biomedical sector.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In this regard, we must uphold our pillar of meritocracy.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: There must be fairness and equal treatment and assessment of workers, which is also a fundamental International Labour Organization commitment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Today, our Singaporean PMEs are well-educated, skilled and seek more in life – meaningful work in line with our values, including meritocracy, equality and progress.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: However, PMEs I have spoken to say that this is not their universal experience.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I cannot help but wonder if, as a result of unchecked conscious and unconscious bias, there may still be instances of nationality bias in hiring and promotion and in today’s context, retrenchments?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The reality is, left unchecked, this would exacerbate the glass-ceiling effect and issues relating to job opportunity for our Singaporean PMEs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This will go some way in levelling the playing field for our Singaporean PMEs and providing our Singaporean PMEs fair hiring opportunities.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I am equally glad that Minister Chan Chun Sing, in his capacity as Minister of Trade and Industry, has emphasised – over the weekend – three very important points.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: First, that there must be fairness and zero tolerance for discrimination of any kind and tough action has to be taken on firms with hiring bias.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Second, the importance of diversity and inclusion, something that I submit is crucial for a developed country and democracy like ours.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Third, the efforts of localisation by transferring of skills to develop a pipeline of local talent.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I therefore submit that Strengthening our Singaporean Core requires a two-fold approach: First, the hiring of foreign PMEs must be based on merit – on their contribution to Singapore and how they complement our local workforce.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Second, we must equip and enable our local workers through relevant and timely reskilling and upskilling to help them remain gainfully employed and employable.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: To augment our efforts to further strengthen the Singaporean Core, I have five suggestions.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: First, ensuring Singaporean PMETs are not left behind by the raising of EP and S Pass qualifying salaries.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Raising the salary criteria for EP and S Pass is timely.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In the same vein, MOM should also consider raising the bar for sectors such as Infocomm Technology and Professional Services, where there are generally more companies on the Fair Consideration Framework watchlist.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: To compound matters further, our Singaporean PMETs working alongside these foreign PMETs performing similar or same jobs may not get a similar pay hike, thereby resulting in serious parity issues.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It does not help that many of our PMETs are now confronted with wage freezes, restraints and cuts.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: For unionised companies, our unions will closely watch the actions of the employers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: For workers in non-unionised companies, I strongly urge them to join as union members and organise themselves, so that we can protect them and ensure that they are fairly treated.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Second, strengthening the Singaporean Core at all Levels through strengthening hiring culture, practices and changing mindsets.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Strengthening the Singaporean Core of PMETs must be at all levels of the hierarchy and not merely addressing entry or lower level PMETs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In large corporations with deep pockets, hiring more Singaporeans at the bottom balloons the denominator to make them look less culpable in actual percentages and numbers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Our efforts must be to address this at all levels and have a tiered approach in our policies and laws, according to different sectors’ needs and circumstances.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: While we introduce new policies to further tighten the various levers, strengthening the hiring culture, practices and changing mindsets across the various organisations which hire foreign PMEs must be at the backbone of these efforts.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: HR leaders I speak to say they may be supportive of the Singaporean Core but in some cases, the hiring managers may have the final say in the eventual choice of the candidate.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In many of these organisations, complex reporting structures and matrix reporting mean that the HR sometimes have little or no say.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In short, it is imperative for not just a change of mindset for the CEO or CHRO but also the mindsets of hiring managers and everyone from end to end in the value chain that are involved in the various HR processes.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: While foreign PMEs are employed in Singapore, there needs to be more intentional reciprocity by multi-national corporations (MNCs) to offer similar regional and global opportunities to our Singaporean PMEs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In this way, our Singaporean PMEs will be able to gain international experience and in turn, add to the calibre of our Singaporean workforce.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I urge the management within MNCs to groom our Singaporean PMEs as part of their leadership identification and development processes.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: By the same token, our Singaporean PMEs must step up, step forward and readily accept these opportunities to take lead and uproot to remote parts of the globe for regional and international exposure and opportunities.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: However, more needs to be done to review the current exemptions of the FCF.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: However, I urge for more transparency on who are these PMEs who fall within this ICT exemption for greater transparency and accountability.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I particularly like the fact that MOM, through its FCF website, encourages all employers, even if they fall within the exemptions, to post their job advertisements on the national jobs portal.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As a pilot, this can be applied to companies that remain on the watchlist after a period of time, such as one year, and have failed to improve or show concerted efforts to strengthen the Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Similarly, we can also impose mandatory audits and penalties such as removing preferential tax and other benefits including curtailment of the award of public sector contracts on companies with discriminatory hiring practices and high proportion of grievance cases if no improvement is made within a stipulated period of time.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Many of our economic incentives appear to be granted based on total headcount created in Singapore, with little mention of support for proactive and sustained local hiring.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Likewise, there should be proactive and sustained knowledge and skills transfer to Singaporeans by the foreign PMEs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: A structured mentoring must be put in place to ensure that skills are transferred from foreign PMEs to our local PMEs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Potential abuse can arise without a tiered approach, for example, economic incentives to expire without more senior Singaporean PME hires within a certain period of time or when there is a failure to transfer skills and knowledge.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Though a very sharp tool, MOM should review if there is a need to legislate areas of the FCF, including providing TAFEP with more legal powers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Pure frameworks, perhaps developed with a fear of losing investments and over-regulation, provide an environment ripe for corporations to circumvent rules.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We need to re-consider the long-held notion of being regarded as "not investment friendly" with legislation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The world has moved on to embrace sustainability and related environmental, social and governance legislation, which encompass fair employment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Fifth, possible tougher measures such as EP quota.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: With the current added measures and above suggestions, I expect to see an eradication of nationality bias and a shrinking watchlist.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Should the above measures still fail and does not bear fruit, the Labour Movement has previously floated the idea to look at relevant quotas, as a response to possible interventions to curb the problem and also address problem sectors that have a notably higher proportion of foreign PMEs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: With these two-tier quota, companies will still be able to hire foreign PMEs with specialised skillsets to drive technology-based initiatives.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The implementation of the quota can be gradual to address the concern by companies that our local PMEs do not have the requisite skills and experience.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The Labour Movement has consistently advocated for a strong Singaporean Core at the heart of our workforce – a Core that keeps us united as a country, even as we welcome those who contribute to our growth, employed based on merit while equipping our local workers to the best of our abilities.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Against current weak economic conditions and employment outlook, strengthening the Singaporean Core is a critical mission for the Labour Movement and an area that needs to be watched carefully and conscientiously.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: To that end, the Labour Movement will continue to work with MOM, employers and professional associations in the fair hiring and continuous reskilling of local workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In many areas such as education, logistics, air and sea transport, biomedical, we aspire and peg ourselves to "best in class" standards – researching and understanding what works well for other countries and positioning ourselves as leaders pushing frontiers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Indeed, it is imperative to introduce the right policies in the face of an evolving economic and domestic environment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We must be mindful of our uniqueness as a city-state and balance our national interests such as the employability of our workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Both methodology and technology adopted in Singapore must be contextualised for our local workforce and for different groups of workers in their various areas of work and at their respective pace of digital acceptance.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We need employers from both MNCs and SMEs, business federations and associations, union leaders who understand the ground, and also academic institutions to actively collaborate – to ensure that current workers and new entrants to the workforce are able, agile and adaptable to changing technology and demands.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The first iteration of the Industry Transformation Maps launched four years ago, in September 2016, articulated these strategies to sustain growth and competitiveness for our industries with a three to five-year horizon.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In that journey, we should evaluate the reasons why Singaporeans are unable to fulfil these existing and future PMET jobs and roles and develop an action plan that combines both a sectoral and functional approach, to rectify this for the longer term.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: To better enable our local PMEs to take on roles and handle tasks in line with industry transformation, there needs to be continuous reskilling and upskilling and intentional career and salary mapping, through formalised set ups such as NTUC's Company Training Committees as well as the efforts by the National Jobs Council and NTUC Job Security Council.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This would help equip our workers to take up roles, especially in industries that have a disproportionate number of foreign PMEs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Such training would be particularly relevant for PMEs in their 40s to 60s, who tend to be more vulnerable and at risk from technological disruption and during economic downturns.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I verily believe that our intention is not to advocate for closed-door policies.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Clearly, market failure exists in our current employment framework.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We can, and must, improve this – by knowing where to flex and where to tighten measures.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We need to guard against abuse of our system, by giving Singaporean PMEs a fair chance at local job opportunities, which will also mitigate any potential brain drain.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: A healthy dose of market intervention is essential to ensure fair play.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This also instils loyalty and fosters a sense of belonging and identity amongst Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is not diametrically opposed to ensuring economic survival for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It is time to pivot and supplement our first-class hard infrastructure with an upgraded soft infrastructure.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In my maiden speech in Parliament in 2011, I said all debates in this House will always be guided by one question: how can we best ensure the survival and success of Singapore and improve the lives of Singaporeans?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We have over the years examined this question in different ways, in and out of this House.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The question has now become more critical than ever.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We begin 2020, full of hope, having just commemorated our Bicentennial last year.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: None of us could have foreseen what was to come: the whole of humanity locked in by a virus; millions of people infected and lives upended; the global economy plunged into the worst recession since the Great Depression; and the way we earn a living, go about our lives and interact with one another, turned on its head.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In Singapore, we mounted a swift and robust response.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: To protect lives, we imposed the circuit breaker.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our healthcare and frontline workers responded vailently, keeping our fatalities very low and bringing down the number of new infections.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our people observe strict discipline to keep each other safe.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But as a small open economy, we cannot defy the full force of this global crisis.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The risk of new waves of infection persists, threatening to derail the gradual reopening of our economy.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Many who have held on to their jobs has seen significant falls in income.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: For those in the most affected sectors like aviation and tourism, recovery will be long-drawn.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We have to tackle these challenges admist the underlying shifts that predated COVID-19.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: There is a backlash against free trade and sharpening nativist instincts because the constant benefits of globalisation have been unevenly distributed.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Technology and innovation are reshaping the nature of work, disrupting jobs and businesses.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Distresses have, in turn, caused societies to be polarised exacerbated by the proliferation of echo chambers on social media.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The uncertainties created by COVID-19 have only accelerated this shifts.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The compound matters, governments around the world have financed massive stimulus packages through borrowing, putting an even greater burden on future generations.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It is against this sombre backdrop that we open our Fourteenth Parliament.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As the President said in her speech, we are at an inflection point in our history.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Now, more than ever, we must ask – how can we best ensure the survival and success of Singapore and improves the lives of Singaporeans in this unprecedented time?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Adapt to change but stay true to our values.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Change will leave us behind if we stand still.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: What would define this term of Government, is how we will adapt that will build a better life for our people.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Even as we keep pace with change, we must stay true to the values that have enabled us to progress all these years.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: By embracing change with courage and confidence, we build our capacity to adapt.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: By staying true to our values, we strengthen our sense of common purpose.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: By working in close partnership, we advance as Singapore together.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I will speak about how we need to adapt as an economy, a society and a people.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Singapore's economic history over the decades has been one of constant adaptation, restructuring and transformation.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Industry players have also found new ways of working together to raise the competitiveness of their industries.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Indeed, bearing fruit is not just a metaphor here.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I met a fruit seller, Jun Sheng, better known as "Ah Boy" at Block 58, market place in Bedok.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In addition to operating a physical store, he sells fruits online and even takes orders via WhatsApp.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Many hawkers and small businesses islandwide are also going digital.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We must do all we can to support our workers and businesses, big or small and make such innovations pervasive.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: While we have made progress in industries' transformation, we must look ahead and prepare ourselves for even faster change and more disruptive change.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: To emerge stronger as an economy, we must strengthen our capacity in four areas.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: First, you must take an even more integrated and coordinated approach to economic transformation.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In our system, tripartism, the Government, businesses and the Labour Movement, working together has been a tremendous source of strength.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Two years back, as chairman of the National Research Foundation, I visited the Netherlands to learn more about their triple helix model of innovation, where government businesses and academia work together to build knowledge, test prototypes and scale innovation.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Like some research triangles in the US, the Dutch have done well.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This model is being expanded to incorporate other dimensions, such as societal responsibility and environmental protection.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In essence, the economy is very complex in how allocates resources, generates innovative ideas and in how returns are distributed across multiple stakeholders.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: While there is a competitive element in this, there are also benefits to be gained from working together for shared prosperity.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Singapore can build on our tripartite partnership to be a test bed that creates deeper linkages with an expanded list of stakeholders, including our education and research institutions, our community groups and interested partners from around the world.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: By doing so, we can create good jobs for our people and new opportunities for our entrepreneurs.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Second, we must redouble our efforts to develop everyone to their fullest potential.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In this way, our people can take on new opportunities and flourish in their chosen fields.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And we have to explore new possibilities for developing our people fully.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Studies in Singapore by Prof Chong Yap Seng show that the physical and mental health of women during pregnancy affects the brain development and behaviours of their babies.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: On-going clinical studies will assess if nutrition and other measures taken during pregnancy and early childhood are associated with better outcomes in both mothers and their children.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The National Research Foundation is expanding on this by supporting research programmes that address the broader goal of enhancing human potential through measures during pregnancy and childhood, including nutrition, parenting and learning and, later, in our studies on how people learn.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Third, we must strengthen our path-finding capacity to find new bright spots amid economic disruption.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: They range from environmental sustainability to smart commerce, supply chain digitalisation and the use of robotics.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This can create new growth markets for our businesses and good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We will invest in incubating and accelerating start-ups and supporting established companies to expand their R&D to build competitive strengths.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Such a vibrant innovation eco-system will build up our path-finding capabilities.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Fourth, we must find new ways to be a vital node with rich and deep interconnections with the rest of the world.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As a small city-state, being open is our strength and opportunity.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Unlike other major cities, we do not have domestic hinterlands that buffer us against shocks.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We cannot take for granted that, in a post-COVID-19 world, we can continue to be the same kind of hub that we used to be.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We must, therefore, forge new forms of connections, such as digital economy agreements, while deepening our linkages with regional markets to ride on Asia's potential.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We must also remain open to investment and talents from around the world.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In this economic climate, we understand that many Singaporeans are anxious about their livelihoods.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our starting point is that our economic strategies must serve the interests of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The foreign investments we attract must create meaningful jobs for our people and strengthen our corporate eco-system.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But to emerge stronger, we must resist any temptation to turn inwards.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We cannot close ourselves to the world or make foreigners unwelcome in our society.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We must always serve the interest of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The best way to ensure that this little red dot, with no natural resources of any kind but with a determined, hard-working, forward-looking people, is to remain useful and relevant to the world.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We do this by keeping our economy vibrant and competitive so that Singaporeans and other people choose to be here to invest and do business, thereby creating good jobs and opportunities for all of us.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Mr Patrick Tay just spoke about ITM 2.0 – and I thank Mr Tay for mentioning about the ITM efforts.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In fact, even in ITM 1.0, there is an explicit linkage between the various components of what we do in developing our people and in job creation.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But Mr Tay is right that we should enhance this to create an even stronger linkage in the form of skills maps and in the form of job redesign and job retraining, re-skilling of our workers to take on those jobs.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And, in particular, we must also make a deliberate effort to develop Singaporeans for leadership roles in companies so that they can take Singapore forward and that Singapore, as an operational and regional headquarters, has what it takes – that it has people, Singaporeans who grow up in a multiracial, multi-religious and multi-cultural environment can connect with people all around us easily and build deep linkages with our friends in the region.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And this is something that we will pursue.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But the same time, we must not undermine the essence of what has made us successful.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Even as we adapt to the changing world, we must stay true to our values, our sense of unity as a people, our composition as a multi-cultural society.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We must stay true to our value to the world as an oasis of harmony in this fractious world.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Even as we evolve our economic strategies, our society, too, is facing new challenges and needs to continue to adapt to sustain the promise of progress for every Singaporean.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We must not let change lead to polarisation.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In the early days of our development, our economy was growing strongly.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: A rising tide lifted all boats and most Singaporeans saw their lives improved by leaps and bounds.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We invested in our people so that they could adapt and grow with our economy.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: High home ownership also gives Singaporeans a share in the fruits of our progress.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As our economy matured, we also strengthened our social safety nets.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Looking ahead, our economy will change at a much more rapid pace.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Disruption to jobs will be more common with greater adoption of technology, such as automation and remote work.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We must, therefore, take an integrated view of our economic and social policies.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As our Labour Movement puts it, "A job is the best form of welfare for our people".

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The Government will continue to invest in our people, match them to new opportunities and bring out the best in all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This way, we will keep social mobility alive.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: At the same time, with major changes in the economy and labour market, will need to adapt our social safety nets and keep inequality in check.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: More workers will fall on hard times and we need to enable them to adjust and bounce back through this crisis and beyond.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Some Singaporeans are taking part in the gig economy, taking on a wide range of jobs, either part-time or full-time.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, our support for self-employed persons will have to evolve accordingly.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We must continue to uplift our lower wage workers and enable our older workers to continue working if they wish to.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Various ideas have been proposed on how we can do this, such as minimum wage, universal basic income and unemployment insurance.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The Government will keep an open mind to all these ideas.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But we must also recognise that there are no magic bullets.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Each of these ideas has its merits as well as unintended effects.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We have to consider the trade-offs and be clear about what works for our context and our time.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Demands on our social safety nets are increasing at a time when our revenue base is growing more slowly and with sharper competition for tax revenues across countries.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, I must caution against looking for what may appear to be cost-less solutions.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Somehow, someone else will have to pay for these schemes.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: At the same time, while we must strengthen our social safety nets, we must do so in a way that reinforces and not undermine an individual's efforts.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: A strong compact maintains a balance between the roles of the individual, family, community and the Government and helps us better cope with change together.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Indeed, social safety nets cannot become a set of shackles.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It should not hold down those we started with less.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It should not create a dependency such that people who get fish for today never learn how to fish for food tomorrow.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It should not breed an entitled class who ask, "What more can you do for me?" A well-designed social safety net protects the vulnerable, invests in human and societal capital and provides a means for those who fall down to bounce back.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It believes in people and lifts the human spirit.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It supports every generation to have aspirations and dreams and for everyone to ask, "What more can we do for one another?" As Members debate on how we can strengthen our support for Singaporeans, let us keep in mind how new enhancements can be funded equitably and sustainably over time and strengthen our people's capacity to not only succeed throughout life but to help others succeed, too.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: These are the values that we must strengthen even as we adapt.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: How can we best ensure the survival and success of Singapore and improve the lives of Singaporeans depends on how well we adapt to change.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And I will now speak on affirming our values as a people.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As we adapt – and, in some cases, make major adjustments because the circumstances we face have changed significantly – we must stay rooted to our values and identity and, above all, our unity as one people.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I have been encouraged to see how COVID-19 has strengthened our sense of common purpose and brought out the best in us.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This sense of unity, through both good times and bad, is rooted in the values enshrined in our Pledge and the distinct Singaporean identity we have evolved through the years.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: During SG50, we honoured those who have brought us this far, in our journey since independence.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In our Bicentennial last year, we explored how we progressed from Singapore to Singaporeans by holding true to our values of openness, multi-culturalism and self-determination and sharing the conviction to stand united and defy the odds as one people.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It will take more effort to maintain this sense of common purpose as our society becomes more diverse.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our society will face new differences along the lines of identity, socio-economic status and political beliefs.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: There will always be different perspectives on subjects like race, language and religion and the rights and obligations of citizenship.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It is essential that we rise above our differences and find common ground.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Occasional setbacks need not trip us in our perseverance to continue to make progress.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Harmony in diversity will always be a work in progress.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We may not always agree, but we cannot afford to let our disagreement turn into division.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We wanted to build on our experience from our Singapore Conversation to engender deep understanding and partnerships among Singaporeans and between our people and the Government.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We know many Singaporeans are keen to play their part and to make a difference.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Two weeks ago, I met Samantha and a group of volunteers who clean up our beach at East Coast Park regularly.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Kiat How, Desmond Tan and I had a follow-up discussion with them via Zoom on Saturday to discuss how we can create a more sustainable Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I was very impressed by the passion and commitment.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We agreed to work together to turn their good ideas into action.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The process of working together will help to foster a culture of respect and expand our common space.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This strengthens our capacity to adapt and change together, and will take time to build up.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The better we adapt to change and stay true to our values, the stronger we can emerge from this and future crises.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The stronger we are at home the more confidence we can be to stick our place in the world and create value with others.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This has been our formula for success and survival.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We are determined to whole a rules-based global order which has taken us to where we are today.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As a small nation that threatens no country, we want to be friends with all and to work with all.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We are both a city-state and a global metropolis.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Maintaining this dual identity will not be easy.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But as long as we are clear about our values and what holds us together, it will be a source of strength that opens up new opportunities.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Let us continue to work with like-minded partners to build a better world for Singaporeans for people around the world and for our future generations.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Since our Independence, we have weathered one crisis after another – from the withdrawal of British forces and the ensuing massive unemployment, to the 1973 oil crisis, the Asian Financial Crisis, SARS, the 2001 IT bubble collapse and the Global Financial Crisis.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: All of us in our 50s and older would have lived through these turbulent periods.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Each time, Singaporeans would have been called upon to show fortitude and resilience, and work in unity with our fellow citizens.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And each time, we have risen to the challenge, adapted and emerged stronger.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: To overcome this crisis, we have to once again draw upon and build on this capacity to adapt and remain united, and stand true to our values.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We can navigate this period of great uncertainty and change, but our policies must set the right tone for the rest of society.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This House must fulfill its duty to articulate and debate policy options to build a better life for our people and to advance Singapore's place in the world.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This is the mandate that has been entrusted to us by Singaporeans.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I trust that all of us, whether in Government or the Opposition, will share this common sense of mission – to serve in the best interests of Singaporeans and Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: My colleagues and I in Government, have listened to the voices of our people.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We have heard and share our people's anxieties.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We acknowledge the concerns and unhappiness that some have voiced.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As the world and our society changes, there will be greater divergence of views.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We will continue to understand our people's concerns and improve your lives.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: For those who are office holders, I encourage them not just to speak about their Ministries' work, but also to share more about their personal convictions and beliefs.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: They are giving their maiden speeches and I believe Singaporeans would want to know who they are and what they stand for.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The longest serving is Mr Goh Chok Tong who served for nearly 45 years, including almost 14 years as our Prime Minister.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: He continued to contribute in many areas, even after stepping down as Prime Minister.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Over the years, I had the privilege of working closely with Mr Goh, including on many trips at ASEAN, ASEM and APEC, where his easy rapport with leaders around the world enabled us to forge many new agreements and many new partnerships.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I remember vividly his advice to meet during the Global Financial Crisis when I was Managing Director of the Monetary Authority of Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It was a lesson that stayed with me and continued to guide much of my work, especially during this crisis.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: After I entered politics in 2001, Emeritus Senior Minister Goh continues to be a good mentor, with his signature mix of humour and wisdom.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Mr Goh has left an indelible mark on many Singaporeans, especially those of us in this House.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: When I last met him, Mr Goh told me he was spending more time with Mrs Goh and their children and grandchildren.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Let us all thank Mrs Goh and their family for being Mr Goh's staunchest and closest supporters all these years.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And I wish our beloved Emeritus Senior Minister a happy retirement.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I also wish to pay tribute to other long-serving parliamentarians, including Boon Wan, Hng Kiang, Swee Say, Yaacob, Charles,Lily, Ho Pin and Cedric.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Mr Goh in 1976, I recall.Boon Wan and Hng Kiang were my bosses at MTI.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I learned a lot from them and they have done much to advance our standing in the world and create new opportunities for our people.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: They may all have left Parliament, but I am confident that they will continue to contribute to nation-building in other ways.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: He is a fiery speaker at election rallies, but when it comes to the crunch, when our national interest is at stake, he stands together with the Government.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: He has deep conviction about language, culture and heritage, and the long-term success of Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: When I last spoke to him, he told me he was very happy playing with his grandchild.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I am also glad he has recovered from his fall and wish him good health.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I trust Mr Singh will, like Mr Low, put our national interests first.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As we face the months and years ahead, let us stand united to weather this crisis.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Even though we were sworn in at two different physical Parliament Houses – the old and the new – we must always be Members of one House.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My speech will cover a variety of topics, organised into three main areas.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: First, I will speak about certain things that have changed in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Second, I will talk about things that must not change.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And third, I will suggest some things that should change.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: First, let me speak about a few things that have changed in Singapore in the aftermath of the last election.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I will speak about the Government's recognition of the office of the Leader of the Opposition, about how Workers' Party Members of Parliament will be organised in Parliament and finally, I will share some thoughts on the presence of our parliamentary colleagues from the Progress Singapore Party.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My view is to take the appointment of the Leader of the Opposition and the motives behind it positively.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Prime Minister has signalled a change in the narrative and culture of how politics and government is to be conducted, and I thank him for that.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We look forward to a different tone of political engagement and the Workers' Party accepts the changes as another step towards a First World Parliament.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government, the Workers' Party and the people of Singapore all believe that politics in Singapore is changing and in some ways changing rapidly.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My personal expectation is that my Workers' Party colleagues and I will have to work extra hard.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We will have to ask ourselves tough questions before critiquing Government policy – the chief of which is, what would we do if we were in charge.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Singaporeans in general would be unfamiliar with the concept of an Opposition in Parliament and as an official part of our political system, let alone the office of the Leader of the Opposition.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the past, popular reference to the Opposition was almost always pejorative, usually centred around the points that the Opposition was out of Government, did not have a mandate, could only talk and as such was ultimately irrelevant.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There was a lacuna in appreciating the value of a parliamentary Opposition as a part of Singapore's parliamentary democracy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With the new changes, it needs to be clear what the Opposition can and cannot do.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The appointment of the Leader of the Opposition is an opportunity for citizens and indeed, politicians, to educate ourselves and understand better what exactly it is that the Opposition does and what its purpose is.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What does it mean to be a check and balance on the Government and how exactly can the Opposition propose alternative policies?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My assessment is that the public expects the Workers' Party and the Opposition in general to play a constructive role in Singapore politics.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It should advance the interests of all Singaporeans, whether they may be in the majority or minority on any particular issue without fear or favour.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For Opposition parties to make greater headway in Parliament, we have to understand that today's political context necessitates the development of a rational and responsible approach to opposition politics that places not just the Singapore Citizen, but Singapore at its core.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The road ahead will not be easy, but anything worthwhile never is.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We will do our best by Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But how much we can do and how much the political conversation evolves for the better will be driven by three things.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One, by the quantity and the quality of information that is shared by the Government in Parliament, and separately, released to the public more generally.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Two, by the resources given by the Government to analyse and use that information for the benefit of the public.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And three, by the willingness of the Government to listen to and implement the alternative ideas suggested.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As far as information is concerned, the Opposition's output will depend very much on whether we can get the input we ask for.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We intend to make targeted inquiries of Government departments and public agencies as such information is essential for crafting alternative policies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On its part, the Government should consider how it can put out more information without being asked to, particularly information and indicators benchmarked against other countries.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In early 2018, I asked a Parliamentary Question about the number of Permanent Residents (PRs) who remained PRs for more than 10, 15, 20 and 25 years respectively, and the common reasons cited by these individuals for not taking up Singapore Citizenship.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The data will also put into stark relief the relevance of referring to someone as a local in our statistical data when it is clear that some PRs do not want to become Singapore Citizens or the state has no plans to extend citizenship to them.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Instead, there could be genuine concerns about how information will be used or perhaps misused to rile pockets of the population since the PR policy is closely tied to immigration and jobs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To that end, later in my speech, I will suggest some alternative approaches for the Government's consideration.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As for resources, I would like to share my understanding of the resources that will be provided to the Leader of the Opposition.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is important for the public to know in formulating their expectations.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Based on these sums, these positions are of necessity, part-time ones.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I should highlight that these are the same resources depended on by PAP Members of Parliament (MPs) who are not political office-holders.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Each PAP backbencher also has only one Legislative Assistant and one Secretarial Assistant, although I should add that they can avail themselves of the additional resources of the People's Association, including the staff at Community Clubs for their grassroots work.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For completeness, let me say that neither Non-Constituency Members of Parliament (NCMPs) nor Nominated Members of Parliament (NMPs) are given these resources.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This would be an opportune time to thank the Legislative Assistants or LAs, both of the PAP and Opposition parties, who have over the years supported Members of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: An administrative assistant has also been made available to the office of the Leader of the Opposition by Parliament.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: By contrast, it is useful to remember that a sitting Government has at its disposal the resources of a Singapore Public Service, a very good one – I might add – of 146,000 full-time officers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Of these, 85,000 are members of the Civil Service.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Leader of the Opposition's office will not have the breadth and depth of the Party in Government in coming up with alternative policies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Nonetheless, the Workers' Party will continue pursuing alternatives we feel are important for Singapore, an example being the proposal for redundancy insurance for workers as put forth in the last term of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We will continue to advance meaningful alternatives for deliberation and debate, and will strive to improve on the quality of the alternatives suggested.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Another change that has happened that led to the appointment of the Leader of the Opposition is that there are more Opposition MPs in Parliament than at any time since the years following our Independence in 1965.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To raise in Parliament what the people cannot do directly is the duty of the Government ruling party and the Opposition.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Workers' Party intends to raise matters in Parliament that are important to the people of Singapore that the Government and PAP backbenchers may not.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We intend to scrutinise policies to the best of our abilities.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To that end, let me set out how the Workers' Party's Members of Parliament will be organised.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With just 10 Members of Parliament – far from the more than one-third necessary to check the PAP's supermajority – it is not feasible for the Workers' Party to set up a shadow Cabinet in the tradition of Westminster parliaments.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There are 16 Ministries in Singapore, including the Prime Minister's Office.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These 16 Ministries have the resources of 37 political office-holders from Parliamentary Secretary upwards.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Despite not being able to shadow each Ministry, we intend to organise our MPs to look into five areas that are critical for Singapore and of huge importance to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The next change that has happened is the first-time presence in Parliament of the Progress Singapore Party.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I wish to welcome their two Non-Constituency Members of Parliament (NCMPs), Mr Leong Mun Wai and Ms Hazel Poa.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What is the relationship of other Opposition parties to the Leader of the Opposition?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In other Westminster parliaments, the Leader of the Opposition is not considered a the leader of all Opposition parties in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This must be so in Singapore as well.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Progress Singapore Party has its own principles and ideology, that are distinct from the Workers' Party.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Mr Leong and Ms Poa may propose policies and promote ideas very different from, and even in disagreement to those of the Workers' Party.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is possible that they may support Government policies that we disagree with or vice versa.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, where our positions match and are in the best interests of Singapore, I look forward to collaborating with the Progress Singapore Party's NCMPs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Taken together, this would make for healthy debate in this House where policies are debated on their merits and principles, rather than in support or opposition to the Government.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Before I leave the subject of the Opposition, I would add that in the United Kingdom, the Leader of the Opposition is sometimes styled as the Leader of Her Majesty's Most Loyal Opposition.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The term "Loyal Opposition" was coined in the Nineteenth century to make clear that opposing the Government was not considered disloyalty to the monarch, or to the state.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I note the Prime Minister also used this term in the aftermath of the last election.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We have proven that we do not oppose the Government for the sake of opposing.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We back the Government when national interests are at stake.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Shortly after COVID struck in January, I said to the House from this very Table: "Workers' Party Members of Parliament agree with the Government when we have to, disagree where we must, in the knowledge that we endeavour for the best outcomes for Singapore and for a unity of purpose when politics must take a back seat, like during the current COVID-19 crisis." That position made in the context of the debate on the Unity Budget is a convenient point for me to transition to the second area I will speak on.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: That is, things that must not change in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: First, Singapore's historical position as a trading nation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Second, the Government's policies and actions on defence and foreign policy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And finally, certain things that are now synonymous with Singapore – multiracialism, the greening of Singapore, the quality of our public libraries and our culture of abhorring corruption.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Investors should know that Singapore will never close for business, no matter how many Workers' Party MPs there are in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We make a living by being relevant to the world and separately as a trustworthy and reliable interlocutor.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Our Police and security agencies keep our country safe.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Our doctors and nurses staff a healthcare system that provides quality care.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These are but some of the reasons why foreign investors put their trust in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Opposition politics and advocacy for Singaporeans cannot ignore Singapore's place in the world and what we offer to the world.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We must still look outward, even as we continually search for a lasting modus vivendi which accommodates the domestic pressures of being economically open, and the reality of a Singapore identity that evolves and crystallises as our nation matures.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Singaporeans do feel patriotic, nationalistic and protectionist even.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These are forces that are not intrinsically negative, but they have to be empathised with and understood by this House.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In turn, Singaporeans should consider Singapore's relevance to the world from a broad perspective.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: After all, all of us, no matter what our political preferences, want our country to be thriving and successful and with a big heart.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Moving on to the second thing that must not change.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These policies are well-considered and they place primacy on Singapore's interest while seeking long-term mutual cooperation with other countries and international organisations.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: They also take into account the realism of international politics and the reality of not just a small state, but our peculiar circumstances too.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We support the Government's efforts in working with our neighbours to bolster ASEAN.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We believe that a successful ASEAN boosts regional security through economic, political and security cooperation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As a small maritime nation and separately, a trading nation, the sanctity of international agreements and adherence to the rule of law is necessary to discourage arbitrary behaviour by more powerful states.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Next, we support the Government's work in continuing various things that have become a part of Singapore's DNA.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Our founding Prime Minister, Mr Lee Kuan Yew was able to lead the achievement of something that many thought impossible at the time – the rooting out of endemic corruption from Singapore society.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We are proud of Singapore's success in doing so and support the Government's continuing work in this area.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If anything, Singapore's position on stamping out corruption should be strengthened so that extra-territorial corruption by Singaporeans is discouraged with as much diligence as domestic corruption.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Equally important is Singapore's emphasis on racial and religious harmony.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These words are almost a cliche in Singapore, and we should be grateful for that, because in many other countries, it is a source of intractable problems.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Workers' Party strongly believes in Singapore's multiracial, multi-religious and multi-cultural community.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is important that all communities support, respect and accommodate each other.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There is much that is right and which should remain the same.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But there is also much that can and should change.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This brings me to my third area – things that should change in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is my conviction that these changes would improve governance and better look after the needs of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Some conversations in Singapore can continue to be divisive unless we decisively create a framework for reasoned conversation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Parliament, using the platform of Select Committees, can operate as an important safety valve and an agent of positive conversations that ought to have a direct impact on policies and laws.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: More significantly, in the information ecology of today's world, misinformation and disinformation campaigns are run online and offline, usually in combination, to manipulate content and hijack narratives.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This House and the Government need to reframe the public narrative on our more pressing issues.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In many countries today, even the mainstream media cannot moderate the conversation without significant public funding.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A recent headline from the magazine Current Affairs put it starkly – the truth is paywalled and the lies are free.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: An apt description of the dilemma facing the mainstream media in the face of some aspects of social media.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One possibility is for more Standing Select Committees to be set up to scrutinise the spending, policies and administration of each Ministry.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The members of these committees would be drawn from a mix of Members in this House, including PAP backbenchers, elected Opposition MPs and NCMPs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Such committees are part of the normal political fabric of other democracies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The UK parliament has cross-party Commons Select Committees that check on each government department, also in the areas of spending, policies and administration.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Those who follow American politics would also be familiar with the various Senate and House committees that are drawn from both Democrats and Republicans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This suggestion is not meant to be a blind copying of the British and American systems, but is made because such committees are an example of parliamentary institutions our democracy can benefit from.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Such Standing Select Committees are not to be confused with Government Parliamentary Committees (GPCs).

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: GPCs are partisan – only PAP Members of Parliament sit on them.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: GPCs were conceived in 1987 when Mr Chiam See Tong was the only Opposition MP left after the removal of Mr J B Jeyaretnam in 1986.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There were no NMPs at the time, nor NCMPs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If not for all Ministries, then perhaps for some of them.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Of course, certain Ministries such as MINDEF and MHA may require the discussion of classified information.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In such cases, cross-party committees could review matters at closed door hearings.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A second possibility for Select Committees would be the formation of more ad hoc committees.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Such committees are already a part of Singapore’s Parliamentary processes, but the Workers' Party recommends that more of them be empanelled.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The purpose of ad hoc Select Committees is to investigate a specific issue and report back to Parliament.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In time, and given their importance, they can be repurposed into permanent Standing Select Committees.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These Select Committees must function as investigators, with no pre-determined agenda, hidden or otherwise.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: They must go where the evidence, obtained through submissions and witnesses, leads them.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, by giving a longer lead time for submissions to be made; publishing written submissions at least two weeks before the hearings; scheduling hearings over more days; and releasing an interim report for public scrutiny that can prompt more written submissions and additional hearings.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
