text: To this end, the President in her Address alluded to potentially difficult conversations that Government would need to have with Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Parliament in committee – rather than in session like it is today – is an excellent platform to hear and truly listen to the voices of Singaporeans in an open way.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The next thing we need to change in Singapore is how we manage and accommodate foreigners in our economy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Their presence gives Singapore a vitality that keeps us economically relevant and also provides jobs and opportunities to our fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Many of us count the foreigners in our midst, regardless of race, language or religion as our friends.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: That openness and friendly attitude must continue as a manifestation of the Singapore spirit and the Singapore we leave behind for future generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But it is precisely because we need foreigners to help power our economy that we need to pay more attention to Singapore workers, some of whom feel excluded, some of whom feel excluded from opportunities created in their homeland.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Of the 47 companies, 30 were financial and professional services institutions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Another example is given of a bank where almost two-thirds are of the same nationality.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The obvious question is: how did those two companies get to those stages without MOM taking action before this?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: MOM’s website states at one point and I quote, “MOM does not tolerate unfair hiring practices and employers who do not give locals a fair chance in hiring and promotion will face scrutiny and stiff penalties if found to have unfair hiring practices.” However, for three-quarters and two-thirds of the PMETs of two companies to be non-Singaporeans of the same nationality, Singaporeans may be justified in asking if MOM has tolerated their unfair hiring practices for some time.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To be fair, this is a complex issue.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, there may be some justification if the bank’s customers are not in Singapore, but are from the same country as the PMETs, and if these customers do not speak any of the languages widely used in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Some have argued that this is what it takes for Singapore to be a global financial hub.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The problem is that we simply do not know enough.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And the vacuum has given space for a more toxic conversation to ferment.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We should nip this forthwith and some details earlier this week from MTI about inter-corporate transferees and remarks by the Minister for MTI have been important.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, more information, and not less, is certainly most helpful.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We can then understand the operating paradigm of such businesses and understand how they intend to make the transition to fair hiring practices.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government also needs to raise its signature in this regard, especially since this is such a hot-button issue, one generating a lot of heat but very little light.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To assist, a Parliamentary Select Committee can investigate the limitations of the workforce and the needs of the economy on the one hand, and the reality of the Singaporean worker in the face of competition and the constraints faced by employers on the other.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This should be considered alongside a more activist approach by the Tripartite Alliance for Fair Employment Practices (TAFEP) in the immediate term.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Surely this tempts recalcitrant employers into trying their luck.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If they practise unfair hiring, all that happens is that they are stopped from hiring unfairly for two years.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Employers only face criminal prosecution if they make false declarations on fair consideration.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And somehow, truthful declarations on fair consideration have allowed two companies to hire up to two-thirds and three-quarters of PMETs of the same nationality.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Needless to say, prosecution only for false declarations is simply not enough.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In tandem with a stronger regime of deterrence, there should be an educational credential assessment for all Employment Pass and S Pass applicants, the cost of which should be borne by the applicant.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This will ensure that only objectively qualified foreigners may work in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Tied closely to the issue of the hiring of foreigners is whether the education system is adequately preparing our citizens for the jobs that are available.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The big banks – OCBC, UOB and DBS – all have workforces that are made up of at least 90% Singapore Citizens and Permanent Residents.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is unclear what proportion are Singapore Citizens.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What are the reasons why these banks cannot be staffed by even more Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The two main justifications given for the hiring of foreigners are first, that they are unable to find Singaporeans with the expertise; and second, that foreigners do jobs that are undesired by Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As it is unlikely that well-paying banking jobs are undesired by Singaporeans, the justification of these banks in hiring foreigners must be that they are unable to find enough Singaporeans with the needed expertise.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If that is true, then we need to ask where the gaps are in our education and lifelong learning training systems.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These gaps must be found and plugged as soon as possible.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Last Friday, MAS responded to The Straits Times queries on the issue of foreign professionals at financial institutions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I agree with MAS that falsehoods on fair hiring are unhelpful and unfair.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On the point of the number of Singaporeans at financial institutions, however, MAS did say that there are some functions and some firms where there is scope to increase the proportion of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: MAS has also said that it would like to see more Singaporeans move into the senior ranks of the financial sector.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: MAS added that there is an urgent need to build the local talent pool in technology-related areas to meet increasing demand.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I was glad to see that MAS made the same points I have made above – that a greater proportion of Singaporeans can be employed at financial institutions and that Singaporeans need to be appropriately educated and trained to take up jobs in the financial sector.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, the seismic political changes in Hong Kong may prompt some international businesses to move to other jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Another thing that we should change in Singapore is raising the value of the work of the Singapore tradesmen.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In Singapore, although our educational institutions train our citizens for such vocations, not enough is done to protect their trades.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Medical professionals, accountants, quantity surveyors, insurance practitioners and even real estate sales professionals have to be properly qualified and certified.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This enables them to earn a wage that is protected from undercutting by the unqualified.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, for trades such as air-conditioner servicing and plumbing, anyone can offer such services.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Uplifting our tradesmen will require a paradigm shift in how workers are viewed and trained.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If it succeeds, it will raise the self-esteem and incomes of Singaporeans who may not be academically inclined but who have acquired valuable skills that many of us in this House would not be able to fully master.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is my view that such a decisive shift will fundamentally alter our understanding of meritocracy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The final point I would like to make on things that should change is on greater help for those who need it most.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Indeed, we ourselves proposed policies along these lines, years ago.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Extending more health and other social benefits comes with a cost.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Could this result in higher income taxes for many Singaporeans and those who work here, for example?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But the benefits will go beyond mere financial help for those who need it.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Will there be a price to pay in terms of higher costs for the end-consumer?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Increasingly, there will be a price to pay if we wish to be "One United People" and move beyond the phrase as an aspiration or worse, a platitude.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Many Scandinavians are content to pay higher taxes because they know this would mean that others in their society will be able to live with greater dignity.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For those who earn higher incomes, to pay higher taxes is a point of pride for many of them.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Singaporean identity which sees community as a central pillar of its DNA should imbibe such thinking with those better-off paying more.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Let us build a kinder and gentler Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As history tells us, change can be for the better or for the worse.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Around 50 years ago, some Asian countries were prosperous and thriving.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Fast forward to today, as a direct result of bad choices and in spite of the best intentions, things have gone awry there.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However Singapore pivots or evolves in the years to come, I believe a reasoned conversation before choices and decisions are made, or not made, will be critical.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These will take time and consume much energy, and we will have to guard against conversations which are hijacked to advance sectional interests that demonise those who have reservations or a different perspective.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I support the Motion in the name of Mr Patrick Tay which gives thanks to the President for her Address delivered on behalf of the Government.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Prior to COVID-19, companies in Singapore have started digitalising to improve productivity, build new capability to access new markets and opportunities.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The way we work, live and interact has significantly changed.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I never thought I would see a day where our borders are closed, people not able to interact freely physically and businesses having to limit their staff from working in the office.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Virtual meetings, e-commerce, digital payments, deliveries, safe distancing and digital tracking have become a way of life.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: First, the concern over jobs and the need to ensure economic growth to support quality jobs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Second, building the Singapore Core and why Singapore must stay open.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: From my house-to-house engagements with residents, many expressed their anxiety over their jobs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Mid-career residents shared that its harder to find equivalent job opportunities when they lose their jobs, that is, quality jobs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I am also hearing from younger residents – their concerns of finding employment.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I met several young residents last week who had recently lost their jobs or had their pay or job scopes reduced due to COVID.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Many are concerned about losing their jobs and livelihoods as the companies they work for are not seeing the same demand for their services and hence need to cut back.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This is, however, not sustainable on a long term.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Companies need support to recover and create jobs for Singaporeans to have good and meaningful work.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This COVID pandemic has forced organisations to rethink how and where they do business to stay resilient.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This pandemic has demonstrated the need for deep capabilities, diversification of markets and supply chains, and the importance of digital capabilities of our companies and workforce.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While no company is spared the impact of this pandemic, we did see that companies with sound business continuity plans, and those who had invested in building capability and digitalisation, were better able to adapt quickly to keep operations and business going.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For small businesses, the ability to adapt and adopt digitalisation has accelerated virtual connectivity and access to new business.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: A simple example is how stalls in our wet markets and hawkers have overcome the physical access restrictions by adapting and selling online.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With access to new customers, some of these businesses are doing better than pre-COVID-19 times.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We must train our younger Singaporeans and reskill our mid-career workers to be ready for the recovery.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Programmes such as traineeship, placements and various skills upgrading initiatives in the SGUnited Jobs and Skills Package allows learning beyond just knowledge to real experience and learning from others to prepare and develop people for these roles.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We must also continue to invest in an innovation and learning ecosystem to build deep local capabilities enabled by a world-class infrastructure.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While helping our SMEs go digital and building digital capabilities are important, I am also glad that in its Addendum to the President’s Address, MCI has outlined how efforts will be made to promote the ecosystem, having the eco-system to support digital transformation.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: International connectivity, growth of local digital champions, progressive regulations and public private partnerships – these are key to building capability and growth of SMEs, who provide 70% of employment in Singapore, as well as markets outside of Singapore which are key for growth.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Now, let me now move on to my second point on why Singapore must stay open.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With job losses and as more jobs are impacted, many Singaporeans are hurting, and many of my residents are questioning if we have too many foreigners working in Singapore and competing for jobs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: There is no easy answer to this, but it is a topic that we must discuss.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While they are not the majority of companies, there are companies hiring a higher proportion of foreign PMETs than their industry peers.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the reduction in the number of jobs available due to COVID, as well as the changes that were seen in the economy to encourage companies to give Singaporeans a fair chance and to ensure foreigners do not undercut Singaporean wages, it is important to have this.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I want to share a little bit about my experience.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Although I currently work for a Singapore company, a large part of my commercial career was with two foreign MNCs in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: My tenure with these two companies was for almost 30 years.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: During my time with both these companies, I worked closely with Singaporeans and foreigners from many countries.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I and many of my Singaporean colleagues had development and many good job opportunities.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Working with a diverse group of colleagues enabled me to learn and develop both in Singapore and in other markets overseas.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Having access to a network of expert talent in and outside of Singapore gave us the ability to compete effectively, build centres of competencies in Singapore or quickly scale up for large projects.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We would otherwise not have been able if these specific skills required had not been available, or we just had not had them available in sufficient numbers.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, I asked myself what is different from the experience many are feeling today?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: One factor could be that despite some periods of challenging business climates, most times the economy was growing.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The other factor which I did not think much about even though it was there was the deliberate People Strategy and Plans that both these MNCs I had worked for had.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Even when there were foreigners in key skilled or leadership positions, and I worked for many of them, there were clear development plans and identified succession plans or pipeline for local talent to fill these roles over time, and that was deliberated every single year.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I myself held many key leadership positions managing business in Singapore and in the region taking over from predecessors who were foreigners and managing both local and foreign teams across the world.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With clear succession planning in place, when I left my last role in the MNC that I was with to pursue new opportunities, the successor to my role is also Singaporean.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I believe that many companies still have such people practices in place.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: However, it could be that the speed and the scale of growth in the last few years, coupled with the disruptions that we have seen, some of these practices may have been sidelined to meet the demands of business.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I believe that while we do have policies in place, we must have, to ensure fair employment practices, more importantly employers must have People Plans to grow and strengthen the Singapore Core.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This requires commitment, not just of the Government, but of the companies both Singapore and foreign to invest and develop skills of Singaporeans, and with a balance of Government policies and enforcement, I think we will get to that balance.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Having jobs is not good enough; we need to have the right support for our workers so that they are ready for the recovery.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I think that is the thing that worries all of us, not just for Singapore, but for the opportunities outside of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: COVID-19 has shown us what happens to many of our businesses and jobs when demand and supply of both products and manpower is shut off.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: During circuit breaker time, that was experiment that I think nobody wanted to see.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But that is a big reminder for all of us – shutting ourselves out is not a solution.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The third point want to make is about staying stronger together.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The challenge we face in the post-COVID-19 world is not about how in Singapore we become better, but how as Singapore we become better.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While there are still risks, this pandemic as with previous crises has once again shown us that together, Singapore, we can overcome difficulties.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What it takes is all of us working together.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Multi-Ministry Taskforce, our businesses and people working together, with each playing our part, has allowed us to keep transmissions low and our people safe while slowing opening up our economy.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We should not wait for a crisis to happen to bring us together.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We need to look at how we come together, tap ideas, expertise across Government and across Government agencies, businesses and our citizenry.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Singapore continues to be an attractive place for doing business and we have a strong talent base.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Together, I am confident that we can and will build a stronger Singapore to meet the aspirations and give Singaporeans hope today and for the future.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: First, the need to accelerate the building of capabilities in our industries, companies and, most importantly, our workforce.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Without such capabilities, our companies cannot respond to opportunities or provide quality jobs, and our people cannot be ready.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Second, Singapore must be connected and stay open.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It allows for access not only for wider market opportunities but also diverse talent and experience which in turn helps to build the Singapore Core.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And finally, we must do it together, whole-of-Government, businesses and citizens.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We will learn, innovate and adapt faster to respond and create opportunities as the uncertain world unfolds before us.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In these unprecedented times, Singapore needs to keep what is good and build on it, refine what can be improved and continue navigating toward a better future.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: My speech will cover three broad themes – first, financial support for Singaporeans; second, foreign workers’ dormitories and, third, riding the wave of a post-COVID-19 world.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Since the beginning of this year, the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance Mr Heng Swee Keat has rolled out four formidable Budgets.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These have gone some way to ease the pain felt by people as a result of the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, there are some Singaporeans who may not stand to benefit from all these schemes but are, nevertheless, adversely affected by the pandemic’s disruption.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For instance, because some of the current schemes assess eligibility based on place of residence rather than whether the Singaporean actually owns the property he or she is residing in, some people may have difficulty tapping on the support they need.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, less well-to-do adult children who may be staying with parents; large extended families living together in the same house; Singaporeans who have recently divorced or single parents returning to stay with their elderly parents; unmarried children or grandchildren waiting to move into BTO flats under construction; or families who recently sold their homes under difficult financial circumstances and who have moved back in with siblings or parents.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Sometimes, the consequence is that Singaporeans are excluded from the Self-Employed Persons Relief Scheme.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: My second suggestion on broadening support for Singaporeans is to assess personal income as an alternative to income on the household per capita basis.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Sometimes, people living in the same "household" do not contribute financially towards each other.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, siblings who are still living in their parents' home but do not subsidise each other’s finances.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Others include situations I have previously described earlier on in my speech.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Members of households could draw substantially different wages.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In such situations, the person drawing a lower income is disqualified from receiving financial support from the Government even though he or she may not have access to those resources that the income on a household per capita basis attributes to him or her.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It also excludes applicants from resources that were supposed to help him or her during the pandemic and, in some instances, prejudices families who are willing to shelter them during this crisis.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Some of the schemes affected are the COVID-19 Support Grant, The Courage Fund for lower income households affected by COVID-19 and the Temporary Relief Fund.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Total Debt Servicing Ratio (TDSR) already helps to ensure that a Singaporean will not overextend himself or herself but will only get a credit line within his or her means.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Revenue can still be raised by retaining ABSD for foreigners.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There looks to be demand for Singapore properties by overseas investors due to Singapore being seen as a stable environment.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, demand from foreigners may not diminish even if ABSD is removed only for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This means that the property market is kept somewhat stable.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The first broad theme of suggestions in my speech, Sir, was related to support available to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The second theme of suggestions are those relating to foreign worker dormitories.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To put this number in context, it is the same number of inspections conducted by MOM last year on foreign worker housing, slightly more than a quarter of inspections and investigations combined.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The high proportion of contraventions is concerning to me and we need to carefully examine whether the system is being abused by operators and whether punitive measures in the relevant legislation are sufficiently deterrent.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Under the Foreign Employees Dormitories Act, the Commissioner may give a compliance directive if the operations are carried out in a careless or incompetent manner, or to avoid a serious and imminent threat to safety and health of residents.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Failure to comply with requirements imposed by a compliance directive is an offence with penalty of a fine not exceeding $50,000 or to imprisonment not exceeding 12 months or to both.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To be fair and encourage responsibility on the part of all parties involved, we could take a balanced approach.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, if the occupier of a dormitory, that is the one in charge of the premises, can prove that he or she had taken all reasonable steps to achieve the criteria on a checklist, it would be prima facie evidence that they had fulfilled their obligations.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: On the other hand, foreign workers themselves staying in the dormitory would also have a similar checklist listing out their own responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Allow me, Sir, to move on to the third broad theme of my speech – suggestions on how to capitalise on the disruption presented by COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The first is in the arena of tertiary education.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The supply of students is no longer limited to geography.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This can enhance Singapore’s reputation around the world and ensure the collection of ideas through the enhanced tapestry of students – Singaporeans and overseas students alike.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In this way, we could look to becoming a global thought-leader in online pedagogy.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In this time of disruption, a second area that Singapore could advance in is in industries that produce virtual products.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These include not only biotech and biosciences but also media and technology, for example, animation or film.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, we have Biopolis which is specially built as a research and development hub at One-North, situated in a place that fosters collaboration between private companies and public scientific and educational bodies.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Fusionopolis was designed to create an environment conducive to growth in information and communications technologies, media, physical sciences and engineering industries.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Metropolis in Buona Vista was meant to be a gateway to One-North with research facilities and business parks situated there and designed to be the headquarters for multinational companies.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: From what I have listed, Sir, we have custom-built state-of-the-art facilities for these sectors situated in places that promote collaboration and generate innovation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, we have a sturdy foundation to ride the waves of biosciences, biotechnology, animation, film and virtual technology.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We have accelerated and robust application-to-grant pathways for certain IP rights.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At this stage, Sir, I should declare that I am a practising lawyer at the Singapore Bar.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Internationally, Singapore is known as an IP hub, with a strong IP office and enforcement working closely with other countries to enable smoother and faster IP protection globally.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Having a strong IP framework is important to encourage innovation in Singapore as it helps generate and protect income from virtual products.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, the point that I am getting at, Mr Speaker, is that there is a regulatory framework to protect inventions squeezed out during the COVID-19 pandemic period.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This makes Singapore attractive and exceedingly relevant to the region and the world.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, we have got good foundational structures to ride the post-COVID-19 wave.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our Bicentennial exhibition last year and especially the five excellent Acts performed at Fort Canning, reflected how Singapore has always been at the crossroads of history and was always enveloped by a time of change in a changing world.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But, even as we are ever surrounded by change, one thing must remain constant and, that is, unity.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Will we, as legislators, lay aside our differences to forge a stronger and brighter future for Singapore together?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How can we forge a better and stronger Singapore together?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As legislators, we come together to debate and refine policy, to lead constructive conversations on what is best for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The policies and the shaping of them – both the result and the process are important.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Often times, especially for fiscal policies, neither extremes are the best, with pitfalls for both.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We cannot pigeonhole ourselves or others as "right-" or "left-leaning” but must have the flexibility to be politically ambidextrous, not being a slave to rigid ideology but always with an eye for doing what is best for Singapore and making sure it works for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Furthermore, we should also be cautious about divisive politics.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That, in my view, is not beneficial for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Divisive politics occurs when we are so entrenched in our position that there is no negotiation for middle ground.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I do not think this would work in Singapore nor would it be beneficial for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to resolve disputes for the best of our country – even if we agree to disagree, the process and the debate allows for a fine-tuning of the points of view.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And if a way around can be found, it places Singapore in good stead.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The ideas proposed earlier regarding foreign worker dormitories, how to engage the seismic shift in tertiary education or ride the waves of a post-COVID-19 world with an excellent IP regime are all aimed at bettering Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What is essential, if we are to ride this storm, is that Singapore’s best interests must always be our goal when advancing our points of view as legislators.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If we are united in that cause, then Singapore wins.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The COVID-19 crisis has affected societies and economies around the world.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As the situation continues to unfold, many try to make sense of what a post-COVID-19 world will be like.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The first would be in English and the latter three will be in Malay.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: First, long-term unemployment concerns and possible need for workforce reallocation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Change is never easy, we fight to hold on and we fight to let go.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In letting go, we also struggle with making sense of the new norm.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Making a mid-career change, especially to a new industry, will not be easy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For many of us, it will be one of the most challenging times in our careers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Today, we face the possibility of another large-scale job reallocation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, the impact is highly disproportionate across different industries.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For now, finance and technology sectors are still doing well, and essential services like healthcare and education are always in demand.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Yet learning new skills for a new industry is time-consuming and challenging, more so for those that require specialised skills, such as in healthcare and technology.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To continue for the long-term or make a switch to move on to a more fulfilling role, further investment in upskilling and education would have to be required.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would the Government consider more incentives for the acquirement of deeper knowledge, including subsidies for full-time degree courses, for example?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And in sectors like healthcare, would the Government look into modified courses so that more people could be quickly trained to get into the jobs and be allowed to upgrade their skills as they serve in the various institutions?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The lower income groups are bearing the brunt of the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many of them have lost their jobs and we may expect more job losses to come in the near future.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Does the Government intend to conduct any form of structured job reallocation beyond nudging towards the Professional Conversion Programmes or PCPs?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can we take this opportunity to direct them to sectors that have been conventionally less popular among Singaporeans and more heavily reliant on foreigners, such as early childhood education, nursing, construction, skilled trades and so on?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Also, what is the Government doing to weed out employers who offer higher pay to foreigners to qualify them for workpass but yet clawback the salary once they get into Singapore?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am told the employers would make this clawback clause as part of the terms of employment and often, they are verbally negotiated.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: F&B businesses run by foreigners are one of the culprits.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Second, coping with the challenges of rising prevalence in remote working and protectionism.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Rising prevalence in remote working and protectionism threatens our survivability as an open economy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the most recent issue of Harvard Business Review, American economist Willy Shih shared his projection on the state of global supply chains in a post-pandemic world.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Manufacturers worldwide will be under greater political and competitive pressure to increase domestic production and grown employment in their home countries.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They will have to reduce or even eliminate their dependence on sources that are perceived as risky and re-think their use of lean manufacturing strategies to minimise inventory held in global supply chains.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our affordable tax regimes, fair and corruption-free business practices and political stability make us an attractive location for start-up companies, and regional headquarters to oversee new supply chains in the region.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I note that Mr Shih also mentioned Singapore's efficient and high-capacity trans-shipment hub as part of the recommended Southeast Asian strategy for moving goods to the major markets.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As part of a longer term strategy, we should continue to build on our manufacturing capabilities, particularly in high-tech and healthcare and biomedical industries.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Moving forward, the demand for comprehensive logistics strategies will be necessary for companies to make sense of post-pandemic production and movement of goods and services.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The question next is, what plans does the Government have to nurture local talents in logistics and even in the maritime industry?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the meantime, we must continue to remain attractive to global corporations.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It remains uncertain if remote working will reduce the need for MNCs to hire locals, but MNCs stimulate the economy through taxes and creating opportunities for SMEs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I wish to record my appreciation to our Health Sciences Authority (HSA) and A*STAR for ensuring the availability and continued review of effective and efficient COVID-19 test kits, which would facilitate business travel without the need for prolonged quarantine measures across the board.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Third, Mr Speaker, is building a Singapore Core in a tight labour market.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Remaining open to global talent is not mutually exclusive to building a local core.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We now have a tight job market with an oversupply of workers chasing too few jobs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It becomes more urgent and imperative than ever to strengthen the Singapore Core and enhance our fair consideration framework as mentioned by many speakers before me.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I have raised this in my maiden speech five years ago, focusing on job discrimination practices and had requested for more teeth for TAFEP and also anti-discrimination legislation, five years ago.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Now is a good time to focus on transferring capabilities from currently employed foreign employees to local workers, with the aim of localising jobs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: First, tackling rising household economic insecurity due to job losses and rising inflation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With mounting retrenchments and job losses comes rising household economic insecurity.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Singapore has no net debt and would have no need to engage in financial repression, but we are an open economy and a price taker, and so we will certainly be impacted by global policies.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For young couples who are planning to start or grow their families, how will this rising household economic insecurity influence their decisions?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Additionally, what will all these mean for our plans to raise the GST and other economic policies?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many young couples cite the cost of living in Singapore as a deterrence from having children.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, how can Singapore be an affordable and conducive place to build a family?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Housing costs remain a key concern for young Singaporean couples who want to remain in Singapore and settle down.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With inflation, the cost of raw materials will only go up.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How will the Government ensure housing remains affordable for young Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I will speak a bit more on this issue.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A key question in the minds of many economists is: what would be the long-term costs arising from the COVID-19 pandemic?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Even if a vaccine, or more than one vaccine, is developed, and everyone is back at work, but what would be the impact on the nature of economic activity?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There is certainly widespread discussion whether the discovery would lead to a U-shaped, V-shaped or L-shaped economic recovery.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The key thing is whether companies and consumers would be able to regain their confidence to embark on a spending pattern.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Or would they hesitate, hold back and become risk-averse?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And this would become the so-called “scarring effect” that would leave a lasting impact on the economy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is like a person who, after going through a trauma, recovers but suffers from a scarring effect on his personality and loses self-confidence.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We would never know which sector of the economy would be more scarred than others, perhaps it is the travel industry (air and cruise) and the entertainment sector, and many other sectors.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Small businesses and households are reeling from the pain of closures and bankruptcies.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Over the last six months, I have met and listened to residents either in-person or virtually, ranging from professional photographers, media professionals and Grab drivers, who sought help, and the Government has provided SIRS and COVID-19 support for them.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: More recently, I have seen residents, who are currently restaurant and now karaoke owners, coming to obtain assistance as well as regulatory changes to allow them to utilise their business spaces for more productive purposes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So far, in the short term, our multiple Budget measures provided the interventions and a kind of insurance to help protect the most vulnerable sections of society and help businesses survive.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But what about the long-term effects of such measures?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Although Government policies cannot prevent people from believing that future pandemics are more likely to occur compared to what they thought previously, good policies can, however, affect how long the on-going crisis will drag on.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The important thing is that we should mitigate the costs of what is known as “belief scarring”.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I hope that the Government will not just view the prevention of bankruptcies as important, but also place importance on the method of prevention and not underestimate its long-term effects on businesses and families.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, we may see more investments in the safe industries like healthcare, food and groceries, and technology.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Global health experts have warned of more possible pandemics to come and we want to stay prepared.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, we will more than likely see less efficient use of commercial space in malls, F&B establishments, tourist attractions, on public transport and planes and so on.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: That brings me back to my earlier point on risk-taking behaviour.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, this scarring effect was seen previously before the 2007/2008 Financial Crisis, few would think of the possibility of a financial collapse.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Today, the fear of a financial collapse has always lingered at the back of the minds of many.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must resist from the temptation of making comparisons, but take charge of what we can control, such as our own lives and our own health.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The Fourteenth Parliament is opening in exceptional times.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The road to recovery will be harsh and bumpy.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The President spoke about COVID-19 reshuffling the deck – revealing new threats alongside fresh opportunities.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This must be the priority for this new term of Government.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: COVID-19 has exposed significant risks in Singapore’s over-dependence on foreign manpower.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Now, more than ever, in an increasingly protectionist world, our employment policies must tilt towards giving priority to Singaporeans for jobs they can do, and put in place proactive development plans to nurture Singaporeans for the skills and experience they lack.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I have met many middle income Singaporeans, working as PMEs, who do not feel secure in their jobs.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: They feel intense competition from the influx of foreign talent and describe incidents of unfair employment practices by employers who display a clear preference for foreigners.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Many Singaporeans believe that they are being passed over for jobs that they can do because foreigners come cheaper, without the employer having to pay for CPF contributions and deal with National Service obligations, or simply because employers prefer to bring their own friends and families from overseas to fill vacancies.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The focus so far has been on giving Singaporeans fair consideration.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Whilst these represent steps in the right direction, I do not think the new measures go far enough.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: First, I would like to reiterate the call I have made repeatedly in past sittings, that Singaporeans should be given priority, and not just be fairly considered, for jobs they can do.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Such a “Singaporean first” employment policy is consistent with other Singapore Government policies where we accord significant benefits and priorities to citizens, whether it be housing, Primary school balloting, school fees or healthcare subsidies.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We must move from a neutral position, where we are content with having employers give Singaporeans "fair consideration" to an assertive position where we expect employers to positively favour – and I repeat, positively favour – the hiring and developing of Singaporeans if they have the skills and experience.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: During my 20 years as an international banker, I have seen how various jurisdictions around the world enforce employment policies that promote the hiring of local talent even as they recognised the need to judiciously tap the international talent pool.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Similarly, even as Singapore continues to welcome the brightest and best from around the world to help our country reach our standards of excellence in every field, we must promote the hiring and training of locals.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: To ensure our economy is undergirded by our strong Singaporean Core, our manpower policies must ensure it happens.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I urge the Government to put in place four key measures.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Apart from requiring that the job vacancy be posted for 28 days, the selection criteria must be completely transparent.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The employer’s final hiring decision must stand up to the scrutiny of others – including the firms’ own employees as well as the authorities.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Hiring based on transparent and objective selection criteria is good for business as it fosters a sense of fair play at the workplace.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This will certainly galvanise the necessary action on the part of employers to reduce reliance on foreigners.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Three, ensure capabilities and skills transfer to local employees.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: For selected sectors, there may be a need to require employers to systematically develop succession plans and capability transfers to locals and have these linked to EP approvals.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Sectors with high concentrations of foreigners should then have their renewals of work passes be contingent on the firms meeting local succession and capability transfer KPIs.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: False declarations should carry penalty under Singapore’s laws.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The current negative sentiment against foreigners will ease when Singaporeans believe that the system takes care of their interests and it means something to be a Singaporean when applying for a job.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: They will be more amenable to hosting international expertise in their midst when they believe that they will benefit from a systematic transfer of skills and knowledge from foreign colleagues.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Singaporeans’ attitudes toward foreigners will be more welcoming and the Government can aid this effort by putting the right systems in place.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Even then, 25 years ago, it was against Canadian law to ask candidates about their age, gender, race, maritial status and disabilities – all things we do routinely in Singapore, as part of our employment process.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: To comply with Canadian laws, HR changed the application forms, removing all reference to these factors and focused the selection completely on job-related skills and experience.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This experience left a deep impression on me – that candidates should indeed be assessed purely on their competencies, skills and experience to do the job – and nothing else.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: In Singapore, despite numerous Government schemes encouraging the employment of older workers and mid-career Singaporeans, I often hear our citizens’ frustrations that their age and previous pay act as barriers to securing new career opportunities.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This, despite genuine effort on their part to lower their expectations of rank and pay.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Employers should institute hiring practices that engender blindness in the workplace towards age, gender, race, disability and everything else that they may discriminate against – for a more diverse representation across all groups.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Employment equity is a matter of dignity – everyone should have an equal opportunity to work and contribute to society.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: At the same time, employers stand to gain from a diversified and competent workforce, one that promotes inclusion in the workplace.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Well-intended assistance to prop up firms who are not viable in a post-COVID-19 world, may inadvertently provide them with artificial life-support to extend their decline, thus hindering the reallocation of labour and resources.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Instead, we should pivot our assistance programmes to help workers find new careers and learn new skills.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: As much as we think JSS will help to save jobs, many citizens shared about their struggles of being "stuck" with employers whose businesses are no longer viable, whilst they experience significant reductions in pay and prospects.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Instead of sinking millions into JSS for these companies, why not help affected workers from distressed firms directly?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: These workers could benefit from the Government’s direct financial assistance – start afresh to seek new careers and undergo training to move to more promising sectors and occupations.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Their future should not have to be so inextricably linked to their companies’ ability to rebound.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Empower the workers to seek a better future for themselves.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: When lower- income residents lose their jobs or experience salary cuts, they have little savings to fall back on.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Every week, I witness the hardship endured by self-employed gig workers, first-hand.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I see the difficulty of many laid-off residents to secure employment and feel their frustration.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: In years past, Singapore has managed to avoid implementing these safety nets– but the world has changed and we should reconsider our position on some of these "sacred cows".

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: In the past, reluctance to do so has been down to the fear of driving away wealthy investors.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: But I believe that, in a world made more turbulent and uncertain by COVID-19, Singapore’s unmatched proposition of a world class infrastructure, rule of law, financial and political stability and now, best-in-class healthcare, is made even stronger.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: As a destination for global wealth assets, Singapore offers peace of mind and will continue to be attractive even if our well-structured tax regime imposes higher rates.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The effects of the pandemic, which have recently included surging stock prices alongside mass unemployment, risk bringing about a more unequal society, more disparate incomes, a wider gulf between rich and poor.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: To be sure, COVID-19 affects everyone, but for lower income citizens, the impact could be devastating.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Our people are frightened and worried – they need our help and they need our assurance.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We, in this House, must lead with compassion, wisdom and courage.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: During the recent General Election, many of us promised our residents that, as they faced the struggles of this pandemic, they would not walk their journey alone.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is time we kept our promise to them.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Throughout my life, I had known the PAP as the Government in charge of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: My assessment at that time was that PAP is a capable Government.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The values expounded by the PAP Government resonate with me – meritocracy, no cronyism, diligence and hard work, a firm stand against corruption.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It is a Government that had performed over the years and gave Singaporeans progress and a better life.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It is a Government which I can support.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Our living standard is still one of the best in the world.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: As President Halimah said in her speech, "countries are fighting to meet their own needs, fueling a new wave of protectionism".

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I believe that many Singaporeans understand the challenges facing us as a small trading nation.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Singaporeans, myself included, also acknowledge that the PAP Government is still a capable government and that it will be able to deliver.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: There will always be policy gaps which I think most of us acknowledge.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: There is no perfect government in the world.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Over the past 14 years as a Member of Parliament, I have met and had many discussions with Government Ministers and senior civil servants.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: But yet, if we do not open our doors to allow skilled and talented foreign workers to Singapore, we risk losing out to international competition for foreign investment.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If foreign investors face severe manpower restrictions and they cannot get the best workers to work here and to grow their companies, why would they come to Singapore?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: But Singapore had overcome the Asian Financial Crisis in 1996; we had defeated SARS in 2003 and we survived the collapse of major financial institutions due to the failure of Lehman Brothers.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: We are a resilient country and together as one people, we will be able to overcome all challenges.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The People’s Association had done a wonderful job in promoting social harmony and integration, racial and religious harmony.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: But come election time, as a people, we are no longer united and instead have become divided.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Debate on policies is supposed to result in better policies for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: But instead of debate on policies, the social media goes on a frenzy as political personalities are attacked during the election.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Just as in many other countries, politics seem to have divided Singapore and this is not good for us as a nation.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The amount of vitriol and hate which I read about in the social media during the election campaign saddens me.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: During the election, the frequent feedback which I have received is that the Government is arrogant; it is not willing to listen; our leaders are out of touch; the leaders are not humble.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Rightly or wrongly, there is also the perception that there is bullying and unfair treatment of people who do not agree with our policies.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, I am glad that the President had devoted an entire section in her speech about "Evolving our Politics".

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I also applaud the Government for recognising the Leader of the Opposition.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I urge the Government to be more open to constructive criticisms and rational debate.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I would submit that the Government must not treat politicians from other parties as enemies.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: We must assume that they want the best for Singapore even if they do not agree with all our Government policies.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And where politicians from other parties and even backbenchers from PAP have good ideas, I urge the Government to acknowledge and consider these ideas.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: After the 2015 election, in my speech to thank the President in 2016, I said that: "Many residents spoke to me about the rejection of confrontational politics.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: They want a government that can work with different organisations which are committed to building Singapore to become a stronger and better nation." Two years later after Parliament prorogued, I again called on the Government to "be a more receptive and kinder government when dealing with people of differing views." I repeat this call for a less confrontational political system, so that Singaporeans can be more united.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If we do not get our politics right, there will be continued distrust in the Government and we will not stand united.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: We will not be able to overcome crises together.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I also urge the leaders of other political parties to condemn the destructive criticisms which push falsehood and twist facts out of context.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Destructive untruths will bring down our country because it instils hatred against fair and decent leaders.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: When we talk about building a fair and just society, my hope is that this means fairness for all Singaporeans regardless of housing type.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In the past budgetary provisions, we have dug deep into our reserves to help those adversely affected by the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: He may have family expenses like medical bills, mortgage instalments, school fees to settle.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: He may have to look after sick elderly parents or look after children with special needs.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: He may not be able to sell his home during a financial crisis.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: During good times, he pays all his taxes dutifully.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: But when times are hard, should the Government decline to help these people just because they have a house with a higher value?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Is the COVID-19 crisis something that they could have predicted?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Our reserves are built on the hard work contributed by all tax payers.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Why do we have the expectation that people do not deserve help simply because they have bigger homes of a higher annual value?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Should we not look at their loss of income?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I rise to thank the President for her speech.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I fully concur with her that we must engage and harness the aspirations and creative energies of all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our lives have changed so much in the past eight months.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This COVID-19 pandemic is providing unprecedented challenges for both our people and society. 2020 has revealed two major realities.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For instance, the companies in our tourism ecosystem such as SIA, hotels and F&Bs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I strongly believe that these challenges provide new opportunities for us to work together as one community, to evolve to meet new realities.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As a fellow Singaporean entrepreneur myself, I stand here to represent and be a strong voice for our companies, especially SMEs, during such extraordinary times.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to broaden our view of enterprises and entrepreneurs as having not only economic value but deep social value at our core.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need more companies to be created with missions that value adds to our society and improves our societal well-being.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, it is crucial that we shift our perspective from looking at an enterprise as an economic entity but also see it as a unit for our society’s progress.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This will mean that at a societal level, each enterprise must reflect our national narrative of "against the odds", "regardless of race, language or religion" and "inclusivity".

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We must be prepared to "learn, unlearn, and relearn".

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to support our companies trying to revive and transform their businesses.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I agree that this requires a significant change in our mindset, but we must do so quickly in such difficult and unusual times.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to question existing assumptions and recalibrate our thinking about enterprises.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Looking at entrepreneurs and enterprises as having both economic as well as societal value at the national level will inspire more entrepreneurs to establish more companies in Singapore, especially young people in their 20s to 30s who want to do more than simply make money.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With more companies on board, we can offer more quality jobs which attract more Singaporeans who desire to work for these companies because it resonates with their aspirations.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In addition, we should not compartmentalise that Corporate Social Responsibility or CSR is separate from entrepreneurship development.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In fact, the concept of CSR is fast becoming nothing more than a "Public Relations".

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Doing well and doing good comes hand in hand.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Authenticity is much talked about and less often reflected.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Today, we must think even beyond delivering double bottom lines and instead build businesses out of a core that integrates societal well-being into its operations.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Every enterprise is an organic entity that evolves over time.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Those that did not begin in high growth sectors can pivot into it over time.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Some successful companies today come from very humble beginnings.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We must support every entrepreneur or business owner in all sectors because society needs them rather than the belief of spotting unicorn winners and only supporting high-tech entrepreneurs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to build into the DNA of the entrepreneur and the enterprise their ability to contribute meaningfully to Singapore society at large.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to value the individual entrepreneur more than the business and walk this journey of evolution alongside them.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our approach with our workers is that we cannot save every job, but we will look after every worker.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our approach for our SMEs and entrepreneurs should be the same.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A good example of a start-up that evolved over time is Alchemy Foodtech.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Alan and his wife, Verleen started Alchemy Foodtech to fight our societal battle on diabetes.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Together, they invented Alchemy Fibre, a patented ingredient that is gluten-free and made from plant crops such as corn, pea and tapioca, to lower the glycaemic index of refined carbohydrates such as rice, bread and noodles while raising their overall fibre content.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: When COVID-19 required restaurants to be closed, and more people began to prepare their own meals at home, the Alchemy team created complementary consumer-friendly products that could be easily used for healthier home-cooked meals.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Today, Alchemy fibre is found in established brands like Boon Tong Kee and working with food manufacturers like Gardenia.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I have known Alan before Alchemy when he and his wife started a company selling soy-based ice cream.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They have evolved from serving desserts to transforming everyday staples.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They are a good example of how an enterprise is an organic entity which evolves through time with a mission of improving our societal well-being.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I deeply hope that we can and will do more to help our entrepreneurs and enterprises.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Increasingly, the world of investing and corporate reporting is shifting towards the ESG model.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Government support measures for our enterprises needs to evolve towards this lens – the way we support and shape enterprises, focus and outcomes.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In this climate of COVID-19 pandemic, we expect to see more business disruptions.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Some entrepreneurs will fail because their business models have been destructed if not disrupted by COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to help these entrepreneurs restart much like how we help budding entrepreneurs to start up.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Seasoned entrepreneurs have years of experience, knowledge and networks that can be potentially wasted if they are unable to restart fast.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to help them with a tangible rebound by assisting them with seed capital and public financing to restart.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With this approach, they can contribute to our economy and society quickly, thereby creating new jobs and benefiting Singapore to emerge faster and stronger.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To help our entrepreneurs restart quickly, our regulatory agencies will need to process new applications faster as it is important to consider the opportunity cost to our society.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To help our entrepreneurs rejuvenate, we need to be more targeted in manpower policies towards different industries.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Industries, such as offshore and marine, travel and hospitality, construction, retail and F&B are already reeling from the impact of COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The additional cost levied on these industries are hard to bare.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Thirdly, we need to further enhance support for businesses who face financial challenges.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The reality is this: as many businesses re- start, they face a mountain of old debt, be it rental arrears or owing to suppliers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
