text: I am sure having a dedicated break will help reduce employee fatigue and burnout.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The lack of adequate WSH protection effectively means that freelancers are cheaper to hire, which pushes more companies to adopt such self-employed arrangements to avoid costs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This is a gap that needs to be plugged!

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We are already half a step towards achieving this, as companies are now required to appoint Safe Management Officers or SMOs, as they re-open for work.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Let us expand the role of these mandatory SMOs beyond the pandemic so that we can work towards creating a safer and healthier workplace for our workers, today.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The future workplace may be upon us sooner than many of us expect.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In my maiden Parliamentary speech in 2016, I spoke at length about the importance of tripartism – the crucial ingredient of Singapore's success story.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Five years on, tripartism is even more critical now, as we deal with this immense scale and unprecedented pace of change that is coming our way.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The Government will need to support the transformation of our businesses and our workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Working together, let us turn this crisis into an opportunity.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: With united resolve, we can emerge stronger and secure a brighter future for our children and grandchildren.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But first, Mr Speaker, Sir, let me thank you for your inspirational speech for all of us to come together and to stand against polarisation.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This indeed reflects the President's call towards unity and common purpose.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And if I can be frank, Mr Speaker, Sir, this is an aspiration, but it is one that may not be politically possible.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Let us not be naive and pretend that the drama of politics and disagreement is something that cannot be constructed.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: There is no "common purpose" to be found unless there is a will to do so.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Our hope, therefore, must be that here is not just a common purpose, but a will for this common purpose to be found.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But while this commonality may be hard in politics, it can be easy and abundant in public life.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And having played football with both of you, I can say that Pritam is the best player amongst the three of us, by far.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And, of course, we all served in the SAF.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And Mr Speaker, Sir, you were a Brigadier-General.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And both Pritam and I, I think we are many ranks below that, but you are certainly a better soldier amongst the three of us.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: So, we all have different vocations, but in our own ways, we all love our country and we want to make lives better for all.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Our unity must lie in the small things – care for each other, love for the family, fighting for the person next to you.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And in difficult times, to help, to be kind and perhaps harder than it sounds, to cut one another some slack.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This is not a criticism but a vote of sympathy on my part.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: If you do not make an exception for a case, you are hard-hearted and ruthless.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: If you do, and you are taken in by a fake application, you are a simpleton being duped and lax with public monies.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Suppose you had a case, an appeal for subsidies for a sheltered home for an old man.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: He is already in a home and under the care of a social worker.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: You speak with the man's wife and his daughter.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This man has family support and is therefore not a suitable candidate for a subsidised sheltered home.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: You discuss with the case officer some more and decide that day care services would be the best option for the old man at the moment.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And this is how it appears to a busy officer, who probably has quite a lot of cases on his desk.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And for him to deny subsidies is entirely sensible.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But this is not how it appears to me.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I come to this case via a resident of mine – actually, it is a very recent case – who had a fall and she was then admitted to hospital.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And during her stay there, the doctor found that her condition was bad due to overwork, advised her to stop working and rest so as to let her body recover.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: After she was discharged, she still has to take care of her husband in his daily needs with her daughter's help.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Yes, this resident is the old man’s wife.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The old man had had a fall and was admitted to a hospital and later a community hospital.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: To be allowed to go home, he needed someone who can take care of him at home.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But she cannot take care of herself, let alone her husband.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: So, they have to put him in a home.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: She unfortunately also had major surgery and a serious illness.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But she did not want to tell her mother and add on to her worries.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: She works as a freelancer but does not have many jobs now because of the current pandemic.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Looking at this family from the outside, the social worker may think that they want to push away their responsibilities and put the old man in a nursing home.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The fact is that they have no ability and no money to take care of him.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: What follows is a heartfelt note from my Residents Committee (RC) Chair who knows the family well and has been helping them for a while.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: She wrote to me and this was just a few days ago and I quote her, "I feel for them, can understand how helpless they are now.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: They wanted to take care of their father and husband but their own health does not allow them.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: They felt sad sending him to a home but they are left with no choice." I read this email over and over again, especially the last line.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And I quote her again, "I really don't know how to move forward to help them after trying all I can; Mr Seah, you are our only hope now.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: So sorry you need to read this; it is like an essay with so many words.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Stay Safe." All of us on both sides of the House would have read or seen cases like these – so many words, but still, not enough to write out a solution.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This is the emotional labour which defines our days and nights as Members of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It is our mission to bear what cannot be borne alone and to be the "only hope" for our residents, so that they do not lose hope nor the will to carry on.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I also ask that they be given some leeway to "make mistakes" that is, to err on the side of being kind.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I also urge for all of us, members of the public, everyone, well to put it bluntly, to calm down!

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Every couple of days, there is a moral panic – someone showing how virtuous, how right, how generous they are and how hard they fight for the underdog.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Often, there is a villain of the piece – the rich driver of the big car, someone who is the wrong place, said the wrong things, the heartless, hapless civil servant, or the politician.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: These cracks they fall through are not wide.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Indeed, over the years, MCYS and, now, MSF and many other parts of the Civil Service, they have already covered many holes and made any cracks a lot very narrow.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: However, the current cracks are not just narrow but they are very now specifically shaped.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We cannot address these by ever increasing the number of rules.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: President Halimah herself said this in her Address and I quote, “We are entering an era of volatility, uncertainty and disruption in people’s lives.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Individuals will need greater social support than before.” The temptation is to construct this support by having yet more schemes, yet more rules.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Next, I want to talk about SMEs and how we can look out for each other.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: So, this same philosophy of kindness and looking out for each other can also apply in the world of business.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: If I now put on my hat as the Group CEO of NTUC Enterprise, let me just share how, in our own little ways, we have done so through our various NTUC entities: Orange Aid, which is part of NTUC Income, works with community partners through social investment in programmes that contribute to empowering youth-in-need through education.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Orange Aid’s flagship, Future Development Programme (FDP), supports tertiary students from ITE and Polytechnics from the lowest income households in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Beyond providing financial assistance for their school fees and living expenses, Orange Aid also equips them with financial literacy skills and giving them personalised career guidance.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But it is more than money which, no doubt, is useful and will complement the various support schemes that the Government is extending to help the many different groups of individuals.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Beyond this, I would also call out to companies and organisations which are doing well to also help others, especially the SMEs, to do well, too.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: So, again, if I can use Fairprice as an example, we have in place the SME Suppliers Support and Development Programme primarily to help small local SMEs.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: First introduced in 2009, the programme gives more favourable trading terms to some 485 SMEs, such as paying them earlier than normal.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Here, I would like to make a shout-out to all to, where possible, support local firms, local producers and local products.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This, in part, is to help our local economy, create jobs, strengthen our local products' resiliency plans and more.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: So, again, as you know, I am also the Group CEO of NTUC Fairprice, we, too, try to play our part.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: As an example, whilst Singapore imports some 75% of its eggs from overseas, mostly from Malaysia, at Fairprice, about 55% of all eggs sold are from local farms.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But I feel proud each time I eat one from our local farms.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: President Halimah said, “Singapore can endure and secure her place in history, only if Singaporeans feel passionately about our country and put our hearts and souls into making this a better home.” This feeling for Singapore is not something abstract.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It lies in the friends we play football with, the eggs we eat, the trust we have in our public servants; it is that feeling of when we are being kind to one another and, perhaps, most of all, when we are proud of the “Made in Singapore” brand.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We are going through the most trying period of our generation and we must unite in our effort to overcome this crisis.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: People with different backgrounds and experience will naturally have different outlooks and opinions.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We should listen respectfully to one another and try to understand different perspectives.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must not allow our society to become polarised.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Let us seek common ground, agree to disagree and be willing to cooperate on solutions acceptable to all and do what is in the best interest of our people and our country.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Today, I would like to speak on how adjustments to our employment policies are needed to help older workers and employees and how we can help the sandwich class.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):   	During this difficult period, workers and employees are increasingly worried about their livelihoods, even more so than the COVID-19 virus.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To-date, we have managed to contain the spread within the community and we look forward to snuffing out the virus in the workers’ dormitories.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singaporeans, especially older workers and employees, are worried about jobs and competition for jobs from foreigners, especially in the financial and ICT industry.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singapore is a very open nation and welcomes foreigners who can contribute.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The employment situation in some other countries is bleak and it is not surprising that there are quite a number of foreigners who are keen to work here.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We need to ensure that the Singaporean Core is strong in our workforce.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My concern is the difficulty of monitoring how companies recruit and whether they adhere to fair hiring practices, especially if the companies are foreign firms or have foreigners in charge of their hiring.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is possible that a minority of such firms or hiring professionals would prefer their fellow countrymen over Singaporeans because of cultural affinity or familiarity or just patriotism, resulting in a bias against Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, I heard that there are also ways around this system.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have heard about how some employers collect monthly fees from their staff.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Both parties benefit from this practice – the bosses can receive additional incomes and the employees qualify for the jobs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must also monitor the number of foreigners in each sector and job function to ensure that we have a strong Singaporean Core to retain industry knowledge and competencies.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There is a social cost to having too many foreign employees in our workforce.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: More resources will be needed, such as accommodation.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Their presence has an impact on our environment, transportation and medical resources.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There is an opportunity cost to the influx of foreign workers to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We need to weigh the benefit and the cost.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must not overlook the cost to our society that may prove too much to pay.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For the sake of social stability, we must pay attention to the number of foreign nationals working and living in our country, taking into account their background details and their impact on the fabric of our society.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But the most important thing is to confirm, to ensure whether that company is really recruiting qualified Singaporean employees, rather than just going through perfunctory processes, "putting on a show", ostensibly to toe the line for MOM's Fair Consideration Framework but, in reality, using "a thousand gestures and poses" to come up with reasons to justify the applications to hire some foreign employees.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Of course, we still welcome foreign talents who can genuinely fill the gaps and really contribute to our economy in special technical areas, as well as visitors to our country for holidays and exhibitions.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In truth, during the Circuit Breaker period, many jobs could be performed at home.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As such, is it necessary for companies to insist on bringing in foreign PMETs to work here?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We need to accelerate the increase in productivity and methodologies in the construction industry to reduce the reliance on foreign workers, allowing our construction sector to retain experienced, skilled, trained and disciplined foreign workers in the continued efforts to increase the productivity of our construction industry.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Government should lead in the use of methodologies that will help contractors boost productivity.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On the other hand, Singaporeans must not have the misconception that the competition is only local.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We need to remember that we are facing global competition.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We need to be able to produce better products than our peers globally.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As consumers ourselves, we also want value for money.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Likewise, if we cannot offer value for money, others will not be buying from us either.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If we lose our competitive edge, we will lose our incomes and jobs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Therefore, we must make sure that we continue to upskill ourselves to stay relevant and employable.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The retention of the newly implemented wage support for employers to employ and retain senior workers and a higher proportional foreign worker quota will reward employers for employing and supporting senior workers with periodical skills upgrading.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, amongst our sandwich class are young families, mid-career workers, middle and lower income families.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Quite a number of PMETs have been affected during this pandemic as well.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Do we have enough family counsellors to guide them through the array of schemes which they can tap into for help?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For the young families, getting married and bringing up children pose a unique challenge during this crisis.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: BTO flats are an integral part of the Singapore Dream.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some young couples shared with me that they are frustrated they could not qualify for the BTO flats they had been attempting to apply; their salaries had increased beyond the income cap over time.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Even though they can afford resale flats and private apartments, they still prefer BTOs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Four- and 5-room flats are often their first pick.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With more people working from home, they need the additional space.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Working from home looks set to become a permanent feature.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our flats need to be re-designed and enlarged to be relevant and useful.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: HDB had often cited land constraints as a limiting factor but we can build upwards.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Nowadays, both parents are working and more seniors are retiring later.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Before the COVID-19 pandemic, I had a chance to visit the Changi Business Park.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: When I stepped into a lift, there were many well-dressed people, apparently foreigners, and were speaking in a language that was foreign to me.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: For the first time, I felt like a foreigner in my own country.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: However, Minister Josephine Teo in MOM's Addendum to the President's address last week, stated that nearly six in 10 locals in the workforce today are employed in professional, managerial, executive and technician (PMET) jobs, which is among the highest in the world.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: But then why some Singaporeans feel like a foreigner in our own country?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I reckon that this is due to the low Total Fertility Rate or TFR in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Thirty years ago, Singapore's TFR was 1.8 babies per female.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This means that for every one local employee, we need to supplement it by almost one foreign worker in Singapore, so as to maintain the existing size of the Singapore workforce; otherwise, our labour force will shrink and Singapore will be in trouble.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: That is well and good, and something which many people probably accept in good times when their jobs and incomes are secure.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: On this note, I am glad that my parliamentary colleague, Mr Patrick Tay, will co-chair the task force to protect local PMEs in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: However, we need to do more than that.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Protecting the Singaporean Core of PMETs is not something that should end once the economy recovers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: We must continue to safeguard this, across all industries and not just pay attention to the financial sector.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: As the CEO of a private company, I often have to collaborate with technology companies, banks, financial institutions and other MNCs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Through these interactions, I have had my fair share of instances where I think to myself, "This is not right".

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In one such instance, I had the opportunity to have lunch with a Head of a delivery company in Singapore before the circuit breaker.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The delivery company is a subsidiary of a MNC with headquarter in Germany and the country Head in Singapore is a Frenchman in his early 30s.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: He admitted that it would be very difficult for him to find a similar opportunity in France given its high unemployment rate.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: He added that many of his expatriate friends had the same experience, that is, it is easier for them to look for good jobs in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Have we made it too easy for foreign "talent" to work in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Especially those in the middle to top management level?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In my admittedly anecdotal experience, I feel that Singaporeans can fill many regional or senior management positions, which are filled by foreigners right now and it is not that they are lacking in any way.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Just recently, I caught up with an acquaintance who used to work as a regional CEO of a start-up company.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Unfortunately, the said company was forced to shut down and he became jobless.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: There are many similar regional roles, in big companies, which he may be suitably qualified.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: But he is having trouble getting these opportunities.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Let us look at what other countries are doing to protect their citizens.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The 457 visa was replaced with a more restrictive visa.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The government also required employers to first try, to try very hard to find an Australian citizen or permanent resident for a job, and only bring in foreign talent when there is no local talent available.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The move was obviously to protect jobs for the Americans.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In a world which is increasingly nationalistic and inward-looking, this is probably not what we want.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Preferential treatment can be detrimental to a country's prospects, especially in Singapore which is international in nature.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: There are many complex reasons why a person is promoted or retained, or why a foreigner is brought in.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: But at a basic level, Singaporeans should be given the opportunities to compete.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The critics may ask is there a need to intervene at all?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: At the base level of zero intervention, strong believers of market forces might argue that natural attrition and adaptability would gradually toughen up Singaporeans who would naturally evolve to compete.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In other words, do nothing and let Singaporeans rise to the challenge.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: At the other extreme, policies could be tweaked to strongly encourage or penalise companies, with the intention of forcefully creating a Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: There is a middle ground of "soft power" and gentle persuasion, where the Government can work together with businesses and unions to jointly seed the appeal of developing a Singaporean Core and explore together how this can best be done.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This National HR Committee could work through the six sub-committees under the Future Economy Council, which oversee ITM developments, to take into account the development of a Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: They would ensure that Singaporeans are a part of the ITM transformation on a meaningful level so that Singaporeans are not left behind.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: There are three main objectives of setting up the National HR committee.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The National HR Committee can have regular meetings with the Head of HR of the major companies in Singapore to understand their manpower concerns and their commitment in building a Singaporean Core in the management team.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: By the way, whether the head of HR of the major companies is helmed by a Singaporean could be a reflection of their dedication to build a Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Whether the company is "major" would be defined in terms of specific turnover, profit and/or number of staff in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Second, the gathering and sharing of data gives us an effective platform to discuss meaningful strategies moving forward.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: It is said, "We don't know what we don't know." By gathering data on PMET workforce composition in major companies will give us an early warning indicators before the situation gets out of hand.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: After all, just like when it comes to disease management, it is much easier to prevent, than to rectify.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The third objective is the active dissemination of best practices.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The Committee could work with these companies to share best practices that develop Singaporean core at the middle and top management levels.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The sharing of data and best practices could push companies to level up.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: For instance, knowing that a company in a particular sector hires 60% to 70% of Singaporeans for its mid and top management levels, might compel other companies in the sector to do some soul-searching.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Over time, the National HR Committee could develop guidelines and blueprint based on the best practices across the industries.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: For instance, if a company has a regional HQ in Singapore, it should have a plan to give their Singaporean executives regional exposure, which might open up opportunities for promotion later on.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This is important because I realise that Singaporeans sometimes lack regional or global exposure, as they are not given opportunities to get it.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The same committee can also receive feedback from these companies and work with institutions of higher learning or training providers, to train Singaporeans who can take on higher level jobs in the near future.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In short, we do not want to impose a strict quota on recruiting foreigners in leadership positions for companies based in Singapore as that will stifle Singapore’s competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: We need to take the bull by its horns.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: We do not want major companies in Singapore to be able to hire foreigners in leadership positions too easily.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: We want these companies to nurture and grow the Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: On this note, I am heartened that Deputy Prime Minister Heng has just reiterated that we need to do all things possible for the benefit of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: We need a fine balance and this could be maintained by a National HR committee led by a Minister.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: As we move forward, with our focus on getting good jobs for Singaporeans, this is an aspect which must become part of our conversation.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: (In Mandarin):   Our current employment situation is very challenging, with frequent retrenchments.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: A few days ago, when I was making house visits, a resident lamented that several of her foreign colleagues had been sent home after their contracts expired.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I comforted her that, at least, her Singaporean colleagues and herself were able to keep their jobs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Indeed, we must try to keep Singaporeans employed.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: However, our birth rate is low: an average of only 1.1 for each female.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Of course, we must maintain a fine balance between the two.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I suggest that we set up a National HR Committee to have regular meetings with the Heads of HR of major companies in Singapore so that we can more effectively build a Singaporean Core in every major company.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: There are three main objectives for setting up the National HR Committee.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: When the National HR Committee discovers that some of these major companies do not even have a Singaporean as the Head of HR, this would be a reflection of their weak dedication towards building a Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This will scare off foreign companies from investing in Singapore and, hence, reduce local employment opportunities.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, foreign investment and foreign companies setting up regional headquarters in Singapore have created jobs for Singaporeans and benefited Singapore.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They are our small and medium-sized enterprises and our youths.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As we progress, we must not forget the disadvantaged ones.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Before that, I would like to declare that I am an employee of a Singaporean bank, a council member of the Institute of Singapore Chartered Accountants administering a supporting small medium audit practices, Chairman of an Institution of Public Character, as well as a member of the Institute of Mental Health's visitors' board.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin):   The past few months have been challenging for many of us as we battle against COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There have been profound changes in so many areas of our lives here in Singapore and around the world.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: None has been spared, particularly the business community.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If more banks and financial institutions participate in these schemes, I am sure that SMEs who need cash flow will be able to receive the loans more quickly and enjoy lower interest rates as well.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The job situation for our young graduates today is also not ideal.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There are layoffs in a number of industries and the situation looks uncertain.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Allow me to share a little about Kwang Jun De, a youth volunteer from Brickland in my constituency.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: His aspiration is to become a business owner who is able to make time to help and serve the community.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Jun De is a business graduate and former President of the NTU Rotaract Club which organises charitable activities.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With the COVID-19 pandemic, it was harder for him to secure interviews with companies he was interested to work in.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: He has taken up a traineeship and is looking forward to picking up new skills and finding out more about the industry that he intends to venture into.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: He hopes that the experience would be useful in the future should he proceed to set up his own business.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The traditional model of work may not be sustainable for youths like Jun De.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Over the next few years, we should focus on building a pipeline of fresh talent and support our youths who aspire to become entrepreneurs.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This was in contrast to five other nations in the poll by the World Economic Forum and an International Internet company.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Across ASEAN, working for SMEs is viewed less favourably by youths.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Traditional SMEs could face challenges in recruiting and retaining the right talents.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How do we ensure that more youths continue new modes of learning by working in SMEs or starting SMEs of their own?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am optimistic that this will boost local start-ups and create jobs during the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Could more initiatives like the "Youth Action Challenge" be organised with Government grants so that more students and youths might step forward?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Participants were asked to pitch their ideas to four judges, outlining their projects, its social impact and how they would implement it before being judged on project feasibility, impact and validation of problem and idea.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is good training for the real world.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Government adopts a "kueh lapis" style of diversified approaches to help the underprivileged.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Government uses similar approaches to help our SMEs through several Government agencies, such as ESG and IMDA, to launch many financing schemes, industry-led training programmes and SME Go Digital programmes to help SMEs.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope that we will have better inter-agency programmes to combine all these projects into a “set-meal” with more synergy, so that the "kueh lapis" can melt easily in their mouth.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In addition to helping SMEs, we also have to remember to support the less privileged in our midst.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I shall be speaking in English to elaborate my points.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In English): There has been a marked increase in anxiety and stress among employees in Singapore since the COVID-19 outbreak.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Those who have lost their jobs would be stressed.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Those who are still employed worry over the likelihood of losing their jobs.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Fresh graduates are anxious about getting suitable jobs in the sector that they desire.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Before COVID-19, Singapore’s social compact was predicated on good economic growth, high employment rate, own responsibility and, as I had said earlier in my Mandarin speech, the "kueh lapis" style social security system.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Post-COVID-19, this new compact needs to be practical and yet creative to ensure there is affordability, availability and quality in the key areas of social security, housing, healthcare, education, public infrastructure and the environment.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Government has a critical role not only in ensuring socially desirable outcomes, but also in pursuing outcomes that are consistent with Singaporeans’ dreams, while not compromising fiscal means and maintaining work incentives.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The construction of this new social compact requires the Government to review and discard long-held beliefs and rigid policy mindsets which are the hurdle and can no longer leave it to market forces to help the less privileged ones.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To me, meritocracy is the key principle which is crucial to Singapore's success.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I spent the first few years of my life living in a rental flat.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I was brought up by my maternal grandparents while my parents took on various odd jobs to support me and my younger sister.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: My father worked as a delivery man and later on as a taxi driver while my mother assembled electronic parts at home and later on, she became a part-time cashier when we were older.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Through perseverance, bursaries and opportunities given to me, I would say that I am doing fine today and hope to give back to the larger Singaporean community.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Ultimately, it instilled in me the idea that, in Singapore, no one will be denied of opportunities if he or she works hard and has the courage to fight on.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: When I was serving in the School Advisory Committee of a neighborhood Secondary school, I came across cases whereby the students skipped classes because they had to take care of their young siblings or sick grandparents as the parents were either in prison or were working long hours.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Their poor academic results are only symptoms and their family issues are the root causes.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Therefore, we must still ensure that everyone has a similar playing field to start from.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And that should start from as young as pre-school.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: No system should stop parents from investing in their own children, but any system should attempt to minimise inequalities.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is heartening that we have more Allied Educators now and I would suggest that this be moved upstream to MOE Kindergartens and the ones operate by the anchor operators.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We can formalise the tripartite partnership between the schools, Social Service Offices (SSOs) and Family Service Centres (FSCs) so that the pipeline of cases can be reviewed regularly.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I also urge new Family Service Centres (FSCs) to be housed together with the SSOs so that there is a better handshake process as clients do not need to repeat their circumstances.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The above-mentioned suggestions illustrate different ways on how we can help the deserving underprivileged Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is a precinct with many BTO flats and executive condominium units.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There are many young families concerned with unemployment as a result of the economic downturn.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Some have young children and are concerned about their future.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I had met many residents who had lost their jobs or had suffered pay cuts.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For one particular case, his nine years old daughter had contracted a rare disease.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I had also met a single mother with two special needs children.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: She suffers from depression as she is constantly worried about her kids and the tight financial situation.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Her former husband has gone missing so she has no alimony to rely upon.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Besides financial assistance, I hope the Government can invest in providing respite care for this group of care-givers just like what we have done for the care-givers of the dementia patients.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is extremely stressful when disadvantaged families have family members who suffer from chronic illnesses, mental illness or have special needs kids.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Financial distress is often intertwined with mental stress.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The United Nations highlighted in May 2020 the need to prioritise mental health during the COVID-19 pandemic, stating that whilst it is a physical health crisis, it has the seeds of a major mental health crisis as well.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope that everyone has the opportunities that I had.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A whole-of-Singapore inclusive approach, where all Singaporeans matter, is key in ensuring that we will continue to maintain a cohesive society while recovering from the pandemic.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This has helped many Singaporeans and has cushioned the impact on our GDP and employment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: These include urging employers to hire fairly and retain Singaporeans over foreigners when both can do the job.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I also like to urge Singaporeans to build up their skills so that they can enhance their suitability for the jobs that are being made available.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I will also share my perspective on the hard truths confronting our nation as we strive to maintain a strong Singaporean Core in the long term.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Today, excluding foreign domestic workers, two-thirds of the workforce in Singapore are Singapore citizens and Permanent Residents, while the remaining one-third are foreigners.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Prior to COVID-19, our economy was growing steadily and we were able to attract foreign investments as well as a sizeable foreign workforce to complement our local workforce.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Although the rise in unemployment rate is lower than what we have seen in advanced economies, such as the United States, we should still be concerned because, unlike many other countries, Singapore has no natural resources to give us buffer.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Our people are our only asset and every Singaporean counts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: How should we strengthen the Singaporean Core through this crisis?

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Some may say that it is about increasing the proportion of Singaporeans in the labour force and reducing our reliance on foreigners.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This is necessary when there is slack in the job market, as we are experiencing in this crisis.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: However, if we want to reduce our reliance on foreigners in a sustained way, we would need to increase our work productivity to bring down our overall demand for labour.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We have made some progress in raising productivity in the last 10 years, but it takes much effort to keep up the momentum.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: And while we have a highly educated population and dynamic workforce, our local labour force is ageing.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Last year, the median age of residents in our labour force was 44 years old.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: At the same time, the proportion of Singapore citizens between 20 and 64 years old will decline.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This is the group that forms the bulk of our labour force.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: To stay competitive against a younger global talent pool, we would have to keep upgrading ourselves or risk being squeezed out in the global competition for good jobs as we strive to grow our economy.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We will need to improve our Total Fertility Rate (TFR) so as to maintain a critical mass of Singaporeans in the labour force and not overly rely on foreigners to sustain our economy.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Increasing our work productivity and "life productivity", which means having more babies, are both not easy to achieve, but we must keep trying.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: In the more immediate term, there are two other areas that we should address to strengthen the Singaporean Core.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: First, employers need to be fair in hiring, retrenchment and developing local talent.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Second, we need to ensure that Singaporeans have relevant skills and are adaptive.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: With growing unemployment this year, there is a heightened sense of anxiety among Singaporeans about job security.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Some people have expressed strong sentiments about foreigners here, especially if they have been retrenched and see that other foreign workers remain in employment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This is compounded if the Singaporean's job search journey has been unsuccessful and companies are still hiring new foreign workers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: In Marymount, residents have similarly shared with me their anxieties about finding jobs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Many have families to support and expenses to upkeep.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I can understand the immense pressure that they are facing.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: In trying to make sense of the continued presence of foreign workforce in Singapore, I find it helpful to look at three categories of jobs that we require foreigners to do.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The first category are jobs in essential services that are not so popular with locals, such as construction workers and cleaners.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: For this category, the reality is that locals may not want these jobs even though we try very hard to transform them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We will need the foreign workforce to complement locals.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Having said that, we ought to move towards a reduced reliance on foreign workers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: How then do we "upgrade" these jobs to make them more appealing to Singaporeans?

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: A good example is in the construction sector.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The adoption of new technologies and digitalisation in construction has created new and higher skilled jobs in the sector.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: With the push for Design for Manufacturing and Assembly, more construction work has shifted off-site to automated production facilities that require production managers and quality assurance personnel, as well as logistics and supply chain planners.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: These jobs offer better work environment for our local PMETs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We should push for similar transformation and job re-design in other sectors, so that we can create good jobs for Singaporeans while reducing our reliance on foreign workers for essential services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The second category of jobs are those that locals want and can do, such as engineers and IT professionals, but for which there are not enough Singaporeans to meet the demand during periods when our economy is growing.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We have foreigners working alongside us in these roles so that jointly, we expand the economic pie which all Singaporeans can benefit from.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: A strong presence of locals in your company not only improves the support for your business in Singapore, but also enhances the resilience of your business in times of border controls that could impact the supply of foreign workers for your company.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: And most importantly, by showing due consideration to the Singaporean Core in this difficult time, the trust that is forged between your Singaporean employees and you will be further strengthened.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This will augur well for you when your business picks up in the future and you need the support of your local workforce.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The third category of jobs are those in global and regional companies that require global teams and certain professionals with highly specialised skills.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Our goal is to get Singaporeans to be part of these global teams comprising diverse foreign and local talent.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We also want companies to contribute to grooming our local talent so that Singaporeans have a fair chance at senior and top management positions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: One company that has done well in this area is Shell.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Ms Tan Chee Wei, a 46-year old Singaporean, is Shell's Vice President of Human Resources for the Asia region.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: In her 18 years of career with Shell, she rose through the ranks from a HR generalist to a global HR Leader.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: She spent a few years in London as a Global HR Advisor and also took on regional roles in organisational development and talent management, before being promoted to Vice President this year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Shell is an employer that values and invests in our local talents.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I hope that more companies would do likewise.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Our foreign workforce policy has largely been driven by the need to support economic growth, so as to create good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We need to continue to stay open and provide businesses with access to global expertise and talent.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: But with rising unemployment in this crisis, we had to tighten work passes for foreigners, and work more closely with employers and unions to uphold fair hiring and retrenchment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Ultimately, for every additional Employment Pass or S Pass that is issued to a foreigner today, we need to be clear that it is so that even more job opportunities will be available to Singaporeans in the future.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: While we ask employers to be fair in hiring and retrenchment, our local workforce needs to be adaptive and skilled in diverse fields, to remain highly employable even as the nature of work changes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: COVID-19 has caused major disruptions to our work and lives.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Some people have lost their jobs as a result.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Some are waiting for the economy to recover before they go back to their previous occupations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Unfortunately, it is hard to tell whether some of these jobs will come back again or will disappear in the new normal.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Amongst the remaining places available, there are over 47,000 jobs, 16,000 traineeships with different companies, and more than 10,000 training places in various Institutes of Higher Learning and other training providers such as NTUC LearningHub.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I have been encouraging my residents and friends who are looking for jobs to seriously consider the SGUnited training and skills programmes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I cannot guarantee that they will be able to get a job immediately after going through one of these courses, but they will certainly be more employable if they pick up new skills and knowledge.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Thirty-two-year-old Muhammad Iskandar Bin Ismail is one example.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Iskandar was an operations officer in the tourism and aviation sector when his job was affected due to COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: To enhance his employability, he took charge of his own upskilling journey and completed a series of courses.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: These included service-related Workforce Skills Qualifications (WSQ) courses, as well as supervisory-level courses on problem solving and decision-making.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Iskandar used his SkillsFuture Credit to defray part of the course fees.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Equipped with new skills, Iskandar successfully found a job as a full-time customer service officer in the retail sector.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Under normal circumstances, we would have preferred Place and Train programmes where a job seeker goes for training as required by his employer after he has secured a job.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: As many businesses have been hit by COVID-19, there are now fewer companies that are prepared to hire in advance now.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: As such, we are pushing for more Train and Place programmes with the hope that Singaporeans who attend these courses will stand a better chance of getting a job when the economy recovers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: COVID-19 has presented us with both challenges and opportunities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We should take this time to re-invest in building our skills.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The best course of action that we can take now is to add to our skills, and remain open to available jobs and training opportunities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Deepening this culture and spirit of lifelong learning will position our local workforce better in the long term.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Openness – our forefathers came from different lands to pursue their dreams on this island that is open to the world.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Multi-culturalism – despite differences of race, language and religion, our forefathers worked together to build thriving communities here.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Self-determination – our people knew that we had to take our fates in our own hands.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: So, we fought for the right to chart our own destiny.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: These values are still very much within us and alive today.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I met some Secondary 2 students from Catholic High School recently and they shared with me their reflections on “The Singapore Identity – What makes a Singaporean?” The students had studied the history of different towns in Singapore and conducted surveys to understand what brings Singaporeans together.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I was heartened that elements of openness, multi-culturalism and self-determination surfaced in their independent analysis of what makes us Singaporean.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Our Singaporean Core may be limited by the size of our citizen population, but we can be mighty if we differentiate ourselves from others by being identified with the values of openness, multi-culturalism and self-determination.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: As a society, we will chart our own destiny, overcome adversity and find opportunities in this crisis.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We must stand together and take care of one another so that no one is left behind in the storm.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: When we have fought together as a people in the battle against COVID-19, the Singapore identity will become even stronger than before.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: As we work together to emerge from this crisis of a generation, it is with a glad heart that I support the President’s call to strengthen our social safety nets and social mobility.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: As an executive from a big automative MNC told me: “Many years ago, Singapore was the only place in the region our expats wanted to live.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But now other cities are pretty nice and when we think about where we want to set up, Singapore doesn’t have what we call the 'halo effect' because the domestic market is so small”.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Technological, social, economic and political forces are reshaping the world, along with Singapore’s place in it.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I think Prime Minister Trudeau put it so well at Davos in 2018: "the pace of change has never been this fast, yet it will never be this slow again." In such a world, the winners will be those who learn faster than others and adapt to change.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I believe Singapore can build a lasting competitive advantage by being the nation that learns the fastest.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Today, I will focus on two things we must prioritise to do that: one, investing in our people; and two, giving them opportunities.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Investing in our people and giving them opportunities.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Since 2015, Singapore has embarked on a bold experiment to get our people to embrace lifelong learning.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is still early days, but I think it is an experiment so bold in its intent and approach, that I think we owe it to ourselves to continue.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Nonetheless, with the fallout from COVID-19, more and more Singaporeans will hope, will want, will demand the courses they attend to lead to a job.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In the late 19th century, the German psychologist, Hermann Ebbinghaus, was among the first to perform experiments to understand how memory works.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, while we talk about steep learning curves, let us not forget about steep forgetting curves.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For this to happen, employers must be a bigger part of the solution.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: First, they must take greater accountability for their employees’ learning.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Second, they must be willing to give more Singaporeans a chance, and look beyond paper and past experience, instead making their hiring and career progression and retention decisions based on skills.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: One of my residents in Woodlands in Sembawang GRC, I will call him Mr Lee, he is in his 50s.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: He wrote to me a few weeks back.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: He had just been retrenched, and wanted my help to support his application for a role in a Government agency.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Reading his resume, I was impressed – he had good technical competencies and he had been promoted several times in his company.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, I thought why settle for the role that he was thinking of.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, I asked a friend with a big data start-up to run it through this fancy matching algorithm that his company had built, that matches people with available job openings, based on the skills on their resume.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I got a list of job openings that had a high match for Mr Lee.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: When I sent the list to Mr Lee, he wrote back to say he appreciated the list, but he did not meet the educational qualifications required.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Sure enough, when I checked the job profiles, they all specified Degree holder.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The next morning, I emailed him, to suggest he try and apply anyway.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: He has yet to get a single interview.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: After completion, Google promises support in the job search as well, with over 50 companies signed up to participate on exclusive job boards and interview days.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is less than what you and I get in SkillsFuture credits.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Whether you are a millennial eager to climb the corporate ladder as quickly as possible, or a mid-career professional looking to make a career change, that probably made you sit up.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And if you are a university, you would probably sit up faster than you can say technology disruption.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Of course, we do not know how many of those who complete the Google Certificate programme will actually get jobs as a result, but it does paint what the future could be like: employers developing their own or collaborating with higher learning institutes and other partners to offer pre-skilling, up-skilling and re-skilling opportunities, from apprenticeships and traineeships, to short courses, to re-skilling bootcamps, along a lifelong learning path where they are able to quickly apply what they learn.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For most employers, it actually makes business sense to do this.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: You see, all businesses need to transform; yet, the skills required for transformation – hard digital skills, transformation skills and soft skills – are all in short supply.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: A company can buy, borrow or outsource these skills to people like myself, but I believe building them by investing in our people, has the biggest payoff in the long term, and is even more relevant today given the global pandemic that restricts movement, and the increased scrutiny on the contribution of business to society.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Ultimately, being known as an employer that invests in and develops its people will help companies attract and retain the best talent.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: To increase opportunities for jobseekers, in particular, we also ask companies to consider if they can hire a little ahead of demand, or to loosen their screening criteria and take a chance on Singaporeans who may not look like the perfect fit in terms of paper qualifications and past industry experience, but have sufficient relevant skills to get in the door and the attitude to learn the rest on the job if they are just given the opportunity.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Some companies will require support to do all this.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For example, for SMEs, Government can play a bigger role, creating platforms to train their employees at scale and at speed, while simultaneously helping the SMEs to transform and redesign their jobs where necessary.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And of course, the Government is already helping.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Adapt and Grow, SGUnited Skills Programme, SGUnited Trainerships are all great schemes, offering much needed hope to our jobseekers.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: According to media reports, they are converting the sceptics.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We need to have more of them and make them sharper.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Today, big data and AI give us insights into the supply and demand for a multitude of skills and using machine learning allows us to be much more surgical in our learning interventions and give us a better shot at landing a job for our people who can use the skills that they have.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But even while we turn to AI, I hope we will always stay open to new possibilities to make our schemes more human.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Yes, but let us not forget, they also need to survive.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, we must find ways to make it easier for our people to take the pathway of learning.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: A good policy, in itself, is not enough.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: People must also trust the implementation – trust that they will be given a fair chance.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But we all know the best schemes do not always work out for everyone.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We have all met them among our residents, our friends – Singaporeans who do not feel they are being given a fair chance.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: If people get a bad taste that, no matter how hard they work, the system is stacked against them, it leads to cynicism.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And because we Singaporeans actually have a strong sense of fairness and rooting for the underdog, if people see too many people around them like that, it can lead to polarisation, which only hurts our competitiveness.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We must continue to address prejudices and correct negative stereotypes and to encourage inclusive workplaces and be willing to have sensible dialogue on these issues.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: If we all – Government, employers and citizens – step up to the plate, our Singaporean workforce will surely be well-positioned to be the fastest in getting the right skills and the most adaptable, able to hold our own against anyone in a competitive and rapidly changing market.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: (In Malay):   I have spoken today about how the Government and, especially companies, can do more to help our people acquire skills and to give them opportunities, looking beyond paper qualifications and past experience.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But we know that the best schemes do not always work for everyone.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We all know friends and family members, who do not feel they are being given a fair chance.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: At the same time, we need to focus our energies on taking advantage of the schemes available for us to learn and progress.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: If we all – the Government, employers and citizens – step up to the plate, I strongly believe we can be the nation that learns the fastest, which will give us a unique advantage, allowing us to remain one of the most competitive economies in the world.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, I would like to conclude by addressing two distinguished groups I now have the incredible privilege to belong to – our Members of Parliament and our business leaders.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: As Members of Parliament, we are the ones that people turn to for help when they are at their lowest. “You are my last resort" – I have heard this too many times.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: How we lead during the coming years could make or break their spirit.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This is what I think about a lot as I try to comfort, encourage, guide and help my residents through these challenging times.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We are used to the Government telling us we have to be better, faster, work harder.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Do excuse my use of a Hokkien word: "mo chai".

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: How do we also provide support and inspiration?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: How do we open doors for them to ease their way through this world?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Call it social capital, call it the human touch.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The battle for hearts and minds can only be won on the ground and we must lead the way.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: (In Mandarin):   	Thank you, Mr Speaker, for allowing me to participate in this debate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: A month ago, a young girl emailed me to inform me that she had seen me and my grassroots leaders working together to resolve school traffic problems in her neighbourhood.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: She also wanted to do her part for the community and had worked out a plan with her two sisters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: They had pooled together her prize money from sports tournaments and their combined Edusave awards money.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: They wanted to donate the entire sum to the community and asked me what use it could be put to.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: It just so happened that my team has been distributing free meals to vulnerable residents at Clementi Avenue 4 since the start of the Circuit Breaker.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I told the girls that their donations would help to cover the costs of five meals and invited their family to join us in the distribution.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The residents were very moved to hear that such young girls had paid for their meals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The mother told me that her father used to be a construction worker and they would have to go without meals at times because his job was unstable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Now that she has the opportunity of guiding her daughters to give back to the community, she has this special sense of satisfaction.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I was also very touched by the mother’s words.
