speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: However, this was a first in my community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Normally, we would issue cheques or grocery vouchers to residents who apply for financial assistance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: During the Circuit Breaker period, we were worried that some of them would not be able to buy their own groceries and meals, which was why we decided to set up this meal programme.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We observed that as many people walked past the distribution point, some who are in need would approach us and apply to join the programme.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Those who are not in need also noticed and commended us for organising such an initiative.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Some residents, like the three sisters, who are in a position to give, even offered to sponsor a few meals or some daily necessities to be distributed together with the meals, giving full play to the kampong spirit of looking out for one another.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This might be a small anecdote, but it does reflect that our community is undergoing changes because of COVID-19.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The pandemic has hit the economy hard and affected the ability of some families to fend for themselves.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: However, it has also ignited the spirit of mutual help in our community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The Government has introduced many large-scale assistance programmes for Singaporeans, but there are finer areas where the grassroots can make themselves useful.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I have seen more residents engage in charitable work and even become volunteers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Our team of volunteers have become more like social workers, actively organising various assistance programmes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: For us Members of Parliament, we also seem to have become a clearing house to match donations to needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The items I have received and given out range from face masks and hand sanitisers to food, second-hand laptops and cash donations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We have been kept busy, but we also learn to adapt, transform and grow.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: During the debate over the past few days, we have had in-depth discussions on economic issues.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: While we will prevail against COVID-19 one day, life will probably not return to what it was.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Rather than long for the past, we can seize the day and shape the future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: While fighting the pandemic, Singaporeans have been surpassing ourselves in many ways.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I am not only referring to the courage of healthcare staff or the dedication of frontline personnel.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I am also referring to ways in which each and every one of us has been stretching ourselves.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: First, many of us have acquired new DIY skills, especially during the Circuit Breaker – cooking, baking, growing vegetables and sewing masks, to name a few examples.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Baking is both a hobby and also a wage-earning skill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Sales of baked goods and desserts were suspended during the Circuit Breaker, but home baking also flourished.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Now, when I make door-to-door visits, I sometimes am presented with cakes made by self-professed “Circuit Breaker Bakers”.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: In the early weeks of the pandemic, face masks were in short supply.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Those who could sew answered the call to make fabric masks for family, friends and strangers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: In the process, I learned that my sewing machine was not as difficult to use as I had imagined – the key was whether I had the motivation to figure it out.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: As for farming, we already have many enthusiastic hobbyists growing plants and vegetables in community gardens all over Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: But with the pandemic disrupting food supply chains, Singaporeans grew concerned about food security.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Looks like we have hopes of grooming more urban farmers!

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Second, we have become more caring towards the vulnerable in society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The meal programme I talked about at the start of my speech is only one among thousands of charity projects.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Many also responded to the call to donate their $600 Solidarity Payment to help those who might need it more.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Third, we have become more appreciative of migrant workers and frontline personnel.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Most of the donated face masks and bottles of hand sanitiser that I had received were from donors who specified that these were meant for frontline personnel, such as cleaners, security guards and pre-school staff.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I have also had the privilege of participating in COVID-19 relief projects for migrant workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I hope these examples of extraordinary efforts would not be ephemeral, but set new benchmarks for ourselves in the post-COVID-19 society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I hope that fellow Singaporeans who have acquired new DIY skills will continue to use them to the benefit of themselves and others.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: In a highly commoditised consumer market, just about anything can be bought ready-made.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: It hardly seems economically efficient to make anything on your own.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: But the pandemic has also brought about a “DIY renaissance”.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: If this leads to a more independent and sustainable approach to living, and greater appreciation for the labour of others, it is not a bad thing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I also hope that our care and concern for the vulnerable, for frontline personnel and migrant workers will be sustained.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The post-COVID-19 society should be one that is caring and cohesive.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I hope those who stepped up to help will continue with long-term volunteering, and that donors continue to support those who need help.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: With times being hard, I can well imagine that cash donations will be harder to come by.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: But even so, I believe there are many who are willing to give their time, or give in kind.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: If we make a conscious effort to encourage, support and mobilise ground-up initiatives, then we would not lose this heightened desire to help one another as we transit into the post-COVID-19 society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The pandemic is a grave threat but also a great force of transformation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The proliferation of work-from-home and flexible work arrangements demonstrates this.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The Government has been encouraging enterprises and individuals to go digital.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Everyone understands the broad direction, but adoption remains uneven on the ground.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: When it comes to enterprise digitalisation, the most challenging segments are neighbourhood enterprises, such as stalls in hawker centres, wet markets and coffeeshops.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Helping seniors go digital, such as learning to use smartphone features, was similarly challenging.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Neighbourhood enterprises count seniors among their most important customers, while many stallholders themselves are seniors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: And the daily lives and consumption preferences of many seniors revolve around the neighbourhood.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: When encouraging stallholders to go digital, some will decline, saying that their customers would not go digital.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: When teaching seniors to use digital technology, some also decline, saying that they would not need it at hawker centres and markets.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: In particular, during the Circuit Breaker, many conventional F&B and retail businesses were affected, while e-commerce and food delivery boomed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Many neighbourhood enterprises began exploring going digital in earnest.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: More people also recognise the benefits of minimising the use of cash and using electronic methods of payment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: These trends have created unprecedented conditions for us to help seniors and neighbourhood enterprises go digital at the same time.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The “Hawkers Go Digital” programme is progressing well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We have also launched Seniors Go Digital, to help seniors gain basic digital know-how.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We know that many seniors have children and grandchildren who are digital natives.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: But they might not have the patience to teach the seniors how to go digital.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Never fear – we have SG Digital community hubs where Digital Ambassadors are prepared to guide seniors one-on-one.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We will also focus on cybersecurity awareness, so that seniors can remain vigilant against potential cyber-crimes and gain confidence in online transactions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: For those with financial difficulty, the Mobile Access for Seniors scheme can equip them with subsidised smartphones and accompanying data plans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Our wish is for more seniors to be familiar with basic digital functions – that they can interact remotely with loved ones and friends, that they can make purchases electronically and to use digital forms of identification to transact online with the Government.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I hope those who take up the challenge can become Digitally Savvy Seniors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: What would a day in the life of a digitally savvy senior look like?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: She could be any “ah ma” in the neighbourhood.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: In the morning, she gets on a bus to the market.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: At the bus stop, she checks the MyTransport.SG app to see when her bus will arrive.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Since she has four or five minutes to spare, she takes a selfie and sends it to the family WhatsApp chatgroup to say good morning to everyone.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: At the market, she buys vegetables and groceries using PayNow on her mobile phone – no need to take out her wallet.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: On her way home, she swings by a parcel locker to collect prescription medication sent by the hospital, saving her a trip to the hospital pharmacy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: She spots what looks like stagnant water in a drain and snaps a photo for the OneService app.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: After getting home, she checks her Healthy365 app to see how many steps she has managed and what rewards she can redeem under HPB’s National Steps Challenge.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Over lunch, she and her husband chat about new articles that they have read using e-Newspaper services on the NLB Mobile app.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: And, since her grandchildren are back home from school, she chats with them over videocall and asks them what they would like her to cook at the next family gathering.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: In the afternoon, her mobile screen lights up with the latest Gov.sg WhatsApp message on the COVID-19 situation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: In the evening, after dinner, she sees a message saying that a pair of trainers she ordered online have now arrived and are ready for collection in-store at a nearby mall.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: She gets her husband to join her on a stroll to the mall, but not before checking spaceout.gov.sg to make sure it is not crowded.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: At the mall, she uses SingPass Mobile for SafeEntry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: And, before going to bed that night, she browses all the well wishes sent by friends in her chat groups and wishes them good night.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This is good for customers and also for business owners.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: It is a tough road between now and the “post-COVID-19 society”.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: But, undeniably, we are seeing encouraging signs as we respond to the immediate challenges posed by the pandemic.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The “post-COVID-19 society” is taking shape bit by bit.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I hope that the “DIY renaissance” will contribute to vibrancy and a sense of autonomy in the post-COVID-19 society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Such a society would also be a Little Red Dot brimming with positive energy, always ready to forge ahead.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I would first like to express my gratitude to the voters of Aljunied GRC for giving me the opportunity to contribute in this House again.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I cherish the trust that you have placed in my teammates and I, and we will do our very best to represent your concerns and work towards a better future for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While we may be called the Opposition for historical reasons, we stand here not necessarily to oppose but to work with Parliamentary colleagues along and across the aisle to refine existing policies and propose new approaches to the challenges we face as a nation.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Singapore's economic, social and security challenges have grown more complex over the years.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The policy responses must rise to the challenge.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: To do so, we need earnest and robust discussions on substantive policy matters both in and out of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Today, I would like to discuss ways in which we can improve how we care for some of the more vulnerable members of our society.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I will touch on the concerns of people with disabilities, means testing, healthcare expenses and welfare of migrant workers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: People with disabilities, or PWDs, are not a homogeneous group but a diverse community.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They include individuals with physical, sensory, intellectual and developmental challenges of varying degrees.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I raised disability issues seven years ago, during my previous term in Parliament, specifically about improving public transport and pedestrian infrastructure accessibility for the visually impaired.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I am glad to see some progress has been made since then, although some gaps still remain.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This could pose a safety risk for visually impaired pedestrians who are out at night.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I hope MOT will reconsider my proposal back then to add vibro-tactile walk indications at the crossings.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These are special buttons positioned at the traffic signals which vibrate when it is safe to walk.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These complement the APS and can continue to operate even late at night without disturbing the peace.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In my conversations with PWDs, the number one issue on their minds is jobs – not unlike many other Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They are not asking for handouts but more equal opportunities in employment.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, PWDs face much higher hurdles and not just because of their disabilities.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: One such hurdle is that it is common for employers to assume PWDs will not be able to perform on the job as well just because of their limitations.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: PWDs have shared with me their unpleasant job search experiences where they met all the job requirements, only to be rejected when the employer learned that they had a disability.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In fact, with modern assistive technologies, PWDs can be as productive at work as their able-bodied colleagues.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Another area that needs to move forward faster with the times is our approach to means testing for social assistance schemes.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The process often requires too much paperwork and imposes an undue burden on the very people we are trying to help.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Mr Leon Perera also raised this issue in a speech on Tuesday.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Some of these documents require applicants to log into Government websites with their SingPass and print out documents such as CPF statements, both of which can be an obstacle for those with no computers and printers at home.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: When they apply for assistance schemes with other Government agencies or need to renew their assistance, the same exercise has to be repeated.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The process for PWDs applying for disability support is not a walk in the park either.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They need to get a doctor certification of their disability and pay the clinic for this service.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Then, they need to repeat this process for every agency they are applying for support from.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: All this is a painfully low-tech way of means testing.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In fact, we already have the capability to integrate and automate such systems.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For example, My Tax Portal from IRAS pulls data from multiple sources to fill in a taxpayer's income deductions and reliefs, and computes their taxable income after just a few clicks.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Government has also been building its capabilities and data analytics.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We clearly have the technical capabilities to collect taxes efficiently and seamlessly.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Can we now develop the same capabilities for dispersing social assistance to deserving individuals and families?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I hope our means testing process will be one of the first to go paperless and presence-less.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: By doing so, deserving citizens can receive the help they need more quickly and conveniently, and will not fall through the cracks just because they have difficulty gathering and submitting the necessary documents.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: My third area of concern is helping Singaporeans cope with the burden of healthcare expenses.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Chronic diseases are imposing an increasing burden on our ageing population.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: MOH has said in its Addendum to the President's Address that it will look into identifying best practices that can help us in our fight to better manage diabetes and other chronic diseases.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: A key challenge in chronic disease management is ensuring that patients follow their treatment regimens and show up for their regular appointments with their family doctors.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I have met residents who have lamented about the high cost of treatment for their chronic conditions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Some have shared about missing appointments because of cost concerns.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, I remain concerned about the limitations of the scheme.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I have two suggestions for MOH to consider.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: First, that MediSave withdrawals be allowed for the treatment of all chronic conditions, not just those on the CDMP list.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will ensure that no one is excluded just because they suffer from a less common chronic condition.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Second, the annual withdrawal limits for MediSave should be removed for patients with sufficient MediSave balances and are over the age of 60.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: To reduce the risk of a buffet syndrome, these two changes can be rolled out first at polyclinics and restructured hospitals, where tight procedures are already in place to ensure that only medically necessary treatment is prescribed.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: (In Mandarin):   	Mr Speaker, healthcare costs are a heavy burden for many Singaporeans, especially those who have been battling chronic diseases for a long time.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Therefore, I hope the Government will further reduce the restrictions on the use of MediSave and help the elderly to reduce the medical expenses that have to be paid in cash.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many residents have complained to us about the high medical costs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Some even forgo follow-up treatment because they cannot afford it.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In the long run, if a patient's condition deteriorates to the point where he has to be hospitalised, the burden will increase, both for the patient and for our healthcare system.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In view of this, I would like to suggest that MOH include all chronic diseases in the list of allowed MediSave withdrawals, and remove the annual withdrawal limits for people over the age of 60.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I believe this arrangement will reduce the mental stress on elderly persons caused by medical expenses and allow them to seek medical treatment with greater peace of mind.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: (In English): Sir, my fourth area of concern is the welfare of migrant workers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These are some of the most disadvantaged yet invisible members of our society.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They are neither voters nor Singaporeans, but they are part of the Singapore community and their interests must be protected too as is befitting a developed country like ours.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: At the heart of the many issues that migrant workers in Singapore face is their lack of bargaining power vis-a-vis other parties like employers, the Government and employment agencies.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This makes them susceptible to being taken advantage of.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The costs include agent fees, course fees and sometimes kick-backs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For both these fees, they take up huge loans and spend many months servicing them on the back of their salaries of about to $500 to $800 a month.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This makes them almost like indentured labour for much of their time in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: A few unscrupulous employers are in on the act, working with illegal agents to profit off the workers they employ.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Because such payments are usually made in cash, there is often no paper trail to prove the offences if they file a complaint with MOM.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Furthermore, workers risk losing their jobs if they are being sent home when their employers find out they have filed a complaint.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I urge MOM to step up enforcement and intelligence-gathering, so that errant parties can be taken to task and made an example of.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We could also set up a jobs portal for employers to list available jobs so that workers do not have to go through intermediaries to find new companies to work for once their contracts end.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will reduce the opportunities for collecting kick-backs and correct some of the power imbalance that currently exists.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The President alluded to this in her Address to.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We have come so far as a country, uplifting the standard of living of generations of our people.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Let us take this progress to the next level as we further improve how we care for the vulnerable members of our society.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: On 24 August 2020, I was privileged to be sworn in at The Arts House, being the Old Parliament House where our Pioneer leaders themselves were sworn in during their time.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Standing in the same Chamber as they had decades before, drove home the sacred duty of being a Member of Parliament (MP), and the importance of what we do here in Parliament.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Like our forefathers, we too are charged with safeguarding the interests of this country.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We now face new challenges, some of which they may not have foreseen.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But I am confident that, by adopting the same spirit that our forefathers had, we can overcome these challenges with perseverance, unity and the conviction to do what is best for our Singapore.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I concur with Mdm President of the need to look out for our lower-wage workforce, many of whom, such as food delivery riders, are also essential workers keeping Singapore afloat throughout the COVID-19 crisis.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many of the people in this House may have heard about or watched the video concerning Mr Abdul Rahman, a food delivery rider who found himself at the tail-end of a National Day mobile column on 9 August this year.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Seizing the moment, Rahman spontaneously waved to some of the onlookers, who then responded with loud cheers in return.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This heartwarming incident was fortunately captured on video and quickly went viral on social media networks that very same day.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I subsequently discovered that Rahman is actually a resident of my constituency and I paid him a visit at his residence in Woodgrove recently.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They earn their wages by being constantly on the road and weathering the elements as they go.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: More or often than not, these are due to the lack of designated parking facilities for delivery riders.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This will provide a win-win situation that reduces the risk of fines and clamping charges for illegal parking, enabling a smoother food collection and delivery process.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In recent years, the threat of climate change has grown ever more urgent, with reports of forest fires and floods making the news more frequently than before.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While Singapore has not seen major environmental disasters in recent years, the world’s rising sea levels may soon become a profound danger that poses a risk to our safety and way of life.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But the world is taking notice of the problem, with many developed countries making a push for "green living" and sustainability to mitigate the effects of climate change.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In a recent survey conducted by Morgan Stanley Research with their summer interns, more than three-quarters of those surveyed plan to increase recycling efforts, while almost half are willing to change their diet to more sustainable food sources.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A sizable portion of them are also reported to prefer the use of electric cars.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We must do the same here in Singapore with regard to increasing awareness and taking action as a society.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For the past few years, I have been involved with green living initiatives at a grassroots level, organising recycling drives for the Bukit Panjang community, and I fully intend to do more as part of what I call my "G.E.L." mission for Woodgrove, with the "G" representing "Green Living"; "E" meaning "Embracing Parenthood" and "L" being "Law Awareness".

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In so doing, hopefully, we can reduce the country’s overall carbon footprint.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Working towards a more inclusive transport system should involve more than just improving public transport per se.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We need to look deeper to better support the less ambulant.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Most of them will opt to take public transport or walk whenever they go out to buy groceries, pick up their grandchildren or go for regular check-ups at the polyclinics as these save money.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But due to the deterioration of their knee joints, it is very strenuous for them to go up and down the stairs of the overhead bridges.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Whenever it rains, they would rather get drenched than to use the overhead bridge.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is even more difficult for those who have mobility issues, let alone those using crutches or wheelchairs.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If we want to encourage more Singaporeans, especially the elderly and the disabled, to use public transport, we should not just focus on how to improve public transport amenities as that may not solve the root of the problem.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We should at the same time, also improve the environment around these public transport.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For example, ensuring that covered walkways are extended to all HDB estates, we have to make sure that these walkways access are barrier-free and that lifts are installed at overhead bridges, especially in areas and along the trails towards where the elderly and mobility handicapped would like to go to, such as Community Clubs, town centres, polyclinics, hospitals and shopping centres.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: (In English): During the term when I served as the School Advisory Committee Chairperson in Zhenghua Primary School, I would conduct motivational talks to the Primary 6 students prior to taking the PSLE, and I would hold intimate chit-chat sessions with their parents before they receive their PSLE results.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: On these occasions, I shared with them my unconventional journey in becoming a lawyer, including the fact that I actually did not do well for my own PSLE.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: With this revelation, I took the opportunity to encourage the parents not to choose schools purely based on their children’s PSLE scores, but where their child’s passion may lie instead.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This will offer students more opportunities to pursue subjects at a level suited to their strengths and interests.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While this is a great leap forward for the country’s education policies, many Singaporeans are far more concerned with the perceived quality of the schools themselves, with the reasoning that only some schools are good, and only the best teachers are in good schools.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: My alma mater, Bendemeer Secondary School, is one such example.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Back then, my parents chose Bendemeer primarily due to convenience’s sake; it was just a two-minute walk away from our HDB block.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They would often walk past the school when returning home and see the school motto – "From Each His Best", eventually growing fond of it.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Till to-date, I remain eternally grateful for the opportunities and encouragements that my teachers had given to me, believing that a Normal (Academic) student can become a lawyer one day if she worked hard for it.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: When I was expecting my daughter back in 2018, the first question one of my friends had asked me was not about the name I was planning to give to my daughter, but whether I had planned on which kindergarten and Primary school for my daughter to enter in future.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I was taken aback by that at first, but she shared with me that this is actually a common question discussed by many parents in the "mummy" chatgroups that she had joined, where the common consensus is that the school which the first child enters is important, as that will make the applications for their subsequent children a lot easier.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As a result of this mentality, many parents when registering their children for Primary 1, typically find themselves vexed by the whole process.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The whole objective of meeting the targets as set forth by this framework is not for schools to eventually be carbon copies of each other, but allow each of them to explore ways to excel with the manpower and resources available to them, enabling their students to feel motivated and inspired to pursue their passion.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: At this juncture, I would like to take this opportunity to wish all teachers, a very Happy Teachers' Day.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: More often than not, residents come to see us when they encounter unfortunate situations, such as when they were scammed of their life savings, or when their spouses had become critically ill or passed on abruptly.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They are invariably helpless and financially-strapped during these periods of time.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: My experience had informed me that prevention is better than cure.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I therefore think that upstream legal education is important, equipping them with knowledge of their rights in order to better prepare them for potential situations concerning legal matters.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: During the course of the past few days of the President’s Motion of Thanks debate, I have observed that everyone in this House – both from the PAP and the Opposition parties – have affirmed the need for our country to stay united and at the same time, keep our economy and society open, and not turn inwards.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I believe that speaks well of the consensus we all share in shaping the overall character and tone of our society.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Ours must always be a diverse, inclusive and multi-cultural Singapore – a nation where everyone has a place and where everyone belongs.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We must uphold the interests of all Singaporeans regardless of their backgrounds and origins.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is what I have observed in my constituency as well.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: During house visits, I often meet residents who share with me that they have worked in Singapore for many years and subsequently decided to establish their roots here.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They purchased a HDB flat and set up a family in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In Parliament, we raise issues that are vital to our people.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Outside Parliament, we listen and serve our people; all of which, we have endeavoured to do, to the best of our abilities for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Manpower and Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: While the system itself is not perfect, but we are doing the best we can.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Manpower and Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And we continue to improve and it continues to be a work-in-progress in terms of how we want to cater to more of taking care of their needs.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Manpower and Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In terms of their coming onboard, employment agencies have access to them first.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Manpower and Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, it is one point that you need to consider.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Manpower and Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have repeatedly engage Embassy officials to highlight to them that they need to work closer with us in terms of working with these employment agencies, to make sure that some of them can be blacklisted, so that we can also identify who they are and dissuade them from coming and using these employment agencies.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Manpower and Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: At a certain length of time, they require to get the approval of their existing employers, and once that period has shortened, has come to the end, when they cannot get the approval towards the end, they can change an employer without getting prior approval.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Manpower and Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, we have actually implemented all that to make sure that there is no need for the migrant workers to go back to re-apply in order to come here again.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Manpower and Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: On top of that, we are also very thankful, we are very grateful to the multiple Non-Governmental Organisations (NGOs) in working with them and continually giving us feedback.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Manpower and Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: If you look at the bulk of them, actually the majority of them stay here for more than two contracts.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Manpower and Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Quite a number of them have actually been here for more than eight years.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Manpower and Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, I thank the hon Member Gerald Giam for bringing this thing up.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Manpower and Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: If he has more ideas, this is constructive feedback, we would welcome them as well.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: One of the points I was trying to make was that it is important to be able to cut out this intermediary that workers have to go through.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I understand that there are jurisdictional problems and being able to reach out to them when they are not in the country.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: But within the country itself, very often, when their contract ends and they need to find another job – I have heard what the Minister said about helping them to be able to find the next job – what I am arguing for is more transparency, not on the part of the Government but more transparency such that the workers will be able to find a job possibly on their own without seeing a need to pay somebody to find them another job.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: We have to put ourselves in the shoes of these workers who are here; they do not understand the language here and they do not have the means to just hop on to MyCareersFuture and find a job.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: So, if there is a way that we can make it more transparent what jobs are available, then they can skip through this intermediary and they do not need to feel a need to pay this kick-back to the intermediary.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In the course of this week's debate, Members have discussed the geopolitical, technological, economic and social trends that have compelled a point of inflection upon us.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: These are forces that are beyond our control.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Yet, we have to address the dislocations they will cause to our businesses, workers and vulnerable groups.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: And, also, we must position ourselves to reap longer term opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: So, the decisions we make now will have a lasting impact on our economy and our society.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Last week, as I took my oath in the old Parliament House, I vividly recall the first time I did so in the same Chamber in 1997 as a newly elected Member of Parliament of the Ninth Parliament of Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: So, Ms Hany Soh would be perhaps surprised to know that there still are a few in this Chamber who took the oath and that includes, if I am not mistaken, the Prime Minister, Senior Minister Teo and, also, I think, Mr Shanmugam.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: But what it reminded me of is the major challenges that successive Parliaments have navigated and the tenets that have helped us prevail against adversity, whilst we held steadfastly to what defined us as a nation – whether it was handling a crisis like the Asian Financial Crisis, SARS, the Global Financial Crisis, or making important shifts such as in population policy or the use of our reserves.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The stakes were high and we had difficult choices to make.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: And each time, we were honest with Singaporeans on the choices and trade-offs.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We sought to foster understanding of our fundamental challenges and forge a consensus on the way forward.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: And Parliament was the key forum for this, and this time is no different.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: So, the question is, what will determine whether this arc of inflection in our history bends in our favour?

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Ultimately, it lies in how we choose to respond.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: And I would like to give my take on that delicate equilibrium and the role that Parliament must play in maintaining it.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Staying open means a willingness to engage with the world, embrace novel ideas and seize new opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: And on the face of it, the need and benefits seem self-evident.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Indeed, even in the course of this week's debate, across the aisle, we all agree that Singapore must remain open in order to create jobs and opportunities for our citizens.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Staying open means greater competition, disruption and constant adaptation to change.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In other words, there are winners and there are losers.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Societies around the world have fractured because of this.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: So, being inclusive is a critical and vital complement to this.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Again, we all agree on this and that we must invest in the skills of our workers, capabilities of our enterprises, have rules of fair play and redistribute benefits.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: As Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat had said, we must redouble our efforts to develop everyone to their fullest potential, to take on new opportunities, flourish in their chosen pursuits.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: So, where does the rubber hit the road?

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: It is in the judgements that we have to make, in translating those principles into policies and putting them into practice; when the macro benefits do not necessarily square with the micro experience; when we have to persuade our workers and union leaders to support technological change that may threaten their jobs, but yet is in our long-term interests; when our economic agencies have to convince investors that they can rely on us to be consistent in our policies, including those that pertain to manpower, even as they make long-term commitments to Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Our citizens must know that their lives and livelihoods are always our priority, that we have their back.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: As Prime Minister said on Wednesday, "The Government will always be on the side of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: What is the point of creating jobs for foreigners, if it does not benefit Singaporeans?" Equally, our international partners must know that we are not just fair weather friends; that we have the political will to stay the course.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Building that trust is the duty of the Government, the Public Service, but, importantly, also of Parliament.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: It is a precious asset that we must not squander.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: I was therefore reassured when the Leader of the Opposition recognised in his speech that the presence of foreign workers, and I quote, "gives Singapore a vitality that keeps us economically relevant and also provides jobs and opportunities to our fellow Singaporeans".

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: I think this is an important signal and a good starting point.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: By all means, let us passionately argue the case to do more for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: But, as Parliamentarians, let us also be careful about what our words convey; in this case, the message we send to those who – to paraphrase Mr S Rajaratnam – have chosen out of conviction to become citizens of Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: How has our openness brought benefits for Singaporeans?

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Our portfolio of Free Trade Agreements or FTAs is a good example.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: As Minister Chan Chun Sing shared earlier this week, our network of FTAs is greater than the sum of its parts; each and every FTA adds to the network effect.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: They also generate demand for local businesses and ancillary legal, financial and other services.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We have also helped our SMEs to benefit from this market access; and invested in our people so that they can take on regional and global roles.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Digital Economy Agreements or DEAs are another way we are striving to keep Singapore open and connected.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: These agreements are the new frontier in the global economic architecture.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: To strengthen our hub status in the digital world, Singapore is actively developing an international network of DEAs.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Clear and harmonised rules, as well as interoperable standards and systems, will enhance cross border digital trade.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: With an open digital trade architecture and safeguards, data can flow more freely and securely across borders, between countries.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This will help more businesses manage their global platforms and digital services out of Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: These DEAs will give a further boost to our infocomm sector.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: It is one of our most promising growth areas, offering interesting and attractive jobs and careers for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: COVID-19 has given the sector, in an ironic way, a further boost, by accelerating the focus on the cloud, connectivity, collaboration because of remote working, and cybersecurity.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: More broadly, the total employment in the infocomm sector has grown over 11% from 2016 to 2019.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Despite this rapid growth, the proportion of locals has held steady at 70%.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This is no mean feat, especially when you consider that the fast growth has also resulted in an intense global competition for scarce talent in this sector.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We want to further increase opportunities for Singaporeans in the sector.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: But our talent policy must take into account the variegated landscape of the tech eco-system, with firms of varying sizes and business models, at different stages of growth, with diverse needs and thus, different staff profiles.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: There are the digital giants like Google, Facebook and Amazon, who have anchored their regional headquarters in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: These firms are at the forefront of global digital innovation and are critical to our ecosystem.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: They hire many Singaporeans, both here and overseas.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: But, because of the nature and scope of their business, they need a globally diverse talent pool; for example in product development and some of the regional headquarter's functions.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Therefore, the proportion of locals may not be as high as the national average, now or even in the steady state.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: For example, firms like Google and Twitter have APAC engineering teams here.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The talent they require include highly skilled product managers and AI scientists, who are globally scarce.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In the long term, these companies can help Singapore become an innovation centre and catalyse the growth of our local tech ecosystem.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We also have local unicorns like Grab and SEA.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: They started with and maintained a Singaporean core, but with their rapid international expansion, they too need a strong complement of regional and global talent to be able to compete.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: At the same time, their increased reach allows Singaporeans in these firms to venture overseas and gain global experience.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Our Large Local Enterprises like Singtel start in the sense from the other end of the spectrum, with a high proportion of local because of where they began.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: As they grow internationally, and branching into new tech areas like cybersecurity and cloud based services, they increasingly are seeking out global talent to complement their Singaporean Core.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Then there are the IT services companies, which play an important role in supporting many other sectors such as finance.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Here, as Minister Josephine Teo has explained in detail, there is more that we can and will do to reduce concentration and over-reliance on foreign manpower while strengthening the pipeline of jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Some had suggested that we could offshore some of their functions as a solution.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: I want to echo Minister Ong Ye Kung's caution.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This is not straightforward, as often there are linkages across different functions.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We should also recognised that with increasing digitalisation, that the scope to work remotely has increased and this, as Minister of State Alvin Tan talked about, earlier this week, can work in our favour or against us.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Do they want to locate those services, the people providing them in Singapore, or would they rather do it remotely.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: And we want them to choose in our favour, when the jobs are the type of jobs that we want Singaporeans to have.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: So, we need a differentiated approach for this diversity of companies in the infocomm sector.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Our challenge is to work with these companies to continue creating career opportunities for Singaporeans, while recognising that we must allow them to have the necessary access to talents that are diverse, especially in emerging areas, in order to strengthen our overall position as a digital tech hub.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: As with globalisation, the digital transformation of our economy must also be inclusive with opportunities for every worker, regardless of his or her background; and every business, regardless of its size or stage of growth.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: MCI's vision is for every business to be digitally-empowered, for every worker to be digitally-skilled and every citizen to be digitally-connected.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We are intensifying our efforts, working with the industry and unions to transform sectors, ease business transitions, create opportunities for jobseekers and reskill workers.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Our goal is to have as many skilled Singaporeans as possible to take up these roles.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: That is why we are scaling up our efforts, both in pre-employment and continuing education.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We also have around 4,500 Polytechnics and ITE graduates annually.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: At the enterprise level, we have enhanced the Productivity Solutions Grant and Enterprise Development Grant, to help our companies, adopt digital solutions and succeed.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: For SMEs in particular, we have the Start Digital, Go Digital and Grow Digital programmes to help them, as the names suggests, at different stages of growth, from when they are formed to as they scale, and eventually as they venture overseas.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We also want to ensure that our digitalisation journey includes every citizen.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: As such, as MCI has stated in our addendum to the President's address, we will ensure that all Singaporeans have a baseline level of affordable digital access and digital skills.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We will help Singaporeans acquire the tools and skills necessary to participate meaningfully in our digital economy and society.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: These include affordable devices, mobile and broadband connectivity, e-payments tools and bank accounts, SingPass and a National Digital Identity to transact securely, We will provide targeted support for our seniors and low-income households.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Senior Minister of State Sim Ann has shared extensively about our digital inclusion efforts, including the Seniors Go Digital Programme and the SG Digital Office, a mobilisation of 1,000 Digital Ambassadors and many more volunteers to galvanise a national movement towards digital transformation.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In short, we will spare no effort in making sure that no one is left behind in our digital transformation efforts.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We do this in every sector, through the work of the Future Economy Committee chaired by Deputy Prime Minister Heng, the National Jobs Council chaired Senior Minister Tharman and, indeed, a slew of other efforts.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Over the past few days, we have witnessed intense debates on a range of issues – our policy priorities, whether and what we should change, and specific measures to be considered.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We have articulated the policy choices and the aspirations and concerns of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In this important and ongoing effort to strike a balance balance between staying open and being inclusive, and building a better future for our citizens, I believe Parliament can and should play a significant role in three ways.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The first is to be the Voice of the People.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The Leader of the Opposition used the Latin term for it, I will stick to English.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The aim is this: we must express the hopes, aspirations, concerns and fears of our citizens at highest forum in our country.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: But, we should not and must not stop there.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We must also be the Voice of Reason.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: To be candid about the challenges we face, honest about the choices and trade-offs, not just about what we want but also what we have to give up to get it.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: And ultimately, what we believe to be in the long-term interest of our citizens.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: And finally, and perhaps most importantly, we must be the Voice of Hope.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Now more than ever, as we deal with unprecedented challenges and seek solutions, we must work with Singaporeans to draw confidence from what we have built up over the past five-and-a-half decades, the challenges that we have faced and overcome, have deep conviction in our strengths and capabilities, and look to the future with belief.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: If we do this, then I think we would have made a signal contribution to our nation building efforts, with a deep engagement of our citizens.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In that spirit of deep engagement, we have paid close attention to calls to broaden access to Parliamentary proceedings, for example through live broadcasts or streaming online.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This is a point that has been made in the past by Mr Pritam Singh, Mr Leon Perera – I think in this Parliamentary session – Mr Faisal Manap.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We had others who have articulated this and, in fact, in today's Forum page in The Straits Times, Mr Wong Weng Fai has also made this plaintive call.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The former Leader of the House and others have previously explained that we already provide timely and comprehensive access to Parliamentary proceedings.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Anyone can watch these proceedings in person from the Strangers’ Gallery.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Every speech and exchange in Parliament is recorded and made available online.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Clips, categorised by topic and speaker, are uploaded within hours of each sitting.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The Hansard is a full written record of Parliamentary proceedings and is available online.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: These already give us the full benefits of transparency, accountability and accessibility.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We have been reluctant to go further for both practical and policy reasons.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Parliament is a forum for serious debate on national issues.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The debate in Parliament should be vigorous, but the tone should be sober.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: An element of cut-and-thrust is unavoidable, even necessary because Members want to show Singaporeans that their concerns are being expressed, and questions asked and answered in Parliament.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: However, it is equally important that Members come to grips with the issues and their complexities and not simply play to the gallery.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: At this point, I am sure Members of the Opposition think this is same line as before.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: And I want to say that we still hold these reservations.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I welcome the Minister's comments that the Government is going to look into this matter.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I note Minister has shared that Government still has those reservations.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I believe the Senior Minister of State in the previous session, Mr Chee Hong Tat, used the word "theatrics" – there was a concern about Parliament being turned into that sort of a forum.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I understand and my colleagues and I have tried to reflect on this.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But it is our view that that element of theatre will be exposed and the public will conclude fairly quickly, if not immediately, fairly quickly who is here to turn Parliament into a theatre and who is here to be serious about Parliament as a forum where serious matters are discussed.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But there is reason to have concerns and that is why I articulated what I did.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, what it means is that at the end of the day it is not axiomatic one way or the other, and it depends on all of us as Parliamentarians to maintain the decorum, the dignity and the integrity of our proceedings through vigorous debate, based on facts and focused on the long-term interests of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In response to Minister Iswaran's point, I would like to reiterate and confirm that PSP is committed to an open and inclusive society and economy.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, we have differences with the Government, probably, with regard to the many issues on how we want to go about achieving that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And I think this Parliament has started the ball rolling to get us in that direction.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Over the last few days, I think we have debated on the issues of foreigners and jobs.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong, are you seeking clarification or are you making a new speech?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: — on the point that our disappointment on DBS still not having the homegrown CEO now is because of the process.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
