text: I want to ask the Minister whether the debate that we are conducting over the last few days when we are questioning certain issues, rebalancing certain issues that we are looking for is against the spirit that he is trying to explain to us just now.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Minister, can you attempt to respond to that?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Indeed, in this Parliament, if the Member had heard the detailed exposition by the Minister for Manpower, for example, we are taking even further measures.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And the Prime Minister has already spelt out that the Government will look at various policies in detail, but never compromising on the fundamentals and always keeping our eye on the long-term interests of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And, indeed, in my comment, I have made the point that we can always advocate the case for doing more for Singaporeans and I have no problems with that.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The issue is when we lament that a Singaporean occupying a certain position is somehow not homegrown.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Then, I think we really have to ask ourselves the question: as Parliamentarians, as elected representatives, what is the message we are sending to our citizens?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I am not sure what the Members means by homegrown, but all our citizens but also, in particular, to those who have, as I said, out of conviction, chosen to be Singaporeans, given up their home citizenship to take up Singapore Citizenship.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And also, what does it say to those who are the spouses, the children of Singapore Citizens who have become naturalised Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, the question I would put to Mr Leong is after this debate and all the information that has been shared, does he still lament that DBS does not have a homegrown CEO?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Does he acknowledge that as one example – and I am only talking about DBS because he raised it – whether he acknowledges that, in fact, much has been done in the organisation.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: There are, in fact, a large number of Singaporeans at the senior levels.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In fact, this is a clarification made by one of our colleagues Derrick Goh.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Unfortunately, the Member was not in the Chamber when the clarification was made.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I still keep to that, although I do appreciate the clarification given by Member Derrick Goh on the senior management of DBS Bank.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: In terms of why I want to keep to my statement is because when I gave the speech, when people listened to the speech, including the new citizens and foreigners in Singapore, they would have appreciated that I said it was over a period of 22 years.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Why did the Government not put in certain safeguards in the process or certain other rules to ensure that we have the skills transfer.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Localisation is not the word anymore, but at least to ensure that Singaporeans will be groomed to take over the job.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: In that context, I do not think that it will taken very, very negatively by the international community.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Foreigners know that we are very, very open.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Then, from there, the first banks that came in and did FX trading, they were foreign banks.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Gradually, we brought in investment banking, wealth management, insurance, so on and so forth.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Now, we are doing green finance and fintech.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I gave quite a lot of data requested by various Members to show that we are holding our own by being open to the world and I think that is the best way for us to grow, that is the best way for us to serve Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Live in the pond and feel that we are great because we are a big fish in the pond.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But open out to the lagoon, open out to the sea.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Have a much more exciting and diverse eco-system but also invest in our own people and hold our own.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I think that would be the wrong approach.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Minister S Iswaran, would you like to add on.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I just want to go back to a point I made in my speech.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: As Parliamentarians, we must be not just the Voice of the People.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That is important, which I think the Member has been articulating – the concerns of the people that he has spoken to.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But we must also be the Voice of Reason.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It is there for the record, for the future and everyone.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Others who are here will all be looking at this.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I think we in this House as elected representatives must hold ourselves up to a higher standard.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: If we do not, then I think we fail our duties as Members of Parliament and I think we ultimately do a disservice to Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I do not recall using this word in my response to Mr Pritam Singh when we were having a discussion on this issue when I was with the Ministry of Communications and Information.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: If my memory serves me correctly, I think we were talking about whether we should have live broadcast of Parliament proceedings and I was explaining to Mr Singh that the demand for such broadcasts was not high.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And then later, we had a discussion about whether instead of a broadcast, maybe it can be done through live-streaming.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And again, if my memory serves me correctly, because this was several years ago, I did say that this is something that we can discuss and review.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: So, I just wanted to clarify that factual point.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I do not think I used the word "theatrics" in my response to Mr Singh.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: To the Senior Minister of State Chee Hong Tat, I do apologise if indeed my memory failed me.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: For some reason, that word "theatrics" was in my mind.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But I think the larger point was about concern that Members of Parliament would play to the gallery.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I believe that was the point but rest assured, I do not mean to misrepresent what the Senior Minister of State said at that point.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: That is why the Hansard is even more effective than live-streaming.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I think that this whole idea of talking about using DBS as an example, maybe I would like to share a perspective having come from the private sector and especially having run a public listed company.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: They have independent directors on the board and there are committees, sub committees, under the ambit of the main board.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Some of the committees are nominating and remuneration committees, and you have the audit and risk management committee.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: All of the transactions, I would say, are done at arm's length basis and the process of selection of a CEO and managing director of a company is subject to a very rigorous process of going through an international search firm, by virtue of meritocratic principles and the best person for the job.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: There are many listed companies, which I think many funds have invested in.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I think Mr Leong himself as the CEO of Timbre Capital, a private equity firm, would have made significant investments in terms of wanting to secure returns for his limited partners (LPs) and people who have invested in his fund.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Perhaps, he can clarify that in companies where we clearly state quotas or perhaps, a certain percentage of the senior management has to be of a certain nationality, would it be something that his private equity firm would freely and happily invest in?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: That is what we are more concerned about in terms of making the investment decision.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Just a quick matter of propriety, in view of what Senior Minister of State Chee Hong Tat has said and he is indeed right.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: This was in response to a letter from a TODAY reader.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, just to make the point clear to Senior Minister of State Chee Hong Tat.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 3.40 pm until 4.00 pm.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Mr Lim Hng Kiang has served our nation with distinction over the past 29 years, and our residents and I appreciate him so much and we propose to build on his work.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: What a privilege it has also been to work with a team of committed volunteers and leaders across the West Coast GRC.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: To the Public Service agencies and NGOs who often go the extra mile to support the needs of our people, we thank you.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: What does it mean to live a life by design?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: And how might we empower our people to do so?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: These are the two questions that I would like to explore this afternoon.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In the past 25 years, serving in the corporate and social sector, I remain energised by two things: to see every youth succeed and to see adults flourish in all that they do.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: A life by design starts when a person's passion and skills intersect with the needs of the world – also known as "finding your niche".

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Here is what I notice when one is operating in their niche.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: You know who you are and who you are not.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: You are energised by what you do and you know the people group you are called to serve.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: When a person finds his or her niche, learning is no longer out of necessity, but a desire.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: You can continually seek out new opportunities to grow so that you can give your best, whether it is at home front, school, work or the community.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: You make these places better than when you first found it.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The second question – how might we empower a life by design?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The first is to clarify possibilities of growth at every age and life stage.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I have shared recently about a colleague of mine who, 10 years ago, then in her late 40s, joined our team.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Her question during the interview was "Am I too old to start a new career in a new sector?" We assured her, "Your age qualifies you.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: It is precisely your age and your experience that we value." Today, at 58, she is flourishing at work.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Her experience, competence and who she is, are impacting lives, honouring both people and results.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: We continue to cheer her on, believing for even greater years ahead of her!

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: We often hear this: "You are too old to do this" or "You are too young to do that".

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: There never seemed to be a right age.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: But if we do not see age as a barrier but rather as a qualifier, then there is nothing stopping us in exploring new possibilities for our lives.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Instead of focusing on limitations, what if we could help our family and our residents identify what they can do at every age and every season of their lives?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This is not about having a positive mindset, but a mindset of possibilities.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: We do not have to be limited to traditional career paths.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Entrepreneurship, volunteerism, participating in the gig economy are also productive options to discovering our niche.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Whether a person is a young graduate, stay-at-home mum, working single, working parent or retiree, we can carry valuable skillsets that our community needs.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: We should support our people to build a holistic life portfolio instead of just a work-focused one.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: They should include competencies beyond formal employment, such as transferable skills and experiences from care-giving, volunteering and personal interests we pursue.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: A familiar example is our stay-at-home mothers, who may aspire to work from home because of the recent work trends.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Many are skilled in wide-ranging areas but may not be sure of their fit in the workforce.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: If we continue to find ways to help our people to consider alternative pathways and identify their full range of skills at different life stages, we open up new possibilities for them and, in the process, strengthen our Singapore Core.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The second thing we can do is to provide opportunities to explore possibilities.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Time and space must be given to explore.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: My friend Mag was in the real estate industry for 20 years before making a switch to become a speech therapist.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: As she crossed her 10-year mark in the industry, she could not see herself doing this work for the rest of her life.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In the journey of exploring possibilities, she was encouraged by friends to volunteer to help children.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Mag discovered then that she really enjoyed being with children.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: She went on to take an early childhood education degree, which led to an advanced diploma in special education and, subsequently, a Masters in Speech Therapy.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Today, Mag is 50 years old and has been a speech therapist for the past five years and she loves her work.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: As a hobby, she has taken up photography, and I am inspired by what she said recently: "Who knows what will happen post-speech therapy?" Mag had time and space to explore possibilities and a boldness to design her life.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: We recognise that not everyone will be able to make time and space for themselves like Mag.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: At the same time, we need to improve towards a work culture that respects the need for rest and recreation.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This brings us to the third point – nurture creativity that opens possibilities that are yet to exist.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Singapore has a super resource still to be maximised – the creative capacities of our people.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: As oil is fuel to industry, so is creativity to the mind.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The more it is used, the more of itself it generates.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: But the opposite is also true, that if we do not tap into the creative capacities of our people, it will diminish and we will miss out on the multi-fold possibilities for our people and our nation.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: First, we can support our people to identify possibilities at every age.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Second, provide time, space and resource to explore them.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: And third, nurture creativity to form new possibilities for Singapore.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I am fully persuaded that if our people live a life by design, we will uncover a new strength of Singapore yet to be seen before.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Our workforce will be increasingly versatile, our families and communities will flourish.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: May we continue the legacy of our forefathers to be a nation by design, transform from the inside out.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: With this, Mr Speaker, I support the Motion.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Being the final speaker on the list, you have given me the privilege to listen to my colleagues' full-hearted views on what Singapore needs to do going forward.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We debated on Singapore's immediate concerns surrounding COVID-19, the Singaporean Core, support for SMEs and strengthening of social compact.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We shared our hope for the future in emerging trends, sustainability and sci-fi.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In this speech, I wish to focus on relevance.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This requires an exploration of our history, a deep reflection of who we are, a stoic acceptance of reality, and a call to stand united in our relevance in the year 3000 and beyond.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: There is a Chinese saying: "夫以铜为镜，可以正衣冠；以史为镜，可以知兴替；以人为镜，可以知得失." To better reflect on our future, it is not enough to dip our fingers into the changing of winds.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: To build our starship, we must weigh anchor, raise the sails and adventure to the past of Bugis pinisi, Chinese junk, Arab dhow and Chola kappal.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We were tossed in the storms of relentless competition, and weathered storms of successes and failures.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Please bear with me for a moment as I recount what is often forgotten.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Earliest known settlements arose in maritime Southeast Asia more than a thousand years ago.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In the west, there was Lambri in present day Aceh between the 13th and 14th centuries.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: And in the east and north of Singapore, Langkasuka in today's Kedah and Tambralinga in south Thailand.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Competition was fierce and there was a fight for relevance and survival.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It did well by being part of sub-regional systems of economic exchange between the peoples in the hills and coastal settlers, and by connecting these local and regional networks internationally – its true, unique competitive advantage to exist.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Wang Dayuan, a Yuan Dynasty traveller, documented his travels to South Asia and Temasek.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In his book, he recollected that Temasek offered products that distinguished it from other ports.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It was "top-quality hornbill casques, lakawood and cotton".

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Hornbill casques, a highly sought after substitute for ivory, were found only in the Malay Peninsula, Temasek, Borneo and the Riau Archipelago.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Lakawood was used as an incense, a red dye and as a disinfectant.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Interestingly, it was available in 19 other regional ports, but only five offered good-quality Lakawood, and Temasek was one of them.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: For one, its success drew much interest from regional powers, including Ayuttaya to the north and the Majapahits based in Java.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: According to some records, without the ability to defend herself, Temasek was brought under the influence of Ayutthaya and its revenue was forwarded to the court.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Temasek was also overly dependent on trade with the declining Yuan Dynasty in China.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: To exacerbate the decline of Temasek, a new port settlement at the Melaka River, seized opportunities offered by the new Ming Court, fundamentally changing trading networks.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This led the merchants who were previously based in Temasek to hollow out and move to the new port-settlement.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Internal conflicts that led to a foreign invasion dealt the final blow.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Temasek, became nothing more than a feeder port.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The age old threats have not disappeared but are supplanted by pandemics propagated by pathogens – created or evolved.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Discord has moved online, anonymous and lethal, disrupting our hard-earned relationships.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: An interconnected world makes us vulnerable to the dictates of others.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: And to add to this conundrum, climate change poses a threat to our future generations.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Only with this understanding, can we seek relevance.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We are a city-state, competing with the most driven.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Relevance is not a simplistic yes or no, one or zero.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Being relevant today does not equate relevance tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This responsibility is not just of the state's but on every Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We must believe that all of us can be ambassadors of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We will develop friendships, advocate for opportunities, and explore areas of cooperation that makes Singapore relevant.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We must operate as an ecosystem of differentiated capabilities.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We can no longer operate linearly, as a single company, a single domain or group.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We must collaborate, and build one another's strength to be a formidable entity that is multi-faceted.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: As an example, legal services have been expensive and time-consuming.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The emergence of Machine Learning and AI have changed the legal landscape.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We are now in a digital age of cross-disciplinary collaboration where lawyers and technologists will work hand in hand and new positions such as legal engineers are becoming part of the profession.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This next example struck a personal chord with me as I first published a peer reviewed journal research on Bi-jective Neural Networks just 15 years ago, building blocks of learning algorithms.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: SmartLaw is working closely with local law firms to create competitive solutions.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: There is a huge potential for this industry which will create more jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The most successful companies today are established because of their ability to develop an ecosystem of capabilities.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: They are able to build layers of different capabilities and products, enabling their users to remain within their ecosystem, adding to their relevance and resilience.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: A dynamic and resilient ecosystem that is differentiated in all levels, layers, and domains.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The years volunteering in the grassroots and organisations such as Tasek Jurong, enforced my belief that we must continue to be open, and open the world for our young to a range of possibilities.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We should encourage our children to learn how to learn, to have omni-directional capabilities.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: I am heartened by the emphasis in the Addendum to the President by MOE on broad based common core curricula.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: At the same time, we must encourage expectation that, it is crucial to achieve mastery in the subject matter of choice.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It requires a culture of embracing its arduousness.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This discussion brings to mind Dr Mark Lim, a teacher with a passion for physics.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: He is a co-founder of Aliena, a homegrown space tech company, which literally believes that the sky is not the limit.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The deep space plasma engines that Aliena is developing aims to bring Singapore's first satellite to the Moon and beyond.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In addition, Aliena has commissioned the region's largest privately owned jet propulsion test facility and nanosatellite integration centre, promoting an eco-system for the co-development of critical satellite platforms.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: A good example would be the collaboration between local IoT company NuSpace and Aliena.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: I say this with great enthusiasm because I too was a plasma dynamics researcher 16 years ago.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Then, we replaced mechanical flight control surfaces using plasma dynamics.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Aliena and Dr Mark is a prime example of how through the pursuit of mastery, young Singapore companies and individuals can leverage on expertise within their domains to do well on a global stage and to break new ground in emerging frontiers such as space, And how an ecosystem fosters the translation of technology to the market in a domain that seem inaccessible.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Through history, technology has never failed to contribute toward the evolution of industries and our way of life.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: With rapid scientific discoveries and high tech engineering, cities and societies, if complacent, can become irrelevant and disconnected from the rest of the world.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We must be courageous to be the leader in emerging technologies.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Technologies such as Quantum computing, AI and advanced materials will eventually shape the future.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Mainstream quantum computing may arrive sooner than anticipated and we must be ready.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Its value extends beyond solving problems faster than conventional computers and holds untapped potential to address global challenges, including climate change, cyber-crime, discovery of drugs and vaccines.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: From a medical standpoint, this would enable researchers to crunch data on more than 40,000 genes from 17,000 genetic samples, approximately 2.5 billion genetic combinations.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This effort may better allow us to better understand the COVID-19 virus strain and to synthesize a viable vaccine.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In fact, this was what happened at Oak Ridge National Lab in Tennessee just recently.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: When the first generation of computers became commercially available, it revolutionised the workforce and created new fields of jobs that never existed.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We must be ready to ride on the next wave of opportunities.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Twenty years ago, in the desire to remain relevant, we started our biomedical industry.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Today, the world faces shortage in technology and equipment in the fight against COVID.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: My work involves addressing this gap, and I witnessed how Singapore is able to bring to bear capabilities in diagnostics, therapeutics and vaccines.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In Therapeutics, we have Tychan, Hummingbird and DSO.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Years ago, had we not had the ambition, the foresight, the guts to make these investments, and put in the hard work, all these would just be a pipe dream, and Singapore would have been dependent on others for survival.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This courage must be coupled with sound strategies reflected in MTI's Addendum to the President's Address.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: I agree with many of our colleagues including the hon Ms Jessica Tan, Mr Melvin Yong, Mr Don Wee and Mr Edward Chia, that these decisions will need to support local SMEs, the bedrock of our economy.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: I agree as well with the hon Mr Patrick Tay, that economic incentives will need to result in proactive and sustained knowledge and skills transfer to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: As I listen to matters highlighted in this debate, I want to acknowledge the tough decisions and hardiness of those who came before us, which under wise stewardship, brought Singapore peace and prosperity.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Singapore's progress is not build on mere rhetoric.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Singaporeans are resilient people that have weathered numerous storms.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The economy will prosper anew and Singapore's children and grandchildren will continue marching forward to build a fairer, ever more just and equal society".

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We are constantly looking into the future but are well aware of our history.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We are small, but courageous in our ambition.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We are diverse but united in our cause.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We will be ordinary unless we make ourselves extraordinary.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: It has been an engaging discussion, with many ideas and suggestions.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: It is clear to us all that COVID-19 has completely transformed our reality.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Externally, Singapore's position – economically, geopolitically – is under threat.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We are disproportionately affected by the global nature of the crisis and tensions between bigger powers.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Within Singapore, our lives have been significantly disrupted and businesses have had to adapt rapidly to survive.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Many of us hope for a quick recovery back to "normal".

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We are finding ways to live and work with the cloud of the pandemic over us, and stay physically and emotionally healthy.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: But I doubt that we will return to life as it used to be.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We must adapt to the waves of change that are upon us.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: First, we have to focus our attention on our immediate challenges but also prepare ourselves for the longer term.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Second, we must renew our compact as a society with justice and fairness as our pledge.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Third, we must engage one another well, both in Parliament but also outside Parliament, and translate our conversations into action.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We are still in the midst of an unfolding crisis.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The pandemic is still raging across the world without any clear end in sight.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: To support economies and jobs that have been devastated, governments around the world have committed trillions of dollars, and debt levels are at record highs.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Our Government's immediate focus is to navigate Singapore through this pandemic and the serious economic downturn because of the very significant risk to our people's lives and livelihoods.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This week, we heard Minister Tan See Leng and Minister of State Gan Siow Huang share how tripartite partners are helping workers to retain their jobs or find new ones.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: But Members have also rightly emphasised the need to think longer term and position ourselves for a strong recovery.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We cannot simply hunker down and wait for things to get better.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Instead, we must prepare ourselves now so that we can capture new opportunities when they come.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We are not starting from scratch, but are building on strong pillars and steady improvements over the years.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In the last 10 years, we have invested heavily in early childhood and continuing adult education, enhanced our healthcare and social service architecture, implemented Industry Transformation Maps to strengthen different economic sectors.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: These fundamentals stand us in good stead to navigate the winds of change now confronting us.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Due to clusters in the dormitories and work sites, companies have had to put projects on hold for months.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Even after workers were cleared, it has not been easy to restart.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Many changes were needed to ensure that workers were safe and despite significant Government support, many construction firms and workers continue to suffer badly.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: But this experience has also strengthened our resolve collectively to transform the construction sector, when the situation stabilises.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We have to drive digitalisation and adopt more advanced building technologies to enhance productivity, and, through this transformation, try to attract more Singaporeans to join this sector.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: It will require the collective efforts of firms, workers and the Government.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This crisis is neither a "pause" nor a "rewind" for Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Instead, if we face this with the right spirit, we can turn this to a "fast-forward".

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Re-imagine new industries and markets for Singapore, learn new skills and discover new careers for ourselves and our children.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Even as we deal with present challenges, we must prepare ourselves for the longer term.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We must keep our resolve and look forward to emerging as a stronger society.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The second area that Members discussed extensively is the social impact of COVID-19 and the challenges it has wrought in our society.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: COVID-19's impact is universal, but it is not equally felt.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Some of us are fortunate to have jobs that allow us to work from home, or we are in sectors that have seen strong demand, like e-commerce.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In the hardest-hit industries, such as aviation, tourism, retail and F&B, workers face steep pay cuts and job losses.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The road to recovery is rocky and uncertain.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Older workers are worried about rising retrenchment figures.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Breadwinners will struggle to keep up with financial commitments if they lose their jobs.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: While essential workers, such as medical staff, cleaners and public transport operators, do not have the luxury of working from home.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: They face risks daily to keep our country running.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This virus has shown us, quite starkly, that "none of us is safe until all of us are safe".

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The broader point is that our well-being very much depends on one another.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: President Halimah has called for this generation of leaders and Singaporeans to forge our new compact.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: If we want Singapore to stay united and strong, we must renew our shared understanding of who we aspire to be.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Minister Maliki said that we must strive to build a fairer and more just society, with equal opportunities and a sense of progress for all.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Many Members, such as Mr Louis Ng, Ms Cheryl Chan and Mr Leon Perera, echoed similar sentiments of inclusiveness and unity.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: These values of justice, equality and unity are enshrined in our Pledge and underpin what Singapore stands for.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We would do well to keep these as our North Star.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Our challenge is, therefore, to find relevant and timely ways of building on what we have.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Some Members, such as Mr Fahmi Aliman and Mr Dennis Tan, have called for us to strengthen social safety nets and even out inequalities.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: At every point, these social programmes were designed with compassion for the vulnerable in our community and with care for those who need a leg up to grasp opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: But we must also go beyond what the Government can do alone.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: It is far more impactful and powerful to have a community of care that provides an eco-system of support.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: What Mr Seah Kian Peng said in this debate struck a chord with me.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: He shared how a person's challenges can be incredibly complex, with interlocking stressors, such as poverty, domestic abuse, disabilities and mental health issues.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And I am sure that many of our Members here, in your work on the ground, have seen how some lower income families struggle with these day-to-day issues.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Harness technology to improve case management and processes.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Preserve our human touch of building trust and empowering and respecting the individual and family.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Not just meeting needs, as Ms Carrie Tan had put it, but partnering them to grow and progress with dignity and respect.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Many have demonstrated this spirit, especially during this tough period.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: One example is Candi and her daughter, Caitlyn.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: A mother-daughter team, they distributed masks with Team Nila and hand sanitisers with the Temasek Foundation.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Caitlyn is seven years old, but Candy, her mother, believes that it is never too early for her to imbibe and learn to help others.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This leads me to my final point on engaging with one another well and turning from dialogue to concrete action.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We have seen and will continue to see a greater contestation of views and ideas – here in Parliament, in civil society, in online discourse.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We will differ on how best to take things forward for Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: But as the Prime Minister emphasised, we cannot afford to allow a diversity in views to lead to distrust or polarisation.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We have different genders, ethnicities and faiths, studied in different schools, worked in different fields.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: I am glad that Members have sought to represent Singaporeans' diverse concerns and spoken on a broad range of topics in the last few days.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Mr Derrick Goh, Mr Don Wee, Mr Edward Chia and Mr Christopher de Souza spoke on behalf of enterprises – their value, their challenges and how to seize more opportunities for growth.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Ms Mariam Jaafar, Mr Desmond Choo, Mr Sharael Taha and many others voiced the deep concerns of workers – how to help them develop their skills all through their careers and protect them from unfair practices at the workplace.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Many Members also highlighted the importance of building a strong Singaporean Core while remaining open to complementary foreign talent.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Prime Minister Lee and Ministers Josephine Teo and S Iswaran have addressed these.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: While Ms Poh Li San, Ms Yeo Wan Ling and Ms Raeesah Khan spoke up for youth and women.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Mr Xie Yao Quan, Ms He Ting Ru and Mr Yip Hon Weng suggested ideas to improve senior care.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Dr Wan Rizal spoke about education; Dr Tan Wu Meng, healthcare; Mr Chong Kee Hiong, housing; Mr Sitoh Yih Pin, culture and sports, and many more.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We thank Members for contributing your views and suggestions.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We have had a vigorous debate these five days and I am sure for many more parliamentary sessions to come.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We may not agree on every issue but, as Mr Murali Pillai and Mr Lim Biow Chuan have pointed out, we can deal with disagreements constructively.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: With empathy and an open mind, using facts and reason, have frank discussions with one another.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We should acknowledge that there are no book answers or straightforward solutions for the challenges that we face.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We will need to grapple honestly and openly with the difficulties that our society faces and will face in all their complexities – whether on our foreign manpower issues, raising the wages of lower income Singaporeans, tackling inequality and many more issues.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: So that through our debates, we not only share with Singaporeans more about the issues, trade-offs and possibilities, but also help find a better way forward for our country.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This may not always be our default way of engaging others in this House.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Sometimes, emotions will run high and we will be tempted to push our point to the fullest.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: But as long as we commit to putting Singapore's interests before our own, it will be possible to find common ground and move forward together.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This will enable us to retain and harness our diversity as a strength and avoid the partisan division and polarisation that we see in other countries taking root here.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Constructive dialogue and engagement extends beyond Parliament to all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Minister Edwin Tong has explained how we hope to harness these as platforms to engage Singaporeans from all walks of life in honest and respectful conversations about the kind of Singapore that we want to build together.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: I have hosted several of these conversations where a myriad of topics were discussed – such as social mobility, racism, xenophobia, our treatment of migrant workers.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Participants were candid and raised suggestions that are worth exploring further.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: For example, some suggested setting up forums where people can talk openly and safely about difficult issues like differences in race, religion, language or class; or reframing how charities work by using new funding models like social impact investing.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We invite all Singaporeans to participate in these conversations, reflect on our experience together during this pandemic and take part first-hand, in the important work of forging a shared consensus.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: But I hope that our conversations will ultimately lead to action and that we will solve problems together and pursue fresh ideas together.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This is the heart of Singapore Together and we have some examples of this.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: But another area we will need collective action is in building a greener and more environmentally sustainable Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Minister of State Desmond Tan and Minister of State Alvin Tan spoke passionately about this.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And as an island city, we are especially vulnerable to its consequences, such as rising sea levels and increasing temperatures.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: That is why we are doubling down on efforts to build a low-carbon climate-resilient Singapore, for our grandchildren and their children.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We will green our buildings, towns and transport network.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Our economy also needs to be more resilient.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Our industries can be more energy-efficient, and we should use more renewable energy like solar power.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In pursuing green growth, we can build expertise that opens up new opportunities – specialised financial or legal services and clean technology.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In June, we shared that we have three such existing networks.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: One of them is the Youth Mental Well-being Network, which Minister Edwin Tong also spoke about earlier.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: I want to highlight the markedly different approach that we took for this network.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: First, we made the network open – anyone could sign up.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Second, we gave the network space to shape their own agenda.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Early on, one participant asked me what the Government aimed to achieve through this network, and I said that we did not want to predetermine where the network would go.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: It is not about the Government setting the agenda all the time, then seeking input from the public.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Instead, the community comes up with ideas and decides what they want to work on, while the Government supports them.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Some participants have stepped up and volunteered to drive this process.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: They have crafted problem statements, eight areas of interest that they want to dive into, such as mental health at school, in the workplace and within families.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We are excited to see where we will go and the fruits of such collaboration.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This Taskforce headed by Ms Anita Fam, President of National Council of Social Service (NCSS), has already gotten down to work.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The genesis of this Taskforce emerged from engagements that NCSS had with many of our charities.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: There was a yearning desire to come together, work on common challenges they faced, magnified during COVID-19, in order to reimagine and develop a social sector that can effectively meet emerging social needs, post-crisis.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And as more themes emerge from our Emerging Stronger Conversations, more Action Networks can be formed in the months ahead.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: They too represent a wholly different way of doing things – again, not just industry providing feedback to Government, but industry actually taking the front seat, taking the lead, and Government as active partners.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: For example, COVID-19 has shown the importance of keeping our supply chains running, especially for a small and open economy like Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: One of the challenges is that many players are involved along the entire supply chain – from shippers and carriers, to air and sea port operators, legal and financial service providers and government regulators.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Along the chain, cargo details need to be tracked, verified and communicated accurately.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: But different players may have different standards, formats and platforms, which complicates the process – some things that are sometimes taken for granted, all this while.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Industry says if we can use digitalisation, make the supply chain more efficient, we can harness opportunities for growth, seize this opportunity during this crisis.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: I joined one of these workshops and heard from participants that this was, to them, the first time something of this scale and nature and complexion was being attempted.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: There was great energy in the room as the participants exchanged many exciting ideas.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: More than ever, in these times, we need all hands on deck to steady the ship.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Every Singaporean can contribute in one way or other.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: To young Singaporeans – we need your energy and your fresh ideas.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The path ahead may be uncertain, but the best way to predict the future is to seek to create it.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We will need your creativity in many exciting areas, your willingness to challenge the status quo.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Climate change, which I mentioned, is one area, but there are many others, such as new applications for digital technology and new ways of organising society to help the low-income and vulnerable.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: To our older Singaporeans – we need your deep experience, your wisdom and your fighting spirit.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: You have seen Singapore through difficult times, from SARS to the Global Financial Crisis.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: At the same time, you may be called upon to learn new skills or trades.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: It will not be easy but we will support you all the way.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: To our enterprises and workers – we need your nimbleness to keep up with the latest changes and your commitment to long-term transformation.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: To our community partners, NGOs, civil society and volunteer organisations – we need your enthusiasm, your spirit, your understanding of the ground and your extensive networks.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The Government cannot reach all the right people at the right times.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: You can be first responders, who can identify and befriend those facing challenges.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We will partner you closely in these efforts.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Singapore Together is one of the rallying cries and spirit that will guide us through this crisis, our commitment to leaving no one behind, making space for differing views and doing our part.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: So, as we lift our heads high, let us face our challenges head-on, dream of a brighter future for our children, and dare to make those dreams a reality.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: "We will be together through thick and thin.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This includes new Members who have made their maiden speeches, and returning Members who have shared their concerns on the back of the uncertainty amidst the COVID-19 crisis.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I am encouraged by all our Members' conviction to improve the lives of all Singaporeans as one Singapore.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: And thank you, Mr Speaker, Sir, for allowing me to round up this debate.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is indeed an unprecedented crisis that has brought about significant impact to the lives of Singaporeans and businesses.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: But it has been a crisis that has also brought out the best in us.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Many have and continue to step forward to volunteer their time, talent and treasures.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Many ordinary people have done extraordinary things including showing appreciation to frontline workers or supporting a community need.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Take, for example, Jacob Neo, a Primary 6 student from Fairfield Methodist Primary School, who penned the lyrics, as quoted in my opening, and melody to an inspiring song "Singapore, Unite as One", as a tribute to healthcare workers earlier this year.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: There were also hawkers who delivered meals to the hungry, as well as generous organisations who returned their Job Support; and individuals who selflessly donated their Solidarity Payments to charity; and countless initiatives launched by many people to look after and support our migrant workers, as they continue to labour for us.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As I listened and read all the speeches delivered by Members of this House, I will endeavour in this closing of mine to string all the recurring themes together into five important areas.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Change is necessary, moving forward, and this also requires us to change mindsets.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In every crisis, there are also opportunities that we must tap on the COVID-19 crisis, to transform and to emerge stronger than before.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Our ability to work effectively together to transform the economy will determine how we come out from this storm.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: By identifying new opportunities for growth, we will ensure the survival and success of Singapore, improve the lives of Singaporeans and build a sustainable eco-system for many generations to come.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Different industries have been impacted differently with several facing structural disruption.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: But if we stay true to the core capabilities, which we have built over the years, we will come out from this storm stronger.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Some promising ideas mentioned by Members include environmental sustainability, smart commerce, supply chain digitalisation and Industry 4.0 and we should take heart that Singapore has benefited from early investments in digital transformation and while we had a head start in the race, COVID-19 has forced us into a sprint while we were mentally preparing for a marathon.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: These new areas and business models will create new jobs and new ways of thinking.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We need to stay positive and see these risks and challenges as opportunities to transform the way we do things.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In the past six months, I have seen firsthand for myself companies which have stagnated and went downhill.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I have also seen how some companies stayed positive with a growth mindset and pivoted quickly and remained afloat and profitable.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Many Members have rightly pointed out equipping the workforce with the right skills and, more importantly, mindset is crucial in driving this transformation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Last year, in support of SkillsFuture, I underwent a fintech foundation programme with our Singapore Fintech Association to get a better understanding of the fintech space and picked up useful knowledge to help me navigate in the fintech space.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The learning has enabled me to gain an understanding of fintech and also open my eyes to new opportunities and possibilities in the fintech space and, of course, emphasising the importance of staying ready, relevant and resilient.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I would also like to thank Deputy Prime Minster Heng for his response to my opening speech on his support to further enhance our Industry Transformation Maps to further develop our people and create more jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In the past five months alone, I have used more virtual conferencing than the past 25 years of my working career.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I believe many of you would agree we had to learn the use an entire spectrum of virtual meeting and conference software, from Webex, MS Teams, Big Marker to Zoom, Skype and Google Meet.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It is really quite a mouthful to swallow.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In a short span of one month during the Circuit Breaker, I have to convert a storeroom of my home into a home office and had to move plans and furnishings in my home into the storeroom to improve my backdrop for live webinars and Facebook live sessions.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As highlighted by President and many Members, jobs remain a core priority for Singapore at this juncture and in the years ahead.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The economic and social disruption brought about by COVID-19 coupled with geopolitics and trade tensions have only served to heighten insecurities and anxieties about jobs for many segments of society, including young fresh graduates from our ITEs, Polytechnics and Universities, low-wage workers as well as older workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I am encouraged that many Members have spoken passionately about the Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In fact, I was doing a count, as we progress through the speeches, and the phrase "Singaporean Core" has been mentioned over 40 times in the last four days alone.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Strengthening our Singapore Core is not and must not be something which divides us.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I take heart that every call to strengthen our Singaporean Core made in these Chambers has not been a call to divide but one to unite.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I take heart that the ideas put forth have been in the pursuit of our key tenets of fairness, equality and with the ultimate aim of progress and growth for our people and our country.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I take heart that while each of us has marked our own journeys, we share the same destination, where we keep our economy strong and competitive so that in turn our workers can have good jobs, not just good jobs, but quality jobs and opportunities that meet their aspirations and improve their lives.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: All around the world, anti-foreigner sentiments are on the rise because of the anxieties of job security, especially when they see that their jobs are overtaken by foreign manpower.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: When Singaporeans lose their jobs, but find that foreigners are still holding onto their PMET jobs, many become unhappy.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We have heard multiple anecdotes from many Members the past week of jobs being filled by foreign manpower and who may not even be as academically qualified.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We will need to grow our economy to create good jobs for Singaporeans and raise the living standards.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: To do this, we need to continue to remain open to attract Investments.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We cannot close our doors to foreigners and foreign investments.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: More Singaporeans will be able to take up the opportunities that these foreign investments create.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: There is a need to bring in foreign manpower to supplement the local workforce and ensure the transferability of niche skills.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Local companies including SMEs will also need skillsets and expertise to grow their business.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I do not think we just want to settle with having the cake and eat it but we want to grow and enlarge the cake, thereby giving Singapore and Singaporeans a bigger and better and also the best slice of it.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: More workers will be impacted and we need to enable them to adjust and bounce back through this crisis and beyond.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It will be especially tough for some group of workers, including low-wage workers and older workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: At the same time, we must not forget our older workers who are generally more vulnerable and are at a higher risk of being retrenched.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: For this group, it will be harder for them to look for another equivalent job and more so at the same pay.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Retraining and upskilling older workers will enable employers to continue finding value in them and be less likely to make them redundant.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I appreciate the call to respond to older workers with a heart, H E A R T which stands for H "holding on to jobs"; E "employment assistance", A "to act fairly", R "relief", T "to tough it out", and to redesign jobs, shift workplace culture and HR policies to institutionalise new possibilities for a maturing workforce.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Government, businesses and citizens must work together and expand opportunities for our senior workforce.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Third, President Halimah also called on all of us to build a fair and just society and to look after our low-wage workers, especially during this crisis.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As we negotiate through these stormy seas, we must not leave anyone behind.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The digital disruption and economic transformation in the next normal and low-touch economy, therefore, must be even more inclusive and further fortify social cohesion.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The new social compact must be practical, balancing the needs of Singaporeans in the areas of social security, affordable and quality housing, healthcare, education, public infrastructure and environment with their aspirations and dreams.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Our starting point in life should not dictate our ending point.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: With hard work, ability and ambition, we can succeed.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: There was also recognition of the trade-offs and sacrifices that women make in their careers to look after their children and to reduce the burden of care-giving.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I was especially reminded by hon Member Mr Louis Ng's example of Oasis water park ladies' toilet in Nee Soon East which he used to illustrate the issue of gender stereotypes.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Related to gender and poverty is a larger conversation about discrimination in our society.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We need to expand our empathy to our minority communities.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It is essential that we rise above our differences and find common ground.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Occasional setbacks need not trip us in our perseverance to continue to make progress.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Harmony in diversity will always be a work-in-progress.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We may not always agree, but we cannot let our disagreement turn into division.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Otherwise, change will cause a rupture in society as we have seen elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Our first President Yusof Ishak did not see our diversity of race, language, religion as an obstacle to progress.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: He saw the diversity as exactly what would make Singapore dynamic and progressive.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Diversity and inclusion is an important area which we must hold dear and fast, too.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It is the heart and spirit of Singapore which is embodied by the Singapore Tapestry, woven out of diversity and adversity.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Its colours brightened by the idealism and energy of our youth or as hon Member Mr Darryl David put it "more like a quilt, nicely handcrafted patchwork", close and dear to us.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Its thread tightly bound by a shared sense of community, culture and, ultimately, destiny.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: To our youths and young people – never stop dreaming or lose that sense of optimism.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is not a lost generation and you are definitely not a "strawberry generation".

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: When I see youths and young people, I see vitality, vigour, tenacity, great courage and ideas.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: There may be attention exerted to the string at the start but when we release the bowstring at the right pull and tension, it will hit the target and mark with perfection and accuracy.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: To our youths and young people, we want to support you for you to realise your dreams, to overcome the crisis of a generation by uniting fellow Singaporeans and leave behind a more beautiful and tightly knitted tapestry as a legacy for generations of Singaporeans to come.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Deep trust and mutual respect will need to form the basis of the relationship between fellow Singaporeans, earned through the help and sacrifices that we give one another.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We need to maintain a profound respect and plurality in Singapore and find shared layers above this diversity.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I hope we can continue to build a culture of openness and trust, and one in which the Government listens, consults and engages regularly and widely with all.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We need to continue to fight for a more caring, compassionate and inclusive society, one with a strong heartware.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Given the upheaval caused by this pandemic, it is our hardware and software that will save lives and livelihoods, but it is about being inclusive in our heartware that will determine whether we will get through this pandemic as One People, One Nation and One Singapore.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: At the same time, new leaders are emerging to take Singapore forward.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Moving forward, both the Government and the Opposition must share the common goal of working together to better Singapore for our people.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We do this with dignity, respect, integrity, courage and grace – not forgetting the hon Member Mr Murali’s exposition of the rhino and lion, and also the indomitable neck-sticking giraffe.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It is crucial to have constructive rational debates to further the interests of Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: For our forebears had fought to bring Singapore forward, for the many storms we have weathered since our independence, including the Asian Financial Crisis, SARS and the Global Financial Crisis, we have prevailed.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We will and we must prevail again today.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We must continue to rise to the challenge, adapt and emerge stronger.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We will need to prepare our lives to overcome this crisis and after this crisis.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We will need to reset, refresh, review, reinvent and rethink our strategies to become successful in the next normal.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We must unite so that our economy will again prosper anew.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We must unite even more so as external forces seek to divide us.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Let us continue to have faith and be of good courage.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I now call upon all the Members of this House to join me in thanking the President for her Address.
